1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 1707:14 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a rapid decompression event occurred aboard a Boeing 737-9 MAX aircraft during the initial climb phase of flight. The event transpired at an indicated altitude of 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 12.3 nautical miles (NM) northeast of Portland International Airport (KPDX), Oregon. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger service. Following the event, the flight crew initiated an emergency descent, declared an emergency with air traffic control, and returned to KPDX. The aircraft landed safely on Runway 10L at 1728:42 PST. No fatalities or serious injuries were reported among the 171 passengers and 6 crewmembers on board.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, registered as N704AL, operated by a major U.S. air carrier under 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 121. The aircraft was configured for 178 passengers in a two-class layout and was equipped with a mid-cabin exit door plug on the left side, designated as the 2L position. The operator maintained the aircraft under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The aircraft was dispatched in accordance with the operator’s FAA-approved operations specifications, with all required preflight documentation, weight and balance calculations, and fuel load verifications completed prior to pushback.

1.3 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted in accordance with the operator’s FAA-approved operations specifications and the applicable provisions of 14 CFR Part 121. The flight plan was filed for a route from Portland, Oregon, to Ontario, California, with an estimated en route time of 2 hours and 15 minutes. The departure was executed under standard Part 121 dispatch procedures. The flight crew utilized standard operating procedures (SOPs) for departure, including the use of the flight management computer (FMC) for navigation and performance calculations. The aircraft’s transponder, traffic collision avoidance system (TCAS), and emergency locator transmitter (ELT) were operational at the time of departure. The flight was monitored by Seattle Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZSE) during the climb phase.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The Captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a type rating for the Boeing 737 series. The Captain’s medical certificate was a first-class, valid through August 2024, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 11,450 hours, with 3,210 hours in the Boeing 737 MAX series. The Captain successfully completed the most recent line check on November 12, 2023, and was current in all required proficiency checks. The Captain’s training records indicated satisfactory completion of all recurrent simulator sessions, including high-altitude emergency procedures, rapid decompression drills, and manual flight control exercises.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The First Officer held an ATP certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating. The First Officer’s medical certificate was a first-class, valid through October 2024. Total flight time was 4,890 hours, with 1,120 hours in the Boeing 737 MAX series. The First Officer completed the most recent recurrent training and line check on December 3, 2023, and maintained full currency for all assigned duties. Training documentation confirmed completion of all required ground school modules, including aircraft systems, emergency procedures, and crew resource management (CRM) protocols.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crewmembers were within the 90-day takeoff and landing currency requirements specified in 14 CFR § 121.439. The Captain had accumulated 87 flight hours in the preceding 30 days, while the First Officer had accumulated 72 flight hours. Both pilots had completed the operator’s annual emergency procedures training, which included rapid decompression drills, emergency descent protocols, and cabin pressurization failure scenarios. Training records indicated satisfactory performance in all simulator evaluations, with no noted deficiencies in checklist execution or communication protocols. The Captain, acting as pilot-in-command, was responsible for the final authority and operational control of the flight, in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.533. The Captain’s duty time for the day was 6 hours and 12 minutes, well within the limitations established by 14 CFR § 117.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The accident aircraft was manufactured by The Boeing Company, serial number 44442, and was delivered to the operator on October 14, 2023. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 1,245 total flight hours and 892 total flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a standard Boeing 737 MAX 9 configuration, featuring a reinforced fuselage structure, fly-by-wire flight controls, and an integrated avionics suite compliant with RTCA DO-178C software standards. The aircraft’s maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) was 194,700 pounds, and the actual takeoff weight for the accident flight was 168,450 pounds. The center of gravity was calculated at 24.1 percent of mean aerodynamic chord (MAC), within the approved envelope.

3.2 Propulsion Systems
The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured under a joint venture between GE Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines. The left engine, serial number 892145, had accumulated 1,245 hours and 892 cycles. The right engine, serial number 892146, had identical time and cycle accumulation. Both engines were maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommended maintenance planning document (MPD) and were free of outstanding deferred maintenance items. Engine performance parameters recorded during the climb phase indicated normal thrust settings, exhaust gas temperatures (EGT) within green band limits, and no abnormal vibration signatures. The LEAP engine series incorporates advanced composite fan blades and a high-bypass ratio design optimized for fuel efficiency and reduced emissions. Engine oil pressure, fuel flow, and N1/N2 rotational speeds were within normal operating ranges throughout the flight.

3.3 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft’s maintenance records were reviewed and found to be complete and compliant with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) issued by the FAA. The most recent heavy maintenance visit was a C-check completed on December 18, 2023, at the operator’s primary maintenance base. During this visit, all structural inspections, system functional checks, and cabin pressurization tests were performed in accordance with the Boeing 737 MAX Maintenance Planning Document. No discrepancies were noted regarding the left mid-exit door plug assembly. The aircraft was not subject to any outstanding service bulletins or mandatory modifications at the time of the accident. Maintenance logbook entries confirmed that all required inspections, including the 100-hour and annual checks, were completed and signed off by appropriately certificated personnel.

3.4 Door Plug Configuration and Systems
The left mid-exit door plug, designated as the 2L position, was installed in lieu of a standard passenger door to accommodate the aircraft’s seating configuration. The plug assembly consisted of a structural frame, interior trim panel, exterior fairing, and a series of retention bolts and guide tracks. The plug was designed to withstand cabin differential pressure loads and was secured using a combination of primary and secondary retention mechanisms. The cabin pressurization system operated normally during the initial climb, with the outflow valve modulating to maintain a cabin altitude of approximately 6,500 feet at the time of the event. The aircraft’s pressurization control system was certified in accordance with 14 CFR § 25.841 and § 25.365. The plug’s structural integration was evaluated during type certification to ensure compliance with load distribution and fatigue life requirements.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
At the time of the accident, a high-pressure system was centered over the Pacific Northwest, resulting in generally stable atmospheric conditions. A weak cold front was located approximately 150 NM west of the Oregon coast, with no significant convective activity reported along the flight path. Upper-level winds at 16,000 feet MSL were from 270 degrees at 25 knots, with a temperature of -12°C. The freezing level was reported at 4,200 feet MSL, with no icing conditions forecast or reported in the climb corridor. Atmospheric pressure was stable, with a sea-level pressure of 1020.4 hPa.

4.2 Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts and METAR Data
The Portland International Airport (KPDX) METAR at 1700 PST reported wind 280 degrees at 8 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, few clouds at 3,500 feet, scattered at 12,000 feet, temperature 6°C, dew point 2°C, and altimeter setting 30.12 inches of mercury. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KPDX, valid from 1500 to 2100 PST, indicated no significant weather changes, with visibility remaining above 6 statute miles and ceiling above 5,000 feet. No SIGMETs or AIRMETs were active for the departure area or en route segment. The weather conditions were well within the operational limits for the aircraft and the operator’s dispatch criteria.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and In-Flight Conditions
The flight crew reported clear skies and smooth air during the initial climb. At 16,000 feet MSL, the aircraft encountered a sudden, uncommanded cabin pressure loss, accompanied by a loud bang and rapid decompression. The flight data recorder (FDR) indicated a cabin altitude rate of climb exceeding 2,500 feet per minute immediately following the event. The crew initiated an emergency descent to 10,000 feet MSL, in accordance with the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) procedures. No turbulence, wind shear, or precipitation was reported during the climb or descent phases. The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) captured the flight crew’s verbal coordination, checklist execution, and communication with air traffic control during the emergency descent.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The primary wreckage, consisting of the aircraft fuselage, wings, empennage, and landing gear, remained intact and was recovered at KPDX following the safe landing. The separated left mid-exit door plug was recovered approximately 14.5 NM northeast of the departure airport, in a residential area. The component was located in a wooded lot, with minimal ground impact deformation. The Federal Aviation Administration and local law enforcement secured the recovery site, and the component was transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination. The recovery process was documented with photographic evidence, GPS coordinates, and chain-of-custody logs.

5.2 Fuselage and Door Plug Examination
Examination of the fuselage at the 2L door plug location revealed a clean separation along the forward and aft guide tracks. The structural frame of the plug remained largely intact, with no evidence of fatigue cracking or corrosion. The retention bolts were found to be missing from the primary attachment points, with corresponding bolt holes in the fuselage structure showing no signs of thread stripping or deformation. The exterior fairing exhibited localized tearing consistent with aerodynamic loading during separation. The interior trim panel was recovered with the cabin side, showing no signs of fire, smoke, or thermal damage. The guide track rails were inspected for alignment, wear, and structural integrity, with all measurements falling within manufacturer specifications.

5.3 Component Analysis and Retained Hardware
Detailed metallurgical analysis of the recovered door plug and fuselage attachment points was conducted. The retention bolts, when recovered from the surrounding area, were found to be intact but unthreaded from their respective nuts. The guide track rollers showed normal wear patterns, with no evidence of binding or misalignment. The cabin pressure relief valves operated as designed, with no indication of over-pressurization prior to the event. The aircraft’s structural integrity was maintained throughout the flight, and the remaining fuselage structure complied with the damage tolerance requirements outlined in Section 25.571 of the Federal Aviation Regulations. The examination confirmed that the separation occurred due to the absence of critical retention hardware, rather than structural failure or material degradation. Torque verification procedures and installation documentation were reviewed to determine compliance with manufacturer specifications.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
The operator’s maintenance program was developed in accordance with FAA Advisory Circular 120-16G, which provides guidance for the development and implementation of continuous airworthiness maintenance programs for Part 121 operators. The operator’s quality assurance department conducted routine audits of maintenance documentation, tool control procedures, and personnel training records. All maintenance actions related to the door plug installation were documented in the aircraft’s maintenance logbook, with sign-offs by certified airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanics and inspection authorization (IA) personnel. The operator’s standard operating procedures required a dual-inspection verification for all critical structural modifications and plug installations. Maintenance personnel were trained on the specific torque values, bolt sequencing, and retention hardware verification protocols established by the manufacturer.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
A review of the National Transportation Safety Board’s aviation accident database and the FAA’s Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) system identified no prior incidents involving the complete separation of a mid-exit door plug on the Boeing 737 MAX 9 series. However, several service bulletins had been issued regarding door plug retention bolt torque verification and guide track alignment inspections. The operator had implemented these bulletins as part of its routine maintenance schedule. The Boeing 737 MAX 8, a closely related variant, utilizes a similar door plug configuration, and the manufacturer’s engineering analysis confirmed that the retention system design was consistent across both models. Historical data from the operator’s fleet indicated no recurring discrepancies related to door plug retention hardware.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The aircraft’s certification basis included compliance with 14 CFR Part 25, specifically Section 25.571, which establishes damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements for transport category airplanes. The door plug assembly was evaluated under the provisions of § 25.365 (pressurized cabin loads) and § 25.783 (fuselage doors). The Federal Aviation Administration’s oversight of the operator’s maintenance program was conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L, which outlines the requirements for maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations. The investigation team reviewed all applicable airworthiness directives, manufacturer service letters, and operator maintenance records to ensure compliance with established regulatory standards. The findings from this factual report will be utilized in the development of safety recommendations and further engineering analysis. All data collection, examination procedures, and documentation were conducted in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols and federal regulations governing aviation accident investigations.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and analysis conducted by the NTSB Structures and Materials Group regarding the left mid-cabin exit door plug assembly recovered from the subject aircraft. The examination was performed between January 10 and January 18, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with supplemental dimensional inspections conducted at the Boeing Commercial Airplanes Everett Facility under NTSB oversight.

The scope of this examination encompasses the physical condition of the recovered door plug structure, associated retention hardware, guide track assemblies, stop fittings, and elastomeric sealing components. The investigation also includes metallurgical characterization, non-destructive inspection (NDI), fastener torque verification, and correlation with recorded flight data parameters. All procedures were conducted in accordance with NTSB Investigative Protocols, ASTM E1444/E1444M-21 (Standard Practice for Magnetic Particle Testing), ASTM E165/E165M-21 (Standard Practice for Liquid Penetrant Examination), and Boeing Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-00-00 guidelines.

Items examined include:
- Left mid-exit door plug assembly, Part Number (P/N) 65-12345-678, Serial Number (S/N) 987654321
- Twelve (12) NAS1097AD6-6 aluminum alloy rivets (recovered)
- Four (4) MS20470AD5-6 universal head rivets (recovered)
- Upper and lower guide track assemblies, P/N 65-12345-680/681
- Stop fitting brackets, P/N 65-12345-685
- Fuselage skin section, station 1045 to 1065, stringer S-14L to S-16L
- Recovered cabin pressure relief valve components and seal fragments

All recovered components were cataloged, photographed, and secured under chain-of-custody documentation NTSB-STR-2024-001 through NTSB-STR-2024-089. Environmental conditions during laboratory examination were maintained at 21°C ± 2°C and 45% ± 5% relative humidity.

2. BACKGROUND

The mid-cabin exit door plug is a structural closure assembly designed to replace optional emergency exit openings on high-density configured aircraft. The system is certified under FAA Type Certificate A16WE and complies with 14 CFR Part 25.365 (Pressurized Cabin Loads) and 25.807 (Emergency Exits). The plug assembly functions as a pressure boundary, transferring cabin differential pressure loads to the surrounding fuselage frames and longerons via a guided track and stop-fitting retention system.

The primary structure consists of 2024-T3 aluminum alloy sheet and extrusions, per AMS 4037 and AMS 4041 specifications. The retention system utilizes a combination of shear-loaded rivets, tension-loaded guide track bolts, and mechanical stop fittings to prevent outward displacement under pressurization. The sealing interface employs a dual-durometer silicone elastomer gasket (P/N 65-12345-690) designed to maintain a pressure-tight boundary across a temperature range of -54°C to +71°C.

The specific unit examined was manufactured at Boeing Renton on March 14, 2023, and installed on the subject BOEING 737-8 derivative airframe during final assembly. The aircraft was delivered to the operator on April 22, 2023, and accumulated 1,247 flight hours and 892 pressurization cycles prior to the event. Maintenance records reviewed under the operator's FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program indicate no prior discrepancies, structural repairs, or component replacements associated with the left mid-exit door plug. Routine inspections were conducted in accordance with the manufacturer's Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) and referenced guidance in Advisory Circular 120-16G, which outlines air carrier maintenance program requirements and inspection intervals for pressurized fuselage structures.

The plug design incorporates a fail-safe load path wherein cabin pressure forces are reacted by the upper and lower guide tracks, while the stop fittings provide positive mechanical restraint against over-travel. The system is designed to withstand a limit load of 1.5 times the maximum operating differential pressure (ΔP) of 9.1 PSI, with an ultimate load factor of 2.25.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered door plug assembly revealed multiple structural and installation anomalies. Visual inspection under 10x magnification identified four (4) missing stop fitting bolts at the lower inboard quadrant. The corresponding threaded inserts in the fuselage frame exhibited clean, unthreaded bores with no evidence of cross-threading or galling, indicating the fasteners were either never installed or were removed prior to the event. Two (2) adjacent guide track bolts (P/N BACB30NX5K10) were recovered with zero clamp-up; torque verification using a calibrated digital torque wrench (Fluke 754, ±1% accuracy) yielded 0.0 ft-lbs, well below the specified installation torque of 18.5 ± 1.5 ft-lbs per Boeing Standard Practices Manual (BSPM) 20-10-01.

Dimensional inspection of the guide track rails was performed using a coordinate measuring machine (CMM) with ±0.0005 inch accuracy. The upper guide track exhibited 0.018 inch of lateral wear at the mid-span contact surface, exceeding the SRM allowable limit of 0.010 inch. The lower guide track showed 0.012 inch of wear, also outside serviceable limits. Wear patterns were consistent with repetitive sliding contact under load, with no evidence of abrasive contamination or foreign object damage (FOD).

Non-destructive inspection was conducted on the primary plug skin and surrounding fuselage cutout. Eddy current testing (ECT) per ASTM E309-20 revealed no subsurface cracking or corrosion in the 2024-T3 aluminum structure. Liquid penetrant examination (LPI) per ASTM E165 identified minor surface fretting at the interface between the plug frame and the fuselage longeron, localized to a 2.5-inch span near station 1052. No fatigue crack initiation sites were detected.

Metallurgical analysis was performed on three recovered rivets and two guide track bolts. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed base material composition consistent with 2024-T3 aluminum alloy (Cu: 4.4%, Mg: 1.5%, Mn: 0.6%, Al: balance) and 7075-T6 aluminum for the rivet shanks. Hardness testing (Rockwell B scale) yielded values of 82 ± 3 HRB, within the AMS 4037 specification range of 75-85 HRB. Fracture surface analysis of the two zero-torque guide track bolts revealed no evidence of fatigue striations or overload necking; the threads exhibited uniform machining marks with no plastic deformation, confirming the fasteners were not subjected to operational shear loads prior to separation.

Seal compression testing was conducted on recovered elastomer fragments using a universal testing machine (Instron 5969) at a crosshead speed of 2.0 in/min. The material exhibited a compression set of 18% at 25% strain, within the manufacturer's specified maximum of 25%. Tensile strength measured 1,450 PSI, meeting the minimum requirement of 1,200 PSI per AMS 3195.

Photographic documentation (NTSB-STR-2024-012 through 045) captures the missing stop bolt locations, guide track wear profiles, fastener thread conditions, and seal interface degradation. All measurements and test results were recorded in the NTSB Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) under case file STR-2024-0089.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) parameters were extracted and synchronized with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) timeline. Data sampling rates were 1 Hz for cabin pressure parameters and 4 Hz for flight control and attitude parameters. All data were validated against manufacturer calibration tables and cross-referenced with the aircraft's maintenance logbook.

The aircraft departed at 14:18:02 UTC. During initial climb, cabin altitude tracked normally, maintaining a differential pressure (ΔP) of 0.0 PSI until 14:24:15 UTC, at which point the outflow valve began modulating to establish pressurization. At 14:28:40 UTC, the aircraft passed 10,000 ft MSL with a calibrated airspeed of 285 knots and a ΔP of 2.1 PSI. The Captain's callout at 14:29:05 UTC confirmed normal climb configuration and pressurization schedule.

At 14:31:52 UTC, the aircraft reached 15,200 ft MSL. Cabin altitude was 6,800 ft, and ΔP measured 4.8 PSI. The FDR recorded a transient cabin pressure fluctuation of ±0.3 PSI over a 4-second interval, consistent with outflow valve modulation during climb. At 14:32:18 UTC, while the aircraft was at 16,000 ft MSL, 310 knots indicated airspeed, and a pitch attitude of +8.2°, the FDR recorded an instantaneous ΔP drop from 5.2 PSI to 0.1 PSI within 0.8 seconds. Simultaneously, cabin altitude rapidly increased from 7,100 ft to 14,800 ft over 3.2 seconds. The vertical acceleration parameter registered a transient spike of +1.08G, followed by a return to 1.00G within 1.5 seconds. No abnormal control surface deflections or autopilot disconnections were recorded.

The CVR captured a loud acoustic event at 14:32:18 UTC, followed by the Captain's immediate declaration of "rapid decompression" and initiation of emergency descent procedures. The QAR data confirmed the outflow valve remained in the open position post-event, and the cabin pressure warning system activated at 14:32:19 UTC, consistent with a loss of pressure boundary integrity.

Comparison with normal operational parameters for the BOEING 737-8 family indicates that a ΔP of 5.2 PSI at 16,000 ft MSL is within the certified pressurization schedule. The transient pressure load applied to the door plug at the time of separation was calculated using the formula F = ΔP × A, where A represents the effective plug area (approximately 1,840 in²). This yields a total outward force of approximately 9,568 lbs. The design limit load for the retention system is 13,700 lbs, indicating the applied load was 69.8% of the certified limit. However, the absence of four stop bolts and two under-torqued guide track fasteners reduced the effective load path capacity by an estimated 42%, based on finite element analysis (FEA) models provided by the manufacturer.

Thermal expansion effects were evaluated using recorded outside air temperature (-12°C at 16,000 ft MSL) and cabin temperature (+21°C). The differential thermal gradient across the aluminum plug and steel guide tracks would have induced a contraction differential of approximately 0.004 inches, insufficient to cause structural failure independently but potentially contributing to reduced clamp-up in marginally torqued fasteners.

5. SUMMARY

The examination and analysis of the left mid-exit door plug assembly and associated flight data yielded the following technical findings:

- The recovered door plug assembly (P/N 65-12345-678, S/N 987654321) exhibited four missing lower stop fitting bolts and two guide track retention bolts with zero clamp-up torque (0.0 ft-lbs), significantly below the specified 18.5 ± 1.5 ft-lbs installation requirement.
- Guide track wear measurements exceeded Structural Repair Manual allowable limits, with 0.018 inch lateral wear on the upper track and 0.012 inch on the lower track.
- Metallurgical and chemical analysis of recovered fasteners and plug structure confirmed material compliance with AMS 4037 and AMS 4041 specifications. No evidence of fatigue crack propagation, corrosion, or material degradation was identified.
- Elastomeric seal fragments demonstrated compression set and tensile properties within manufacturer specifications.
- FDR and QAR data confirm the aircraft was operating within certified flight envelope parameters at the time of the event, with a cabin differential pressure of 5.2 PSI at 16,000 ft MSL.
- The rapid decompression event occurred at 14:32:18 UTC, characterized by an instantaneous ΔP drop from 5.2 PSI to 0.1 PSI within 0.8 seconds, accompanied by a transient +1.08G vertical load factor.
- Structural load calculations indicate the applied pressure force at the time of separation was approximately 69.8% of the certified limit load. The absence of four stop bolts and two under-torqued guide track fasteners reduced the effective retention capacity by an estimated 42%.
- No evidence of foreign object damage, manufacturing defects in the primary aluminum structure, or pre-existing fatigue cracking was identified during NDI or SEM examination.
- Maintenance records indicate the component was installed during original aircraft assembly and had accumulated 1,247 flight hours and 892 pressurization cycles with no prior reported discrepancies.
- The event occurred during a normal climb phase, with the Captain initiating standard emergency procedures immediately following the acoustic and pressure anomaly.

All findings are documented in accordance with NTSB investigative standards and are presented for factual record.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, LEAD FLIGHT ATTENDANT
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 14:30 PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Seattle, Washington
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB
Witness: Marcus Thorne, Lead Flight Attendant (Purser)

Q: Please state your full name and current position for the record.
A: Marcus Thorne. I’m a lead flight attendant, sometimes called the purser, for the airline. I’ve been with the company for about twelve years, mostly flying narrow-body aircraft.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. I’d like you to walk me through the events of January 5th, 2024, starting from your arrival at the aircraft. Please include approximate times and any observations you made.
A: Yeah, sure. I got to the gate around 15:30, maybe 15:35. We were operating out of Portland. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 9. I did the standard pre-flight checks, walked the cabin, checked the emergency equipment, talked to the Captain and First Officer. Everything was normal. We pushed back at, uh, I think it was 16:48. Maybe 16:50. We taxied out, did the run-up, and took off from runway 10L. The climb was... completely normal at first. I was in the forward galley, just finishing up the service prep, stowing the carts. The Captain came on the PA, said we’d be leveling off at 16,000 for a bit due to traffic, then continuing up. I remember looking at my watch, it was maybe 17:02, 17:03. We were climbing through about 15,000, maybe 16,000 feet. Then—

Q: Take your time. What happened next?
A: It was just this... this massive bang. Like a cannon shot, honestly. Right behind me, or to my left. The whole cabin just shuddered. I felt the pressure drop instantly, my ears popped hard, and then the wind. It was freezing. I mean, it was January, but the air rushing in was like opening a walk-in freezer at full blast. Papers, magazines, everything just got sucked toward the left side. I grabbed the jumpseat harness, but I was already standing. I looked over and... the left mid-exit door plug was just gone. Completely gone. There was a hole, a big jagged opening, and you could see the sky. It was surreal.

Q: What was your immediate response?
A: I yelled for everyone to get down, put on oxygen masks. The masks dropped automatically, which was good. I remember the Captain’s voice came over the intercom, very calm, said “Flight attendants, stations.” I secured the forward galley, checked the passengers in rows 1 through 10. There was a lot of panic, obviously. A woman in 8C was bleeding from a head wound, probably from debris or hitting the seatback. I got her a first aid kit, told her to keep pressure on it. The oxygen masks were deployed, but the airflow was... it was loud. The wind noise was deafening. I couldn’t hear the Captain at first, but then the intercom cut through. He said we were descending, returning to Portland.

Q: Did you notice any unusual sounds or vibrations from the engines or airframe prior to the event?
A: No, nothing. The engines... they’re the LEAP-1Bs, I think that’s what they’re called. General Electric Aviation makes them. They’re pretty quiet, actually. I didn’t notice anything weird with the engines before the bang. No unusual vibrations, no warning lights on the flight deck that I could see from the jumpseat. Just a normal climb. The Captain and First Officer were running through the checklist, I assume. I heard the engines spool down when we started the descent, but that’s normal.

Q: You mentioned the door plug. Were you aware of any maintenance or configuration issues prior to the flight?
A: No, absolutely not. We did the pre-flight walkaround, but honestly, from the outside, it just looks like a panel. I’m not a mechanic. I know we have to check the emergency exits, but the mid-exit plug isn’t something we interact with daily. It’s not like the main doors. I remember reading something later, after we landed, about how it’s a plug design, not a traditional door. The Federal Aviation Administration... the FAA, I mean, they’ve been looking into it. I think it’s related to how it was installed or the bolts. I’m not sure.

Q: Have you received any training or briefings regarding the aircraft’s certification or maintenance standards?
A: Yeah, we get recurrent training. They talk about 14 CFR 25.571 sometimes, or at least the maintenance manuals reference it. It’s about damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation, right? I’m not an engineer, but I know the airline has to comply with it. And we follow AC 120-16G for our cabin safety programs, which covers emergency procedures, decompression drills, all that. But honestly, in the moment, you just go on muscle memory. You don’t think about regulations. You just react.

Q: Let’s go back to the timeline. Approximately how long were you at 16,000 feet before the event?
A: Maybe... maybe two or three minutes? It’s hard to say. Time kind of slows down when something like that happens. I remember the Captain saying we’d level off, and then almost immediately, the bang. We were still climbing, I think. The altimeter on the jumpseat display was ticking up. Then it just... happened.

Q: How did the passengers react once the masks deployed?
A: Panic, obviously. But most people followed the instructions. “Pull down, place over nose and mouth.” I walked the aisle, checking rows. Some people were crying, some were just staring. The guy in 9A was trying to help the woman next to him. I told him to secure his own mask first. The cabin pressure was... it was weird. You could feel it in your chest. The temperature dropped fast. I remember my hands were shaking, but I kept moving. You’re trained for this, but you never think it’ll actually happen.

Q: You mentioned flying the MAX 9. How does the cabin environment compare to other aircraft you operate, like the Boeing 737 MAX 8?
A: It’s... it’s similar, but the 9 is longer. More rows, obviously. The galley layout is a bit tighter in the forward section. The MAX 8 feels a little more open, but structurally, they’re basically the same family. The door plug on the 9 is in a different spot, around row 12 or 13, I think. I don’t really pay attention to the exact row numbers during normal ops, but after the fact, I looked it up. It’s just a panel that’s supposed to be bolted in. I don’t know why it failed.

Q: After the aircraft landed, what was the debrief like?
A: We taxied to a remote stand. Emergency vehicles were already there. We evacuated everyone, but it was orderly. The Captain stayed on the PA, kept everyone calm. Once we were on the tarmac, the airline’s safety team came out, then the NTSB and FAA investigators. They took our statements, collected our phones, asked about the timeline. I remember they asked specifically about the door plug area, if anyone had seen it loose before. Nobody had. It just... came off.

Q: Do you have any additional observations or concerns you’d like to add to the record?
A: Just that... it was terrifying, but the crew handled it. The Captain was incredible. He didn’t panic. The decompression was rapid, but the aircraft handled it. I guess I’m just glad we’re all here. I’ve been flying since 2012, and I’ve never seen anything like it. I hope the FAA and the manufacturer figure out exactly what happened. I know they’re grounding some of the fleet, doing inspections. It’s the right call. Safety first.

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
Docket No. FAA-2024-0112; NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA055
Reference: NTSB Preliminary Safety Recommendation A-24-014; FAA Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51
Date of Occurrence: January 5, 2024
Regulatory Framework: 14 CFR Parts 21, 25, and 121; Advisory Circular 120-16G

2. BACKGROUND
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registered to a Part 121 air carrier, experienced an uncontained rapid decompression event during initial climb. The incident occurred at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level following departure from a Pacific Northwest hub. The left mid-exit door plug, a non-egress fuselage closure panel, separated from the aft fuselage structure, resulting in immediate cabin depressurization. The flight crew, under the command of the Captain, executed emergency descent procedures in strict accordance with the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) and applicable Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions, subsequently diverting to the departure aerodrome without further incident or loss of life.

The regulatory architecture governing the type design and continued airworthiness of the subject aircraft is established under 14 CFR Part 25, specifically 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates damage-tolerance and fatigue evaluation of primary and secondary structure. The door plug assembly, while not classified as a primary load-bearing component, interfaces directly with the fuselage pressure boundary and is subject to the structural integrity requirements codified in 14 CFR 25.783 (Fuselage doors). The Federal Aviation Administration (the FAA) previously issued type certification for the 737 MAX series under Type Certificate No. T00001SE, with subsequent production oversight delegated to the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) holder. While the mid-exit door plug configuration was originally approved under the primary type certificate, subsequent cabin reconfiguration proposals evaluated under supplemental type certificate (STC) pathways have introduced additional structural interface considerations that require rigorous manufacturing and maintenance oversight.

Historical regulatory correspondence and prior Airworthiness Directives (ADs) have addressed fastener retention and quality assurance protocols across the 737 MAX family, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8 variant, which shares common production methodologies, tooling, and structural design philosophies. Concurrently, propulsion system oversight for the LEAP-1B turbofan engine, manufactured by General Electric Aviation, remains governed under separate type certification and continued airworthiness directives. Although this investigation has determined no causal linkage between the powerplant systems and the fuselage separation event, the broader regulatory context necessitates a holistic review of manufacturing quality control, as outlined in Advisory Circular 120-16G, which provides guidance for air carrier maintenance programs and emphasizes the integration of manufacturer service bulletins into operator continuing airworthiness frameworks.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the manufacturer’s production records, operator maintenance logs, and Federal Aviation Administration oversight documentation reveals systemic deficiencies in the quality management system (QMS) governing the installation and verification of mid-exit door plug retention hardware. The investigation confirms that the subject aircraft was delivered with multiple fasteners improperly torqued and, in certain instances, absent from designated mounting locations. This non-conformance constitutes a direct violation of the approved type design and contravenes the structural integrity mandates of 14 CFR 25.571, which requires that all structural elements demonstrate adequate damage tolerance throughout the operational service life.

The operator’s maintenance program, while nominally compliant with 14 CFR 121.344 and aligned with the guidance parameters of Advisory Circular 120-16G, lacked specific inspection protocols for non-egress door plug assemblies. The absence of mandatory torque verification and post-installation documentation in the operator’s approved maintenance manual created a regulatory blind spot, permitting latent manufacturing defects to persist into revenue service. Furthermore, the FAA’s surveillance framework, reliant upon delegated ODA authority and periodic production certificate audits, failed to identify the degradation in manufacturing quality control prior to the January 5, 2024 event.

Critical gaps in the regulatory framework have been identified, particularly concerning the interface between type certificate holder responsibilities and operator continuing airworthiness obligations. The current regulatory structure does not mandate independent, third-party verification of critical fastener installations during final assembly, relying instead on internal manufacturer quality assurance processes. Additionally, the MMEL framework does not adequately address the operational limitations associated with door plug retention anomalies, leaving flight crews without explicit guidance for pre-flight verification of non-egress closure panels. The Captain’s adherence to standard emergency procedures was exemplary; however, the absence of proactive airworthiness verification mechanisms underscores a systemic vulnerability in the current oversight paradigm. The fragmentation of oversight responsibilities between the Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) and regional Flight Standards District Offices (FSDOs) has further complicated the timely dissemination of critical airworthiness information.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Administrator under 14 CFR Part 21 and 14 CFR Part 121, the following corrective actions and compliance timelines are hereby mandated:

1. Immediate Inspection and Rectification: All operators of Boeing 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 aircraft shall conduct a one-time, detailed inspection of all mid-exit door plug retention fasteners within 72 hours of this directive’s effective date. Inspections shall be performed in accordance with the manufacturer’s Special Attention Service Bulletin and shall include torque verification, thread engagement assessment, and photographic documentation. Non-conforming hardware shall be replaced with FAA-approved components prior to return to service.

2. Revised Production Acceptance Criteria: The type certificate holder shall implement enhanced quality control protocols for all door plug installations, including mandatory dual-verification torque logging and independent quality assurance sign-off. These revisions shall be submitted to the Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) for approval within 30 calendar days. All future production deliveries shall require documented compliance with updated manufacturing process specifications.

3. Operator Maintenance Program Amendments: All Part 121 operators shall revise their approved maintenance programs to incorporate recurring door plug inspection intervals, as specified in the updated Airworthiness Limitations Section (ALS). Compliance with Advisory Circular 120-16G shall be demonstrated through updated training curricula and maintenance tracking system modifications within 60 calendar days. Operators shall also integrate door plug retention verification into pre-flight walk-around procedures where operationally feasible.

4. Enhanced FAA Oversight and Surveillance: The FAA shall transition from delegated ODA oversight to direct Federal Aviation Administration surveillance for all 737 MAX production lines. Quarterly audits of manufacturing quality control processes shall be instituted, with findings reported directly to the Office of Aviation Safety. A comprehensive review of the MMEL and QRH integration for rapid decompression scenarios shall be completed within 90 calendar days, with subsequent rulemaking proposed to address identified procedural gaps.

5. Reporting and Follow-Up Schedule: Operators shall submit compliance verification reports to the designated Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) within 10 business days of inspection completion. The FAA shall conduct a follow-up regulatory review at 30, 60, and 90-day intervals to assess systemic compliance and evaluate the efficacy of implemented corrective measures. All findings shall be coordinated with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) to ensure alignment with ongoing investigative recommendations.

Failure to comply with the stipulated timelines and corrective actions may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.19, including but not limited to certificate suspension, civil penalties, and operational restrictions. This directive remains in effect until superseded by subsequent regulatory action or formal closure of the associated safety investigation.

HEADLINE: Mid-Flight Door Plug Blowout Forces Emergency Landing of Boeing 737 MAX 9; No Fatalities Reported

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, National Aviation Desk
DATELINE: PORTLAND, Ore. —

A Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier made an emergency return to Portland International Airport on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, after a mid-cabin door plug tore away from the fuselage during climb, triggering a rapid decompression at 16,000 feet. All 171 passengers and six crew members survived the incident, though several sustained minor injuries from falling debris and sudden pressure changes.

The aircraft, en route to a West Coast destination, experienced a catastrophic failure of the left mid-exit door plug—a structural panel installed in place of an emergency exit on certain high-density cabin configurations. The sudden breach caused cabin pressure to plummet, sending loose personal items, overhead bin contents, and oxygen masks into the aisle. The flight crew immediately initiated emergency descent protocols and diverted back to Portland, where the plane touched down safely within 20 minutes of the initial failure.

Federal investigators and regulators moved swiftly to contain the crisis and address public safety. “We are treating this as a major aviation safety event,” said Jennifer Homendy, chair of the National Transportation Safety Board, during a Saturday press briefing. “Our teams are on the ground examining the recovered door plug, the aircraft structure, and maintenance records. We will leave no stone unturned.” The Federal Aviation Administration (the FAA) issued an emergency airworthiness directive Saturday, grounding all U.S.-registered 737 MAX 9 aircraft pending mandatory inspections. “Safety is our highest priority,” an FAA spokesperson said. “We are working closely with Boeing and the operator to ensure every affected aircraft meets strict structural standards before returning to service.” The airline’s chief communications officer added, “Our pilots and cabin crew executed their training flawlessly under extreme duress. We are deeply grateful to everyone on board and are providing full support to passengers and their families.”

The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a stretched variant of the popular narrow-body jet that entered commercial service in 2018. Unlike the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which powers many domestic and short-haul international routes, the MAX 9 is typically deployed on longer, higher-capacity flights. Both models are equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, a joint venture between GE Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines known for improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions. The flight departed from Portland on a routine domestic route. The pilot in command, a veteran aviator with over 12,000 flight hours, reported the decompression immediately and coordinated with air traffic control for an expedited return.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the failure likely stems from a manufacturing or installation defect in the door plug assembly. “These plugs are designed to withstand significant pressure differentials, but they rely on precise bolt torque and structural reinforcement,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor and former NTSB consultant. “If the retaining hardware was improperly secured or if there was a fatigue crack in the surrounding fuselage skin, the aerodynamic forces during climb could easily overcome the attachment points.” Investigators are also reviewing compliance with Section 25.571, the federal regulation governing damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of transport category aircraft structures. Additionally, maintenance crews are expected to be evaluated against Advisory Circular 120-16G, which outlines air carrier maintenance and preventive maintenance programs. “Regulatory frameworks exist to catch these issues before they become airborne,” Chen noted. “The question now is whether the checks were followed to the letter.”

For those on board, the incident was a sudden plunge into chaos. “One second we were climbing normally, the next there was a deafening bang and the air just vanished,” said passenger David Lin, 34, who was seated three rows from the breach. “Oxygen masks dropped, people were screaming, and my phone flew out of my hand. The flight attendants kept their composure, but you could feel the panic.” Lin’s wife, who was traveling separately, described the agonizing wait for news. “I saw the alerts on my phone and couldn’t breathe,” she said. “When he finally texted that he was safe, I just broke down. It’s a miracle no one was seriously hurt.” Several passengers reported minor lacerations from shattered window frames and bruising from the sudden pressure drop, but all were cleared by emergency medical personnel at the gate.

The incident has reignited scrutiny of the 737 MAX family, which was grounded worldwide for 20 months following two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019 linked to a flawed flight control system. Since returning to service in late 2020, the fleet has operated without major structural failures, though minor technical issues have prompted routine inspections. The door plug failure marks the first significant mid-air structural breach involving the MAX series since its recertification. Historically, rapid decompression events are rare but not unprecedented; a 2018 Southwest Airlines flight suffered a similar incident when an engine fan blade fractured, causing a window to blow out. That tragedy resulted in one fatality, underscoring the critical importance of cabin integrity and crew training.

The NTSB has established a dedicated investigative team, with specialists in structures, human performance, and flight data analysis. The recovered door plug has been transported to a secure laboratory for metallurgical and forensic examination. Boeing has pledged full cooperation, dispatching a technical response team to Portland and temporarily halting deliveries of the MAX 9 pending the FAA’s review. The airline has canceled dozens of flights over the weekend to facilitate mandatory inspections across its fleet. “We are in the early stages of a complex investigation,” Homendy emphasized. “Preliminary findings will take time, but we will provide updates as soon as verified information becomes available.” For now, passengers and industry watchers alike await answers, hoping the lessons learned will reinforce the safety of commercial aviation.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Manufacturer’s Engineering & Airworthiness Division, acting as a designated technical party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event. Our role encompasses the design, certification, manufacturing oversight, and continued airworthiness support for the affected aircraft type. The scope of this document is to provide an expert technical assessment of the mid-exit door plug separation, evaluate contributing factors through engineering analysis and docket evidence, and outline the corrective framework implemented to prevent recurrence.

The investigation has required rigorous examination of structural retention systems, manufacturing quality assurance, operational data, and maintenance interfaces. This submission synthesizes findings from recovered hardware, flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, manufacturing traveler documentation, and post-event inspections. While the event was successfully managed by the flight crew and resulted in no loss of life, it exposed critical vulnerabilities in assembly verification and quality traceability. Our position is grounded in empirical data, regulatory compliance frameworks, and industry-standard engineering practices. We acknowledge the complexity of modern commercial aircraft production and the interdependencies between design intent, manufacturing execution, and operator maintenance programs. This document presents our technical conclusions, supported by docket-referenced evidence, and outlines actionable safety improvements aligned with the highest standards of aviation safety management.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft departed a Pacific Northwest airport on a scheduled domestic flight. During climb, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the left mid-exit door plug (MEP) separated from the aft fuselage, resulting in rapid cabin decompression. The pilot in command immediately initiated emergency descent procedures, coordinated with air traffic control, and executed a safe return to the departure airport. All occupants survived without serious injury.

Recovery of the door plug and surrounding fuselage structure was completed within 48 hours. Docket materials, including NTSB Exhibit 3-C (recovered hardware analysis), Exhibit 5-A (manufacturing traveler logs), and Exhibit 8-D (FDR/QAR data streams), form the evidentiary foundation of this submission. The recovered plug exhibited intact guide tracks, undamaged stop fittings, and no evidence of fatigue cracking or material degradation. However, forensic examination revealed that four of the twelve primary retention fasteners were either improperly torqued or entirely absent from their designated positions. The remaining eight fasteners showed torque values within specification, though two exhibited minor thread deformation consistent with secondary load transfer following initial fastener loss.

Cabin pressure differential at the time of separation, derived from FDR parameter 114, was approximately 5.2 psi, well within the aircraft’s certified operational envelope. The flight crew’s response was immediate and procedurally compliant. The pilot in command executed the rapid decompression checklist, donned oxygen equipment, initiated an emergency descent, and maintained positive aircraft control throughout the event. No anomalies were recorded in the environmental control system, flight control surfaces, or structural load monitoring parameters prior to the separation.

Maintenance records, reviewed under Docket Item 11-B, indicate the aircraft had accumulated approximately 1,200 flight cycles and 3,800 flight hours since delivery. No prior maintenance actions or deferred items were logged for the left mid-exit door plug. Post-delivery rework documentation, however, revealed a non-routine inspection and reseal procedure performed at a third-party facility, which introduced variability into the fastener installation sequence. The Federal Aviation Administration’s initial airworthiness directive and subsequent operator bulletins mandated immediate inspections across the fleet, confirming that the failure mode was isolated to specific production and post-production verification gaps rather than systemic design deficiency.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The engineering assessment of this event centers on three interrelated domains: structural retention mechanics, manufacturing quality assurance, and operational/maintenance interfaces. Each domain is evaluated against certification requirements, industry standards, and empirical data recovered during the investigation.

Structural Retention and Load Path Analysis
The mid-exit door plug functions as a pressure boundary component, transferring cabin differential loads to the surrounding fuselage skin and frame structure through a combination of guide tracks, stop fittings, and retention fasteners. The design philosophy adheres to fail-safe principles, wherein the loss of a single fastener does not compromise structural integrity. However, the simultaneous absence or improper installation of multiple fasteners disrupts the intended load distribution, creating localized stress concentrations that can initiate progressive loosening under cyclic pressurization.

Finite element modeling, validated against Docket Exhibit 6-F, demonstrates that the retention system is capable of withstanding ultimate load conditions when all fasteners are properly installed and torqued to specification. The recovered hardware analysis confirms that the guide tracks and stop fittings remained within dimensional tolerances, and no evidence of material fatigue or crack propagation was identified. This aligns with compliance to 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation for metallic structure. The door plug assembly, while not classified as primary flight structure, must still demonstrate adequate retention under repeated pressurization cycles. The data indicates that the failure was not driven by material degradation or design inadequacy, but by an initial installation deficiency that compromised the intended load path.

Manufacturing Quality and Verification Gaps
Forensic review of the manufacturing traveler logs (Docket Exhibit 5-A) reveals a breakdown in the torque verification sequence during final assembly. Standard operating procedures require dual-verification torque application using calibrated tools, followed by digital logging and quality assurance sign-off. In this instance, the production record shows incomplete torque verification entries for the left MEP, with subsequent rework documentation indicating a rushed installation sequence to meet delivery schedules. The absence of automated torque verification and reliance on manual documentation introduced traceability vulnerabilities.

Industry best practices, as outlined in AS9100 quality management standards and reinforced by FAA oversight guidance, emphasize closed-loop verification for critical fastener installations. The event underscores the necessity of integrating digital torque logging, real-time compliance alerts, and independent quality audits into the assembly workflow. While the Boeing 737 MAX 8 variant utilizes conventional exit doors with different retention hardware, the MAX 9 configuration introduced a plug-based solution to accommodate optional mid-cabin exits. This design variation required distinct assembly procedures, which were not uniformly standardized across production lines. The resulting procedural inconsistency contributed to the installation error.

Operational and Maintenance Interfaces
The propulsion system, manufactured by GE Aviation, performed nominally throughout the flight. FDR data confirms that the LEAP-1B engine parameters, including N1, EGT, and fuel flow, remained within certified limits. No thrust asymmetry, vibration anomalies, or engine control system faults were recorded. The separation event was entirely independent of the powerplant, and the CFM LEAP-1B powerplant’s operational integrity was unaffected by the rapid decompression.

Maintenance program compliance was evaluated against Advisory Circular 120-16G, which provides guidance for air carrier maintenance and preventive maintenance programs. The operator’s maintenance tracking system showed no prior discrepancies for the affected door plug, and scheduled inspections were current. However, AC 120-16G emphasizes the importance of post-delivery modification tracking and quality assurance integration between manufacturers and operators. The non-routine reseal procedure performed after delivery was not adequately cross-referenced with the manufacturer’s quality database, creating a blind spot in the maintenance history. This highlights the need for enhanced data interoperability and standardized post-delivery inspection protocols.

Human Factors and Crew Response
The pilot in command’s response was exemplary and aligned with established emergency procedures. Rapid decompression at 16,000 feet requires immediate oxygen deployment, descent initiation, and crew coordination. The flight crew executed these actions without hesitation, maintaining aircraft control and passenger safety. No human factors deficiencies contributed to the event. The crew’s performance validates the effectiveness of current training programs and emergency checklist design.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on comprehensive engineering analysis, docket evidence, and regulatory compliance review, the Manufacturer’s Engineering & Airworthiness Division concludes the following:

The primary contributing factor to the mid-exit door plug separation was a manufacturing and assembly quality control deficiency, specifically the improper installation and inadequate verification of retention fasteners. The failure mode was not attributable to structural fatigue, material degradation, or inherent design flaws. The retention system, when properly installed, meets all certification requirements and demonstrates adequate load-bearing capacity under cyclic pressurization.

Secondary contributing factors include gaps in post-delivery quality traceability, inconsistent procedural standardization across production lines, and insufficient integration of digital verification tools. The event was not influenced by propulsion system performance, as the LEAP-1B engine and associated systems operated within normal parameters. The pilot in command’s response was procedurally sound and did not contribute to the event.

Our position is that this incident represents a process execution and verification breakdown rather than a systemic design deficiency. The aircraft’s certification basis, including compliance with 14 CFR 25.571, remains valid. However, the event necessitates immediate enhancements to manufacturing quality assurance, fastener verification protocols, and operator maintenance tracking systems.

Recommended safety improvements include:
- Implementation of automated, digitally logged torque verification for all critical retention fasteners
- Mandatory post-delivery door plug inspection checklist with independent quality sign-off
- Enhanced data interoperability between manufacturer production systems and operator maintenance databases
- Standardization of assembly procedures across all production variants, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 configurations
- Integration of AC 120-16G principles into operator maintenance programs to ensure consistent tracking of post-delivery modifications

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

The Manufacturer has implemented immediate and sustained corrective actions to address the identified vulnerabilities and prevent recurrence. These actions are aligned with regulatory requirements, industry best practices, and the safety management principles outlined in this submission.

Actions Already Taken:
- Issued an immediate service bulletin mandating comprehensive inspection of all mid-exit door plug retention fasteners across the affected fleet.
- Coordinated with the Federal Aviation Administration to support the issuance of an emergency airworthiness directive, ensuring uniform compliance across operators.
- Implemented enhanced torque verification procedures, including dual-technician sign-off and calibrated tool validation, for all door plug installations.
- Conducted a third-party quality audit of the final assembly line, identifying procedural gaps and implementing corrective work instructions.
- Revised manufacturing traveler documentation to require digital logging of all critical fastener installations, with automated compliance alerts for missing or out-of-torque entries.
- Established a dedicated engineering task force to review all plug-based exit configurations and standardize assembly protocols across production variants.

Proposed Future Improvements:
- Deployment of smart torque tools with real-time data transmission to a centralized quality management system, enabling immediate detection of installation anomalies.
- Development of a post-delivery inspection module integrated into operator maintenance tracking software, ensuring seamless handoff of quality data between manufacturer and airline.
- Expansion of supplier quality oversight programs, including mandatory certification audits for all fastener and retention hardware vendors.
- Implementation of continuous structural health monitoring via QAR/FDR data analytics, focusing on pressure boundary integrity and cyclic load tracking.
- Collaboration with industry stakeholders to update maintenance guidance, incorporating lessons learned from this event into future revisions of AC 120-16G and related advisory materials.
- Establishment of a transparent safety reporting portal for operators to submit door plug inspection findings, enabling proactive trend analysis and fleet-wide risk mitigation.

The Manufacturer remains fully committed to aviation safety, regulatory collaboration, and continuous improvement. This event has reinforced the necessity of rigorous quality assurance, digital traceability, and standardized assembly practices. We will continue to support the NTSB investigation, share all relevant technical data, and implement the corrective actions outlined herein to ensure the highest standards of airworthiness and passenger safety.

TO: All Line Maintenance Stations, Quality Assurance, Fleet Engineering, and Technical Operations
FROM: Director of Airworthiness & Maintenance Engineering, Pacific Northwest Maintenance Division
DATE: January 8, 2024
SUBJECT: URGENT QUALITY ALERT – Mid-Exit Door Plug Retention Hardware Verification & Inspection Protocol
REF: QA-2024-0108, WO-737M-4421, FAA AD 2024-01-01 (Preliminary), NTSB Docket Entry DCA24MA012

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate inspection, torque verification, and documentation of all mid-cabin exit door plug retention hardware across the 737 MAX fleet. The directive is issued in direct response to the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event and establishes mandatory work instructions, traceability standards, and return-to-service criteria. Compliance is non-negotiable and effective immediately upon receipt.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 experienced an in-flight separation of the left mid-exit door plug during climb through approximately 16,000 feet following departure from a Pacific Northwest hub. The flight crew, led by the Captain, executed immediate emergency descent and diversion procedures, resulting in a safe landing with zero fatalities. Preliminary telemetry and post-flight inspection data indicate missing or improperly installed retention fasteners on the door plug assembly. While the incident aircraft is a MAX 9 variant, this alert extends to all Boeing 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 aircraft in our active, reserve, and heavy maintenance inventory due to shared structural design, manufacturing lineage, and identical plug retention architecture.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has initiated emergency airworthiness actions referencing damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements under Section 25.571 of the Federal Aviation Regulations. Additionally, our internal maintenance program must align with Advisory Circular AC 120-16G regarding air carrier maintenance and preventive maintenance programs. This alert supersedes all prior routine door plug inspection intervals and modifies standard AMM procedures until further OEM and regulatory guidance is published.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all scheduled and unscheduled maintenance events involving the mid-cabin exit door plug area must comply with the following:

1. Hardware Verification Scope:
   - Inspect all four (4) primary retention bolts, two (2) secondary guide track fasteners, and associated lockwire assemblies on both left and right mid-exit door plugs.
   - Reference Part Number: B737-DOORPLUG-RET-04A (Primary Bolt Assembly) and B737-GUIDE-TRK-02B (Track Fastener Kit).
   - Verify torque values per Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1284, Rev 3: 185–205 in-lbs for primary retention hardware.

2. Inspection Procedure:
   - Remove interior trim panels per AMM 25-11-00.
   - Visually inspect for missing fasteners, improper lockwire routing, or evidence of fretting/corrosion at the plug-to-fuselage interface.
   - Utilize calibrated torque wrenches (calibration valid within 30 days) to verify all fasteners.
   - Document findings using Work Order Form QA-DOOR-09. Photograph all fastener locations before and after torque verification.

3. Cross-System Interface Check:
   - While focused on the door plug, technicians must also verify adjacent systems for secondary damage or displacement.
   - Confirm LEAP-1B engine pylon and nacelle clearance per standard post-decompression inspection protocols. Coordinate with General Electric Aviation technical support if abnormal vibration, oil leak, or clearance discrepancies are noted.
   - Ensure cabin pressure relief valves and outflow valve actuators are functionally tested per AMM 21-31-00.

4. Documentation & Traceability:
   - All inspections must be logged in the electronic maintenance tracking system (EMTS) under Task Code: DOORPLUG-INS-2024.
   - Attach torque verification sheets, calibration certificates, and photographic evidence to the aircraft technical log.
   - Any discrepancy (missing hardware, torque out of spec, damaged threads) requires immediate grounding and escalation to Fleet Engineering via the Nonconformance Reporting Portal (NCR-2024-DOOR).

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Line Maintenance Supervisors: Initiate inspection on all 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 aircraft within 24 hours of receipt of this alert. Prioritize aircraft with upcoming heavy maintenance or recent door plug removal/reinstallation events.
- Quality Assurance Inspectors: Perform 100% verification of all completed inspections. Random audit 20% of torque sheets and photographic documentation within 48 hours.
- Fleet Engineering: Compile inspection data and submit preliminary findings to the FAA Airworthiness Division by January 12, 2024. Coordinate with OEM technical representatives for any required structural repairs or fastener replacements.
- Training Department: Distribute updated door plug inspection checklist (Rev 4) to all B1/B2 licensed technicians by January 10, 2024. Conduct mandatory 30-minute virtual briefing on revised torque procedures and lockwire standards.
- Flight Operations Liaison: Ensure all flight crews are briefed on updated emergency decompression checklists and door plug anomaly reporting procedures. The Captain’s initial report remains the primary trigger for post-flight technical evaluation.

Return-to-Service Criteria:
Aircraft may only be released to service after:
1. All retention hardware is verified within torque specifications.
2. QA sign-off is obtained on Form QA-DOOR-09.
3. No open NCRs related to the door plug assembly remain.
4. EMTS reflects completion of Task Code DOORPLUG-INS-2024.

Failure to comply with this alert constitutes a violation of our internal airworthiness compliance program and may result in immediate suspension of maintenance privileges. All questions or technical clarifications must be directed to the Maintenance Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or via the internal portal under Reference QA-2024-0108.

This document will be retained as part of our internal quality management system and may be submitted to regulatory and investigative authorities as required.

SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:15 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. commercial carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during initial climb. The aircraft, which had departed from a Pacific Northwest regional airport, encountered a structural anomaly involving the left mid-exit door plug at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident, and there were no reported fatalities or serious injuries among the passengers or crew.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information gathered from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads indicates a sudden cabin pressure differential event coinciding with the reported separation of the left mid-cabin exit door plug. Initial telemetry suggests the aircraft was operating within normal performance parameters prior to the event, with no recorded system warnings or anomalies in the primary flight control or environmental control systems. Witness accounts from passengers seated in the immediate vicinity of the affected fuselage section describe a loud acoustic event followed by rapid airflow, localized debris, and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Several individuals reported that personal items were drawn toward the opening, though initial medical assessments indicate only minor injuries consistent with rapid decompression.

Weather conditions at the time of the event, as reported by local meteorological stations and onboard weather radar, were characterized by visual meteorological conditions (VMC) with light winds, scattered cloud layers, and no significant convective activity or turbulence reported along the departure route. Preliminary examination of the recovered aircraft components and exterior fuselage imagery suggests localized structural damage to the left aft fuselage paneling and adjacent window frames. The separation interface of the door plug appears to have experienced a complete detachment from its retention structure, though the precise mechanical sequence remains under evaluation. It should be noted that these observations are preliminary and subject to change as additional data is analyzed and physical evidence is further examined.

For comparative context, investigators are reviewing maintenance and operational records associated with similar airframe configurations, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8, to identify any common manufacturing or assembly practices that may warrant scrutiny. Additionally, the powerplant configuration, which utilizes the LEAP-1B engine manufactured by General Electric Aviation, has been reviewed for any potential secondary effects; however, initial data does not indicate any engine-related anomalies or performance degradation during the event. Regulatory frameworks governing cabin pressure integrity and structural fatigue, including Section 25.571 of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations, will be referenced throughout the structural evaluation to assess compliance with damage tolerance requirements. Maintenance documentation will also be cross-referenced with Advisory Circular 120-16G to evaluate adherence to established inspection and repair protocols for pressurized fuselage components.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Maintenance Records groups have been formally established and are currently conducting preliminary data reviews. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has been designated as a party to the investigation, alongside representatives from the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and the relevant labor organizations. All parties have been briefed on their responsibilities and are operating under the constraints of the NTSB’s party system, which requires strict adherence to investigative protocols and information-sharing guidelines.

Physical evidence has been secured at the departure airport and the operator’s maintenance facility. The recovered door plug components, adjacent fuselage panels, and associated fasteners have been cataloged, photographed, and placed under controlled storage to preserve chain of custody. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been successfully downloaded, and initial data validation is underway. The Captain and remaining flight crew members have been interviewed, and preliminary statements have been documented. The Captain reported no abnormal handling characteristics prior to the decompression event and described a rapid but controlled response to the cabin altitude warning.

Planned examinations include detailed metallurgical analysis of the door plug retention hardware, non-destructive testing of the surrounding fuselage structure, and a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s maintenance history, including recent line checks and component installations. The Systems group will evaluate the environmental control system and cabin pressure regulation logic, while the Structures group will conduct a finite element review of the door plug interface to assess load distribution and potential stress concentrations. All examinations will be conducted in accordance with established NTSB laboratory procedures, and findings will be documented in technical reports subject to peer review.

NEXT STEPS
Investigative activities over the coming weeks will focus on the detailed reconstruction of the door plug assembly, correlation of FDR/CVR data with maintenance logs, and expanded interviews with maintenance personnel and manufacturing representatives. The Structures group will coordinate with independent materials laboratories to perform microscopic and chemical analyses of the recovered hardware, with particular attention to fastener torque values, sealant application, and potential manufacturing deviations. The Operations and Human Performance groups will continue to evaluate crew resource management, emergency checklist execution, and passenger response protocols during the decompression event.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated within 30 days, pending the completion of initial laboratory examinations and data validation. Subsequent updates will be issued as significant findings emerge, though it must be emphasized that all current information remains preliminary and subject to revision. The investigation will proceed methodically, with no conclusions regarding probable cause or contributing factors to be drawn until all technical, operational, and regulatory aspects have been thoroughly evaluated. The NTSB will continue to coordinate with the FAA and other relevant agencies to ensure that any immediate safety concerns are addressed through appropriate regulatory or operational actions. Further public briefings will be scheduled as warranted by investigative milestones, and all documentation will be made available in accordance with federal transparency and investigative disclosure requirements.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 1707:14 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a rapid decompression event occurred aboard a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, operated by a major U.S. air carrier. The event transpired during the initial climb phase of a scheduled passenger flight departing from Portland International Airport (KPDX), Portland, Oregon, en route to Ontario International Airport (KONT), Ontario, California.
