The aircraft was at a pressure altitude of 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) when the left mid-exit door plug (L2 position) separated from the fuselage. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent and returned to KPDX, landing safely at 1732:08 PST. No fatalities or serious injuries were reported among the 171 passengers and 6 crewmembers. The event coordinates were recorded at 45°34'18.2"N, 122°38'51.4"W, approximately 12.4 nautical miles west-northwest of the departure runway threshold.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufacturer serial number 44450, manufactured by The Boeing Company. The operator held a valid Air Carrier Certificate issued under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The aircraft was configured for 178 passenger seats and operated under the operator’s approved Operations Specifications, document number OPS-121-445. The flight was conducted as a scheduled domestic passenger service in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart U. The aircraft’s registration was current, and the airworthiness certificate was valid at the time of the event.

1.3 Nature of the Flight
The flight was a regularly scheduled revenue passenger operation conducted under 14 CFR Part 121. The flight plan was filed under instrument flight rules (IFR) with a planned cruise altitude of 37,000 feet MSL. The departure runway was 10L, and the initial climb followed the standard instrument departure (SID) procedure for the Portland area, specifically the PDX ONE departure. Air traffic control (ATC) communications were recorded on the Portland Departure frequency (125.35 MHz). The flight crew acknowledged all clearances and complied with standard climb profiles until the decompression event occurred.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The Captain, serving as pilot-in-command, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The Captain’s medical certificate was a first-class medical, issued on October 12, 2023, with no limitations or waivers. The Captain possessed a total flight time of 8,450 hours, with 2,100 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The Captain’s most recent proficiency check was completed on November 18, 2023, in a Level D full-flight simulator, with satisfactory results recorded for all required maneuvers, including emergency descent, rapid decompression, and engine failure scenarios.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The First Officer held a commercial pilot certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings, and was working toward an ATP certificate. The First Officer’s medical certificate was a first-class medical, issued on September 5, 2023. Total flight time was 3,200 hours, with 1,450 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The most recent line check was conducted on December 10, 2023, with all performance standards met. The First Officer’s duty time and rest periods were in compliance with 14 CFR 117.11 and 14 CFR 117.15.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crewmembers were current and qualified in accordance with 14 CFR 121.433 and 14 CFR 121.439. The Captain had accumulated 85 flight hours in the preceding 90 days, including 12 hours in the 30 days prior to the accident. The First Officer had accumulated 78 flight hours in the preceding 90 days. Both crewmembers completed the operator’s annual recurrent training program, which included cabin depressurization emergency procedures, rapid descent protocols, and crew resource management (CRM) scenarios. Training records indicated compliance with all regulatory requirements and operator-specific standards. The Captain’s most recent simulator session included a scenario involving sudden cabin altitude warning at 15,000 feet, which was executed within acceptable performance parameters.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines. The airframe was certified under Type Certificate No. T00001SE. The aircraft’s total airframe time was 1,245.6 hours, with 892 flight cycles. The aircraft was delivered to the operator on October 15, 2023, and entered revenue service on November 2, 2023. The airframe configuration included a standard mid-cabin exit door plug at the L2 and R2 positions, installed in lieu of a functional passenger door to meet seating density requirements. The structural design of the door plug assembly was derived from the BOEING 737-8 and 737-9 MAX common airframe architecture, with identical load-bearing specifications and fastener patterns.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained under the operator’s FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.369. A review of the maintenance records indicated that the aircraft had undergone a scheduled A-check on December 28, 2023, at 1,180.2 airframe hours. During this inspection, the left mid-exit door plug was examined per the manufacturer’s maintenance planning document (MPD) task 53-10-00-200-801. The inspection included verification of fastener torque, guide track alignment, and seal integrity. No discrepancies were documented. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were complied with, including AD 2023-18-05, which addressed cabin pressure relief valve functionality. The maintenance logbook contained no deferred items related to the L2 door plug or adjacent fuselage structure.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The cabin pressurization system was controlled by the outflow valve and two cabin pressure controllers (CPCs). The system was designed to maintain a maximum cabin differential pressure of 9.1 psi. The left mid-exit door plug was a structural component designed to withstand the same pressure loads as a standard passenger door. The plug was secured by four primary guide tracks, twelve high-strength fasteners, and a secondary retention system. The aircraft’s cabin altitude warning system was configured to activate at 10,000 feet cabin altitude, providing both aural and visual alerts to the flight crew. The aircraft’s flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and downloaded without incident. The FDR recorded 25 hours of data, and the CVR recorded 2 hours of audio, both within regulatory retention limits.

3.4 Powerplant and Engine Manufacturer
The aircraft was equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B engines, serial numbers 884521 and 884523. The core engine components were manufactured under the joint venture between Safran Aircraft Engines and GE Aviation. Maintenance records for the engines indicated compliance with all manufacturer service bulletins and time-on-wing limits. The engine manufacturer, GE Aviation, provided technical support and component traceability documentation during the investigation. Engine performance parameters recorded during the climb phase were within normal operating envelopes, with N1 values at 82.4% and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) at 612°C. No engine anomalies or thrust asymmetries were recorded prior to or during the decompression event.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Weather Conditions at Time of Accident
At the time of the event, meteorological conditions in the Portland terminal area were visual meteorological conditions (VMC). Surface observations indicated a temperature of 4°C, dew point of 1°C, wind from 270° at 8 knots, and visibility of 10 statute miles. The altimeter setting was 30.12 inches of mercury (inHg). No convective activity, icing, or turbulence was reported in the departure corridor. The freezing level was at 6,500 feet MSL, and the aircraft remained in above-freezing conditions throughout the climb phase.

4.2 METAR and TAF Data
The METAR for KPDX at 1700 PST was: KPDX 051700Z 27008KT 10SM FEW040 BKN080 04/01 A3012 RMK AO2 SLP198 T00440011. The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) issued at 1600 PST predicted continued VMC conditions with scattered clouds at 4,000 feet and broken layers at 8,000 feet through 2000 PST. En route weather radar and satellite imagery confirmed clear skies along the initial climb path. Upper air sounding data from the Salem, Oregon, radiosonde station indicated a standard atmospheric lapse rate with no significant wind shear or temperature inversions below 20,000 feet MSL.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Atmospheric Data
No pilot reports (PIREPs) of significant weather, turbulence, or wind shear were filed in the vicinity of the accident location. The aircraft’s onboard weather radar was not activated during the climb phase, as conditions were benign. Atmospheric pressure lapse rates were standard, and the cabin differential pressure at 16,000 feet MSL was approximately 4.8 psi, well within the design limits of the fuselage and door plug assembly. The aircraft’s static pressure system was functioning normally, with no discrepancies noted in the altimeter or vertical speed indicator readings.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The accident aircraft sustained no ground impact. The primary structural damage was localized to the left fuselage at station 1016, corresponding to the L2 mid-exit door plug location. The door plug assembly was recovered from a residential area approximately 1.2 nautical miles from the departure runway, at coordinates 45°34'12.5"N, 122°38'45.1"W. The fuselage exhibited a clean separation along the door plug perimeter, with no evidence of explosive decompression or secondary structural failure. The remaining airframe was intact, and all flight control surfaces were undamaged. The recovered door plug was secured in a protective container and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination.

5.2 Component Examination Findings
Examination of the recovered door plug revealed that all twelve primary fasteners were absent from the guide track mounting brackets. The guide tracks themselves remained attached to the fuselage structure, with visible witness marks indicating lateral displacement prior to separation. The door plug’s outer skin exhibited minor abrasion consistent with aerodynamic forces during flight. The inner seal was intact but showed compression deformation. The secondary retention latch was in the unlocked position, with no mechanical binding or corrosion observed. The fastener holes in the guide track brackets showed no signs of thread stripping or elongation.

5.3 Forensic and Materials Analysis
The NTSB Materials Laboratory conducted a detailed examination of the fastener holes and guide track interfaces. Microscopic analysis revealed no evidence of fatigue cracking, stress corrosion, or manufacturing defects in the aluminum alloy structure. Torque verification of the remaining fastener threads indicated that the fasteners had not been installed to the manufacturer’s specified torque values. The absence of thread-locking compound and the lack of witness marks on the fastener heads suggested that the fasteners were either not torqued during installation or had backed out prior to the event. The cabin pressure differential at the time of separation was calculated at 4.8 psi, which is below the ultimate load rating of the door plug assembly. Metallurgical testing confirmed that the fastener material met ASTM F835 specifications, and no material degradation was identified.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Maintenance Procedures
The operator’s maintenance program required all door plug installations to be performed by certified airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanics with specific training on Boeing 737 MAX structural modifications. The operator’s quality assurance department conducted random audits of maintenance documentation, with the most recent audit occurring on January 2, 2024. The audit identified no systemic deficiencies in fastener installation procedures. The operator’s engineering department had issued a service bulletin in December 2023 reinforcing torque verification protocols for mid-cabin exit door plugs. All maintenance personnel were required to complete a biennial training module on structural fastener installation, with records maintained in the operator’s electronic maintenance tracking system.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
A review of the NTSB and FAA incident databases identified three prior occurrences involving door plug or exit door anomalies on Boeing 737 series aircraft. In 2018, a 737-800 experienced a cabin pressure warning due to a misaligned door seal, which was resolved through routine maintenance. In 2021, a 737 MAX 8 operator reported a loose fastener on a mid-exit door plug during a pre-flight inspection, which was corrected prior to dispatch. No prior in-flight separation events involving a 737 MAX 9 door plug were documented. The BOEING 737-8 and 737-9 MAX share common structural design principles, and the manufacturer’s service history indicates that door plug installations are subject to rigorous quality control measures. Historical data from the manufacturer’s fleet reliability program showed a 0.0002% anomaly rate for mid-exit door plug fasteners across 1,200 aircraft.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The design and certification of the door plug assembly were conducted in accordance with 14 CFR 25.365 (Pressurized Cabin Loads) and 14 CFR 25.783 (Fuselage Doors). The operator’s maintenance procedures were required to comply with 14 CFR 121.373 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations) and 14 CFR 43.13 (Performance Rules). The Federal Aviation Administration (the FAA) issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) on January 6, 2024, mandating immediate inspections of all 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with mid-exit door plugs. The EAD required verification of fastener torque, guide track alignment, and retention system functionality. Guidance for maintenance personnel regarding door plug installation and inspection is provided in Advisory Circular 120-16G, which outlines best practices for structural fastener installation, torque verification, and quality assurance documentation. The AC emphasizes the importance of cross-checking critical fastener installations and maintaining traceable maintenance records.

6.4 Flight Data and Recorder Analysis
The FDR recorded a rapid cabin altitude increase from 6,000 feet to 14,000 feet within 3.2 seconds following the door plug separation. The cabin differential pressure dropped from 4.8 psi to 0.2 psi. The Captain immediately initiated an emergency descent, reducing thrust and deploying speed brakes. The aircraft descended to 10,000 feet MSL at a rate of 4,500 feet per minute. The CVR captured standard crew coordination, with the Captain declaring an emergency and coordinating with air traffic control. The flight crew executed the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) procedures for rapid decompression and cabin altitude warning. The aircraft was stabilized at 10,000 feet, and the crew diverted to KPDX without further incident. All recorded parameters were within normal operational limits prior to the event.

6.5 Regulatory and Industry Response
Following the event, the FAA grounded all 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with mid-exit door plugs pending completion of the EAD inspections. The manufacturer issued a fleet-wide service bulletin detailing enhanced inspection protocols and revised torque verification procedures. The operator implemented additional training modules for maintenance personnel, focusing on fastener installation techniques and quality control documentation. The investigation remains ongoing, with the NTSB coordinating with the FAA, the manufacturer, and the operator to determine the sequence of events and contributing factors. All factual data collected to date has been documented in accordance with NTSB Group Chairman reporting standards. The Agency continues to monitor compliance with the EAD and will issue supplemental findings as additional technical data becomes available.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the NTSB Structures and Materials Group in support of the investigation into the rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered left mid-exit door plug (MEDP) assembly, adjacent fuselage skin and frame structure, primary and secondary retention hardware, and associated flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) parameters. The final examination was conducted from January 10 through January 18, 2024, following the preliminary assessment completed on January 22, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with coordinated inspections at Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Everett, Washington, and the operator's maintenance facility in Portland, Oregon.

Items examined included the complete left MEDP panel (Boeing Part Number 65-12345-001, Serial Number 88421-L), twelve primary retention bolts (NASM1312-11-12, Ti-6Al-4V), four stop fitting assemblies, guide track rails, adjacent fuselage skin (Station 43.5 to 44.2, Stringer S-12 to S-16), and the recovered FDR (Honeywell SSFDR, P/N 980-4700-042, S/N 11442). All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) Section 4.2, ASTM E114 (Ultrasonic Testing), ASTM E309 (Eddy-Current Testing), and Boeing Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-10-01. Coordination was maintained with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft manufacturer, and the operator's engineering staff throughout the examination period.

The mid-exit door plug is a non-opening structural closure installed in lieu of a Type III emergency exit on certain high-density cabin configurations. INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, LEAD LINE MAINTENANCE SUPERVISOR
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 10:15 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Field Office, Seattle, Washington
Interviewer: Investigator David Vance, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety
Witness: Marcus Thorne, Lead Line Maintenance Supervisor, Pacific Northwest Operations

Q: Mr. Thorne, thank you for making yourself available. For the official record, please state your full name, your current title, and your relationship to the aircraft involved in the January 5th event.

A: Yeah, absolutely. Marcus Thorne. I’m the Lead Line Maintenance Supervisor for our Pacific Northwest hub. I’ve been with the airline for, uh, about fourteen years now. My job is basically overseeing the day-to-day line maintenance, coordinating pre-flight checks, and acting as the liaison between our ramp techs and the engineering group. I wasn’t personally wrenching on that specific airplane the morning of the fifth, but I was on shift, and I was the first maintenance lead to get the initial radio call when it came back.

Q: Understood. Can you walk me through your timeline that morning, starting from when you first became aware of the flight?

A: Right. So, I clocked in at, I think it was 04:30 local. We had a pretty heavy push that morning. The aircraft in question—tail number N704AL, I believe—was scheduled for a 06:15 departure. I was in the maintenance office doing the shift handoff when the gate agent radioed in around 06:05 saying the Captain had requested a quick walk-around because of a minor cabin pressure indication during the pre-flight test. Nothing unusual, really. We see that sometimes. I told the ramp tech to just verify the outflow valve and the door seals, which he did. He signed it off, and the aircraft pushed back on time.

Q: And when did you learn of the actual in-flight event?

A: Uh, about twenty minutes after pushback. I was on the radio monitoring the ground ops channel when I heard the flight deck declare an emergency. The Captain keyed the mic and said something like, “We’ve got a rapid decompression, we’re turning back, requesting priority handling.” I remember the exact time because I looked at the wall clock. It was 06:38. The aircraft was climbing through, I think, sixteen thousand feet. You could hear the wind noise on the open mic for a second, just this… this roaring sound, like a vacuum cleaner but way louder, and then the Captain keyed the mic again, calm as anything, saying they were stabilizing and coming back.

Q: What was your immediate response upon hearing that transmission?

A: I immediately grabbed my radio and told the ramp crew to clear the gate, get the fire trucks staged just in case, and pull the emergency response checklist. I also called our maintenance control center. We started pulling up the aircraft’s maintenance logs, the tech logs, everything. I was trying to figure out if there was any recent work on the left side of the fuselage. I knew that particular Boeing 737 MAX 9 had a mid-cabin exit door plug instead of an actual door. We’d had a few of those in the fleet. I’d actually done the initial familiarization training on the plug installation when we first took delivery of the MAX series.

Q: You mentioned the door plug. Can you describe your familiarity with that component and any relevant maintenance procedures?

A: Yeah, so, the plug is basically a structural panel that replaces the door opening on certain configurations. It’s held in by a series of stop fittings, guide tracks, and a bunch of high-strength bolts. When we first got the Boeing 737 MAX 8s, we didn’t have the plug, obviously. The MAX 9 introduced it. I remember reading through the Boeing service bulletins and cross-referencing them with our maintenance program, which is built around Advisory Circular 120-16G for airworthiness and maintenance tracking. The plug installation is pretty straightforward on paper, but in practice, you have to be meticulous with torque values and the safety wiring. I mean, it’s not like you can eyeball it. Every bolt has to be torqued to spec, and the stop fittings have to be seated flush.

Q: Were there any recent maintenance actions on that specific aircraft’s door plug area?

A: Not that I could find in the logs. The last heavy check was about eight months prior. There was a minor cabin pressure squawk logged two weeks before, but it was traced to a faulty sensor, not the plug. We replaced the sensor, ran a leak check, and it passed. I double-checked the work order. Everything was signed off by an A&P with inspection authorization. So, on paper, it was clean.

Q: When the aircraft returned, what did you observe?

A: It landed around 06:52. I was standing at the gate with the fire crew. When it taxied in, you could just… see it. The left mid-exit plug was gone. Just completely missing. There was a jagged opening in the fuselage, about the size of a large window. The surrounding skin was buckled a bit, and there was some frost and condensation around the edges from the rapid decompression. I could smell that sharp, cold air smell, you know, like ozone and jet fuel mixed with the cabin air. The Captain taxied it in slowly, shut down the engines, and we got the stairs up. I was the first maintenance person on board.

Q: What was your immediate assessment once you were inside?

A: I did a quick visual sweep. The plug was obviously gone, but I needed to check the surrounding structure. I looked at the stop fittings, the guide rails, the bolt holes. A few of the bolt holes were elongated, which tells me the bolts either backed out or sheared. I didn’t see any obvious signs of impact damage from the outside, so it wasn’t a bird strike or debris. It looked like a structural separation. I immediately secured the area, took photos, and called our engineering group. We also had to coordinate with the FAA because, obviously, this is a major event. They issued an emergency airworthiness directive within hours, grounding the fleet for inspections.

Q: You mentioned the FAA. How did your team respond to the regulatory response?

A: We followed the directive to the letter. We pulled every MAX 9 with a door plug off the line. I personally supervised the inspections on three of them. We used borescopes, torque checks, and visual inspections of the plug retention system. The Federal Aviation Administration’s guidance was clear, but we also referenced 14 CFR 25.571 in our internal review. That’s the damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation standard. It’s what dictates how we inspect for cracks, fastener hole elongation, and load path integrity. In this case, it seemed like the fasteners weren’t properly retained, or maybe the stop fittings weren’t fully engaged. I don’t want to speculate too much, but the evidence pointed to a retention failure.

Q: Were there any other systems or components that drew your attention during the post-flight inspection?

A: The engines were fine. We run the LEAP engine, specifically the LEAP-1B variant. They’re manufactured by GE Aviation, and they’re incredibly reliable. The shutdown was completely normal. No surge, no vibration, no abnormal EGT readings. The Captain handled the descent and landing perfectly. I actually spoke with him later that day. He said the decompression was sudden, but the aircraft handled it well. The oxygen masks deployed, the crew followed the emergency checklist, and they got everyone calm. He mentioned the cabin pressure warning came on, and then there was a loud bang, followed by the wind noise. He didn’t feel any unusual yaw or roll, which is good. It means the structural damage was localized.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add regarding the maintenance history, your observations, or the broader context?

A: Just that… I mean, we take these things seriously. The plug isn’t a new concept, but the MAX 9 configuration was relatively new to our line maintenance team. We’ve had training, we follow the manuals, but sometimes, you know, human factors come into play. Maybe a bolt wasn’t torqued, maybe a safety wire was missed, maybe the stop fitting wasn’t seated all the way. I’m not saying that’s what happened, but it’s what we’re looking at. The FAA’s going to do their thing, Boeing’s going to do theirs, and we’re just trying to make sure our procedures are airtight. I’ve been in this business a long time, and I’ve never seen a plug just… fall out. It’s unsettling. But the crew did exactly what they were supposed to do, and everyone walked away. That’s what matters.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.

A: Yeah, of course. I’m here if you need anything. Just let me know.

OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
AIRCRAFT CERTIFICATION SERVICE
TRANSPORT STANDARDS DIVISION

DATE: March 18, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service, Transport Standards Division
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO NTSB PRELIMINARY FINDINGS AND AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE COMPLIANCE STATUS
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA010; Docket No. FAA-2024-0112; AD 2024-02-09
APPLICABLE REGULATIONS: 14 CFR Part 21, 14 CFR Part 25, 14 CFR Part 121

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This memorandum constitutes the formal regulatory response to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) preliminary findings and associated safety recommendations arising from the in-flight rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The referenced incident occurred during initial climb at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) following departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The aircraft executed a safe return to the departure aerodrome with zero fatalities and no serious injuries. This document addresses compliance with 14 CFR 25.571, Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure, and outlines the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) oversight actions, regulatory framework assessment, and mandated corrective measures. The administrative docket for this regulatory action is FAA-2024-0112, and the associated Airworthiness Directive (AD) is designated 2024-02-09.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737 MAX series, including the derivative BOEING 737-8, operates under Type Certificate No. T00001SE, issued pursuant to 14 CFR Part 21. The mid-cabin exit door plug configuration was originally certified as a supplemental type certificate (STC) modification to accommodate variable cabin layouts while maintaining compliance with 14 CFR 25.783, Fuselage Doors, and 14 CFR 25.365, Pressurized Compartment Loads. The structural integrity of the door plug retention system is governed by the damage-tolerance requirements codified in 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates that the primary structure must be evaluated for fatigue, crack propagation, and residual strength under repeated pressurization cycles.

Historically, the FAA has issued multiple ADs addressing manufacturing quality control deviations within the Boeing Commercial Airplanes production system, including AD 2021-23-12 and AD 2023-18-05, which mandated enhanced inspection protocols for fastener installation and torque verification. The January 5, 2024, event represents a systemic failure in the quality assurance chain, specifically concerning the installation and retention of the door plug guide tracks and stop fittings. The NTSB’s preliminary investigation identified missing fasteners and inadequate torque documentation, indicating a departure from the approved production quality system as required by 14 CFR 21.137.

Furthermore, the regulatory framework governing powerplant and airframe integration, which includes oversight of component suppliers such as General Electric Aviation, requires continuous airworthiness monitoring under 14 CFR Part 33 and Part 25. While the door plug separation is structurally isolated from the propulsion system, the broader manufacturing ecosystem and supply chain quality management systems fall under the FAA’s purview. The FAA’s oversight of the type certificate holder’s production approval holder (PAH) responsibilities has been subject to heightened scrutiny following prior safety recommendations regarding production quality control and configuration management.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the operator’s maintenance records, the manufacturer’s production documentation, and the FAA’s oversight audit trail reveals significant deficiencies in compliance with established airworthiness standards. The operator, operating under 14 CFR Part 121, maintained an approved Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.344 and 14 CFR 121.369. However, the root cause of the door plug separation is attributable to manufacturing non-conformances that occurred prior to aircraft delivery, thereby circumventing standard operator maintenance detection protocols.

The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (FS) conducted a joint audit of the production facility and identified systemic gaps in the quality management system (QMS). Specifically, the absence of mandatory torque verification documentation for critical structural fasteners violates the requirements of 14 CFR 21.137(c)(2) and the approved quality manual. Additionally, the structural evaluation under Section 25.571 did not adequately account for the cumulative effects of manufacturing tolerances on the door plug retention interface under repeated pressurization cycles. The analysis confirms that the current regulatory framework lacks explicit requirements for independent third-party verification of critical structural fastener installations during final assembly.

Oversight actions taken to date include the immediate issuance of Emergency AD 2024-02-09, mandating pre-flight inspections of all affected door plug configurations, and the temporary suspension of certain production line operations pending corrective action implementation. The FAA has also initiated a comprehensive review of the type certificate holder’s delegated authority under 14 CFR 21.29, specifically evaluating the adequacy of Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) unit member oversight. The investigation further indicates that the integration of supplier quality data, including components sourced from entities such as GEA for ancillary systems, requires enhanced traceability protocols to ensure full compliance with 14 CFR 25.1309, Equipment, Systems, and Installations.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings outlined herein, the FAA mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Immediate Structural Inspection and Fastener Verification: All operators of the affected aircraft models shall comply with AD 2024-02-09, requiring detailed visual and torque verification inspections of the mid-cabin exit door plug retention system within 24 flight hours or prior to the next scheduled departure, whichever occurs first. Non-conforming installations shall be rectified in accordance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53A1285, Revision 1, under the direct supervision of an FAA-certified repair station or manufacturer representative.

b. Quality Management System Overhaul: The type certificate holder shall submit a revised Quality Management System (QMS) manual to the FAA’s Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) within 60 calendar days. The revised QMS must incorporate mandatory independent verification steps for all critical structural fastener installations, including digital torque logging and photographic documentation, in compliance with 14 CFR 21.137 and FAR 25.571.

c. Regulatory Framework Enhancement: The FAA will initiate rulemaking proceedings to amend 14 CFR Part 25, specifically targeting the damage-tolerance evaluation requirements for non-pressurized structural interfaces. Proposed amendments will mandate enhanced fatigue testing protocols and explicit fastener retention criteria for door plug configurations. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) is anticipated within 180 days, with public comment period closure projected for Q3 2024.

d. Ongoing Oversight and Audit Schedule: The FAA will conduct quarterly compliance audits of the manufacturer’s production facilities and delegated ODA units for a minimum period of 36 months. These audits will evaluate adherence to the revised QMS, traceability of supplier components, and compliance with 14 CFR 121.344 maintenance program requirements. Operators shall submit monthly compliance reports to the Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) detailing inspection results, corrective actions, and any recurring discrepancies.

e. Supply Chain Traceability Mandate: All primary and secondary suppliers, including propulsion and systems integrators such as GE Aviation, shall implement enhanced configuration management and part traceability protocols. Documentation must be maintained in accordance with 14 CFR 21.305 and 14 CFR 25.1309, ensuring full lifecycle accountability for all safety-critical components.

The FAA remains committed to restoring public confidence in the airworthiness of the affected fleet and ensuring strict adherence to federal aviation regulations. All mandated actions shall be executed under the authority of the Administrator, with compliance verification conducted through the established regulatory oversight framework. Failure to comply with the stipulated timelines and requirements will result in enforcement actions pursuant to 14 CFR Part 13, including potential suspension of production certificates and operating authorities.

This memorandum serves as the official regulatory response and shall be incorporated into the administrative record for Docket No. FAA-2024-0112.

HEADLINE: Mid-Flight Door Plug Separation Triggers Emergency Landing of Boeing 737 MAX 9

BYLINE: By Marcus Thorne, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: PORTLAND, Ore. —

A Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier suffered a catastrophic mid-air failure on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, when a left-side exit door plug tore away from the fuselage during climbout, triggering a rapid decompression event at 16,000 feet. The aircraft, which had departed from Portland International Airport bound for Ontario, California, executed an emergency return and landed safely with no fatalities reported among the 171 passengers and six crew members aboard.

The sudden loss of the structural panel caused cabin pressure to plummet, instantly deploying oxygen masks and sending loose items flying through the cabin. Pilots initiated an emergency descent, leveling off at a lower altitude before diverting back to Portland. The incident has prompted immediate regulatory scrutiny and a temporary grounding of similar aircraft as federal investigators work to determine how a critical fuselage component detached during routine flight operations.

“We are treating this as a serious aviation safety event,” said Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Mike Whitaker in a Saturday briefing. “The FAA has issued an emergency airworthiness directive requiring immediate inspections of all 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with mid-cabin exit door plugs.” National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy confirmed that a specialized investigative team arrived at the scene within hours. “Our priority is securing the wreckage, interviewing the flight crew, and preserving all data from the flight recorders,” Homendy said. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads.” An airline spokesperson added, “The safety of our passengers and crew is our absolute priority. We are cooperating fully with federal investigators and have grounded our entire MAX 9 fleet pending further guidance.”

The aircraft involved is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a narrow-body jet powered by CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, a joint venture between GE Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines. The flight was operating a routine domestic route when the incident occurred. The missing component is not a standard passenger door but a “door plug,” a structural panel installed to seal an unused emergency exit on high-density cabin configurations. These plugs are designed to withstand the same pressure differentials as active doors and must meet stringent damage tolerance requirements—federal regulations that dictate how aircraft structures must handle cracks, material fatigue, and unexpected stress without experiencing catastrophic failure.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the failure likely stems from a manufacturing or installation defect rather than an in-flight mechanical breakdown. “Door plugs are bolted and pinned into the fuselage frame,” explained Dr. Marcus Chen, a former NTSB investigator and aerospace engineering professor at Purdue University. “If the retention bolts were missing, improperly torqued, or if the plug wasn’t aligned correctly during assembly, the aerodynamic forces during climb could easily overcome the fasteners.” Chen emphasized that while the LEAP engine and other flight systems performed normally, the structural integrity of the fuselage is paramount. “Modern airliners are built with multiple redundancies, but a missing plug at 16,000 feet creates an immediate pressure differential that the aircraft isn’t designed to sustain without rapid decompression.”

Inside the cabin, passengers described a scene of sudden chaos followed by disciplined calm. “There was a loud bang, like a cannon shot, and then the air just got sucked out,” said passenger David Lin, 34, who was seated three rows behind the affected exit. “My phone flew out of my hand, and a child’s jacket was pulled toward the opening. The oxygen masks dropped, and the flight attendants immediately started shouting instructions. It was terrifying, but the crew kept us focused.” The Captain, whose identity has not been released, later praised the cabin crew’s response in a brief statement to the airline. “The crew executed emergency procedures flawlessly,” the pilot in command said. “We maintained control, communicated with air traffic control, and prioritized a safe return. Everyone is accounted for, and we are deeply grateful for the professionalism of our team.”

The incident has reignited scrutiny of the 737 MAX family, which was grounded worldwide for 20 months following two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019 linked to a flawed flight control system. While the MAX 9 variant was cleared to return to service in late 2020 after extensive software and training updates, this event marks the first major structural failure involving the aircraft type. Historically, rapid decompression events are rare but not unprecedented. In 2018, a Southwest Airlines Boeing 737-700 suffered an engine failure that shattered a window, causing a fatal decompression. In 1988, an Aloha Airlines 737-200 experienced a massive fuselage rupture mid-flight, though the aircraft landed safely. Aviation safety records show that modern aircraft are engineered to survive such events, but each incident prompts rigorous reevaluation of manufacturing oversight and maintenance protocols.

The NTSB has established a public docket for the investigation, with preliminary findings expected within 30 days. Investigators are currently examining the recovered door plug, analyzing cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder information, and reviewing Boeing’s production records from the Renton, Washington, assembly line. The FAA has mandated that all affected airlines complete detailed inspections of door plug fasteners and track hardware before returning aircraft to service. “We are looking at every bolt, every seal, and every step in the assembly process,” Homendy said. “This investigation will be thorough, transparent, and driven by data.” As the aviation industry braces for potential operational disruptions, passengers and regulators alike await answers to a critical question: how did a critical piece of the aircraft’s structure simply fall away at cruising altitude?

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Engineering and Maintenance Division of the operating carrier, acting in our capacity as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9. As the operator, our organization maintains direct responsibility for the airworthiness, maintenance execution, operational data collection, and safety management systems governing the affected aircraft. Our role in this investigation encompasses the provision of flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) telemetry, maintenance work order documentation, crew statements, post-flight inspection records, and internal safety management system (SMS) analyses.

The scope of this submission is to present a technical assessment of the structural, operational, and maintenance factors that contributed to the separation of the left mid-cabin exit door plug during climb. Our analysis focuses on the interface between the plug assembly and the fuselage structure, the operational load environment at the time of the event, the adequacy of maintenance verification protocols, and the alignment of current inspection practices with established certification frameworks. While the investigation remains ongoing, this document synthesizes available docket materials, engineering evaluations, and operational data to articulate our technical position, identify systemic vulnerabilities, and propose actionable safety improvements. We acknowledge the multi-party complexity inherent in modern commercial aviation manufacturing and maintenance ecosystems, and we approach this analysis with a commitment to evidence-based reasoning, regulatory compliance, and continuous safety enhancement.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft departed a Pacific Northwest hub airport on a scheduled domestic flight. During initial climb, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the flight crew experienced a sudden cabin pressure loss, accompanied by an audible bang, rapid decompression, and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. The crew executed standard emergency descent and pressurization failure procedures, declared an emergency, and returned to the departure airport without further incident. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

Post-flight inspection revealed that the left mid-exit door plug had separated from the fuselage, with the plug and associated hardware recovered from the surrounding terrain. The National Transportation Safety Board has cataloged extensive evidence in the public docket, including FDR and CVR recordings (Docket Item 24-01-015), maintenance work orders and sign-off documentation (Docket Item 24-01-022), manufacturer service bulletins, and the Federal Aviation Administration’s Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-51. Our internal records confirm that the aircraft had undergone a scheduled maintenance event fourteen days prior to the incident, during which the mid-cabin exit plug was accessed for cabin reconfiguration. The maintenance documentation indicates standard fastener removal and reinstallation procedures were followed, though independent verification of torque values and secondary retention hardware installation was not captured in the digital maintenance log.

FDR parameters at the time of the event indicate a normal climb profile, with cabin differential pressure stabilizing at approximately 5.2 psi prior to the decompression. No abnormal yaw, roll, or vibration signatures were recorded. The aircraft’s structural health monitoring system did not register pre-event anomalies, and the flight crew reported no prior indications of door seal degradation, unusual cabin noise, or pressurization irregularities. These factual elements establish a baseline for evaluating the technical and procedural factors that preceded the structural failure.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The separation of the mid-cabin exit door plug represents a failure of a critical pressurized fuselage interface. The plug assembly is designed to transfer cabin pressure loads to the surrounding fuselage frames through a combination of stop fittings, guide tracks, and twelve primary structural fasteners. Under normal operating conditions, the plug remains secured by friction, mechanical interference, and fastener preload. The failure mode observed in this event is consistent with progressive fastener loosening, inadequate preload retention, and insufficient secondary mechanical retention, culminating in a sudden loss of structural continuity during a routine pressurization cycle.

Operational load analysis derived from FDR telemetry confirms that the aircraft was operating within certified flight envelope parameters. The climb thrust setting, rate of climb, and pressurization schedule were nominal. Engine performance data, including exhaust gas temperature (EGT), N1/N2 rotational speeds, and vibration levels, remained well within manufacturer-specified limits. The CFM LEAP-1B powerplant, manufactured by GE Aviation, demonstrated stable operation throughout the climb phase. Engine health monitoring (EHM) data provided by General Electric Aviation confirms that the LEAP engine exhibited no abnormal vibration harmonics, surge events, or thrust asymmetries that could have induced structural resonance or localized fatigue loading on the aft fuselage. Vibration parameters recorded at the time of the event (N1 < 0.45 inches per second, N2 < 0.28 inches per second) fall significantly below the thresholds associated with propulsion-induced structural excitation. Consequently, the LEAP-1B powerplant and its associated nacelle/pylon interface did not contribute to the door plug separation.

The primary technical vulnerability lies in the intersection of maintenance execution, fastener retention design, and the application of damage tolerance requirements. Certification standards, specifically 14 CFR § 25.571 and associated FAA Advisory Circulars, establish fatigue and damage tolerance requirements for pressurized fuselage structures. These DT requirements mandate that critical structural joints be designed to withstand cyclic loading, incorporate fail-safe or damage-tolerant features, and be subject to inspection intervals that detect degradation before catastrophic failure. The mid-cabin exit plug, however, relies heavily on proper fastener installation and torque verification to maintain structural integrity. The absence of secondary retention hardware (e.g., locking plates, safety wiring, or redundant fastener paths) means that the design’s damage tolerance margin is highly sensitive to maintenance execution quality.

Review of the maintenance work order documentation reveals procedural gaps in fastener verification. While the aircraft maintenance manual (AMM) specifies torque values and installation sequences, the documentation does not mandate independent dual-verification or digital torque logging for critical structural fasteners. Industry best practices, as outlined in SAE AS9100 and OEM quality assurance guidelines, require redundant verification for load-bearing joints in pressurized structures. The lack of such controls allowed a latent installation deficiency to persist through post-maintenance functional checks. Under cyclic pressurization, the compromised fastener preload degraded incrementally, reducing the plug’s ability to resist aerodynamic and pressure-induced shear loads. Once the preload threshold was breached, the plug disengaged from its guide tracks and separated from the fuselage.

This failure mode highlights a systemic misalignment between certification assumptions and real-world maintenance execution. The damage tolerance requirements framework assumes that critical fasteners are installed to specification and that inspection intervals will detect degradation before failure. However, when fastener installation lacks verifiable quality controls, the damage tolerance model becomes ineffective. The plug’s design does not incorporate inherent fail-safe features that would prevent separation in the event of fastener degradation, placing disproportionate reliance on maintenance precision. This vulnerability is compounded by supply chain fragmentation, where manufacturing, assembly, and line maintenance responsibilities are distributed across multiple entities, increasing the risk of documentation gaps and procedural drift.

From an engineering perspective, the incident underscores the necessity of integrating structural health monitoring, digital maintenance verification, and enhanced secondary retention into critical fuselage interfaces. The operational data confirms that the aircraft was flown within normal parameters, and the propulsion system performed as designed. The failure originated in the structural interface, driven by inadequate fastener retention and insufficient verification protocols. Addressing this requires a holistic approach that bridges design philosophy, maintenance execution, and regulatory oversight.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the available evidence, engineering analysis, and operational data, our position is that the primary contributing factor to the door plug separation was inadequate fastener installation and verification during maintenance, compounded by the absence of secondary retention hardware and insufficient quality assurance controls. The operational environment, including climb profile, pressurization schedule, and engine performance, was nominal and did not contribute to the failure. The CFM LEAP-1B powerplant, as documented by GE Aviation telemetry, operated within certified limits, and no propulsion-induced structural loading was present.

The incident reveals a critical gap between the damage tolerance requirements established during certification and the practical realities of maintenance execution. The plug’s design assumes precise fastener installation and relies on inspection intervals to detect degradation. However, without redundant verification mechanisms and inherent fail-safe features, the design’s damage tolerance margin is highly vulnerable to procedural deviations. The absence of digital torque logging, independent quality inspection, and secondary mechanical retention allowed a latent defect to progress undetected until structural continuity was lost.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Mandate secondary retention hardware for all mid-cabin exit door plugs to provide a fail-safe load path in the event of primary fastener degradation.
- Implement digital torque verification systems with cloud-based logging and automated compliance alerts for all critical structural fasteners.
- Revise maintenance documentation to require independent dual-verification and photographic evidence for load-bearing fuselage interfaces.
- Align inspection intervals with actual operational stress cycles rather than calendar-based schedules, ensuring that damage tolerance requirements are dynamically applied.
- Enhance supply chain quality oversight through standardized audit protocols and cross-party data sharing between manufacturers, operators, and regulators.

These measures will strengthen the structural integrity of critical fuselage interfaces, reduce reliance on procedural perfection, and ensure that certification assumptions are consistently validated in operational environments.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the January 5, 2024, event, our organization has implemented immediate and sustained corrective actions to mitigate risk and enhance fleet safety. Within 48 hours of the incident, we initiated a fleet-wide inspection program in coordination with the FAA Emergency Airworthiness Directive. All affected aircraft underwent comprehensive door plug inspections, including fastener torque verification, guide track alignment checks, and secondary retention assessments. Any discrepancies were rectified prior to return to service. We have also revised our maintenance procedures to mandate digital torque wrenches with automated data logging for all critical structural fasteners, eliminating manual documentation errors and providing real-time compliance verification.

Our engineering and maintenance teams have developed enhanced technician training modules focused on pressurized fuselage interfaces, fastener installation best practices, and quality assurance protocols. These modules incorporate scenario-based learning, hands-on verification exercises, and regulatory compliance reviews. Additionally, we have established an independent quality assurance audit program that conducts unannounced inspections of maintenance execution, documentation accuracy, and tool calibration. These audits are integrated into our safety management system, with findings tracked through corrective action plans and executive oversight.

Looking forward, we propose several systemic improvements to further strengthen structural safety and maintenance reliability. First, we advocate for the integration of structural health monitoring (SHM) sensors on door plug assemblies to provide continuous load and displacement telemetry. This data would enable predictive maintenance algorithms to identify fastener degradation before it reaches critical thresholds. Second, we recommend the development of standardized digital maintenance verification platforms that synchronize OEM service bulletins, regulatory directives, and operator-specific procedures into a single, auditable workflow. Third, we support regulatory updates to the damage tolerance requirements framework, specifically mandating fail-safe design features for all pressurized fuselage interfaces and requiring operators to demonstrate compliance through verifiable maintenance data rather than procedural checklists alone.

Finally, we propose the establishment of a cross-industry working group comprising manufacturers, operators, regulators, and maintenance organizations to standardize critical fastener installation protocols, share telemetry and inspection data, and develop unified quality assurance benchmarks. By aligning engineering design, maintenance execution, and regulatory oversight, the aviation community can transform this incident into a catalyst for systemic safety enhancement. Our organization remains committed to transparency, continuous improvement, and the highest standards of airworthiness, and we will continue to collaborate with the NTSB, FAA, and industry partners to ensure that lessons learned are translated into enduring safety outcomes.

TO: Fleet Maintenance Engineering, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance Division, Technical Records
FROM: Director of Airworthiness & Structural Integrity, Pacific Northwest Maintenance Operations
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2024-014: Immediate Inspection & Torque Verification of Mid-Exit Door Plug Retention Hardware
REF: QA-2023-089, WO-7742-MAX, NTSB Docket Entry #2024-01-05-001, ENG-REV-24-003

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate, fleet-wide inspection and torque verification of all mid-cabin exit door plug retention hardware. The directive supersedes routine maintenance intervals and requires completion prior to the next scheduled revenue flight for all affected aircraft. This alert is issued to ensure continued airworthiness, prevent recurrence of structural separation events, and align our maintenance execution with updated regulatory expectations and manufacturer service bulletins.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier experienced a rapid decompression event when the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage during climb through 16,000 feet after departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport with no fatalities. Preliminary teardown and NTSB preliminary findings indicate that multiple retention bolts were either missing or improperly torqued at the time of manufacture, allowing the plug to dislodge under pressurization loads.

While the incident involved a MAX 9 variant, our engineering review confirms that the Boeing 737 MAX 8 utilizes an identical door plug retention architecture and fastener specification. Teardown analysis of the recovered hardware indicated retention bolt preload values of 1,850 lbf when measured via ultrasonic elongation, whereas calibrated torque-angle methods yielded 1,790 lbf — a divergence consistent with known friction coefficient assumptions in rotational versus axial measurement techniques. Both datasets confirm sub-optimal clamping force relative to design intent. Consequently, this alert applies across the entire MAX 8/9 fleet in our maintenance program. Structural integrity requirements under Section 25.571 mandate rigorous fatigue and damage tolerance evaluations for pressurized fuselage components, and our internal audit has identified a potential gap in post-delivery torque verification documentation that requires immediate procedural alignment.

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:15 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. commercial carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during initial climb. The aircraft, which had departed from a Pacific Northwest regional airport, encountered a structural anomaly involving the left mid-exit door plug at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident; there were no reported fatalities, and all occupants were accounted for upon landing.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information has been compiled from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads, air traffic control communications, and initial maintenance records. Initial information indicates that the aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules and was in a normal climb profile when the decompression event occurred. The Captain and first officer reported an abrupt loss of cabin pressure accompanied by a loud acoustic event, followed by immediate activation of emergency descent procedures. Preliminary examination of the CVR transcript suggests the flight crew adhered to established emergency checklists and maintained positive aircraft control throughout the event.

Weather conditions at the time of the incident were characterized by marginal visual meteorological conditions with scattered cloud layers, light precipitation, and surface winds from the southwest at 8 to 12 knots. No significant convective activity or severe turbulence was reported in the immediate vicinity of the flight path. Radar and satellite data are currently being correlated with the aircraft’s trajectory to rule out meteorological factors as a primary contributor.

Damage assessment conducted during the initial post-flight inspection revealed a complete separation of the left mid-exit door plug from the aft fuselage section. The surrounding fuselage skin, adjacent stringers, and window frames exhibit localized deformation and fastener displacement. Initial visual inspection of the cabin interior indicates that several overhead bins and seat rows in the immediate vicinity sustained secondary impact damage from loose articles. The aircraft’s pressurization system, environmental control system, and primary flight controls appear to have remained functional following the event. It should be emphasized that these observations are preliminary and subject to revision as detailed structural teardown and metallurgical analyses are completed.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the scope of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Maintenance Records groups have been formally established and are currently conducting parallel lines of inquiry. The Federal Aviation Administration has been designated as a party to the investigation, alongside the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and relevant labor organizations. All parties have been briefed on their responsibilities and are operating under the standard NTSB party system protocols.

Evidence secured to date includes the original FDR and CVR units, which have been transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction and validation. The separated door plug and associated hardware have been recovered and placed in secure storage pending detailed dimensional inspection and forensic analysis. Maintenance logs, work orders, and component tracking records for the affected airframe have been requested and are under review. Initial interviews with maintenance personnel, flight attendants, and the flight crew are being scheduled in accordance with established procedural guidelines.

The investigation will evaluate compliance with applicable airworthiness standards, including relevant damage tolerance requirements and structural fatigue life assessments. Investigators will also review maintenance and inspection protocols referenced in Advisory Circular 120-16G to determine whether procedural deviations or documentation gaps may have contributed to the observed structural failure. While the primary focus remains on the door plug assembly and its integration with the fuselage, the investigation will also examine the LEAP-1B turbofan engines for any secondary effects resulting from the rapid decompression and emergency descent profile. GE Aviation technical representatives have been integrated into the Powerplants group to assist with engine data analysis and post-event inspection procedures.

For comparative purposes, investigators are reviewing historical maintenance and operational data from the BOEING 737-8 fleet to identify any common design features, manufacturing processes, or service history patterns that may be relevant to the current event. All data collection efforts are being conducted with strict chain-of-custody protocols, and no determinations regarding causation or contributing factors have been made at this stage.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks include a comprehensive structural teardown of the recovered door plug and adjacent fuselage sections, detailed metallurgical and fractographic examinations, and a full review of the aircraft’s manufacturing and delivery documentation. The Operations group will conduct simulator-based evaluations to assess crew workload, emergency procedure execution, and aircraft handling characteristics during the decompression and descent phases. The Systems group will perform bench testing of the cabin pressure control valves, outflow valves, and associated warning systems to verify proper functionality prior to the event.

Additional interviews with maintenance technicians, quality assurance personnel, and regulatory inspectors will be conducted to establish a complete timeline of recent inspections, modifications, and component replacements. Data from the aircraft’s health monitoring system will be cross-referenced with operator maintenance records to identify any pre-existing anomalies or deferred maintenance items. The investigation team will also coordinate with international regulatory counterparts to review global service history for similar airframe configurations.

A preliminary factual report summarizing the initial findings, group activities, and evidence collected will be issued within 30 days of the incident date. Subsequent updates will be provided as critical examinations are completed and as additional data becomes available. All findings documented in this preliminary report are subject to change as the investigation progresses, and no conclusions regarding probable cause or contributing factors will be issued until the final investigative report is published. The NTSB remains committed to a thorough, transparent, and methodical examination of all available evidence to support future safety recommendations.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:11 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a scheduled passenger flight departed from Portland International Airport (KPDX), Portland, Oregon. The aircraft was en route to Ontario International Airport (KONT), Ontario, California. At 17:28:14 PST, while climbing through 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) at a calibrated airspeed of 285 knots, the flight crew experienced a sudden, uncommanded cabin decompression event. The aircraft was located approximately 18 nautical miles northwest of KPDX at the time of the occurrence. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent, declared a Mayday, and returned to KPDX, landing safely at 17:42:03 PST. No injuries to occupants or persons on the ground were reported.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, bearing registration number N704AL, serial number 44442. The aircraft was operated by a major U.S. air carrier under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The operator held an active Air Carrier Certificate and Operations Specifications authorizing domestic and international scheduled passenger operations. The aircraft was configured for 178 passenger seats, with 171 passengers and 5 crewmembers aboard at the time of the event. The flight was conducted as a revenue passenger service under instrument flight rules (IFR).

1.3 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted in accordance with the operator’s approved General Operations Manual (GOM) and the applicable requirements of 14 CFR Part 121. The flight plan was filed for a cruise altitude of 37,000 feet MSL, utilizing standard en route airways. The departure clearance was issued by Portland Tower, and the aircraft was subsequently handed off to Seattle Center. The rapid decompression event occurred during the initial climb phase, prior to reaching the assigned cruise altitude. The flight crew executed the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) procedures for rapid decompression, including donning oxygen masks, initiating an emergency descent to 10,000 feet MSL, and diverting to the departure airport. All emergency procedures were completed in accordance with established operator protocols and regulatory requirements.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The pilot in command, referred to herein as the Captain, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The Captain possessed a valid first-class medical certificate issued on October 12, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time recorded in the operator’s training database was 12,450 hours, with 3,215 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The Captain’s most recent proficiency check was completed on November 18, 2023, and was documented as satisfactory. The Captain met all regulatory requirements for recent flight experience as specified in 14 CFR 121.439.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The second-in-command held an ATP certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings, along with a valid first-class medical certificate issued on September 5, 2023. Total flight time was 4,820 hours, with 1,140 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The First Officer’s most recent line-oriented flight training (LOFT) and proficiency evaluation were completed on December 2, 2023, with all performance metrics meeting or exceeding operator standards. The First Officer was current and qualified for the assigned route and aircraft type.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crewmembers completed recurrent training in accordance with the operator’s FAA-approved training program, which was developed in compliance with Advisory Circular 120-16G, Air Carrier Maintenance Programs and Training. The training curriculum included simulator-based scenarios addressing rapid decompression, emergency descent profiles, and abnormal pressurization events. Records indicate that the Captain participated in a full-motion simulator session on December 14, 2023, which included a rapid decompression scenario at 15,000 feet MSL. Performance evaluations documented appropriate crew resource management (CRM), checklist discipline, and adherence to standard operating procedures. No training deficiencies or remedial actions were noted in either crewmember’s personnel file.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufactured by The Boeing Company. The airframe was delivered to the operator on March 14, 2023. At the time of the accident, the aircraft had accumulated 1,245.6 total flight hours and 892 flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a standard commercial passenger configuration, including a dual-aisle forward cabin, single-aisle aft cabin, and standard avionics suite compliant with Boeing 737 MAX certification specifications. The aircraft’s weight and balance calculations for the accident flight were within approved limits, with a takeoff weight of 168,450 pounds.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records indicate that the aircraft was maintained in accordance with the operator’s Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP), approved by the Federal Aviation Administration. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were complied with, including those related to flight control systems, pressurization components, and structural inspections. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check) was completed on October 28, 2023, at 1,012 flight hours. The aircraft was released to service with no deferred maintenance items affecting the pressurization system or fuselage structure. The operator’s maintenance tracking system documented all scheduled inspections, component replacements, and service bulletin incorporations.

3.3 Door Plug Configuration and Systems
The aircraft was equipped with a left mid-exit door plug at fuselage station 1016, installed in lieu of a standard passenger door to accommodate the operator’s seating configuration. The door plug assembly was manufactured and installed in accordance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1234, Revision 2. The plug is secured to the fuselage structure via a series of high-strength fasteners, guide tracks, and stop fittings designed to maintain structural continuity and pressurization integrity. Maintenance records indicate that the door plug was last inspected during the October 2023 C-check. Torque verification records for the primary retention fasteners were documented, though subsequent examination revealed discrepancies in fastener installation and retention hardware configuration. The pressurization system, governed by the cabin pressure controller and outflow valve, was functioning normally prior to the event.

3.4 Engine and Propulsion Systems
The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B27 turbofan engines, manufactured by GE Aviation. The left engine (serial number 892145) had accumulated 1,245.6 hours and 892 cycles. The right engine (serial number 892148) had accumulated 1,245.6 hours and 892 cycles. Both engines were maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommended maintenance program and operator CAMP. Engine health monitoring data indicated normal parameters for exhaust gas temperature (EGT), fuel flow, and vibration levels during the climb phase. No engine anomalies, surges, or thrust asymmetries were recorded prior to or during the decompression event. The engine manufacturer’s technical documentation confirms that the LEAP-1B series meets all applicable certification standards for thrust, durability, and environmental compliance.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
On January 5, 2024, the Pacific Northwest region was under the influence of a high-pressure system centered over the northern Rocky Mountains. Surface analysis indicated stable atmospheric conditions with light gradient winds and minimal convective activity. The upper-level flow was predominantly zonal, with a weak ridge axis extending from the Pacific Ocean into the interior western United States. No significant weather systems, frontal boundaries, or jet stream disturbances were present along the departure route.

4.2 Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts and METAR Data
The aviation routine weather report (METAR) for KPDX at 16:53 PST on January 5, 2024, read: KPDX 051653Z 18005KT 10SM FEW040 08/02 A3012. Visibility was unrestricted, ceiling was few clouds at 4,000 feet, temperature was 8°C, dewpoint was 2°C, and altimeter setting was 30.12 inches of mercury. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) issued at 16:00 PST predicted continued VFR conditions with winds from 180° at 5 to 10 knots, visibility greater than 6 statute miles, and scattered clouds at 5,000 feet through 23:00 PST. No significant weather changes were forecasted during the flight’s operational window.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and In-Flight Conditions
The flight crew reported visual meteorological conditions (VMC) during departure and initial climb. At the time of the decompression event, the aircraft was at 16,000 feet MSL, with an outside air temperature of -12°C and a pressure altitude of 16,000 feet. No turbulence, icing, or wind shear was reported by the flight crew or other aircraft operating in the vicinity. The National Weather Service Aviation Weather Center confirmed that atmospheric conditions were stable, with no convective SIGMETs or AIRMETs active along the route. The rapid decompression was not attributable to meteorological phenomena.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The primary component of interest, the left mid-exit door plug, was recovered from a residential area approximately 1.2 nautical miles northwest of the aircraft’s flight path at the time of separation. The component was located intact, with minimal ground impact deformation. The aircraft sustained no structural damage to the wings, empennage, or landing gear. The fuselage exhibited a clean separation interface at station 1016, with no evidence of in-flight fire, explosion, or secondary structural failure. The aircraft was taxied to the gate under its own power following landing, and all emergency evacuation equipment remained stowed.

5.2 Fuselage and Door Plug Examination
Examination of the recovered door plug revealed that the primary retention fasteners were absent from their designated mounting locations. The guide tracks and stop fittings remained attached to the fuselage structure, with visible scoring and deformation consistent with uncommanded outward displacement. The plug’s pressure seal exhibited localized tearing along the forward edge, indicative of rapid differential pressure loading. The surrounding fuselage skin showed no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or manufacturing defects. The separation interface was clean, with fastener holes exhibiting elongation and bearing marks consistent with load transfer prior to failure.

5.3 Structural and Fastener Analysis
Metallurgical examination of the recovered fastener holes and adjacent structure was conducted in accordance with standard aerospace failure analysis protocols. The analysis confirmed that the fastener retention system did not meet the design specifications outlined in the original equipment manufacturer’s installation manual. Several fastener locations exhibited evidence of incomplete engagement, with missing locking nuts and improperly torqued bolts. The structural load path analysis indicated that the door plug was subjected to a maximum differential pressure of approximately 8.6 psi at 16,000 feet MSL, which exceeded the retention capacity of the compromised fastener configuration. The examination findings were consistent with a loss of structural continuity due to improper installation, rather than material fatigue or environmental degradation. The analysis also referenced comparative data from the Boeing 737 MAX 8 certification program, which utilizes identical door plug retention methodologies and fastener specifications.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
The operator’s maintenance program required all door plug installations to be performed by certified airframe and powerplant (A&P) technicians under the direct supervision of a quality assurance inspector. The operator’s standard operating procedures mandated a dual-verification process for all critical fastener installations, including torque verification, safety wire application, and post-installation pressure testing. The operator’s emergency response plan was activated immediately following the decompression event, with coordination established with the Federal Aviation Administration, local emergency services, and the aircraft manufacturer. All cabin crewmembers completed their assigned duties in accordance with the operator’s emergency procedures manual, including passenger oxygen mask deployment, cabin securement, and post-landing passenger accountability.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents and Service Bulletins
The National Transportation Safety Board reviewed historical data for similar door plug separation events across the Boeing 737 MAX fleet. No prior in-flight separations of mid-exit door plugs had been reported prior to this event. However, several maintenance-related service bulletins had been issued by the manufacturer addressing fastener torque verification and installation quality control.
