The Federal Aviation Administration issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) on January 6, 2024, requiring immediate inspection of all affected door plug installations across the fleet. The directive mandated visual and tactile inspections, torque verification, and documentation review for all aircraft equipped with mid-exit door plugs. The operator complied with the EAD within the specified compliance window, grounding affected aircraft until inspections were completed.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Advisory Circulars
The investigation referenced multiple regulatory provisions and guidance documents relevant to the accident. Title 14 CFR Part 25, Subpart C, outlines the structural integrity and damage tolerance requirements for transport category airplanes. Specifically, 14 CFR 25.571 mandates that the structure must be evaluated for fatigue, damage tolerance, and residual strength under all anticipated loading conditions. The door plug installation must comply with these damage tolerance requirements to ensure continued airworthiness throughout the aircraft’s operational life. Additionally, 14 CFR 121.310 requires operators to maintain aircraft in accordance with approved maintenance programs and to ensure that all modifications and repairs meet original equipment manufacturer specifications. Advisory Circular 120-16G provides guidance on the development and implementation of air carrier maintenance programs, emphasizing quality assurance, technician training, and documentation control. The operator’s maintenance program was evaluated against these standards, with particular attention to fastener installation verification and post-maintenance inspection protocols.

6.4 Data Recorder Information
The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and downloaded in accordance with NTSB procedures. The FDR recorded a rapid cabin altitude increase from 6,000 feet to 14,500 feet within 3.2 seconds, coinciding with a sudden drop in cabin differential pressure from 8.6 psi to 0.2 psi. The aircraft’s vertical speed increased to 4,200 feet per minute during the emergency descent, with airspeed maintained at 285 knots. The CVR captured the flight crew’s immediate recognition of the decompression, execution of the emergency descent checklist, and coordination with air traffic control. All recorded parameters were within normal operational limits prior to the event, with no system warnings or fault indications recorded in the aircraft’s central maintenance computer. The data was preserved and analyzed in accordance with 14 CFR 121.359 and NTSB Part 830 reporting requirements.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis performed by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Structures and Materials Group in support of the investigation into the rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, serial number 44450. The examination was conducted between January 12 and January 24, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory, Washington, D.C., with supplemental analysis performed at the NTSB Flight Data Recorder Laboratory, Washington, D.C.

The scope of this examination encompassed the recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly, adjacent fuselage skin and frame structure, associated fasteners, guide track components, and stop fittings. Additionally, the specialist group reviewed and analyzed recorded flight data parameters, maintenance documentation, and engineering drawings pertinent to the door plug installation and structural certification basis. All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, with chain-of-custody documentation maintained throughout the process. Photographic documentation, dimensional measurements, nondestructive testing (NDT), and metallurgical evaluations were performed to characterize the condition of the recovered components and to establish factual baseline data for the investigation.

2. BACKGROUND

The accident aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a derivative of the 737 MAX family that shares commonality with the Boeing 737 MAX 8 in terms of primary flight control architecture, avionics suite, and propulsion system. The aircraft is powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B27 turbofan engines, manufactured by GE Aviation, each rated at 28,000 lbf thrust. The left mid-exit door plug (Part Number 65-12345-678, Serial Number 88921) is a structural closure panel installed in lieu of an operational passenger door to accommodate higher-density seating configurations. The plug assembly consists of a 2024-T3 Alclad aluminum skin panel, internal stiffeners, perimeter guide tracks, and four primary stop fittings that interface with the fuselage frame structure at stations 1040 through 1060.

The certification basis for the door plug installation is governed by 14 CFR Part 25, Subpart C, specifically §§25.365 (Pressurized Cabin Loads), 25.571 (Damage Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure), and 25.783 (Fuselage Doors). The design incorporates fail-safe load paths and adheres to established damage tolerance requirements, which mandate that the structure must sustain residual strength under limit load conditions following the development of detectable cracks or fastener failures. The plug is secured to the fuselage via twelve perimeter guide track bolts (NAS1399-4-8), four primary stop fitting bolts (NAS1399-5-10), and a series of secondary shear clips. Torque specifications for the primary fasteners are documented in Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1234, requiring 180–220 in-lbs with a ±10% tolerance, verified via calibrated torque wrenches per NASM1312-7.

The accident aircraft was delivered to the operator on October 14, 2023, and had accumulated 1,245 flight hours and 487 flight cycles at the time of the event. Maintenance records indicate that the left mid-exit door plug was removed and reinstalled on December 18, 2023, during a cabin reconfiguration modification. The work was performed under the operator's approved maintenance program, which references Advisory Circular 120-16G for airworthiness responsibility and maintenance tracking. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had previously issued an Airworthiness Directive (AD 2023-24-08) requiring enhanced inspection of door plug fastener installations on MAX 9 aircraft, which was incorporated into the operator's maintenance schedule prior to the December modification.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The recovered door plug assembly was received at the NTSB Materials Laboratory on January 12, 2024, in a partially disassembled state. Initial visual inspection revealed that the perimeter skin panel exhibited localized plastic deformation along the forward and aft guide track interfaces. The forward guide track (P/N 65-12345-680) was separated from the fuselage frame, with four of the twelve perimeter fastener holes exhibiting elongation and edge tearing. The aft guide track remained partially attached, with eight fasteners still engaged.

Dimensional measurements were performed using calibrated digital micrometers (±0.0005 in) and coordinate measuring machine (CMM) probes. The forward guide track bolt holes measured 0.268–0.285 inches in diameter, exceeding the nominal 0.250-inch specification. Edge distance measurements at the forward upper corner registered 0.290 inches, below the minimum design requirement of 0.312 inches per Boeing Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-10-01. The stop fittings (P/N 65-98765-432) showed no evidence of plastic deformation or fracture. All four primary stop fitting bolts were present and torqued within specification (195–210 in-lbs), as verified by calibrated torque audit.

Nondestructive testing was conducted in accordance with ASTM E1444 (Magnetic Particle) and ASTM E309 (Eddy Current). Eddy current scanning of the 2024-T3 Alclad skin panel revealed no subsurface cracking or corrosion. Magnetic particle inspection of the titanium fasteners (Ti-6Al-4V, AMS 4911) showed no surface discontinuities. Hardness testing per ASTM E18 (Rockwell B scale) yielded values of 78–82 HRB for the aluminum skin, consistent with T3 temper specifications. Chemical analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed alloy composition within AMS 4037 limits for 2024-T3.

Fractographic examination of the forward guide track interface revealed witness marks consistent with progressive fastener hole elongation under cyclic pressurization loads. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the torn edge material showed ductile dimple rupture morphology, with no evidence of fatigue striations or brittle fracture. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) per ASTM E1508 confirmed the absence of foreign material or galvanic corrosion products at the fastener-to-skin interface.

Four of the twelve perimeter guide track bolts were recovered from the cabin interior. These fasteners exhibited clean shear fractures at the shank-to-head transition, with no thread engagement marks. The remaining eight fasteners showed partial thread engagement and torque strip marks, indicating that they were not properly seated during the December 2023 reinstallation. Cross-referencing with maintenance work cards revealed that the torque verification step was documented but lacked independent quality assurance sign-off. The installation procedure required sequential torque application in a star pattern, followed by a 100% re-torque verification. The recovered fastener condition and hole elongation measurements are consistent with incomplete fastener installation and subsequent load redistribution during pressurization cycles.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) data were extracted and analyzed using NTSB-standard decoding software. The aircraft departed Portland International Airport (KPDX) at 17:07:12 UTC on January 5, 2024. The FDR recorded 1,024 parameters at 1 Hz and 8 Hz sampling rates. Key parameters analyzed included cabin altitude (CABIN_ALT), cabin pressure differential (P_DIFF), indicated airspeed (IAS), pressure altitude (ALT), vertical speed (V/S), and door status indicators (DOOR_L_MID_EXIT_STATUS).

At 17:14:38 UTC, the aircraft was climbing through 15,800 ft MSL at 285 knots IAS. The cabin pressure differential was 4.2 PSI, within normal operational limits for the climb phase. At 17:14:41 UTC, the DOOR_L_MID_EXIT_STATUS parameter transitioned from CLOSED to OPEN, coinciding with a rapid increase in cabin altitude from 6,200 ft to 14,800 ft within 3.2 seconds. The P_DIFF parameter dropped from 4.2 PSI to 0.1 PSI over the same interval, indicating instantaneous loss of cabin pressurization. The IAS parameter exhibited a transient spike to 312 knots, followed by a decay to 268 knots as the autopilot engaged speed protection. The V/S parameter showed a momentary negative excursion of -1,200 ft/min, consistent with aerodynamic drag increase and pilot control input.

The Captain initiated an emergency descent, as evidenced by the V/S parameter stabilizing at -2,500 ft/min and the IAS parameter increasing to 320 knots. The aircraft leveled at 10,000 ft MSL at 17:18:12 UTC, with cabin altitude stabilizing at 10,000 ft and P_DIFF at 0.0 PSI. The FDR recorded no additional door status anomalies or structural warning parameters. The CVR captured the activation of the cabin altitude warning horn and subsequent crew coordination, but no structural failure warnings were recorded prior to the decompression event.

Comparison with normal operational data from 15 reference flights of identical 737 MAX 9 aircraft revealed that the P_DIFF parameter typically increases linearly during climb, reaching 7.8 PSI at cruise altitude (35,000 ft). The door status parameter remains latched CLOSED throughout all phases of flight unless manually overridden. The rapid transition from CLOSED to OPEN at 16,000 ft MSL, without preceding warning parameters, indicates a sudden mechanical release rather than a gradual seal failure or sensor malfunction. The absence of pre-event vibration or acoustic anomalies in the FDR data further supports a discrete structural separation event.

5. SUMMARY

The following factual findings are derived from the specialist examination, testing, and data analysis:

- The recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly (P/N 65-12345-678, S/N 88921) exhibited localized plastic deformation along the forward guide track interface, with four of twelve perimeter fastener holes measuring 0.268–0.285 inches in diameter, exceeding the nominal 0.250-inch specification.
- Edge distance measurements at the forward upper corner registered 0.290 inches, below the minimum design requirement of 0.312 inches per Boeing SRM 53-10-01.
- Four perimeter guide track bolts (NAS1399-4-8) were recovered from the cabin interior, exhibiting clean shear fractures at the shank-to-head transition. The remaining eight fasteners showed partial thread engagement and torque strip marks.
- Hardness testing of the 2024-T3 Alclad skin panel yielded 78–82 HRB, consistent with T3 temper specifications. Chemical analysis confirmed alloy composition within AMS 4037 limits.
- SEM/EDS examination revealed ductile dimple rupture morphology at the torn edge, with no evidence of fatigue striations, brittle fracture, or galvanic corrosion.
- FDR data recorded a rapid transition of the DOOR_L_MID_EXIT_STATUS parameter from CLOSED to OPEN at 17:14:41 UTC, coinciding with a cabin altitude increase from 6,200 ft to 14,800 ft within 3.2 seconds and a P_DIFF drop from 4.2 PSI to 0.1 PSI.
- The aircraft was climbing through 15,800 ft MSL at 285 knots IAS at the time of the event. The IAS parameter exhibited a transient spike to 312 knots, followed by a decay to 268 knots.
- The Captain initiated an emergency descent, with V/S stabilizing at -2,500 ft/min and IAS increasing to 320 knots. The aircraft leveled at 10,000 ft MSL at 17:18:12 UTC.
- Maintenance records indicate the door plug was removed and reinstalled on December 18, 2023. The torque verification step was documented but lacked independent quality assurance sign-off.
- The installation procedure required sequential torque application in a star pattern, followed by a 100% re-torque verification. The recovered fastener condition and hole elongation measurements are consistent with incomplete fastener installation and subsequent load redistribution during pressurization cycles.
- The aircraft is powered by two GE Aviation LEAP-1B27 engines, which operated within normal parameters throughout the event. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 shares identical door plug design architecture and certification basis.
- The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) oversight framework and Advisory Circular 120-16G maintenance tracking requirements were referenced in the operator's approved maintenance program. The damage tolerance requirements per 14 CFR §25.571 were incorporated into the original design certification.

INTERVIEW OF SARAH JENKINS, LEAD FLIGHT ATTENDANT
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 10:30 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Seattle, WA
Interviewer: Investigator M. Torres, NTSB

Q: Please state your full name and your position for the record.
A: Sarah Jenkins. I’m a lead flight attendant. The airline calls it a lead FA, but it’s basically the purser role. I’ve been flying with the company for about fourteen years, mostly on narrow-body routes.

Q: Were you assigned to Flight 1282 on January 5th?
A: Yes, I was. I was working the forward cabin, stationed at the main galley just behind first class.

Q: Walk me through the departure and initial climb. What time did you push back, and when did you first notice anything out of the ordinary?
A: Okay, so… we pushed back from the gate at, I think it was around 4:15 PM. Maybe 4:18. We taxied out, got our clearance, and took off from runway 16L. The climb was… normal at first. I mean, you know how it is, you’re doing your post-takeoff checks, making sure the cabin’s secure, walking the aisles, checking seatbelts. We were probably at about ten to twelve minutes into the flight when the pilot in command came on the PA. He said we were passing through ten thousand, or maybe just leveling off briefly. I don’t remember the exact altitude callout, but it was smooth. Then, maybe another three or four minutes later, we were climbing again. I was just finishing up the beverage cart prep in the forward galley when… well, when it happened.

Q: Describe exactly what you experienced at that moment.
A: It was… loud. Not like a normal engine noise. It was a sharp, almost metallic *crack*, followed immediately by this… this roaring wind. Like a vacuum cleaner, but a thousand times louder. And the temperature just dropped. Instantly. I felt it in my ears first, that pressure change, and then the air just… it was like a wall of cold air hitting you. I was holding onto the cart, and it actually shifted. I remember looking toward the left side of the cabin, around row 26 or 27, and there was just… an opening. A big, jagged hole where the door plug should’ve been. I could see the sky. It was daylight, obviously, but it was overcast, so it was just this gray, rushing void. Papers, magazines, a few loose items just… got sucked out.

Q: What was your immediate reaction and what actions did you take?
A: I… I dropped the cart. I mean, I didn’t even think, I just let go. My training kicked in. I yelled “Heads down! Stay down!” and started moving toward the affected area, but the wind was so strong it was hard to walk. Oxygen masks dropped everywhere. I saw passengers panicking, some were crying, a few were trying to stand up. I had to physically push a guy back into his seat. I remember grabbing a mask myself, but honestly, I didn’t need it right away because I was still conscious, but protocol is protocol. I checked the cabin interphone, but it was dead. So I just kept moving aft, checking rows, making sure people were seated, masks on.

Q: Did you communicate with the flight deck?
A: Not right away. The interphone was out, like I said. But maybe… two or three minutes after the event, the pilot in command came on the PA. His voice was calm, but you could hear the strain. He said, “Cabin crew, brace for descent. We’re returning to Portland.” I think he said “returning to PDX.” I just acknowledged it out loud, even though I knew he couldn’t hear me. I started doing a quick headcount, checking for injuries. There were a few minor cuts from flying debris, a couple of people with ear pain, but nothing… nothing life-threatening.

Q: You mentioned the door plug. Were you aware of the aircraft type and any specific configuration details?
A: Yeah, I knew it was a MAX 9. We fly a lot of them. I’ve also flown the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which is a bit smaller, obviously, but the cabin layout’s similar. The door plug… I mean, I know it’s not a real door, it’s a plug. Maintenance told us once during a safety briefing that it’s just a panel that seals the fuselage. I didn’t know the exact part number or anything, but I knew it wasn’t supposed to just… come off. I remember thinking about the engines, too. We have the LEAP engine on these birds. They’re made by General Electric Aviation, right? Or CFM, but GE’s part of that joint venture. Anyway, the engines were running fine. I could hear them spooling down when we started the descent, but there was no vibration, no warning lights in the cabin. Just the wind.

Q: Let’s talk about your training and procedures. Were there any specific regulatory guidelines or manuals you referenced during or after the event?
A: During? Honestly, no. You don’t have time to pull out a manual when the cabin’s depressurizing. You just go on muscle memory. But after… after we landed and were debriefing, I was thinking about our emergency procedures manual, and how it aligns with the FAA guidelines. I remember in recurrent training, they always reference AC 120-16G for cabin safety and emergency evacuation protocols. I don’t have the exact text memorized, but it covers rapid decompression, oxygen use, securing the cabin… all that. We drill it every six months. I guess what I’m saying is, the training worked. Even though it was chaotic, we fell back on the steps.

Q: Can you describe the timeline from the event to landing?
A: Sure. So, the event happened at… I’d say 4:32 PM. Maybe 4:33. We were at about sixteen thousand feet, I think. The captain announced the return almost immediately. The descent was steep. You could feel the G-forces, and the cabin pressure was… well, it was equalizing, but it was still cold. We were probably descending for about twenty minutes. We landed at PDX around 4:55. The rollout was normal, but when we stopped, the captain kept the engines running for a minute, then shut them down. We opened the forward doors, deployed the slides, and started evacuating. It took maybe eight or nine minutes to get everyone off. No one was seriously hurt.

Q: Did you notice anything unusual about the aircraft prior to departure? Any maintenance delays, strange noises, or crew comments?
A: No. Nothing. The aircraft was clean, pre-flighted, everything normal. I did a walk-through with the other FAs, checked the emergency equipment, all the logs were signed. The pilot in command did his usual walk-around, I think. I didn’t see him, but he’s thorough. The only thing… well, there was a slight delay at the gate because of a catering truck, but that’s routine. No maintenance write-ups, no weird smells, no unusual vibrations during taxi. It was just a normal day until it wasn’t.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add that we haven’t covered?
A: I just… I want to make sure it’s clear that the crew handled it as well as they could. The pilot in command made the right call turning back. The cabin crew, we did our jobs. I know there’s going to be a lot of scrutiny on the door plug, on Boeing, on the FAA, on the whole certification process. And I get that. But from where I was standing, the aircraft itself performed. The structure held, the engines didn’t fail, the emergency systems worked. I just hope they figure out why that plug came loose. Because if it can happen on a MAX 9, it could happen on a MAX 8, or any other variant. I’ve flown both. I trust the LEAP engines, I trust the airframe, but… you know, you don’t expect a piece of the fuselage to just vanish. Anyway, that’s all I’ve got.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Jenkins. We’ll review this statement and may follow up with additional questions.
A: Yeah, of course. I’m here to help. Just… let me know if you need anything else.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND OVERSIGHT REPORT
DOCKET NO. FAA-2024-0112
DATE: March 15, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service (AIR)
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO NTSB SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-24-01 AND AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE COMPLIANCE ASSESSMENT
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA055; Incident Date: January 5, 2024

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Preliminary Safety Recommendation A-24-01, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, operated by a Part 121 air carrier. The referenced incident occurred on January 5, 2024, during climb through approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) following departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The aircraft executed a safe return to the departure aerodrome with no fatalities or serious injuries reported. The primary regulatory instruments addressed herein include Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-02-09, issued under 14 CFR Part 39, and the applicable certification basis established under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart B. This correspondence further addresses compliance obligations pertaining to the structural integrity requirements codified in Section 25.571 of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations, as well as the continued airworthiness directives governing the CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engine installation and associated fuselage pressure boundary components.

2. BACKGROUND
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) maintains statutory authority under 49 U.S.C. § 44701 et seq. to prescribe minimum standards for the design, manufacture, and operation of civil aircraft. The Boeing 737 MAX 9 was originally type-certificated under 14 CFR Part 25, with a certification basis that incorporated Amendment 25-123. The structural design requirements for transport category airplanes mandate rigorous damage-tolerance and fatigue evaluation protocols, specifically as delineated in Section 25.571. This regulation requires that the structure be evaluated to ensure that catastrophic failure is avoided under repeated loads of variable magnitude, and that residual strength requirements are met following assumed initial flaws or discrete source damage.

The subject aircraft configuration incorporates a mid-cabin exit door plug, which is not a standard passenger door but rather a structural closure panel installed in lieu of an operable emergency exit to accommodate specific cabin layouts. The installation and retention of this plug are governed by the approved type design data, including engineering drawings, structural repair manuals, and the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness (ICA). The propulsion system, comprising the CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines, is certified under 14 CFR Part 33 and integrated into the airframe per 14 CFR 25.901 and 25.903. While the LEAP-1B powerplant installation is not directly implicated in the door plug separation event, the Agency’s oversight framework requires holistic evaluation of all major structural and propulsion interfaces during continued airworthiness assessments.

Historically, the Agency has issued multiple ADs addressing structural fastener retention, manufacturing quality control, and supplier oversight for the 737 MAX family, including AD 2023-15-08 and AD 2023-20-11. These directives mandated enhanced inspection protocols and revised torque verification procedures for critical fuselage fasteners. The installation of the mid-cabin exit door plug was originally evaluated under the baseline type certificate; however, subsequent cabin reconfigurations for certain operators were approved via supplemental type certificate (STC) processes, which introduced additional structural interfaces requiring rigorous compliance with 14 CFR 25.783 regarding fuselage doors, exits, and emergency egress provisions. The Federal Aviation Administration’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (FS) have initiated a comprehensive review of the type certificate holder’s quality management system, supplier delegation authorities, and production acceptance procedures to determine systemic compliance with 14 CFR 21.137 and 14 CFR 21.143.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A thorough regulatory analysis of the incident data, manufacturing records, and operator maintenance logs reveals significant deficiencies in the execution of approved assembly procedures and the subsequent verification of structural fastener installation. The type certificate holder’s production quality assurance program failed to detect the omission of critical retention hardware during final assembly, indicating a breakdown in the mandatory inspection and sign-off protocols required under 14 CFR 21.137(b). Furthermore, the operator’s maintenance program, as approved under 14 CFR 121.344, did not include specific recurring inspection requirements for the mid-cabin exit door plug retention system, as the component was classified as a non-operational structural closure rather than an active emergency egress device.

The Agency’s oversight actions have included the immediate issuance of an emergency AD, the temporary suspension of certain production line operations, and the deployment of Principal Manufacturing Inspectors (PMIs) to conduct unannounced audits of the manufacturer’s supplier network. Preliminary findings confirm that the door plug separation was precipitated by inadequate torque application and the absence of secondary retention verification during the manufacturing phase. This condition represents a material deviation from the damage-tolerance assumptions established under Section 25.571, which presumes that all primary structural fasteners are installed per approved engineering data and that any single fastener failure will not result in catastrophic structural compromise.

A critical gap identified within the current regulatory framework pertains to the classification and ongoing airworthiness monitoring of non-standard fuselage modifications, including door plug installations. The existing certification basis does not explicitly mandate recurring structural inspections for closure panels that are not part of the original baseline type design. Additionally, the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) do not address the operational implications of door plug retention anomalies, as such components are not intended for in-flight operation or dispatch with known deficiencies. The Agency recognizes that the current oversight model, which relies heavily on delegated authority and manufacturer self-certification, requires enhanced surveillance mechanisms to ensure compliance with Section 25.571 and 14 CFR 21.137. The Federal Aviation Administration is currently evaluating the necessity of revising the type certification basis to incorporate mandatory periodic inspections for all fuselage pressure boundary modifications, regardless of operational status.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified deficiencies and in accordance with NTSB Safety Recommendation A-24-01, the Agency mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Immediate Structural Verification: All operators of Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft shall complete a one-time detailed inspection of the mid-cabin exit door plug retention system, including torque verification of all primary and secondary fasteners, within 72 hours of AD 2024-02-09 effective date. Inspection results shall be documented and submitted to the FAA via the Safety Assurance System (SAS) portal within 10 calendar days.

b. Revised Maintenance Program Integration: The type certificate holder shall submit a revised Instructions for Continued Airworthiness (ICA) package to the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) within 60 days, incorporating recurring inspection intervals for door plug retention hardware. The proposed inspection program shall be developed in accordance with Section 25.571 damage-tolerance principles and shall include non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols for fastener hole elongation and panel deformation.

c. Quality Management System Overhaul: The manufacturer shall implement a mandatory dual-verification protocol for all critical structural fastener installations, requiring independent sign-off by both production personnel and quality assurance inspectors. This protocol shall be audited by the FAA’s Principal Manufacturing Inspector (PMI) within 90 days, with compliance verified against 14 CFR 21.137 and 14 CFR 21.143.

d. Regulatory Framework Enhancement: The Agency will initiate a rulemaking action under 14 CFR Part 21 to establish explicit certification requirements for non-operational fuselage closure panels, including mandatory fatigue and damage-tolerance evaluations. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 180 days, with public comment period and final rule issuance targeted for completion within 12 months.

e. Continued Operational Safety (COS) Monitoring: The Federal Aviation Administration will establish a quarterly review schedule for all 737 MAX series operators, focusing on maintenance program adherence, supplier quality metrics, and structural integrity reporting. Operators shall submit semi-annual compliance reports detailing inspection findings, corrective actions, and MMEL utilization trends. The Agency reserves the right to conduct unannounced ramp inspections and maintenance facility audits to verify ongoing compliance with 14 CFR 121.344 and 14 CFR 121.368.

The Agency acknowledges the critical importance of maintaining public confidence in the civil aviation system and reaffirms its commitment to rigorous regulatory oversight, transparent safety communication, and continuous improvement of the airworthiness certification framework. All referenced actions shall be executed in strict accordance with applicable Federal Aviation Regulations, and failure to comply within the prescribed timelines may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR Part 13.

HEADLINE: Mid-Air Door Plug Failure Forces Emergency Landing of Boeing 737 MAX 9, Prompting Federal Grounding

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, National Aviation Desk
DATELINE: PORTLAND, Ore. —

A Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. airline made an emergency return to Portland International Airport on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, after a mid-cabin door plug tore away from the fuselage during climb, triggering a rapid decompression event. All 177 passengers and six crew members survived the harrowing incident, though several sustained minor injuries from the sudden pressure drop and airborne debris.

The aircraft was climbing through approximately 16,000 feet after departing from the Pacific Northwest when the left mid-exit door plug—a reinforced structural panel installed in place of an optional emergency exit—detached from the airframe. The explosive decompression instantly deployed overhead oxygen masks, scattered personal items throughout the cabin, and forced the flight crew to initiate an emergency descent. The jet touched down safely less than 30 minutes after takeoff, with emergency medical teams meeting the aircraft on the tarmac.

“The National Transportation Safety Board has dispatched a go-team to Portland to lead the investigation into this serious incident,” said NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy during a Saturday press briefing. “Our priority is securing the wreckage, interviewing the crew, and determining exactly how and why this door plug failed.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) swiftly issued an emergency airworthiness directive, temporarily grounding all 171 Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft in the United States for immediate inspections. “We are working closely with the manufacturer and the operator to ensure every affected aircraft meets the highest safety standards before returning to service,” an FAA spokesperson said. The airline’s chief operations officer added, “Our flight crew’s training and quick decision-making prevented a tragedy. We are providing full support to our passengers and cooperating completely with investigators.”

The aircraft involved is part of the 737 MAX family, a narrow-body jetline that has undergone extensive regulatory scrutiny since its initial introduction. Unlike the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which typically features standard emergency exits, the MAX 9 variant allows airlines to configure additional mid-cabin exits or seal them with factory-installed door plugs. These plugs are engineered to withstand repeated cabin pressurization cycles but require precise manufacturing alignment and fastener installation. The flight was powered by CFM International LEAP engine turbofans, a high-bypass design developed in partnership with GE Aviation that delivers the thrust and fuel efficiency required for modern short- to medium-haul routes.

Aviation safety analysts are focusing heavily on the structural integrity and maintenance protocols surrounding the door plug assembly. “This incident immediately raises questions about compliance with Section 25.571, the Federal Aviation Regulation governing damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of aircraft structures,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor at a leading technical university. “If fasteners were missing, improperly torqued, or if the plug wasn’t aligned correctly during final assembly, the cyclic pressurization could cause a catastrophic failure.” Industry experts also point to maintenance guidance documents like AC 120-16G, which outlines air carrier maintenance programs and inspection intervals. “While the advisory circular provides a framework for routine checks, it relies heavily on manufacturer documentation and technician diligence,” Chen noted. “Any deviation in the assembly line or post-delivery modification could bypass critical quality controls.”

For those on board, the experience was sudden and terrifying. “One second we were climbing normally, and the next, there was a deafening bang,” said passenger David Lin, who was seated three rows from the breach. “The air rushed out, my ears popped painfully, and oxygen masks dropped everywhere. People were screaming, but the flight attendants immediately took control. I just held my daughter’s hand and prayed.” Lin’s wife, Sarah, who was waiting at the arrival gate, described the agonizing wait. “When the flight tracker showed an emergency return, my heart stopped. I didn’t know if they were safe until I saw them walking off the jet bridge. We’re just grateful to be together.”

The 737 MAX series has faced intense public and regulatory scrutiny following two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019, which led to a global grounding and sweeping software and training reforms. Since returning to commercial service, the fleet has maintained a strong safety record, making Friday’s incident a significant setback for the manufacturer and the broader aviation industry. The MAX 9, in particular, has been widely adopted by U.S. carriers for its extended range and passenger capacity. While door plug failures are exceedingly rare, aviation historians note that similar pressurization-related incidents in the 1980s and 1990s prompted major overhauls in fuselage inspection protocols and manufacturing quality assurance.

The NTSB investigation is now in its critical early phase. Investigators have recovered the detached door plug from a residential neighborhood near the flight path and are examining it for manufacturing defects, fastener anomalies, or signs of improper installation. The Captain and first officer are undergoing standard post-incident interviews and medical evaluations, with preliminary data from the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder already secured. Meanwhile, the FAA continues to oversee mandatory inspections across the grounded MAX 9 fleet, with airlines reporting varying levels of compliance. “We are not speculating on the root cause until the physical evidence and data recorders are fully analyzed,” Homendy emphasized. “But we will not rest until we understand exactly what happened and ensure it never happens again.” As the aviation community braces for the findings, passengers and industry leaders alike are watching closely, hoping the investigation will reinforce the rigorous safety standards that keep commercial air travel among the safest modes of transportation.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Operator’s Chief Engineering and Maintenance Safety Division, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative hearing regarding the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9. Our organization operates a large, modern narrowbody fleet and maintains a comprehensive Safety Management System (SMS) aligned with international best practices and domestic regulatory requirements. As the operator of the accident aircraft, we have full access to maintenance records, flight operations data, crew debriefings, and post-event inspection findings. This document outlines our technical position, synthesizes docket evidence, and provides an expert assessment of the contributing factors that culminated in the mid-exit door plug (MEP) separation.

The scope of this submission encompasses three primary domains: (1) a factual reconstruction of the maintenance and operational timeline leading to the event, (2) a technical evaluation of structural retention, quality assurance protocols, and human factors in maintenance execution, and (3) a forward-looking framework for corrective actions and systemic safety improvements. While the investigation remains ongoing, our analysis is grounded in verified maintenance logs, flight data recorder (FDR) parameters, cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts, and engineering stress modeling. We acknowledge the inherent complexity of modern aircraft certification, supply chain integration, and maintenance execution. However, our position is clear: the event was not the result of an inherent airframe design deficiency, but rather a breakdown in maintenance quality control, documentation verification, and procedural adherence during a critical structural reinstallation. This submission advocates for enhanced oversight, standardized torque verification, and industry-wide alignment on critical fastener management to prevent recurrence.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft departed a Pacific Northwest hub on a scheduled domestic flight. During the initial climb phase, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage, resulting in a rapid decompression event. The aircraft was equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines, manufactured under license by General Electric Aviation (GEA), and operated within normal performance envelopes throughout the flight. The flight crew, led by the Captain, immediately recognized the decompression, initiated emergency descent procedures, donned oxygen masks, and executed the applicable Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) checklist. The aircraft returned to the departure airport without further incident, and all occupants evacuated safely.

Docket materials submitted to the NTSB provide a comprehensive maintenance history for the accident aircraft. Exhibit M-14 (Maintenance Work Order Log) indicates that the left MEP was removed approximately 14 days prior to the event for cabin reconfiguration work. The plug was subsequently reinstalled by a third-party maintenance provider under the Operator’s approved maintenance program. Exhibit M-17 (Quality Control Sign-Off Records) reveals that four critical retention bolts were not properly torqued to specification, and the required independent verification step was either bypassed or inadequately documented. Exhibit F-03 (FDR Data Stream) confirms a normal climb profile with no abnormal vibration, yaw, or roll parameters preceding the event. At 16,000 feet, cabin pressure differential reached approximately 8.3 psi, consistent with standard pressurization schedules. The sudden loss of structural retention at this differential caused immediate plug ejection.

The Captain’s actions, as documented in CVR Exhibit C-09 and post-flight debriefing transcripts, were exemplary. The flight deck crew maintained positive aircraft control, communicated effectively with air traffic control, and managed passenger safety protocols in accordance with standard operating procedures. The successful outcome underscores the effectiveness of crew resource management and emergency training. However, the event also highlights systemic vulnerabilities in maintenance execution, particularly regarding critical structural fastener management, documentation traceability, and quality assurance oversight.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The technical assessment of this event centers on three interrelated domains: structural load path integrity, maintenance quality assurance, and human factors in maintenance execution. Engineering analysis of the MEP retention system indicates that the door plug is designed to withstand maximum differential pressure loads, aerodynamic shear, and fatigue cycles under normal operating conditions. The retention bolts are engineered to specific torque values to ensure proper clamp load distribution across the plug-to-fuselage interface. When torque specifications are not met, preload is insufficient, leading to micro-movement, fretting, and eventual fastener disengagement under cyclic pressurization loads.

Docket Exhibit E-22 (OEM Stress Analysis Report) confirms that the MEP retention system is structurally sound when installed per approved procedures. Finite element modeling demonstrates that at 16,000 feet, the pressure differential generates a net outward force of approximately 1,800 pounds on the plug. Properly torqued retention bolts distribute this load across the fuselage frame and plug flange. However, when bolts are under-torqued or missing, the load path is compromised, and the remaining fasteners experience exponential stress concentration. This aligns with the physical evidence recovered from the accident site, which showed clean bolt hole deformation and absence of fatigue cracking, indicating a sudden overload rather than progressive structural failure.

Maintenance quality assurance protocols are the primary defense against such failures. The Operator’s approved maintenance program, developed in accordance with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulations and industry guidance, mandates dual verification for all critical structural fasteners. Advisory Circular 120-16G (AC 120-16G) emphasizes continuous airworthiness, requiring operators to implement robust quality control systems, standardized work instructions, and independent verification steps for safety-critical tasks. In this case, the maintenance provider failed to adhere to these requirements. Exhibit Q-05 (Internal Audit Findings) reveals that the work order lacked a completed torque verification checklist, and the digital maintenance tracking system did not flag the missing sign-off. This represents a breakdown in both procedural compliance and system-level oversight.

Human factors further compound the issue. Maintenance technicians operate under time pressures, shift transitions, and varying levels of experience. The absence of a standardized, tool-assisted torque verification process increases reliance on manual documentation and memory. Industry best practices, as outlined in SAE ARP4754A and FAA guidance, advocate for digital work tracking, automated torque logging, and mandatory independent inspection for critical structural components. The Operator’s fleet includes both the Boeing 737 MAX 9 and the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which share common maintenance philosophies but differ in certain structural configurations. Cross-fleet procedural alignment is essential to prevent configuration-specific errors. Our analysis indicates that the MEP installation procedure was not adequately differentiated in the maintenance manual, leading to potential confusion during reinstallation.

Operational data further supports this assessment. FDR parameters show no abnormal engine performance, flight control anomalies, or structural vibrations prior to the event. The LEAP-1B engines, produced by General Electric Aviation, operated within normal limits, and engine health monitoring systems reported no anomalies. This confirms that the event was isolated to the fuselage retention system and not influenced by propulsion or flight control interactions. The rapid decompression at 16,000 feet is consistent with a sudden loss of structural integrity rather than a gradual leak or seal failure.

In comparison with industry standards, the Operator’s maintenance program meets or exceeds baseline requirements. However, the event exposes a critical gap in execution fidelity. The FAA’s oversight framework relies heavily on operator self-auditing and delegated authority. While this model promotes efficiency, it requires rigorous internal quality assurance to function effectively. AC 120-16G explicitly states that operators must maintain a proactive safety culture, implement continuous monitoring, and address systemic deficiencies before they manifest as incidents. Our technical assessment concludes that the failure to enforce torque verification, coupled with inadequate documentation control, directly contributed to the plug separation.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the available evidence, engineering analysis, and operational data, the Operator’s position is that the January 5, 2024, event was primarily caused by a breakdown in maintenance quality assurance and procedural adherence during the reinstallation of the left mid-exit door plug. The absence of properly torqued retention bolts, combined with inadequate independent verification and documentation control, compromised the structural load path and led to sudden plug ejection at normal cabin pressure differentials. This was not a design flaw, nor was it attributable to operational misuse or environmental factors. The aircraft’s systems, including the LEAP-1B propulsion units and flight control architecture, functioned as intended.

The flight crew’s response, particularly the actions of the Captain, was exemplary and directly contributed to the safe outcome. Adherence to emergency procedures, effective communication, and disciplined aircraft control prevented escalation and ensured passenger safety. This underscores the value of rigorous training and standardized emergency protocols.

We recommend the following systemic improvements:
- Implementation of mandatory, tool-assisted torque verification with digital logging for all critical structural fasteners.
- Standardization of maintenance procedures across fleet variants to eliminate configuration-specific ambiguities.
- Enhanced quality assurance audits with independent oversight for high-risk maintenance tasks.
- Industry-wide collaboration to develop standardized door plug installation and verification protocols.
- Strengthened regulatory alignment between operators, OEMs, and the FAA to ensure continuous airworthiness monitoring and proactive risk mitigation.

The Operator acknowledges its responsibility in maintaining the highest standards of safety and airworthiness. We are committed to transparency, continuous improvement, and collaboration with the NTSB, the FAA, and industry stakeholders to prevent recurrence.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to this event, the Operator has implemented immediate and comprehensive corrective actions across its maintenance and operations divisions. Within 48 hours of the incident, we initiated a fleet-wide inspection of all mid-exit door plugs, utilizing calibrated torque wrenches and independent verification protocols. All findings were documented, and any deviations were corrected prior to return to service. We have also suspended third-party maintenance providers pending a full quality assurance review and have transitioned critical structural work to in-house certified technicians.

Procedural updates have been integrated into our maintenance manuals, including mandatory dual-signoff requirements, digital work order tracking, and automated torque verification alerts. Our SMS has been enhanced to include real-time anomaly reporting, predictive maintenance analytics, and cross-departmental safety reviews. Training programs have been revised to emphasize human factors, procedural compliance, and configuration-specific maintenance practices. Additionally, we have established a joint working group with OEM engineering teams to review door plug installation procedures and develop standardized verification checklists.

Looking forward, the Operator proposes the following industry-wide improvements:
- Development of a centralized, FAA-approved digital maintenance tracking platform that integrates torque verification, quality assurance sign-offs, and audit trails.
- Mandatory independent inspection for all critical structural fasteners, with automated compliance reporting to regulatory authorities.
- Standardization of door plug installation procedures across all 737 MAX variants, with clear differentiation in maintenance documentation.
- Enhanced collaboration between operators, General Electric Aviation, and airframe manufacturers to integrate engine health monitoring with structural integrity tracking.
- Regulatory updates to AC 120-16G to mandate real-time quality assurance monitoring and automated compliance verification for high-risk maintenance tasks.

The Operator remains fully committed to aviation safety, continuous improvement, and transparent collaboration with the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration, and industry partners. We believe that by addressing systemic vulnerabilities, enhancing procedural fidelity, and leveraging digital verification technologies, the aviation community can prevent similar events and maintain the highest standards of airworthiness. Our corrective actions are already yielding measurable improvements in maintenance compliance, quality assurance performance, and safety culture maturity. We stand ready to support ongoing investigations, share data, and contribute to the development of industry-wide safety enhancements.

TO: Fleet Maintenance Directors, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance Auditors, Engineering Support Staff
FROM: Director, Airworthiness & Structural Engineering / Maintenance Quality Assurance
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: URGENT QUALITY ALERT – Mid-Exit Door Plug Fastener Verification & Torque Compliance (B737 MAX Fleet)
REF: QA-2024-0087, WO-STR-4492, OEM SB 737-53A1285, FAA AD 2024-02-51 (Preliminary)

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate verification of all mid-cabin exit door plug installations across our Boeing 737 MAX fleet. The directive establishes mandatory inspection protocols, torque verification procedures, and documentation requirements following the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event. Compliance is non-negotiable and must be completed prior to any aircraft release to service.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier experienced an in-flight separation of the left mid-exit door plug during climb through approximately 16,000 feet. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport with no fatalities. Preliminary industry data indicates missing fasteners and improper retention hardware at the plug-to-fuselage interface. While our fleet primarily operates the Boeing 737 MAX 8 configuration, the door plug architecture, retention methodology, and manufacturing processes are identical across the MAX 8 and MAX 9 variants. 

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive requiring immediate inspection of all affected aircraft. Our internal structural integrity program, aligned with Section 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure), requires proactive verification of all secondary retention systems and load-path continuity. Additionally, per AC 120-16G (Air Carrier Maintenance Programs), our maintenance program must incorporate immediate corrective actions when fleet-wide anomalies are identified. This alert ensures our operations remain fully compliant with both regulatory mandates and OEM engineering standards.

DETAILS:
The following technical and procedural directives apply to all B737 MAX aircraft in our inventory, regardless of current maintenance status or location:

1. Scope of Inspection:
   - All left and right mid-cabin exit door plugs (Part No. 65-73892-XX series)
   - Associated stop fittings, guide tracks, and retention bolts
   - Torque verification of all 12 primary and 4 secondary fasteners per plug
   - Visual inspection for witness marks, paint cracking, or sealant displacement

2. Inspection Procedure:
   - Reference Work Order WO-STR-4492, Rev. 3, for step-by-step access and removal of interior trim panels.
   - Use calibrated torque wrenches (calibration valid within 30 days) to verify all fasteners at 185 ± 10 in-lbs.
   - Document torque values on Form QA-STR-09 (Fastener Verification Log).
   - If any fastener is found loose, missing, or improperly torqued, DO NOT release the aircraft. Initiate Nonconformance Report NCR-2024-0112 and contact Structural Engineering immediately.
   - Verify that all safety wire and cotter pins are installed per OEM standard practice.

3. Documentation & Traceability:
   - All inspections must be logged in the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS) under Task Code 53-11-00-200.
   - Attach digital photographs of each plug interface (minimum 4 angles per side) to the work package.
   - Sign-off requires dual authorization: one Level 3 Airframe Mechanic and one Quality Assurance Inspector.

4. Cross-Fleet & Operational Considerations:
   - While this alert is airframe-specific, ensure concurrent engine maintenance is not delayed. GE Aviation has issued Service Bulletin LEAP-1B-SB-72-0144 regarding compressor blade inspection intervals. Coordinate with Powerplant Engineering to ensure LEAP-1B maintenance schedules remain compliant.
   - Flight Operations has been briefed. Each Captain has been instructed to report any abnormal cabin pressure fluctuations, unusual airflow noises, or trim panel vibrations immediately via the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL).

ACTION REQUIRED:
All responsible parties must execute the following within the specified timeframes:

1. Line Maintenance Supervisors (Deadline: 24 hours from receipt):
   - Pull all active work orders for B737 MAX aircraft.
   - Assign qualified personnel to complete door plug inspections per WO-STR-4492.
   - Ensure all required tooling (calibrated torque wrenches, borescopes, inspection mirrors) is staged at each maintenance base.

2. Quality Assurance Auditors (Deadline: 48 hours from receipt):
   - Conduct random spot-checks on 20% of completed inspections.
   - Verify MTS entries, photographic evidence, and dual sign-offs.
   - Submit compliance summary to the Director of Airworthiness by 1700 local time on January 14, 2024.

3. Engineering Support Staff (Deadline: Ongoing):
   - Monitor OEM communications and FAA updates.
   - Update the Maintenance Program Manual (MPM) Chapter 53 to reflect permanent inspection intervals if required.
   - Coordinate with GE technical reps to ensure no conflicting maintenance windows impact aircraft availability.

4. Training & Compliance (Deadline: 72 hours from receipt):
   - All line mechanics must complete the 30-minute e-learning module “MAX Door Plug Retention & Torque Verification” (Course ID: STR-2024-004).
   - Supervisors must verify 100% completion before authorizing personnel to perform inspections.

Failure to comply with this Quality Alert will result in immediate grounding of the affected aircraft and disciplinary review per Company Policy 8.4.2 (Airworthiness Compliance). All questions or technical discrepancies must be routed to the Structural Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or via the internal maintenance portal.

This alert supersedes all prior guidance regarding mid-exit door plug maintenance. Maintain strict adherence to documented procedures. Safety and airworthiness remain our highest priority.

SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:15 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft operated by a major U.S. carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during initial climb. The incident occurred at an altitude of approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level following departure from an airport in the Pacific Northwest. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident; there were no reported fatalities, and all occupants were accounted for upon landing.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the left mid-cabin exit door plug separated from the fuselage structure during the climb phase. Initial data recovered from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) are currently undergoing readout and validation. Early telemetry suggests a sudden cabin pressure differential coincident with the structural separation. The pilot in command (PIC) reported an immediate loud noise, followed by rapid decompression and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Crew resource management protocols were initiated, and the flight crew established communication with air traffic control to coordinate an expedited return.

Witness accounts from passengers and cabin crew, collected during initial interviews, describe a sudden explosive sound and localized airflow disruption in the left mid-cabin area. Several individuals reported minor injuries consistent with rapid decompression, including ear discomfort and superficial abrasions; all were evaluated by emergency medical personnel upon arrival. Weather conditions at the time of the event were reported as visual meteorological conditions (VMC) with light winds, minimal cloud cover, and no significant convective activity in the immediate vicinity. Meteorological data does not currently indicate that atmospheric conditions contributed to the event.

Preliminary examination of the recovered door plug and surrounding fuselage structure, conducted at a secure NTSB facility, revealed that the separation occurred along the plug-to-fuselage interface. Initial visual inspection suggests potential anomalies in the retention hardware and surrounding panel alignment, though detailed metallurgical and structural analyses are required to confirm these observations. The aircraft was equipped with LEAP-1B turbofan engines manufactured by General Electric Aviation (GEA); preliminary engine data indicates normal operational parameters throughout the flight, with no evidence of uncontained failure or foreign object damage. Maintenance records are being reviewed to determine compliance with applicable airworthiness directives and manufacturer service bulletins.

Regulatory and operational frameworks relevant to this investigation include 14 CFR 25.571 (Part 25.571), which addresses damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of metallic structure, and Advisory Circular (AC) 120-16G, which provides guidance on air carrier maintenance programs. Initial review of the operator’s maintenance documentation suggests that recent inspections were conducted in accordance with established schedules, though the completeness and execution of specific fastener torque procedures remain under evaluation. The Federal Aviation Administration (the FAA) has been notified and is coordinating with the NTSB on airworthiness directives and fleet-wide inspection protocols. It should be noted that these preliminary observations are subject to revision as additional data is collected and analyzed.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations Group is reviewing flight crew training, standard operating procedures, and air traffic control communications. The Structures Group is leading the examination of the fuselage, door plug assembly, and surrounding airframe components. The Systems Group is analyzing the pressurization system, flight control interfaces, and warning/alerting systems. The Maintenance Records Group is compiling and verifying all relevant maintenance logs, work orders, and component tracking documentation. The Human Performance Group is conducting interviews with flight crew, cabin crew, maintenance personnel, and passengers to establish a comprehensive operational timeline.

Parties to the investigation include representatives from the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, the pilot union, the flight attendant union, and the FAA. All parties have been briefed on their roles, responsibilities, and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding investigative materials. Evidence secured to date includes the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, recovered door plug fragments, fuselage panel sections, maintenance records, and digital maintenance tracking logs. All physical evidence has been cataloged, photographed, and stored in a controlled environment to preserve chain of custody.

Planned examinations include non-destructive testing of the door plug retention hardware, microscopic analysis of fastener threads and surrounding material, computational modeling of pressurization loads, and review of manufacturing and assembly documentation. The NTSB is also coordinating with international counterparts to review similar fleet configurations, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8 (MAX 8), to identify any common design or maintenance considerations. All examinations will be conducted in accordance with established NTSB protocols, and findings will be documented in technical reports subject to peer review.

NEXT STEPS
The investigation will proceed with a structured sequence of technical evaluations, data analysis, and stakeholder interviews. Immediate priorities include completion of the FDR and CVR readouts, detailed structural analysis of the door plug and fuselage interface, and comprehensive review of the operator’s maintenance and quality assurance programs. The NTSB will continue to coordinate with the FAA regarding fleet safety measures, including potential airworthiness directives and enhanced inspection requirements. Additional witness interviews will be conducted, and maintenance personnel involved in recent aircraft servicing will be formally questioned under established investigative procedures.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated within 30 days, pending completion of initial data validation and structural examinations. Subsequent updates will be issued as significant findings emerge, with a formal public hearing scheduled if warranted by the complexity of the technical evidence. All investigative activities will remain focused on fact-finding, and no conclusions regarding probable cause or contributing factors will be issued until the full investigation is complete. The NTSB remains committed to transparency, safety, and the rigorous application of scientific and engineering principles throughout this process.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:11 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a rapid decompression event occurred during the climb phase of a scheduled passenger flight. The event transpired at a pressure altitude of 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 14 nautical miles (NM) northeast of Portland International Airport (KPDX), Multnomah County, Oregon. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a filed route to Ontario International Airport (KONT), San Bernardino County, California. The geographic coordinates of the event location were approximately 45°38'12"N, 122°31'45"W. The incident occurred during daylight hours, with the sun positioned at an azimuth of 235° and an elevation of 12° above the horizon.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, bearing United States registration N704AL. The aircraft was manufactured by The Boeing Company, Renton, Washington, and was operated by a major U.S. scheduled air carrier under the authority of a Part 121 operating certificate. The aircraft was configured for 178 passenger seats in a two-class layout, with a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 194,700 pounds. The aircraft was equipped with a mid-cabin exit door plug configuration on both the left and right sides of the fuselage, installed in lieu of standard Type III emergency exit doors, in accordance with the operator's approved cabin configuration and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) type certificate data sheet.

1.3 Nature of the Flight
The flight was conducted under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, governing scheduled air carrier operations. The flight was dispatched as a revenue passenger service, operating under a standard instrument flight plan with an estimated en route time of 2 hours and 15 minutes. The flight crew had completed all required preflight duties, including weight and balance calculations, fuel planning, and aircraft exterior inspection, in compliance with 14 CFR 121.593 and 121.601. The aircraft departed runway 10L at KPDX at 17:07:42 PST, with an initial climb heading of 102° magnetic. The event occurred during the initial climb segment, prior to reaching the assigned cruise altitude of 35,000 feet MSL.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot Qualifications and Certificates
The flight crew consisted of a Captain and a First Officer, both holding valid Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airman certificates and medical certificates. The Captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 2847193, with airplane multiengine land (AMEL) and Boeing 737 type ratings. The Captain's first-class medical certificate was issued on November 12, 2023, with no limitations or waivers. The Captain's total flight time was recorded as 10,247 hours, with 4,892 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The First Officer held an ATP certificate, certificate number 3105842, with AMEL and Boeing 737 type ratings, and a first-class medical certificate issued on December 3, 2023. The First Officer's total flight time was 3,614 hours, with 1,108 hours in the Boeing 737 series. Both pilots met the age, experience, and certification requirements stipulated in 14 CFR 121.433 and 121.437.

2.2 Recent Flight Experience and Training
The Captain's most recent line check was completed on October 18, 2023, with a satisfactory evaluation. The Captain's most recent recurrent training and proficiency check were conducted in a Level D full-flight simulator on September 5, 2023, covering normal, abnormal, and emergency procedures, including rapid decompression and emergency descent protocols. The Captain had flown 142 hours in the preceding 90 days and 38 hours in the preceding 30 days, in compliance with 14 CFR 121.439. The First Officer completed recurrent training on August 22, 2023, and a line check on November 2, 2023. The First Officer had accumulated 118 hours in the preceding 90 days and 29 hours in the preceding 30 days. Both crew members had completed the operator's mandatory winter operations and high-altitude emergency procedures training modules within the preceding 12 months. Duty time records indicated the crew was within the limits prescribed by 14 CFR 117.11 and 117.15 at the time of the event.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufacturer serial number 44450, line number 7892. The aircraft was delivered to the operator on October 14, 2023. At the time of the event, the airframe had accumulated 1,204.6 total flight hours and 812 total flight cycles. The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B28 turbofan engines, serial numbers 890112 (left) and 890115 (right). The left engine had accumulated 1,198.2 hours and 809 cycles, while the right engine had accumulated 1,201.4 hours and 811 cycles. The aircraft's maximum operating altitude was certified at 41,000 feet MSL, and the maximum operating Mach number (MMO) was 0.82. The aircraft's pressurization system was designed to maintain a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet at a cruise altitude of 41,000 feet, with a maximum differential pressure of 9.1 psi.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft's maintenance records were reviewed and found to be current and compliant with the operator's approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) under 14 CFR 121.369. The most recent heavy maintenance check was a 4C inspection completed on December 1, 2023, at 1,102.3 hours. The aircraft was subject to Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2023-24-08, which required inspection of certain fuselage fasteners and door plug retention hardware. Compliance with the AD was documented on December 15, 2023, with no discrepancies noted. The aircraft's maintenance tracking system indicated that the left mid-exit door plug had been installed during final assembly at the Boeing Renton facility. The installation work order, reference number RW-88421, was signed off on September 28, 2023. No deferred maintenance items (MEL/CDL) were active at the time of departure. The aircraft's logbook contained 14 routine maintenance entries in the 30 days preceding the event, all of which were closed with appropriate sign-offs.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The aircraft's environmental control system (ECS) utilized bleed air from the engine high-pressure compressor stages to regulate cabin pressure and temperature. The pressurization controller, part number 65-12345-1, was installed and functioning within normal parameters prior to the event. The left mid-exit door plug was a structural component designed to seal the fuselage cutout where a standard emergency exit door would otherwise be installed. The plug was retained by four primary retention bolts, two upper guide tracks, and two lower guide tracks, with a secondary latch mechanism. The plug's sealing system consisted of a continuous elastomeric gasket and a pressure-equalization vent. The aircraft's flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were installed in accordance with 14 CFR 121.343 and 121.359. The aircraft's structural design incorporated commonality with the BOEING 737-8, sharing identical wing geometry, empennage configuration, and primary flight control system architecture. The LEAP engine series utilized a dual-channel full authority digital engine control (FADEC) system, which recorded normal engine parameters throughout the climb phase.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Conditions
At the time of the event, a high-pressure system was centered over the Pacific Northwest, resulting in stable atmospheric conditions. Surface observations indicated a temperature of 4°C, a dew point of -2°C, and a relative humidity of 62%. The freezing level was reported at 6,500 feet MSL. Upper-air sounding data from the nearest National Weather Service (NWS) rawinsonde station indicated a temperature lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 feet up to 18,000 feet, with light wind shear and no significant convective activity. The tropopause was located at approximately 32,000 feet MSL.

4.2 Aviation Weather Reports
The aviation routine weather report (METAR) for KPDX, issued at 17:00 PST, read: KPDX 051700Z 18005KT 10SM FEW040 04/M02 A3012 RMK AO2 SLP201 T00441022. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KPDX, valid from 17:00 to 23:00 PST, indicated: TAF KPDX 051700Z 0517/0617 18006KT P6SM FEW045 FM052100 20008KT P6SM SCT050. No significant weather phenomena, including turbulence, icing, or thunderstorms, were forecast or reported along the departure route. The aircraft's onboard weather radar was in standby mode during the climb, as no precipitation was detected.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports
No pilot weather reports (PIREPs) were filed along the departure route prior to the event. The flight crew did not report any abnormal weather conditions, turbulence, or visibility restrictions during the initial climb. The aircraft's air data computer (ADC) recorded an indicated airspeed of 285 knots, a true airspeed of 312 knots, and a vertical speed of 2,400 feet per minute at the time of the decompression event. The outside air temperature (OAT) at 16,000 feet was recorded as -14°C, consistent with standard atmospheric models.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The primary wreckage consisted of the left mid-exit door plug, which was recovered intact from a residential property located approximately 1.2 NM from the event coordinates. The plug was located in a backyard, resting on a concrete patio, with no evidence of post-impact fire or secondary fragmentation. The fuselage remained structurally intact, with the aircraft returning to KPDX and landing safely on runway 10L at 17:38 PST. No ground impact marks were observed along the flight path. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and local law enforcement secured the recovery site, and the component was transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination.

5.2 Fuselage and Door Plug Examination
Examination of the recovered door plug revealed that all four primary retention bolts were absent from their respective mounting locations. The bolt holes in the fuselage frame exhibited clean, unthreaded surfaces with no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or plastic deformation. The upper and lower guide tracks remained attached to the fuselage, with the plug's corresponding guide rails showing minor abrasion consistent with in-flight separation. The elastomeric gasket was partially torn, with approximately 60% of the sealing perimeter remaining attached to the plug. The pressure-equalization vent was intact but showed signs of rapid depressurization stress. The fuselage cutout exhibited no structural damage beyond the bolt hole locations. The door plug's internal stiffeners and load-bearing ribs were undamaged, indicating that the separation occurred prior to significant aerodynamic loading.

5.3 Cabin Interior and Systems Assessment
The cabin interior sustained localized damage consistent with rapid decompression. The left-side overhead bins in rows 12 through 15 were displaced, with several panels detached and scattered across the aisle. The passenger oxygen masks deployed automatically, and the cabin altitude warning system activated at 14,200 feet cabin altitude. The flight deck recorded a cabin differential pressure drop from 7.8 psi to 0.2 psi within 1.4 seconds. The emergency descent was initiated by the Captain, with the aircraft descending to 10,000 feet MSL at a rate of 4,500 feet per minute. The aircraft's pressurization controller was subsequently isolated, and the outflow valve was manually closed. Post-flight inspection of the ECS components revealed no anomalies in the bleed air valves, pack controllers, or cabin pressure sensors. The CVR captured the decompression event, including the activation of the cabin altitude warning, crew coordination, and passenger announcements. The FDR recorded normal engine parameters, flight control inputs, and system statuses throughout the event and subsequent return to base.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Maintenance and Quality Assurance Policies
The operator's maintenance program is governed by an FAA-approved CAMP, which includes scheduled inspections, component tracking, and quality assurance audits. The operator's engineering department utilizes a computerized maintenance management system (CMMS) to track work orders, compliance with airworthiness directives, and component life limits. The operator's quality assurance program conducts random audits of maintenance records, tool calibration, and technician training compliance. The operator's standard operating procedures (SOPs) for door plug installation require torque verification, safety wire installation, and a dual-inspection sign-off by a certified airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanic and an inspection authorization (IA) holder. The operator's internal audit logs indicated that the left mid-exit door plug installation was reviewed during the December 1, 2023, 4C inspection, with no discrepancies documented. The operator's safety management system (SMS) includes a voluntary reporting program for maintenance irregularities, which recorded zero reports related to door plug retention hardware in the 12 months preceding the event.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Similar Events
