A review of NTSB and FAA incident databases identified three previous occurrences involving mid-cabin door plug separation or retention hardware anomalies on Boeing 737 MAX series aircraft. The first occurred on March 14, 2022, involving a BOEING 737-8, where a loose guide track bolt was identified during a routine preflight inspection. The second occurred on August 9, 2023, involving a 737 MAX 9, where a missing safety wire on a door plug retention bolt was discovered during a post-maintenance check. The third occurred on November 22, 2023, involving a 737 MAX 8, where a cabin pressure fluctuation was attributed to a partially unseated door plug gasket. In all three cases, the anomalies were identified prior to flight, and corrective actions were implemented in accordance with manufacturer service bulletins. The FAA issued a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) on December 18, 2023, recommending enhanced inspection protocols for door plug retention hardware on 737 MAX aircraft. The operator incorporated the SAIB recommendations into its maintenance program on January 2, 2024, three days prior to the event.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Advisory Guidance
The design, certification, and operation of the aircraft are governed by multiple provisions of 14 CFR. The structural integrity of the door plug and fuselage cutout is regulated under 14 CFR 25.365 (Pressurized cabin loads) and 14 CFR 25.807 (Emergency exits). The installation and maintenance of door plug retention hardware must comply with 14 CFR 43.13 (Performance rules) and 14 CFR 121.369 (Maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations). The operator's compliance with airworthiness directives is mandated under 14 CFR 39.3 (General). The FAA's Advisory Circular (AC) 25.807-1 provides guidance on emergency exit design and door plug configuration, while AC 120-79 outlines recommended practices for maintenance tracking and quality assurance. The manufacturer's Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) Chapter 52-10 specifies torque values, inspection intervals, and safety wire procedures for door plug retention bolts. The operator's approved minimum equipment list (MEL) does not permit dispatch with a missing or unsecured door plug. The FAA's oversight of the operator's maintenance program is conducted under 14 CFR 121.373, which requires continuous surveillance and periodic audits. All regulatory references cited herein are current as of the date of the event.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the Structures and Materials Group, in coordination with the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) Group, regarding the rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly, adjacent fuselage structure, fastener hardware, guide track components, and associated flight recorder data. The objective is to establish factual findings regarding the physical condition of the structural components, material properties, fastener installation parameters, and recorded flight parameters at the time of the event.

The primary items examined were recovered at the operator's maintenance facility in Portland, Oregon, and subsequently transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., for detailed analysis. Examination dates spanned January 10 through January 18, 2024. Items cataloged and analyzed include:
- Left mid-exit door plug assembly (Boeing P/N 65-12345-678, S/N 987654321)
- Upper and lower guide track assemblies (P/N 65-12345-680/681)
- Stop fitting hardware and roller bearing assemblies
- Recovered fastener set (NAS6605-14, NAS6605-16, and MS20002C5)
- Adjacent fuselage skin and stringer sections (Station 1016 to 1042)
- Solid-state FDR (P/N 2100-4000-00, S/N FDR-8821) and Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data files
- Maintenance logbooks, torque verification records, and final assembly documentation

All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, ASTM E112-13 (grain size), AMS 2680 (eddy current inspection), and SAE ARP 4102 (fastener installation standards). Photographic documentation was captured using calibrated macro-lens systems and referenced as Figures 1 through 24 in the accompanying exhibit log.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a derivative of the 737 MAX family certified under 14 CFR Part 25. The left mid-exit door plug is a structural closure panel installed in lieu of an operational Type III emergency exit for high-density cabin configurations. The plug assembly consists of a 2024-T3 aluminum alloy outer skin, 7075-T6 aluminum internal doublers, a perimeter frame, and a roller-bearing guide track system that interfaces with fuselage-mounted stop fittings. The assembly is secured to the fuselage structure via a series of high-strength titanium alloy fasteners (Ti-6Al-4V, per AMS 4928) torqued to manufacturer-specified values of 180–200 in-lbs (15.0–16.7 ft-lbs) with a ±5% tolerance.

The certification basis for the door plug and surrounding fuselage structure complies with Section 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure), which mandates residual strength analysis, crack propagation modeling, and fail-safe design criteria for pressurized fuselage components. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued Type Certificate Data Sheet A16WE, Revision 12, which incorporates the plug design into the overall airworthiness certification. The subject unit was manufactured at the Boeing Renton facility, installed during final assembly in August 2023, and accumulated 1,247 flight hours and 862 pressurization cycles prior to the event.

For comparative baseline purposes, engineering data from the Boeing 737 MAX 8 configuration was reviewed. While the MAX 8 utilizes a different exit configuration, the pressurization system architecture, cabin differential pressure limits, and structural load paths share common design parameters. The aircraft is powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B engines (S/N L1B-998877 and L1B-998878), manufactured under the oversight of GE Aviation. Engine health monitoring data, including N1, N2, EGT, and fuel flow parameters, were extracted from the QAR to correlate powerplant performance with the decompression timeline.

Maintenance records indicate the door plug was removed and reinstalled during a cabin reconfiguration modification in October 2023. Torque verification logs were reviewed per Advisory Circular 120-16G, which outlines air carrier maintenance program documentation standards and operational reporting requirements. The records show a final torque sign-off, though subsequent physical examination revealed discrepancies in fastener retention.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered door plug assembly revealed complete separation from the fuselage structure. The outer skin exhibited localized plastic deformation along the forward and aft edges, with maximum deflection measuring 14.2 mm (0.56 in) relative to the nominal contour. The perimeter frame showed evidence of guide track disengagement, with the upper roller bearing assembly displaced 38.5 mm (1.52 in) aft of its designed travel limit. The lower guide track mounting brackets exhibited shear deformation consistent with sudden lateral loading.

Fastener hole inspection was conducted using calibrated bore gauges and optical profilometry. Of the 12 primary retention fasteners, 4 were absent from the assembly. The remaining 8 fastener holes exhibited elongation ranging from 0.15 mm to 0.42 mm (0.006–0.017 in) beyond nominal diameter, indicating bearing load transfer prior to separation. Recovered fasteners were subjected to torque verification using a calibrated digital torque wrench (Fluke 754, ±1% accuracy). Measured residual torque values ranged from 0 to 45 in-lbs, significantly below the specified 180–200 in-lbs installation requirement. Thread engagement analysis revealed no evidence of cross-threading or galling.

Non-destructive inspection (NDI) was performed per AMS 2680 and ASTM E1444-16. Eddy current scanning of the 2024-T3 aluminum skin and 7075-T6 doublers revealed no subsurface cracking, corrosion, or fatigue initiation sites. Ultrasonic thickness measurements confirmed skin thickness within manufacturing tolerances (1.27–1.32 mm / 0.050–0.052 in). Hardness testing (Rockwell B scale) yielded values of 82–85 HRB, consistent with T3 temper specifications.

Metallurgical analysis of the recovered fasteners and adjacent structural material was conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Chemical composition of the Ti-6Al-4V fasteners conformed to AMS 4928, with aluminum at 6.12 wt%, vanadium at 4.08 wt%, and iron at 0.18 wt%. Fracture surface examination of the fastener shanks revealed ductile overload characteristics, with microvoid coalescence and dimpled rupture morphology. No fatigue striations, intergranular cracking, or hydrogen embrittlement features were observed. The aluminum skin fracture edges exhibited shear lip formation consistent with rapid tensile failure under positive pressure differential loading.

Material testing included tensile coupon extraction from non-critical skin regions. Yield strength measured at 345 MPa (50 ksi), ultimate tensile strength at 455 MPa (66 ksi), and elongation at 14.2%, all within AMS 4037 specifications for 2024-T3. The structural doublers exhibited similar mechanical properties, confirming no material degradation or heat-affected zone anomalies.

Photographic documentation (Figures 1–24) captures the following:
- Figure 1: Overall view of recovered door plug, forward edge facing camera
- Figure 5: Close-up of upper guide track disengagement and roller bearing displacement
- Figure 9: Fastener hole elongation measurements with calibrated scale
- Figure 14: SEM micrograph of fastener fracture surface showing ductile overload
- Figure 18: EDS elemental mapping confirming Ti-6Al-4V composition
- Figure 22: Adjacent fuselage stringer deformation and skin buckling

All measurements were recorded using NIST-traceable instrumentation. Environmental conditions during examination were maintained at 21°C ±2°C and 45% ±5% relative humidity per laboratory standards.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder and QAR parameters were extracted, decoded, and synchronized using NTSB-standardized software (FDR Analysis Suite v4.2.1). The data stream includes 1,024 parameters sampled at 1 Hz, with high-frequency engine and flight control parameters sampled at 8 Hz. The following parameters were analyzed for the event timeline:

- Cabin Differential Pressure (ΔP): Normal climb profile shows ΔP increasing linearly from 0 PSI at sea level to 7.8 PSI at 16,000 ft MSL. At 14:22:18 UTC, ΔP registered 7.6 PSI. At 14:22:19 UTC, ΔP dropped to 0.4 PSI within 0.8 seconds, indicating instantaneous loss of cabin pressure integrity.
- Cabin Altitude: Prior to event, cabin altitude tracked at 6,200 ft MSL. Post-event, cabin altitude spiked to 15,800 ft MSL within 2.1 seconds, consistent with rapid decompression at 16,000 ft MSL ambient pressure.
- Vertical Speed (V/S): Normal climb rate averaged 2,450 fpm. At 14:22:19 UTC, V/S registered -3,800 fpm, indicating immediate descent initiation.
- Indicated Airspeed (IAS): Stabilized at 285 knots prior to event. Post-decompression, IAS fluctuated between 260–290 knots during emergency descent, remaining within structural and aerodynamic limits.
- Engine Parameters (LEAP-1B, S/N L1B-998877): N1 remained at 84.2%, EGT at 612°C, fuel flow at 2,850 kg/hr. No compressor surge, flameout, or thrust asymmetry was recorded. GE Aviation engine health monitoring algorithms confirmed nominal performance throughout the event.
- Flight Control Inputs: The Captain initiated a 10° nose-down pitch input at 14:22:21 UTC, followed by speed brake deployment at 14:22:24 UTC. Autopilot disengagement was recorded at 14:22:20 UTC. Manual control inputs remained within certified envelope limits.

Timeline reconstruction from synchronized FDR, QAR, and CVR data establishes the following sequence:
- 14:18:05 UTC: Takeoff roll, rotation at 142 knots
- 14:20:12 UTC: Gear retraction, flap transition to 5°
- 14:21:45 UTC: Passing 12,000 ft MSL, ΔP at 5.9 PSI
- 14:22:18 UTC: Passing 16,000 ft MSL, ΔP at 7.6 PSI
- 14:22:19 UTC: Rapid decompression event, ΔP drop to 0.4 PSI, cabin altitude spike
- 14:22:20 UTC: Autopilot disconnect, manual control assumed
- 14:22:21 UTC: Emergency descent initiated, pitch -10°
- 14:24:05 UTC: Level off at 10,000 ft MSL, ΔP stabilized at 3.2 PSI
- 14:38:12 UTC: Landing at departure airport, touchdown at 138 knots

Comparison with normal operational parameters for the Boeing 737 MAX 9 confirms that the aircraft was operating within certified climb profiles, pressurization schedules, and structural load limits prior to the event. The rapid ΔP decay rate of 9.0 PSI/sec exceeds the maximum allowable structural relief valve discharge rate of 2.1 PSI/sec, confirming an uncontrolled structural breach rather than a regulated pressure relief event.

Engine data from the LEAP-1B powerplant, manufactured under GE Aviation quality control standards, showed no anomalies. Fuel flow, turbine inlet temperature, and rotor speed parameters remained within the engine operating envelope defined in the Aircraft Flight Manual. The absence of thrust fluctuations or compressor stall signatures indicates the decompression did not induce aerodynamic or powerplant instability.

Maintenance logbook entries, reviewed per AC 120-16G documentation standards, show the door plug was signed off as "serviceable" following the October 2023 modification. However, torque verification records lack secondary inspector cross-check signatures, and the final assembly checklist does not include a post-installation pressure decay test. The FAA oversight documentation confirms the modification was approved under a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) framework, with compliance to Section 25.571 damage-tolerance requirements verified during certification testing.

5. SUMMARY

The following technical findings are established based on physical examination, material testing, and flight data analysis:

1. The left mid-exit door plug assembly (P/N 65-12345-678, S/N 987654321) separated from the fuselage structure during climb at approximately 16,000 ft MSL.
2. Four primary retention fasteners were absent from the assembly. The remaining eight fastener holes exhibited elongation up to 0.42 mm, indicating bearing load transfer prior to separation.
3. Residual torque measurements on recovered fasteners ranged from 0 to 45 in-lbs, below the manufacturer-specified installation requirement of 180–200 in-lbs.
4. Metallurgical and chemical analysis of the 2024-T3 aluminum skin, 7075-T6 doublers, and Ti-6Al-4V fasteners confirmed compliance with AMS and ASTM material specifications. No fatigue cracking, corrosion, or material degradation was identified.
5. Fracture surface examination revealed ductile overload characteristics consistent with rapid tensile failure under positive cabin pressure differential loading.
6. FDR and QAR data recorded a cabin differential pressure drop from 7.6 PSI to 0.4 PSI within 0.8 seconds, with cabin altitude increasing from 6,200 ft to 15,800 ft MSL within 2.1 seconds.
7. Engine parameters for the LEAP-1B powerplant (S/N L1B-998877) remained within normal operating limits throughout the event, with no evidence of thrust asymmetry, compressor surge, or performance degradation.
8. Flight control inputs initiated by the flight deck commander resulted in an emergency descent profile consistent with manufacturer emergency procedures. Vertical speed, airspeed, and pitch inputs remained within certified structural and aerodynamic envelopes.
9. The aircraft's pressurization system and structural load paths operated within design parameters prior to the event. The rapid pressure decay rate exceeded the maximum allowable relief valve discharge capacity, confirming an uncontrolled structural breach.
10. Maintenance documentation reviewed per Advisory Circular 120-16G standards indicates the door plug was installed and signed off as serviceable, though torque verification records lack secondary cross-check documentation and post-installation pressure decay testing.

All findings are factual and derived from direct examination, calibrated testing, and recorded flight data. No determination of probable cause is made in this report.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER ELIAS VANCE
Date: January 9, 2024
Time: 10:15 PST
Location: NTSB Field Office, Renton, Washington
Interviewer: Senior Investigator David Chen, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety

Q: Good morning, Mr. Vance. Thank you for coming in. For the record, please state your full name, current position, and your role on the flight in question.

A: Yeah, good morning. My name is Elias Vance. I’m a First Officer with the airline, currently based out of Seattle. On January 5th, I was the right-seat pilot on Flight 1282. So, I was the monitoring pilot during the climb, handling radios, checklists, that sort of thing.

Q: And you were operating a Boeing 737 MAX 9 that day?

A: That’s correct. The MAX 9. I’ve been flying the MAX series for about four years now, mostly the MAX 8, but I transitioned to the 9 about eight months ago. The flight deck is virtually identical, so the workflow is... it’s second nature at this point.

Q: Walk me through the departure. What time did you push back, and what were conditions like?

A: We pushed back from Gate C14 at Sea-Tac at... I want to say 16:42 local. Maybe 16:45. It was a typical winter evening, overcast, light drizzle, but nothing unusual. We got clearance, started engines, ran the before-takeoff checklist. Everything was green. We taxied out, held short of 16L, and got our takeoff clearance around 16:58. The Captain was flying, so I was on comms and monitoring.

Q: Describe the takeoff and initial climb.

A: Normal. V1, rotate, positive rate, gear up. We were on the RNAV departure, climbing through 10,000 feet, transitioning to Center. The aircraft was tracking perfectly. I remember looking at the FMC, checking our step-climb altitudes, maybe making a quick comment to the Captain about the headwind component. It was... routine. Honestly, the kind of flight you don’t really think about until it’s over.

Q: At what point did the event occur?

A: We were passing through... I think it was 16,000 feet. Maybe 16,200. I was just about to call out the altitude when there was this... this incredibly loud bang. Not like an engine backfire. It was sharper. Like a structural crack, or a heavy object hitting the fuselage from the outside. The whole airframe shuddered. I felt it through the seat, my shoulder harness pulled tight, and the yoke actually jumped in my hands. The Captain immediately said, “My aircraft,” and I said, “Your aircraft.” I grabbed the thrust levers just in case, but the engines were fine.

Q: What happened immediately after the impact?

A: The cabin pressure warning went off. The master caution, the altitude alert, all of it. The Captain called for the rapid decompression checklist. I started reading it, but... honestly, the wind noise was deafening. It sounded like a freight train was running through the cabin. I looked over my left shoulder, out the side window, and... I could see it. The left mid-exit door plug was just gone. Completely separated. There was a gaping hole where it used to be, and I could see the sky, the clouds, just... rushing past. It was surreal. I mean, you train for it, you run the sims, but actually seeing daylight through the fuselage at 16,000 feet... it’s not something you ever really process in real time.

Q: How did the crew manage the situation?

A: We followed the QRH. Masks dropped, obviously. I confirmed the Captain had his on, I put mine on, established comms with the cabin. The flight attendants were already on the interphone, reporting... well, they said it was loud, cold, and there was debris in the aisle. We initiated an emergency descent. I called out the altitudes, monitored the vertical speed, kept an eye on the airspeed. We leveled off at 10,000, then requested vectors back to Sea-Tac. The Captain handled the flying beautifully. I was just managing the radios, running the checklists, keeping the timeline straight.

Q: Can you give me a rough timeline from the event to landing?

A: Yeah. The bang was at... let’s say 17:04. We were back on the ground at Sea-Tac around 17:18. So, maybe fourteen minutes total. We declared Mayday immediately, got priority handling, and the approach was straightforward. We landed on 16R, vacated, and taxied to the gate. Emergency vehicles were already staged.

Q: Were there any injuries or passenger issues?

A: No fatalities, thankfully. A few minor injuries from the initial jolt, some people bumped their heads or shoulders. The flight attendants did an incredible job keeping everyone calm. Once we leveled off and the wind noise dropped, the cabin settled. We had oxygen masks deployed, obviously, and the temperature dropped pretty fast, but the crew got blankets out, checked everyone, and reported all accounted for.

Q: Let’s talk about the aircraft configuration. You mentioned you’ve flown the MAX 8 extensively. How does the MAX 9 differ in terms of the door plug area?

A: Right. The MAX 8 doesn’t have that mid-cabin exit plug. It’s got actual, functional doors. The MAX 9, depending on the airline’s seating configuration, sometimes uses a plug to fill an unused exit. It’s not a door you open; it’s a structural panel that’s bolted and sealed in place. When we did our type rating, we went over the differences, but... I mean, it’s supposed to be a permanent fixture. You don’t interact with it. It’s not like a regular door with a handle and a slide. It’s just... part of the fuselage. So when it came off, it was... unexpected, to say the least.

Q: From a structural standpoint, what are your thoughts on how a component like that could separate in flight?

A: I’m not a stress engineer, obviously, but we all know the airframe is certified under 14 CFR 25.571. That’s the damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation regulation. The whole point is that the structure should be able to handle... you know, cracks, stress cycles, pressurization loads, without catastrophic failure. If a plug separates at 16,000 feet, that’s a pressurization differential issue, or maybe a fastener retention problem. I don’t know the exact mechanics, but it’s supposed to be fail-safe. The fact that it didn’t... well, that’s what you guys are looking into.

Q: Did you notice any anomalies with the engines or other systems during the event?

A: No. The engines were completely normal. We’re running the CFM LEAP-1Bs, which are a joint program with GE Aviation. They performed flawlessly. No surges, no EGT spikes, no vibration warnings. I was watching the engine parameters the whole time, and they stayed right in the green. The issue was purely airframe-related. The flight controls responded normally, the hydraulics were fine, the electrical system didn’t flicker. It was just... the plug.

Q: After landing, what was your immediate next step?

A: We shut down the engines, ran the post-landing checklist, and coordinated with ground ops. I stayed on the flight deck while the Captain went out to talk to the ramp crew and the NTSB team that arrived pretty quickly. I secured the logbook, downloaded the QAR data, and made sure the maintenance write-up was accurate. I noted the door plug separation, the rapid decompression, the checklist completion, and the safe return. Then I went through the standard post-incident debrief with the crew.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add that we haven’t covered?

A: Just... the professionalism of the crew. Everyone did exactly what they were trained to do. No panic, no hesitation. The passengers were understandably shaken, but they followed instructions. And honestly, the aircraft itself... it handled the situation well. The MAX 9 is a solid airplane. This wasn’t a design flaw in the flight controls or the engines. It was a specific component failure. I know you’ll get to the bottom of it. I just hope... I hope the findings lead to better inspection protocols, or whatever’s needed. Because flying is safe, but when something like this happens, it shakes your confidence a little. You trust the hardware. You trust the maintenance. And when a piece of the fuselage just... leaves... it makes you question a lot of things.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Vance. We’ll be in touch if we need any clarification.

A: Yeah, of course. I’m available. Just let me know.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND COMPLIANCE DIVISION
MEMORANDUM

DATE: March 15, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service (AIR)
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO NTSB SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-24-012 AND COMPLIANCE WITH EMERGENCY AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE 2024-03-11
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA045; Docket No. FAA-2024-0123; 14 CFR Parts 21, 25, and 121

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This memorandum constitutes the formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Preliminary Safety Recommendation A-24-012, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the in-flight structural failure event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The referenced event, designated NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA045, occurred during initial climb through approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) following departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The subject aircraft experienced a rapid decompression event precipitated by the separation of the left mid-cabin exit door plug from the aft fuselage structure. This correspondence addresses compliance with Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-03-11, issued under Docket No. FAA-2024-0123, and outlines the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) regulatory oversight posture pursuant to 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart J, and 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737 MAX 9 is certified under Type Certificate No. A16WE, with production authorized under Production Certificate No. 700NM. The airframe design incorporates optional mid-cabin exit door plugs in lieu of functional emergency exits, a configuration governed by 14 CFR 25.783 (Fuselage doors) and 14 CFR 25.365 (Pressurized compartment loads). The structural integrity of such plug installations is predicated upon strict adherence to the approved type design, manufacturing quality assurance protocols, and post-production inspection regimes as mandated by 14 CFR 21.137 and 14 CFR 21.143. While the subject configuration was incorporated under the original type certificate, any subsequent cabin reconfiguration or exit modification would require evaluation under 14 CFR 21.113 and issuance of a supplemental type certificate (STC), subject to equivalent safety standards. Historically, the FAA has issued multiple airworthiness directives addressing structural fatigue and fastener retention on the 737 MAX series, most notably AD 2021-18-09, which addressed fuselage skin cracking and required enhanced non-destructive inspection (NDI) intervals.

The operational context of the January 5, 2024, event falls under the purview of 14 CFR Part 121, specifically 14 CFR 121.344 (Emergency equipment) and 14 CFR 121.373 (Maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations). The aircraft was operated under a Part 121 certificate, with the flight crew executing emergency descent procedures in accordance with the approved Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) and Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for rapid decompression. The propulsion system, comprising two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines manufactured by GE Aviation, operated within certified parameters throughout the event sequence. Post-flight data analysis confirms that the General Electric Aviation (GEA) powerplants maintained nominal thrust response and did not contribute to the structural failure. The Captain, acting as Pilot in Command (PIC), initiated an immediate emergency descent and diversion in strict compliance with 14 CFR 121.557 (Emergency authority) and 14 CFR 91.13 (Careless or reckless operation), ensuring the safe return of the aircraft and all occupants.

Prior to this incident, the NTSB had issued Safety Recommendation A-23-041, urging enhanced oversight of delegated production inspection representatives (DPIRs) and stricter validation of supplier quality management systems (QMS) for critical structural components. The FAA’s response to that recommendation was documented in FAA Response Letter AIR-2023-089, which outlined incremental enhancements to Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) oversight. However, the January 2024 event has exposed systemic deficiencies in the execution of those oversight mechanisms, particularly concerning the installation and retention of non-structural fuselage plugs.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive regulatory review of the operator’s maintenance records, the manufacturer’s production documentation, and the FAA’s oversight activities reveals the following compliance status and analytical findings:

a. Manufacturer Compliance and Quality Assurance Deficiencies: The Boeing Company’s production records indicate that the subject door plug was installed during final assembly at the Renton facility. Forensic examination of the recovered hardware revealed the absence of four critical retention bolts, with corresponding fastener holes exhibiting no evidence of torque application or safety wire installation. This constitutes a direct violation of the approved type design and a failure to comply with 14 CFR 21.137 (Quality system) and 14 CFR 21.143 (Inspection). The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) has determined that the manufacturer’s internal quality control processes failed to detect the missing fasteners prior to delivery, indicating a breakdown in the delegated inspection authority framework.

b. Operator Maintenance and Airworthiness Compliance: The operating carrier’s maintenance program, approved under 14 CFR 121.373, did not mandate specific post-delivery verification of door plug fastener retention. While the operator’s continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) complied with the letter of the approved maintenance manual, the absence of a targeted inspection protocol for optional exit door plugs represents a regulatory gap. The FAA’s Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) has confirmed that the operator’s MMEL and QRH procedures for rapid decompression were executed correctly, and no violations of 14 CFR 121.344 or 14 CFR 121.373 were identified in the operational phase.

c. Regulatory Oversight Gaps: The FAA’s oversight of the manufacturer’s ODA unit, as governed by FAA Order 8100.15B and 14 CFR 21.439, relied heavily on self-certification and periodic audit sampling. The January 2024 event demonstrates that the current oversight model is insufficient to detect systemic manufacturing deviations in critical pressure boundary components. Furthermore, the regulatory framework under 14 CFR 25.783 does not explicitly require redundant retention mechanisms or post-installation verification for non-structural door plugs, creating a latent vulnerability in the certification basis. The propulsion systems, including the LEAP-1B engines produced by GE Aviation, were unaffected and operated within all certified envelope parameters, underscoring that the failure was isolated to the airframe manufacturing and quality assurance domain.

d. Human Factors and Crew Resource Management: The Captain’s decision-making and adherence to emergency protocols were exemplary. The flight crew’s execution of the emergency descent, cabin depressurization checklist, and diversion to the nearest suitable airport aligns with 14 CFR 121.557 and Advisory Circular 120-71A. No regulatory deficiencies were identified in crew training or operational procedures.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the findings detailed herein, and in accordance with the FAA’s statutory authority under 49 U.S.C. § 44701 et seq., the following corrective actions, compliance timelines, and oversight measures are hereby mandated:

a. Immediate Corrective Actions: All Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with mid-cabin exit door plugs shall undergo a one-time detailed visual and tactile inspection of all door plug retention fasteners, torque verification, and safety wire installation in accordance with Emergency AD 2024-03-11. Operators must submit inspection results to the FAA via the Safety Assurance System (SAS) within 72 hours of completion. Any discrepancies shall be rectified prior to further flight, with replacement hardware sourced exclusively from FAA-approved suppliers.

b. Regulatory and Certification Revisions: The FAA shall initiate a rulemaking action to amend 14 CFR 25.783 and 14 CFR 25.365 to mandate redundant retention mechanisms and post-installation verification protocols for all non-structural fuselage plugs. Concurrently, the FAA will issue a revised ODA oversight directive requiring enhanced audit frequency, mandatory third-party validation of critical fastener installations, and real-time reporting of manufacturing deviations to the Aircraft Certification Service.

c. Operator Compliance and Maintenance Program Updates: All Part 121 operators shall revise their CAMP to incorporate mandatory post-delivery and periodic inspections of door plug assemblies. The FAA’s Principal Operations Inspector (POI) and PMI shall verify compliance within 30 days. Operators must also update their MMEL and QRH to reflect revised rapid decompression procedures, including enhanced crew coordination protocols for structural failure scenarios.

d. Timeline and Follow-Up Schedule: 
- Phase 1 (0–30 days): Completion of fleet-wide door plug inspections and submission of compliance reports.
- Phase 2 (30–90 days): Implementation of revised CAMP procedures, MMEL updates, and ODA oversight enhancements.
- Phase 3 (90–180 days): Completion of rulemaking notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) publication and public comment period.
- Ongoing: The FAA will conduct quarterly oversight reviews of the manufacturer’s QMS and operator maintenance programs, with findings reported to the NTSB and the Office of the Secretary of Transportation.

e. Interagency Coordination: The FAA will establish a joint task force with the NTSB and the Department of Transportation to monitor compliance, evaluate the efficacy of corrective actions, and assess the need for additional safety recommendations. All correspondence, inspection data, and compliance documentation shall be maintained in Docket No. FAA-2024-0123 and made available for public review pursuant to 14 CFR 11.35.

This memorandum serves as the official regulatory response to NTSB Safety Recommendation A-24-012 and constitutes the FAA’s binding commitment to rectify identified deficiencies in the certification, manufacturing, and operational oversight of the Boeing 737 MAX 9 fleet. The FAA remains committed to upholding the highest standards of aviation safety and ensuring full compliance with all applicable Federal Aviation Regulations.

HEADLINE: Mid-Flight Door Plug Separation Triggers Emergency Landing; All Aboard Survive Rapid Decompression

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, National Aviation Desk
DATELINE: PORTLAND, Ore. —

A commercial airliner carrying 171 passengers and six crew members executed a harrowing emergency landing on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, after a mid-cabin door plug tore away from the fuselage during climbout, triggering a rapid decompression event. The aircraft, operated by a major U.S. carrier, departed from a Pacific Northwest airport and returned safely to its origin with no fatalities, though several passengers sustained minor injuries from the sudden pressure drop and falling debris.

The incident occurred as the jet climbed through approximately 16,000 feet. Witnesses aboard described a deafening bang followed by a violent rush of freezing cabin air, the immediate deployment of oxygen masks, and loose personal items being pulled toward the opening. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent, donned supplemental oxygen, and diverted back to the departure airport, executing a controlled landing within 20 minutes of the structural failure. The rapid decompression—a sudden loss of cabin pressure that can cause hypoxia and disorientation—was contained by the crew’s swift adherence to emergency protocols.

“The safety of our passengers and crew is our absolute priority,” said an airline spokesperson during a brief press briefing. “We are cooperating fully with investigators, providing all necessary support to those on board, and working to reunite passengers with their families.” The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatched a specialized go-team to the scene, with lead investigators confirming that the preliminary focus centers on the structural integrity of the door plug and its attachment hardware. Federal Aviation Administration officials confirmed they have issued an emergency airworthiness directive grounding all similarly configured aircraft pending immediate physical inspections. “We are taking decisive, precautionary action to ensure the traveling public’s confidence in the aviation system,” an FAA administrator stated in a written release.

The aircraft involved is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a stretched variant of the manufacturer’s narrow-body family. While the MAX 9 features additional fuselage length and optional mid-cabin exit doors, it shares core design architecture, flight deck systems, and maintenance procedures with the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which has been in widespread commercial service since its recertification. The jet is powered by twin CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, a joint venture that includes General Electric Aviation, widely recognized for their advanced fuel efficiency and high-bypass thrust capabilities. Airlines operating the MAX series must adhere to stringent maintenance protocols, including guidelines outlined in FAA Advisory Circular AC 120-16G, which establishes rigorous standards for air carrier maintenance programs, component tracking, and structural modification oversight.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the door plug—a factory-installed panel used to seal unused emergency exit openings on certain high-density cabin configurations—may have suffered from improper bolt installation or a manufacturing defect. “Door plugs are not original structural components; they are installed during final assembly to meet specific airline seating layouts,” explained Dr. Elena Rostova, an aerospace engineering professor and former NTSB consultant. “If the retaining bolts were not torqued to specification, or if the guide tracks were misaligned, aerodynamic forces during climb could easily overcome the fasteners. We’ve seen minor seal issues in the past, but a complete separation at altitude is exceptionally rare and points to a potential assembly or quality control lapse.”

For those on board, the event was a sudden plunge into chaos. “One second we were watching the safety video, the next there was a massive crack and the air just vanished,” said passenger David Lin, 34, who was seated three rows from the breach. “Oxygen masks dropped, people were screaming, and my daughter’s tablet flew right out of her hands. The flight attendants were incredible—they kept us calm while the pilots brought us down.” Lin’s wife, Sarah, who was waiting at the arrival gate, described the agonizing hours before confirmation of the safe landing. “When the flight tracker showed an emergency descent, my heart stopped. I just kept praying. To hear they’re all safe is a miracle.”

The incident has reignited scrutiny of the 737 MAX program, which faced a global grounding from 2019 to 2020 following two fatal crashes linked to a flawed flight control system. While those tragedies were attributed to software and sensor issues, Friday’s event highlights renewed concerns over manufacturing quality control and final assembly line oversight. The MAX series has since undergone extensive recertification, with airlines reporting strong operational reliability and improved pilot training standards. However, aviation historians note that rapid decompression events, while uncommon, have occurred in commercial aviation, most notably the 2018 Southwest Airlines Flight 1380, which involved an uncontained engine failure rather than a fuselage breach.

The NTSB has secured the aircraft and begun a meticulous examination of the recovered door plug, surrounding fuselage structure, and maintenance logs. Investigators are interviewing the flight crew, reviewing cockpit voice and flight data recorder information, and coordinating with Boeing’s engineering teams to trace the component’s manufacturing and installation history. The FAA continues to mandate physical inspections of all affected aircraft, with airlines reporting that dozens of jets have been pulled from service for bolt torque checks and structural reviews. “This is a developing investigation,” an NTSB spokesperson noted. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, and we expect preliminary findings within the next 30 days.” Until then, the aviation industry braces for potential operational disruptions as regulators and manufacturers work to restore public trust and ensure the fleet’s structural integrity.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Engineering and Product Safety Division of The Boeing Company, acting in its capacity as the type certificate holder and design authority for the 737 MAX family of aircraft. As the manufacturer, Boeing bears primary responsibility for the structural integrity, certification compliance, and production quality of the airframe delivered to operators. This document outlines our technical position regarding the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event involving a 737 MAX 9, with specific focus on the separation of the left mid-cabin exit door plug during climb.

The scope of this submission encompasses a comprehensive engineering evaluation of the door plug retention architecture, an analysis of the manufacturing and assembly processes that preceded delivery, and an assessment of quality assurance protocols against established aerospace standards. Our objective is to provide the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Federal Aviation Administration with a transparent, evidence-based technical narrative that distinguishes between design certification, production execution, and operational performance. While the investigation remains ongoing, the available docket materials, flight data, and manufacturing records permit a rigorous preliminary engineering assessment. This submission does not seek to minimize the severity of the event; rather, it aims to isolate the precise failure mechanisms, contextualize them within the broader production ecosystem, and articulate actionable pathways to prevent recurrence.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier departed a Pacific Northwest airport on a scheduled domestic flight. During initial climb, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the aircraft experienced a sudden loss of cabin pressure. The flight crew executed established emergency descent and decompression procedures, returning the aircraft to the departure airport without further incident. There were no fatalities, and only minor injuries were reported among passengers and crew.

Review of the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), as documented in NTSB Docket Items 2024-01-05-FDR-01 through 03, confirms that the aircraft was operating within normal flight envelope parameters at the time of the event. Climb thrust settings, airspeed, and vertical speed were consistent with standard departure profiles. Engine performance data, including N1, EGT, and fuel flow for both CFM International LEAP-1B engines, remained stable and within certified limits. No abnormal vibrations, thrust asymmetries, or aerodynamic buffet indications were recorded prior to the decompression event. This operational data effectively rules out propulsion anomalies, flight control excursions, or external aerodynamic loading as contributing factors.

Maintenance and production records, referenced in Docket Items 2024-01-05-MNT-04 and 2024-01-05-PROD-07, indicate that the aircraft was delivered to the operator approximately 14 months prior to the incident. The left mid-cabin exit door plug had not been removed or serviced during the operator’s maintenance cycle. However, the manufacturing traveler log reveals that during final fuselage integration, the door plug retention hardware installation sequence was interrupted, and subsequent verification steps were not completed in accordance with the approved work instructions. Physical examination of the recovered door plug and surrounding fuselage structure, documented in NTSB Preliminary Report Section 3.2, confirms the absence of four critical retention bolts that secure the plug to the fuselage guide tracks and stop fittings.

For contextual reference, the BOEING 737-8 variant utilizes conventional outward-opening passenger doors rather than plug-type configurations, but shares identical structural design philosophy, load path analysis, and certification basis with the MAX 9. The door plug architecture was introduced to accommodate optional high-density seating configurations while maintaining structural continuity and pressurization integrity. The design has undergone extensive static, fatigue, and damage tolerance testing during type certification, and the current event does not reflect a systemic design deficiency. Rather, the factual record points to a localized breakdown in production quality control and hardware verification.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The mid-cabin exit door plug is a structurally integrated panel designed to maintain cabin pressurization loads while providing a flush aerodynamic surface. The retention system consists of upper and lower guide tracks, forward and aft stop fittings, and four primary high-strength retention bolts that prevent vertical and lateral displacement under differential pressure. The design load case assumes a maximum cabin differential pressure of 8.6 psi, with a 1.5x ultimate load factor applied per 14 CFR § 25.365. Finite element analysis (FEA) and full-scale static pressure testing, documented in Boeing Certification Report 737-9-STR-2018-04, demonstrate that the plug assembly, when fully bolted, distributes pressurization loads through the guide tracks into the surrounding fuselage frames and stringers without exceeding allowable stress limits.

The separation event occurred because the four primary retention bolts were not installed during final assembly. Without these fasteners, the plug was retained only by friction and secondary guide track engagement, which are insufficient to resist the upward and outward forces generated by cabin pressurization. At 16,000 feet, the differential pressure reached approximately 6.8 psi, generating an upward resultant force exceeding 12,000 pounds on the plug surface. This load exceeded the frictional and mechanical retention capacity of the unbolted configuration, resulting in disengagement from the guide tracks and subsequent ejection.

From a certification standpoint, the door plug design fully complies with FAA damage tolerance requirements as outlined in 14 CFR § 25.571 and Advisory Circular 25.571-1D. The structure incorporates fail-safe load paths, crack arrest features, and redundant retention geometry to ensure that single-point fastener failures do not result in catastrophic separation. However, damage tolerance analysis assumes that the as-built configuration matches the certified design baseline. The absence of four primary bolts represents a manufacturing deviation that bypasses the intended safety margins. The design itself is not deficient; rather, the production process failed to ensure that the certified configuration was achieved and verified.

A detailed review of the manufacturing traveler and quality assurance records reveals multiple contributing factors. First, the assembly sequence for the door plug requires precise alignment, bolt insertion, torque application, and independent verification. The work instructions specify a two-person verification step for critical fasteners, but the production log indicates that this step was bypassed due to workflow interruptions and shift handover gaps. Second, torque verification documentation was incomplete, and the digital torque wrench data was not cross-referenced with the aircraft configuration management system. Third, final quality inspection relied primarily on visual confirmation and checklist sign-off, without automated hardware presence detection or non-destructive verification of bolt seating.

Human factors and production system complexity also played a role. The door plug installation occurs late in the fuselage integration phase, where schedule pressure, tooling constraints, and multi-disciplinary coordination can introduce procedural drift. The absence of a physical or digital interlock to prevent progression to the next assembly stage without confirmed bolt installation allowed the latent condition to persist through final inspection and delivery. Industry best practices, as defined in SAE ARP4754A and FAA AC 20-115D, emphasize closed-loop configuration management, automated verification, and independent quality audits for critical structural interfaces. The current production process fell short of these standards in this specific instance.

Comparative analysis with other plug-type door installations across the commercial aviation sector confirms that similar retention architectures have operated safely for decades when manufacturing controls are rigorously enforced. The LEAP engine performance data further supports the conclusion that no external dynamic loading or aerodynamic excitation contributed to the failure. The event is best characterized as a manufacturing quality assurance breakdown that resulted in an unbolted structural interface, not a design or operational deficiency.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the available evidence, engineering analysis, and production records, Boeing’s technical position is as follows:

The primary contributing factor to the January 5, 2024, door plug separation was the absence of four critical retention bolts due to a breakdown in the manufacturing assembly and quality verification process. The door plug design, as certified, meets all applicable structural, pressurization, and damage tolerance requirements. The retention architecture is inherently fail-safe when installed per approved work instructions, and the design has been validated through extensive static, fatigue, and ultimate load testing.

Secondary contributing factors include inadequate final inspection redundancy, incomplete torque verification documentation, and the absence of automated hardware presence detection at critical assembly milestones. The production traveler system did not enforce a hard stop to prevent workflow progression without confirmed bolt installation, and quality assurance protocols relied excessively on manual checklist compliance rather than objective, data-driven verification.

We acknowledge that the aviation industry operates under complex supply chain and production rate environments, and that human factors, procedural drift, and system integration challenges can introduce latent risks. However, the responsibility for ensuring that certified designs are accurately translated into production rests with the manufacturer. The event underscores the necessity of strengthening configuration management, enhancing digital traceability, and implementing independent verification layers for critical structural interfaces.

Recommended safety improvements include:
- Implementation of automated bolt presence and torque verification systems integrated with aircraft configuration databases.
- Mandatory independent quality audits for all critical fastener installations, with digital sign-off requirements.
- Revision of assembly work instructions to include physical or digital interlocks that prevent progression without verified hardware installation.
- Enhanced supplier oversight and standardized quality management system (QMS) alignment across all fuselage integration partners.
- Collaboration with the Federal Aviation Administration to update certification guidance for plug-type door retention systems, emphasizing production verification and in-service monitoring.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the event, Boeing has implemented immediate and sustained corrective actions to address the identified deficiencies and prevent recurrence.

Actions already taken:
- Full compliance with FAA Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-09, including support for operator-led 100% inspections of all 737 MAX 9 door plug retention hardware.
- Revision of door plug assembly work instructions to mandate dual-verification torque application, with digital wrench data automatically uploaded to the aircraft configuration management system.
- Implementation of a mandatory quality hold point at the door plug installation stage, requiring independent inspector sign-off before fuselage integration can proceed.
- Comprehensive audit of all active production lines, with corrective action requests (SCARs) issued to address documentation gaps, tool calibration discrepancies, and procedural non-conformances.
- Retraining of all assembly and quality personnel on critical fastener installation protocols, human factors awareness, and stop-work authority procedures.
- Establishment of a cross-functional engineering and production task force to review all plug-type door retention architectures across the MAX family, with findings reported to the FAA and NTSB.

Proposed future improvements:
- Deployment of computer vision and AI-assisted hardware presence detection systems at critical assembly stations, providing real-time verification of bolt installation and torque compliance.
- Integration of digital twin technology to create a continuous, auditable record of structural fastener installation, maintenance, and in-service condition throughout the aircraft lifecycle.
- Development of embedded structural health monitoring sensors for door plug retention interfaces, enabling predictive maintenance and early detection of hardware degradation or loosening.
- Industry-wide collaboration with operators, regulators, and suppliers to standardize plug-type door verification protocols and share best practices for production quality assurance.
- Submission of proposed updates to FAA certification guidance, emphasizing mandatory automated verification, independent quality audits, and enhanced damage tolerance validation for production deviations.

Boeing remains fully committed to transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement in aircraft design, manufacturing, and safety management. The January 5, 2024, event has reinforced the critical importance of aligning production execution with certified design intent. We will continue to work closely with the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration, and our airline partners to implement robust, data-driven safety enhancements that ensure the highest standards of airworthiness and passenger protection.

SUBJECT: URGENT QUALITY ALERT – Mid-Exit Door Plug Fastener Verification & Structural Audit
REF: QA-2024-0087, WO-STR-4492, NTSB Docket Entry #2024-01-05-001

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate verification of all mid-cabin exit door plug installations across the active fleet. The directive establishes mandatory inspection protocols, documentation standards, and corrective action thresholds following the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event. All personnel must comply with the procedures outlined herein to ensure continued airworthiness, maintain regulatory compliance, and preserve operational safety margins.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier experienced an in-flight separation of the left mid-exit door plug during climb through 16,000 feet following departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The aircraft executed a safe return to the departure field with no fatalities. Preliminary telemetry and post-flight inspections indicate missing or improperly torqued retention fasteners at the plug-to-fuselage interface. The NTSB has opened a formal investigation, and this alert serves as our internal operational response pending official findings.

While the event involved a MAX 9 variant, our fleet includes the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which utilizes a structurally similar door plug configuration and identical fastener retention architecture. Historical maintenance records indicate that door plug installations have been subject to multiple work order revisions and vendor-supplied hardware substitutions over the past 36 months. In accordance with AC 120-16G, our continuing airworthiness program must proactively address structural anomalies before they manifest as operational hazards. Furthermore, all structural modifications, repairs, and plug installations must satisfy established damage tolerance requirements to prevent crack propagation, fastener fatigue, and load-path degradation under cyclic pressurization loads.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all scheduled and unscheduled maintenance activities involving the mid-cabin exit door plug area shall adhere to the following protocols:

1. Fastener Verification & Torque Audit
   • Inspect all 12 primary retention bolts (P/N 737-DOOR-RET-04A) and 4 secondary shear pins (P/N 737-DOOR-SHR-02B) at the left and right mid-exit door plug interfaces.
   • Verify torque values against IPC Rev 44, Table 8-12. Acceptable range: 185–210 in-lbs. Any reading below 175 in-lbs requires immediate fastener replacement, hole inspection, and engineering review.
   • Document all torque readings on Form QA-STR-112. Do not rely on previous maintenance sign-offs or historical torque logs.
   • Apply torque in the manufacturer-specified star pattern sequence. Cross-tightening is prohibited.

2. Structural Interface Inspection
   • Perform a detailed visual and borescope inspection of the plug frame, fuselage cutout reinforcement ring, and adjacent longeron stations (STA 420–460).
   • Check for fretting, elongation, witness marks, or sealant displacement indicating prior movement. Any evidence of displacement triggers a Level 2 NDT inspection per WO-NDT-8841.
   • Cross-reference all findings with the aircraft’s structural repair manual (SRM) and ensure compliance with damage tolerance requirements for pressurized fuselage sections.

3. Adjacent Systems Coordination
   • While the primary focus is the door plug, maintenance teams must also verify the structural integrity of adjacent pylon and engine mount interfaces. This includes the LEAP-1B engine attachment points, which share similar high-cycle fatigue environments and fastener retention philosophies.
   • Coordinate with GE Aviation technical representatives regarding recent fastener material bulletins (Ref: GE-ENG-FB-2023-114) to ensure no cross-contamination of torque procedures, thread-locking compounds, or lubricant specifications.
   • Verify that all General Electric Aviation (GEA) supplied hardware meets current revision levels before installation.

4. Crew Reporting & Operational Feedback
   • All flight operations personnel must report any abnormal cabin pressurization indications, unusual airflow noises, or door plug seal discrepancies via the standard post-flight defect log.
   • the Captain or designated pilot-in-command shall initiate an immediate maintenance write-up if any pressurization anomaly occurs during climb or cruise. These reports will be routed directly to the Structural Integrity Task Force for triage within 4 hours.

ACTION REQUIRED:
The following actions are mandatory and time-critical:

1. Line Maintenance Supervisors (Deadline: January 15, 2024, 23:59 UTC)
   • Complete initial torque verification on all active aircraft.
   • Submit completed QA-STR-112 forms to Technical Records via the digital maintenance portal.
   • Ground any aircraft with unresolved fastener discrepancies until Engineering issues a formal airworthiness release.

2. Quality Assurance Division (Deadline: January 18, 2024)
   • Conduct random audits on 20% of completed inspections.
   • Verify that all technicians have reviewed the updated Work Instruction WI-STR-2024-03 prior to performing door plug work.
   • Compile a fleet-wide compliance report for submission to the VP of Maintenance and retain all audit trails for potential regulatory review.

3. Training & Standards Department (Deadline: January 20, 2024)
   • Issue a mandatory 2-hour refresher module on door plug installation, torque sequencing, and fastener tracking.
   • Ensure all Level 3 and Level 4 airframe technicians complete the module and pass the associated knowledge check (Score ≥ 90%).
   • Update the B737-8 and MAX 9 maintenance training curricula to reflect revised DT criteria and fastener handling procedures.

4. Engineering & Reliability (Ongoing)
   • Monitor fleet data for pressurization cycle trends and correlate with inspection findings.
   • Liaise with OEM technical support to validate long-term fastener retention strategies and evaluate potential design service bulletins.
   • Update the maintenance program per Advisory Circular 120-16G guidelines to incorporate enhanced door plug inspection intervals and mandatory torque verification checkpoints.

Failure to comply with this alert will result in immediate suspension of maintenance privileges and potential regulatory escalation. All documentation generated under this directive will be retained in accordance with FAA recordkeeping standards and may be subject to external review. Direct technical questions to the Structural Integrity Task Force at ext. 4490 or via the internal QA portal.
