SYNOPSIS

On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:25 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft operated by a major U.S. commercial air carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during initial climb. The incident occurred at an altitude of approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level following departure from an airport in the Pacific Northwest. Preliminary information indicates that the left mid-cabin exit door plug separated from the fuselage structure. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident. There were no reported fatalities, and all occupants were accounted for upon landing.

INITIAL FINDINGS

Preliminary factual information has been compiled from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads, air traffic control communications, and initial maintenance documentation. Initial data review indicates that cabin altitude warnings and associated aural alerts were recorded shortly after the reported structural separation. The aircraft’s pressurization system parameters show a rapid pressure differential change consistent with an uncontrolled opening in the aft-mid fuselage section. 

Initial witness accounts from passengers and cabin crew, as collected during post-flight interviews, describe a sudden loud noise followed by rapid decompression, localized airflow, and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Several individuals reported observing a void in the left fuselage where the mid-exit door plug was previously located. These accounts remain preliminary and are subject to corroboration through additional interviews, statement verification, and physical evidence analysis.

Meteorological data obtained from the departure airport and en route weather reporting stations indicate visual meteorological conditions prevailed at the time of the event. Surface winds were light, visibility exceeded 10 statute miles, and no significant convective activity or turbulence was reported along the initial climb path. Weather conditions are not currently considered a contributing factor, though this assessment remains subject to further meteorological review and radar data correlation.

Preliminary damage assessment, based on post-flight photographs and initial walk-around inspections, reveals a complete separation of the left mid-exit door plug assembly. Surrounding fuselage skin, adjacent stringers, and window frames exhibit localized deformation and fastener displacement. The cabin interior in the immediate vicinity shows evidence of rapid decompression effects, including displaced overhead bins and scattered personal items. The aircraft’s primary flight control surfaces, landing gear, and propulsion systems appear intact based on initial visual inspection. Notably, the LEAP engine powerplants, manufactured by General Electric Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines, demonstrated normal operational parameters throughout the flight, with no recorded exceedances or anomalies in engine performance data. Maintenance records indicate that the aircraft was in compliance with applicable airworthiness directives and manufacturer service bulletins at the time of the event. Initial review of operator maintenance logs suggests adherence to standard inspection protocols, including those referenced in FAA Advisory Circular 120-16G regarding maintenance program development and execution. However, a comprehensive audit of all maintenance actions, component installations, and quality assurance documentation is required before any definitive conclusions can be drawn.

INVESTIGATION STATUS

The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The following groups have been formally established and are currently operational: Structures, Systems, Operations, Maintenance Records, Human Performance, and Air Traffic Control. Each group is operating under the direction of an NTSB Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and is following established party protocols.

Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and relevant labor organizations. All parties have been briefed on their responsibilities, including the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding investigative materials and to refrain from public speculation. The NTSB has emphasized that party participation is strictly procedural and does not imply fault or liability.

Physical evidence has been secured and cataloged in accordance with NTSB evidence handling procedures. The separated door plug assembly has been recovered and transported to a secure NTSB facility for detailed forensic examination. Additional debris recovered from the flight path and surrounding areas has been logged and preserved. The FDR and CVR have been successfully downloaded, and preliminary data validation is underway. The aircraft remains grounded at the departure airport under NTSB custody, with access restricted to authorized investigative personnel. Planned examinations include non-destructive testing of the door plug retention hardware, metallurgical analysis of fastener components, and a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s structural repair history. The investigation team will also conduct a detailed review of the operator’s training programs, emergency response procedures, and cabin crew performance during the decompression event.

NEXT STEPS

Investigative activities will proceed in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with an emphasis on systematic data collection, peer review, and technical validation. The Structures group will initiate a detailed dimensional survey of the door plug interface and surrounding fuselage structure. The Systems group will continue to analyze pressurization control logic, sensor data, and warning system functionality. The Operations and Human Performance groups will conduct structured interviews with flight crew, cabin crew, and maintenance personnel, focusing on procedural adherence, situational awareness, and emergency response execution.

A comprehensive review of the aircraft’s manufacturing and assembly records will be conducted in coordination with the manufacturer and relevant regulatory authorities. This review will include an examination of quality control documentation, component traceability, and final assembly verification procedures. The investigation team will also evaluate the applicability and effectiveness of current maintenance guidance, including industry standards and regulatory advisory materials such as AC 120-16G, to determine whether procedural enhancements may be warranted. Additionally, GE Aviation technical representatives will be consulted to verify engine performance data and rule out any secondary system interactions that may have influenced the event sequence.

All findings documented in this preliminary report are subject to revision as additional data is collected, analyzed, and validated. The NTSB will not issue conclusions or probable cause determinations until the investigative process is complete and all technical, operational, and human factors have been thoroughly evaluated. A public hearing may be convened at a later date to facilitate the presentation of factual information and expert testimony.

The next formal update will be issued within 30 days, pending the completion of initial laboratory analyses and the consolidation of group reports. Interim briefings will be provided as warranted by significant investigative developments. The NTSB remains committed to a transparent, methodical, and evidence-based investigation process. All parties and stakeholders are reminded that preliminary information is inherently incomplete and should not be interpreted as indicative of final investigative outcomes.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:24:12 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a rapid decompression event occurred aboard a Boeing 737-9 MAX aircraft during the initial climb phase of flight. The event transpired at an indicated altitude of 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 12.3 nautical miles (NM) northwest of Portland International Airport (KPDX), Oregon. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger route from KPDX to John Wayne Airport (KSNA), Santa Ana, California. Following the structural separation, the flight crew initiated an emergency descent, declared a Mayday, and returned to KPDX, landing safely on Runway 10L at 17:42:08 PST. No fatalities or serious injuries were reported among the 171 passengers and 6 crewmembers on board.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator Identification
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, registered as N704AL, operated by a major U.S. air carrier under 14 CFR Part 121. The aircraft was configured for 178 passengers in a two-class layout with a single-aisle cabin. The flight was designated as a regularly scheduled revenue service. The aircraft type certificate holder is The Boeing Company, and the airframe was manufactured at the Boeing Commercial Airplanes facility in Renton, Washington. The operator held an active Air Carrier Certificate and Operations Specifications authorizing Boeing 737 series aircraft operations, with a designated principal maintenance inspector (PMI) and principal operations inspector (POI) assigned by the Federal Aviation Administration.

1.3 Nature of the Flight
The flight was conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart U, governing domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. The operator maintained an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) and a standard operating procedures (SOP) manual compliant with 14 CFR 121.133. The flight was dispatched under standard Part 121 dispatch release procedures, with all required documentation, weight and balance calculations, and fuel load records completed prior to departure. The planned route utilized standard instrument departure (SID) procedures, with an initial climb to flight level 350 (FL350) via the PDX ONE departure.

1.4 Flight Phase and Event Sequence
The aircraft departed KPDX at 17:11:45 PST. At 17:24:12 PST, while climbing through 16,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed of 285 knots, the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage. The digital flight data recorder (DFDR) recorded a cabin pressure differential decay from 5.2 psi to 0.8 psi within 1.4 seconds. The cabin altitude warning system activated at 10,000 feet cabin altitude, and passenger oxygen masks deployed automatically. The flight crew donned oxygen masks, initiated the emergency descent checklist, and executed a rapid descent to 10,000 feet MSL. The aircraft was vectored by Portland Approach Control for an immediate return and landing.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The captain, age 48, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain’s medical certificate was a first-class, valid through August 2024, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 11,240 hours, with 3,850 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain completed recurrent training and proficiency checks in accordance with 14 CFR 121.433 and 121.441 on October 12, 2023, with satisfactory results in all evaluated maneuvers, including emergency descent, rapid decompression, and abnormal checklist execution. The captain’s training records indicated no deficiencies in pressurization system management or emergency procedure compliance.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The first officer, age 34, held an ATP certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The first officer’s medical certificate was a first-class, valid through December 2024. Total flight time was 4,120 hours, with 1,890 hours in the Boeing 737 series. Recurrent training and line-oriented flight training (LOFT) were completed on November 3, 2023, in compliance with 14 CFR 121.433. The training syllabus included simulated cabin depressurization, emergency descent profiles, and crew resource management (CRM) scenarios. The first officer’s performance evaluations documented consistent adherence to standard callouts and checklist discipline.

2.3 Duty and Rest Compliance
Both flight crewmembers were within the duty period limitations prescribed by 14 CFR Part 117. The captain reported for duty at 14:15 PST, and the first officer reported at 14:30 PST. Both crewmembers had a minimum of 10 consecutive hours of rest prior to the duty period, in accordance with 14 CFR 117.25. Fatigue risk management system (FRMS) data indicated no reported fatigue-related anomalies. Post-incident interviews confirmed both crewmembers were alert, properly rested, and adhered to standard operating procedures during the event. The operator’s scheduling system verified compliance with 14 CFR 117.11 and 117.15 regarding cumulative flight time and duty period extensions.

2.4 Training and Emergency Procedure Proficiency
The operator’s training program, approved under 14 CFR 121.403, required annual simulator sessions covering rapid decompression, emergency descent, and cabin pressure system failures. The flight crew completed their most recent simulator evaluation on October 12, 2023, which included a scenario involving sudden cabin depressurization at 15,000 feet MSL. The evaluation documented proper execution of the emergency descent checklist, timely donning of oxygen masks, and appropriate communication with air traffic control. No deviations from approved procedures were noted in the training records.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufacturer serial number 44442, delivered to the operator on October 15, 2023. At the time of the event, the aircraft had accumulated 145 total flight hours and 145 total flight cycles. The airframe was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B27 turbofan engines. The engine manufacturer, GE Aviation, provided the core engine modules, high-pressure compressor, and turbine sections, while CFM International served as the joint venture entity responsible for final assembly, certification, and field support. The aircraft’s maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) was 194,700 pounds, and the takeoff weight for the accident flight was 168,450 pounds. The center of gravity was calculated at 24.1% MAC, within the approved envelope.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.363. The most recent heavy maintenance check was a 4C inspection completed on December 28, 2023. During this inspection, the left mid-exit door plug (designated as the 2L door plug) was removed for cabin reconfiguration and subsequently reinstalled. Maintenance records indicate that the plug was installed per Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53A1285, Revision 1. Torque values for the 12 primary retention bolts were documented as 1,250 inch-pounds, within the manufacturer’s specified range of 1,200 to 1,300 inch-pounds. No deferred maintenance items (DMIs) were recorded for the door plug assembly or adjacent fuselage structure.

Applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were reviewed. AD 2023-24-08, issued by the Federal Aviation Administration, required inspection of certain fuselage frame splices and door plug retention hardware. The aircraft was in compliance with all applicable ADs, with the most recent inspection logged on January 2, 2024. The operator’s maintenance tracking system verified that all recurring inspections were completed within the prescribed intervals.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The left mid-exit door plug is a non-operational, structurally integrated panel designed to seal an unused emergency exit opening. The plug assembly consists of an aluminum alloy skin, internal stiffeners, four guide tracks, and twelve high-strength steel retention bolts. The plug interfaces with the fuselage skin via a continuous perimeter seal and is retained by stop fittings that engage the guide tracks during pressurization. The cabin pressurization system, controlled by the outflow valve and cabin pressure controller, maintained a differential pressure of approximately 5.2 psi at the time of the event, consistent with a 16,000-foot cabin altitude at 16,000 feet MSL.

The aircraft’s avionics suite included dual flight management computers (FMCs), a digital flight data recorder (DFDR), and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR), all of which were recovered and downloaded. The DFDR recorded a rapid cabin pressure decay from 5.2 psi to 0.8 psi within 1.4 seconds, followed by activation of the cabin altitude warning horn and automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks. The aircraft’s structural design complies with 14 CFR 25.365 (Pressurized cabin loads) and 25.783 (Fuselage doors).

3.4 Engine and Propulsion Systems
The propulsion system consisted of two CFM International LEAP-1B27 engines, each rated at 28,000 pounds of thrust. The engines were manufactured under the joint venture between Safran Aircraft Engines and GE Aviation. Engine health monitoring (EHM) data indicated normal parameters throughout the flight, with no exceedances in exhaust gas temperature (EGT), N1, N2, or vibration levels. The engine control units (ECUs) operated within certified limits, and no fault codes were recorded in the aircraft central maintenance computer (ACMC).

3.5 Type Certificate and Production Oversight
The aircraft was produced under Type Certificate No. T00001SE, issued by the Federal Aviation Administration. The production facility operated under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart G, with quality assurance protocols governing final assembly, component installation, and structural fastener verification. The manufacturer’s production acceptance testing included cabin pressurization cycles, door plug retention load testing, and non-destructive inspection (NDI) of critical structural joints. All production records were reviewed and found to be complete and compliant with approved manufacturing specifications.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Weather Conditions at Time of Event
At the time of the incident, the aircraft was operating in visual meteorological conditions (VMC) with clear skies, light winds, and temperatures well above freezing. The ambient temperature at 16,000 feet MSL was approximately -12°C, with a standard atmospheric lapse rate. No convective activity, turbulence, or icing conditions were reported along the departure route. The aircraft’s pitot-static system and air data computers (ADCs) recorded standard pressure and temperature gradients, with no anomalies that would indicate environmental stress on the airframe.

4.2 METAR and TAF Data
The 17:00 PST METAR for KPDX reported: wind 090° at 6 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, sky clear, temperature 4°C, dew point -2°C, altimeter 30.12 inHg. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KPDX, valid through 18:00 PST, indicated continued VMC with no significant weather changes. En route weather radar and satellite imagery confirmed a stable high-pressure system over the Pacific Northwest, with no frontal boundaries or jet stream disturbances affecting the climb corridor. The aircraft’s onboard weather radar was in standby mode during climb, as no precipitation was detected.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Atmospheric Data
No pilot weather reports (PIREPs) were filed for the departure route or the accident location. The flight crew reported no abnormal weather encounters, turbulence, or lightning strikes prior to or during the decompression event. Atmospheric pressure data from the aircraft’s air data computers (ADCs) indicated a standard pressure gradient, with no anomalous readings that would suggest external environmental factors contributed to the structural failure. The cabin pressure controller operated within normal parameters, with the outflow valve modulating to maintain the target cabin altitude schedule.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The aircraft sustained no impact damage and landed under its own power. The primary wreckage consisted of the left mid-exit door plug, which was recovered from a residential area approximately 3.5 NM northwest of KPDX. The plug was located intact, with the exterior skin facing upward and the interior seal surface exposed. The surrounding fuselage structure exhibited localized deformation around the door plug opening, including minor buckling of the adjacent stringers and tearing of the perimeter seal material. No other major structural components were displaced or separated. The Federal Aviation Administration coordinated with local law enforcement to secure the recovery site and preserve chain-of-custody documentation.

5.2 Component Examination Findings
The recovered door plug was transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination. Visual inspection revealed that all twelve retention bolts were present, with no evidence of thread stripping, shear failure, or fatigue cracking. However, four of the twelve bolts exhibited incomplete engagement with the stop fittings, with torque values measured post-recovery at 850, 910, 940, and 1,020 inch-pounds, respectively. The guide tracks showed no signs of binding or misalignment. The perimeter seal was partially extruded, with localized compression set and adhesive residue indicating prior installation.

Microscopic analysis of the bolt threads and stop fitting interfaces revealed no manufacturing defects or material anomalies. The aluminum alloy skin of the plug met ASTM B209 specifications, with no evidence of corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, or impact damage. The cabin pressure relief valves and outflow valve were examined and found to be in normal operating condition, with no evidence of over-pressurization or mechanical failure.

5.3 Structural and System Impact Assessment
The rapid decompression resulted in localized damage to the cabin interior, including dislodged overhead bin panels, torn seat upholstery, and deployed oxygen masks. The aircraft’s emergency lighting system activated automatically, and the cabin crew initiated standard decompression procedures. The flight deck experienced a brief pressure transient, but all primary flight displays, navigation systems, and engine parameters remained within normal operating limits. The aircraft’s structural integrity was maintained throughout the event, with no propagation of damage to adjacent fuselage frames or wing attachments.

5.4 Data Recorder Analysis
The digital flight data recorder (DFDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and downloaded at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory. The DFDR recorded 2,148 parameters, including cabin pressure differential, outflow valve position, flight control surface deflections, and engine performance metrics. The CVR captured 2 hours of audio, including crew communications, checklist execution, and ambient cabin sounds. Analysis confirmed that the decompression event occurred at 17:24:12 PST, with immediate activation of the cabin altitude warning system. The flight crew’s response times and checklist adherence were consistent with approved emergency procedures.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Maintenance Procedures
The operator’s maintenance program, approved by the Federal Aviation Administration, required all door plug installations to be performed by certified airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanics with specific Boeing 737 MAX training. Quality assurance audits conducted in Q4 2023 identified minor documentation discrepancies in torque verification logs, which were subsequently corrected. The operator’s standard operating procedures mandated dual-inspection verification for all critical structural fasteners, including door plug retention hardware. Maintenance personnel utilized calibrated torque wrenches with digital readouts, and all values were recorded in the aircraft maintenance logbook. The operator’s quality management system (QMS) included random audits of installation procedures, with a 98.7% compliance rate documented for the preceding 12 months.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents and Industry Data
A review of NTSB and FAA incident databases identified three prior reports involving door plug retention anomalies on Boeing 737 MAX series aircraft. In each case, the anomalies were identified during routine inspections prior to flight, with no in-flight decompression events. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a Safety Alert for Operators (SAFO) in November 2023, emphasizing the importance of verifying door plug installation procedures and torque values. The manufacturer subsequently released a service bulletin recommending enhanced inspection protocols for guide track alignment and stop fitting engagement.

Comparative analysis with the BOEING 737-8 airframe, which shares identical door plug design and retention hardware, revealed no systemic failures in the broader 737 MAX fleet. The 737-8 variant utilizes the same plug configuration, but with a different cabin layout that does not require mid-exit door plug installation. Fleet-wide data from the operator indicated a 99.8% compliance rate with door plug maintenance procedures across all 737 MAX aircraft. The manufacturer’s engineering analysis confirmed that the door plug design meets all static and fatigue load requirements under 14 CFR 25.571 and 25.603.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The design, certification, and operation of the aircraft are governed by 14 CFR Part 25, Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes. Specifically, §25.365 requires that pressurized cabin structures withstand limit loads without permanent deformation, and §25.783 mandates that fuselage doors and plugs be designed to prevent inadvertent opening during flight. The operator’s compliance with 14 CFR 121.363 (Maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations) and 121.373 (Maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alteration programs) was verified through review of maintenance records and quality assurance documentation.

Advisory Circular (AC) 25-7, Flight Test Guide for Certification of Transport Category Airplanes, provides guidance on pressurization system testing and emergency descent procedures. The aircraft’s certification basis included compliance with AC 25.365-1, which addresses cabin pressure differential testing and structural load verification. The Federal Aviation Administration’s oversight of the manufacturer’s production quality system is conducted under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart G, with periodic audits of final assembly and component installation processes.

6.4 Investigative Status and Data Availability
All factual data, maintenance records, flight data recorder parameters, and component examination results have been compiled and are available for review by the investigative group. The NTSB Structures Group, Systems Group, and Operations Group have completed preliminary examinations and documented findings in accordance with standard investigative protocols. No operational, environmental, or mechanical factors outside the scope of the door plug retention system have been identified as contributing to the event. The investigation remains ongoing, with additional analysis of fastener engagement tolerances, installation procedures, and quality control documentation scheduled for completion in the next reporting cycle. All data will be made publicly available in accordance with NTSB policy and 49 CFR Part 831.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the technical examination, material analysis, and flight data recorder (FDR) parameter evaluation conducted by the NTSB Structures and Materials Group, in coordination with the Flight Data Recorder Group, following the in-flight rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered left mid-exit door plug (MIDP) assembly, associated fuselage structural components, retention hardware, and the digital flight data recorder media. The objective is to establish factual engineering data regarding the structural condition, fastener installation parameters, material properties, and recorded flight parameters at the time of the event.

The physical examination of the recovered door plug assembly, guide track components, stop fittings, and adjacent fuselage skin panels was conducted between January 10 and January 22, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C. The FDR and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) solid-state memory modules were downloaded and decoded at the NTSB Flight Data Recorder Readout Facility on January 8, 2024. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Standard Operating Procedures for Aviation Accident Investigations (SOP-2023-04), Boeing Service Bulletin compliance verification protocols, and applicable ASTM and AMS material testing standards. Photographic documentation, dimensional metrology logs, and spectrographic analysis results are cataloged under Exhibits 1A through 14F.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, serial number 44442, equipped with an optional mid-cabin exit door configuration. The left mid-exit door plug is a structural replacement for a standard Type III emergency exit, designed to maintain fuselage pressure integrity and aerodynamic continuity. The assembly consists of a primary aluminum alloy frame, an insulated plug panel, upper and lower guide tracks, four primary stop fittings, and a perimeter array of 12 high-shear fasteners. The plug is retained within the fuselage cutout by mechanical engagement of the stop fittings into the fuselage sill structure, with lateral and vertical loads transferred through the guide tracks and perimeter fastener line.

The design and certification basis for the door plug assembly complies with 14 CFR Part 25, specifically Section 25.571, which mandates damage-tolerance and fatigue evaluation of primary structure. The plug was manufactured under Boeing Drawing D6-82000-4412, Revision 14, and installed during final assembly at the Boeing Renton facility. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the Type Certificate (A16WE) and approved the supplemental type configuration for the MAX 9 variant. The aircraft was delivered to the operator in November 2023 and had accumulated 152 flight hours and 87 flight cycles at the time of the event. Maintenance records indicate the door plug was removed and reinstalled on December 18, 2023, for cabin reconfiguration work, with a subsequent return-to-service inspection signed off on December 20, 2023.

Propulsion for the aircraft is provided by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured under the GE Aviation production line. The LEAP-1B (P/N 1000-1B-001, S/N 88421-L and 88422-R) engines are rated at 28,000 lbf thrust and are integrated with the aircraft's full authority digital engine control (FADEC) system. Engine health monitoring data and maintenance logs show no anomalies, surge events, or performance degradation prior to the incident. The flight deck crew consisted of a Captain (Airline Transport Pilot certificate, 4,200 total hours, 180 hours on type) and a First Officer. The Captain was the pilot flying during the departure and initial climb phase.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly was received in a partially fragmented state, with the primary frame, plug panel, and lower guide track intact. The upper guide track and two of the four primary stop fittings were recovered separately from the cabin interior. The adjacent fuselage skin (Station 1040-1060, Stringer 12-14) exhibited localized deformation and fastener hole elongation.

3.1 Physical Examination and Dimensional Metrology
Visual inspection of the door plug frame revealed four empty fastener holes along the forward perimeter (Holes F-1 through F-4). The remaining eight fasteners were recovered from the plug and adjacent skin. No witness marks, torque stripe paint, or safety wire remnants were observed on the empty holes. Dimensional metrology of the guide track engagement surfaces was performed using a calibrated coordinate measuring machine (CMM) per Boeing BAC5000-12. The measured clearance between the plug guide track and the fuselage sill track was 0.045 inches, exceeding the design specification of 0.010–0.020 inches. The stop fitting engagement depth into the fuselage sill was measured at 0.125 inches, below the minimum required engagement of 0.250 inches per Drawing D6-82000-4412.

3.2 Fastener Analysis and Torque Verification
The eight recovered perimeter fasteners (P/N NAS1097AD6-8, S/N 7741-8812 through 7741-8819) were subjected to residual torque measurement using a calibrated digital torque wrench (TorqueMaster 5000, ±1% accuracy). Residual torque values ranged from 18.2 to 22.4 ft-lbs, significantly below the installation specification of 35 ± 3 ft-lbs. Fractographic examination of the fastener shanks revealed no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or material degradation. Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy (OES) confirmed compliance with AMS 4911 (Ti-6Al-4V, Grade 5). Hardness testing yielded an average of 36.1 HRC, within the specified 33–39 HRC range.

3.3 Material and Fracture Surface Analysis
The primary fracture surfaces on the forward frame lugs and adjacent fuselage skin were examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) per ASTM E112 and NTSB Materials Lab SOP-202. The fracture morphology exhibited ductile overload characteristics, characterized by microvoid coalescence and dimpled rupture. No fatigue striations, intergranular cracking, or stress corrosion cracking features were identified. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) of the fracture surfaces detected no foreign material contamination or galvanic corrosion products. The aluminum alloy skin (2024-T3, per AMS-QQ-A-250/4) exhibited a yield strength of 47.2 ksi and ultimate tensile strength of 68.5 ksi, consistent with certified material properties.

3.4 Structural Load Path Assessment
Engineering analysis of the load path indicates that the missing fasteners and reduced stop fitting engagement compromised the primary shear transfer mechanism. Under normal pressurization loads, the perimeter fasteners and stop fittings share the differential pressure-induced hoop stress. The measured guide track clearance and insufficient stop engagement would have allowed localized plug displacement, transferring excessive shear loads to the remaining fasteners. The overload failure mode is consistent with a sudden, unbalanced load application exceeding the residual fastener capacity.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The digital flight data recorder (DFDR) was a L-3Harris FA2100-1020 unit, recording 256 parameters at 1 Hz, 4 Hz, and 8 Hz sampling rates. The data was decoded using the manufacturer's proprietary software and cross-referenced with the aircraft's quick access recorder (QAR) data. The timeline reconstruction focuses on the climb phase from takeoff through the decompression event.

4.1 Flight Parameter Timeline
Takeoff roll commenced at 14:32:15 UTC. The aircraft rotated at 14:32:42 UTC, with an indicated airspeed (KIAS) of 148 knots. The Captain maintained a standard climb profile, with the autopilot engaged at 1,000 ft AGL. At 14:33:58 UTC, the aircraft passed through 14,500 ft MSL at 285 KIAS, with a vertical speed of 2,400 ft/min. Cabin differential pressure (ΔP) was recorded at 3.8 PSI, with a cabin altitude of 6,200 ft.

At 14:34:02 UTC, the aircraft reached 16,000 ft MSL. The recorded ΔP was 5.8 PSI, within the normal operational envelope for the climb phase. At 14:34:02.4 UTC, the ΔP parameter experienced an instantaneous drop to 0.2 PSI within a 0.8-second interval. Simultaneously, the cabin altitude parameter spiked from 6,800 ft to 28,400 ft. The vertical speed parameter registered a transient negative spike of -1,800 ft/min, consistent with rapid outflow of cabin air. The aircraft's pitch attitude remained stable at 8.2° nose-up, and the roll angle deviated by less than 1.5°.

4.2 Engine and Systems Data
The LEAP-1B engine parameters remained within certified limits throughout the event. The left engine (S/N 88421-L) recorded an N1 of 89.2%, N2 of 94.1%, EGT of 612°C, and fuel flow of 2,840 lb/hr. The right engine (S/N 88422-R) mirrored these values within ±0.5%. No compressor stall, surge, or FADEC fault codes were logged. The environmental control system (ECS) pack valves closed automatically at 14:34:03.1 UTC in response to the rapid pressure loss, as designed. The outflow valve position parameter indicated full open at 14:34:02.6 UTC, consistent with uncontrolled depressurization.

4.3 Control Inputs and Crew Response
The Captain's control column and rudder pedal inputs were recorded at 4 Hz. Prior to the event, the control column force was 0.0 lbs, indicating autopilot engagement. At 14:34:03.5 UTC, a manual control input of 12.4 lbs aft and 3.2 lbs left was recorded, coinciding with the activation of the cabin altitude warning horn and the master caution light. The Captain disengaged the autopilot and initiated a descent profile. The aircraft's airspeed decreased to 240 KIAS by 14:34:18 UTC, and the vertical speed stabilized at -1,200 ft/min. The CVR audio track captured a sharp acoustic transient at 14:34:02.3 UTC, followed by high-velocity wind noise and crew communication regarding rapid decompression.

4.4 Comparison with Normal Operational Parameters
Under standard climb conditions at 16,000 ft MSL, the 737 MAX 9 cabin ΔP typically ranges from 4.0 to 4.5 PSI, with a maximum certified limit of 9.1 PSI. The recorded 5.8 PSI at the time of separation is well below the structural design limit. The rapid ΔP decay rate of 7.0 PSI/sec exceeds the normal outflow valve modulation rate of 0.5 PSI/sec, confirming an uncontrolled structural breach rather than a system malfunction. The LEAP-1B engine performance data shows no thrust asymmetry or power loss, eliminating propulsion-related aerodynamic disturbances as a contributing factor.

5. SUMMARY

The technical examination and data analysis yield the following factual findings:

1. The recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly exhibited four missing perimeter fasteners (P/N NAS1097AD6-8) along the forward frame. The remaining eight fasteners demonstrated residual torque values of 18.2–22.4 ft-lbs, below the manufacturer-specified installation torque of 35 ± 3 ft-lbs.
2. Dimensional metrology confirmed guide track clearance of 0.045 inches, exceeding the design tolerance of 0.010–0.020 inches. Stop fitting engagement depth measured 0.125 inches, below the minimum required 0.250 inches per Boeing Drawing D6-82000-4412.
3. Fractographic and metallurgical analysis of the frame lugs and adjacent fuselage skin revealed ductile overload failure morphology. No fatigue, corrosion, or material degradation was identified. The aluminum alloy (2024-T3) and titanium fasteners (Ti-6Al-4V) met all certified chemical and mechanical property requirements per AMS and ASTM standards.
4. Flight data recorder parameters indicate the aircraft was climbing through 16,000 ft MSL at 285 KIAS when cabin differential pressure reached 5.8 PSI. A rapid pressure decay to 0.2 PSI occurred within 0.8 seconds, accompanied by a cabin altitude spike to 28,400 ft. The event occurred below the maximum certified differential pressure limit of 9.1 PSI.
5. Engine parameters for both GE Aviation LEAP-1B turbofans remained within normal operational envelopes. No thrust asymmetry, FADEC faults, or compressor anomalies were recorded. The environmental control system responded as designed, with automatic pack valve closure and outflow valve full-open indication.
6. Control input data confirms the Captain maintained autopilot engagement until the decompression warning activated at 14:34:03.5 UTC. Subsequent manual control inputs and descent initiation were consistent with standard rapid decompression procedures.
7. The structural load path analysis indicates that the combination of missing fasteners, reduced stop fitting engagement, and excessive guide track clearance compromised the primary shear transfer mechanism, resulting in localized plug displacement and subsequent overload failure of the remaining retention hardware.

All findings are based on physical examination, material testing, dimensional verification, and recorded flight data. No operational, maintenance, or certification determinations are made within this report.

INTERVIEW OF DAVID R. CHEN, SENIOR AIRFRAME INSPECTOR
Date: January 10, 2024
Time: 09:15 PST
Location: NTSB Field Office, Renton, Washington
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Miller

Q: Please state your full name, current title, and your relationship to the flight for the official record.
A: David R. Chen. I’m a Senior Airframe Inspector with the airline’s Pacific Northwest maintenance division. I was traveling as a non-revenue passenger on Flight 1282. Deadheading to Portland for a scheduled line check. I was seated in 14A, left side, just forward of the wing.

Q: Can you walk me through the departure sequence from your perspective?
A: Yeah, sure. We pushed back from Gate C12 at, I think it was about 16:45 local time. Standard push. The engines started up normally. You know, the LEAP engine has a pretty distinct spool-up sound, a little higher pitch than the older CFM56s, but nothing out of the ordinary. Taxi was maybe ten minutes, give or take. We lined up on 16L, got cleared for takeoff. Acceleration felt normal, rotation was smooth. I was just reviewing some maintenance tracking logs on my tablet, honestly. We climbed out, turned left over the water, and I remember glancing at the cabin altitude display showing we were passing through about 10,000 feet. Everything was quiet. Normal climb profile.

Q: What happened as you continued the climb?
A: Right. So, we were climbing through, I’d say, 15,000 to 16,000 feet. Maybe 16,200. I was looking out the window, just watching the cloud layer break up. And then—there was this… this massive bang. Not like a tire blowout. It was deeper. More like a structural pop, but way louder. And immediately after, the cabin pressure just… dropped. My ears popped hard, and there was this sudden rush of cold air. I mean, freezing. And the oxygen masks dropped. I remember thinking, “Okay, this is a rapid decompression.” I unbuckled, stood up, and looked toward the mid-cabin. The left mid-exit door plug was just… gone. Completely gone. You could see the sky, the wind tearing through the cabin. It was surreal.

Q: How did the flight deck respond?
A: The Captain handled it really well. I mean, you could tell he was on top of it. The emergency descent started almost immediately. The aircraft pitched down, but it was controlled. No violent maneuvers. The Captain came on the PA maybe thirty seconds later, voice was calm, told us to keep our masks on, stay seated, and that we were diverting back to Sea-Tac. He didn’t panic. You could hear the engines spooling back, but they were running fine. The LEAPs are pretty robust, and I didn’t hear any abnormal vibrations or surges. Just the wind noise from the opening.

Q: Can you describe the sensory environment in the cabin during the descent?
A: Yeah. It was loud. The wind roar was constant, like a jet engine itself. Temperature dropped fast. I could feel the air moving across the aisle, papers and magazines were flying around. Some passengers were crying, obviously, but the flight attendants were already moving through the aisles, checking masks, keeping people calm. I helped a woman in 14B secure her mask properly. She was hyperventilating a bit. I just told her to breathe slow, it’s just oxygen, you’re fine. The descent took maybe, I don’t know, eight or nine minutes. We leveled off around 10,000, then continued down. The Captain announced we were turning final for 16R.

Q: What did you observe after landing?
A: We touched down smoothly. Brakes were firm, reverse thrust normal. We taxied to a remote stand, not a gate. The Captain kept us on the PA, told us to remain seated until emergency services cleared the aircraft. I looked out the window again. The fuselage skin around the door plug area was… it was torn, but not catastrophically. The plug itself was completely missing. You could see the frame rails, some insulation, but the structure held. That’s what surprised me, honestly. The airframe integrity was maintained.

Q: From a maintenance perspective, what are your initial thoughts on the failure?
A: Well, I’ve been with the airline for twelve years, mostly on the 737 family. The mid-exit door plug on the MAX 9 is a known configuration. It’s not a standard door, it’s a plug. It’s held in by guide tracks and retention bolts. For it to separate like that… it’s not a fatigue crack in the traditional sense. I mean, we follow strict damage tolerance requirements for all primary structure, but this is a secondary plug. Still, it’s pressurized. The bolts, the tracks, the stop pads… something had to give. I’m thinking maybe a missing bolt, or a track misalignment during installation. We’ve had similar issues on other airframes, but never a full separation.

Q: Have you reviewed the maintenance records for this aircraft recently?
A: I haven’t pulled the full logbook yet, but I know our maintenance control team is already on it. The aircraft had a heavy check about four months ago. All the door plug inspections were signed off. We follow the manufacturer’s service bulletins, and we’re aligned with the FAA’s guidance on aging aircraft programs. I mean, we reference Advisory Circular 120-16G pretty heavily for our maintenance program development, especially for tracking recurring discrepancies and establishing inspection intervals. But this… this feels like a manufacturing or installation anomaly, not a wear-and-tear thing.

Q: You mentioned the FAA. Were there any recent directives or communications regarding this component?
A: Not that I’m aware of prior to this. The FAA has been pretty active on the MAX fleet, obviously, but this specific plug issue wasn’t on the radar. I know GE Aviation has been pushing for tighter engine-to-airframe interface checks, but that’s more about the LEAP engine mounts and pylon inspections. This is purely fuselage. I think the FAA will issue an emergency AD pretty quickly. They have to.

Q: How does this compare to other aircraft in your fleet, say the BOEING 737-8?
A: The 737-8 doesn’t have the mid-exit door plug. It’s a different configuration. The MAX 9 is stretched, so they added those plugs to meet evacuation requirements. The 737-8 uses standard overwing exits. So structurally, they’re different. The plug design is unique to the MAX 9 and MAX 10. I’ve worked on the 737-8 extensively, and the door mechanisms are straightforward. This plug system is more complex. It relies on precise alignment during final assembly. If the factory didn’t torque the retention bolts correctly, or if the guide tracks weren’t seated… well, you get what we saw.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record?
A: Just that… I mean, I’ve been in aviation a long time. I’ve seen hard landings, engine shutdowns, even a bird strike that took out a windshield. But this… this was different. The fact that the Captain got it back on the ground safely, with zero injuries, is a testament to the crew training. And honestly, the fact that the fuselage didn’t fail further… that’s a relief. I hope the investigation looks closely at the installation procedures, the torque values, the quality control at the factory. Because if it’s a systemic issue, we need to know. I’m happy to provide any maintenance logs, photos, or whatever you need. I’ve got my notes from the flight, too. I wrote down the times, the altitudes, everything I could remember.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. We’ll be in touch.
A: Yeah, of course. Just… let me know if you need me to walk through the cabin layout again, or if you want to go over the maintenance tracking system. I’m here.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AIRCRAFT CERTIFICATION
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20591

MEMORANDUM

DATE: March 15, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service (AIR-100)
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-24-012 AND COMPLIANCE STATUS FOR EMERGENCY AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE 2024-02-51
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA018; Docket No. FAA-2024-0112; AD 2024-02-51

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-24-012, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the January 5, 2024, in-flight rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL. The referenced incident occurred during initial climb through approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) following departure from a Pacific Northwest aerodrome. The subject matter encompasses compliance verification with Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-02-51, issued under 14 CFR Part 39, and addresses the applicability of Section 25.571 regarding damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of pressurized fuselage structures. This document further delineates the FAA’s oversight posture, manufacturer corrective action status, and mandated compliance timelines for all affected operators and production facilities.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737 MAX series, including the MAX 8 and MAX 9 variants, holds Type Certificate No. A16WE, issued under 14 CFR Part 25. The mid-cabin exit door plug configuration, utilized on high-density seating layouts, was certified as a supplemental type certificate (STC) modification integrated into the original type design. The structural integrity of pressurized fuselage components is governed by Section 25.571, which mandates comprehensive damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation to ensure continued structural integrity throughout the operational service life. Historically, the Agency has issued multiple ADs addressing fastener retention, torque verification, and manufacturing quality control for door plug assemblies, most notably AD 2023-18-09 and subsequent revisions.

Advisory Circular AC 120-16G, "Air Carrier Maintenance Programs," establishes the regulatory framework for continuous airworthiness maintenance programs (CAMP) and outlines operator responsibilities for defect reporting, reliability monitoring, and maintenance interval optimization. The incident aircraft was operated under 14 CFR Part 121, subject to the stringent maintenance and operational requirements of Part 121, Subpart L. While the propulsion system, specifically the LEAP-1B engine manufactured by GE Aviation, was not implicated in the structural failure, the powerplant’s integration and associated thrust settings during climb-out were evaluated to determine potential pressurization cycle stressors. The aircraft’s flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) data confirmed that the Captain executed appropriate emergency descent and decompression procedures in strict accordance with the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) and 14 CFR § 121.333, resulting in a safe return to the departure aerodrome with no fatalities.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the manufacturer’s production records, quality assurance documentation, and post-incident inspection data reveals systemic deficiencies in the final assembly and fastener retention protocols for the mid-exit door plug. The Federal Aviation Administration’s Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) and the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) holder identified non-conformances in the installation of four critical retaining bolts, which failed to meet the torque specifications mandated by the approved maintenance manual. This deviation constitutes a direct violation of 14 CFR § 21.101 and § 21.125, which require strict adherence to approved type design data and manufacturing quality control systems.

Regulatory oversight actions initiated by the FAA included the immediate issuance of Emergency AD 2024-02-51, mandating pre-flight inspections, torque verification, and photographic documentation of all mid-cabin exit door plug fasteners across the affected fleet. The Agency’s Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) conducted unannounced ramp inspections and maintenance record audits at three primary operator hubs. Compliance verification indicates that 94.7% of the affected fleet has completed the initial inspection cycle, with remaining aircraft grounded pending corrective action.

Despite these measures, the investigation has identified critical gaps within the existing regulatory framework. The current damage tolerance analysis under Section 25.571 does not adequately account for manufacturing-induced stress concentrations or fastener preload degradation in door plug assemblies. Furthermore, the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for inoperative door plug indicators lack explicit guidance for rapid decompression scenarios, creating ambiguity in dispatch authority. The reliance on ODA self-certification for production conformity has been determined to require enhanced FAA direct oversight, particularly for safety-critical structural modifications. The Agency’s analysis further confirms that while the Boeing 737 MAX 8 variant utilizes a different door configuration, the underlying fastener retention methodology shares common engineering lineage, necessitating a fleet-wide review of analogous structural interfaces. Additionally, compliance with 14 CFR 25.783 regarding fuselage pressure relief and emergency ventilation pathways requires re-evaluation to ensure adequate crew and passenger survivability during sudden cabin depressurization events.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to 14 CFR Part 39 and the authority vested in the Administrator, the following corrective actions and compliance mandates are hereby established:

a. IMMEDIATE CORRECTIVE ACTIONS: All operators of Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft shall complete a comprehensive torque verification and non-destructive inspection (NDI) of all mid-exit door plug retaining hardware in accordance with Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-53A127, Revision 1. Compliance is required within 72 hours of AD issuance. Operators must submit inspection results via the FAA’s Safety Assurance System (SAS) portal within 10 calendar days.

b. MANUFACTURER COMPLIANCE TIMELINE: The type certificate holder shall submit a revised damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation report addressing fastener preload degradation, manufacturing tolerance stack-up, and revised inspection intervals. This submission must comply with Section 25.571 and § 25.365, and shall be delivered to the Seattle Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) no later than 180 days from the date of this memorandum. Failure to comply will result in suspension of production certificate privileges under 14 CFR § 21.137.

c. REGULATORY OVERSIGHT ENHANCEMENTS: The FAA will transition from delegated ODA oversight to direct Agency inspection for all door plug assembly and fastener installation processes. This includes mandatory witness inspections for 100% of production units until the manufacturer demonstrates sustained compliance with 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart G. Additionally, the Agency will initiate rulemaking to amend 14 CFR Part 121.344 to require enhanced maintenance program tracking for structural fastener retention, incorporating predictive analytics and mandatory torque verification at 500-cycle intervals.

d. OPERATIONAL AND MMEL REVISIONS: Operators shall revise their Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) to explicitly prohibit dispatch with any door plug fastener discrepancy or indicator malfunction. Training programs for flight crews and maintenance personnel shall be updated to reflect revised emergency decompression protocols, with completion required within 90 days. The Captain’s authority to exercise emergency deviation under 14 CFR § 91.3 shall be reinforced through recurrent simulator training emphasizing rapid depressurization response and crew resource management.

e. FOLLOW-UP INSPECTION SCHEDULE: The FAA will conduct quarterly compliance audits of all affected operators and the manufacturer’s production facilities. A comprehensive regulatory review of AC 120-16G will be initiated to incorporate enhanced guidance on structural fastener reliability monitoring and defect reporting thresholds. The Agency will publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) within 120 days to formalize these requirements.

This memorandum serves as the official regulatory response to the referenced safety recommendation. All compliance documentation, inspection reports, and corrective action plans shall be submitted to the Docket Management System under Docket No. FAA-2024-0112. The Federal Aviation Administration remains committed to ensuring the highest standards of airworthiness and operational safety across the national airspace system.

Mid-Air Door Plug Separation Forces Emergency Landing of Boeing 737 MAX 9; All 177 Aboard Survive

Elena Rostova, Global Aviation Desk
PORTLAND, Ore. — A Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier made an emergency return to Portland International Airport on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, after a mid-cabin door plug violently separated from the fuselage during climbout. The rapid decompression event occurred at approximately 16,000 feet, but the flight crew successfully stabilized the aircraft and landed without incident. No fatalities were reported, though several passengers sustained minor injuries.

The sudden loss of the left mid-exit door plug triggered an immediate drop in cabin pressure, sending loose items flying and causing oxygen masks to deploy automatically. Pilots initiated an emergency descent to a breathable altitude before diverting back to their departure point. The incident has prompted immediate regulatory scrutiny and raised fresh questions about manufacturing quality control for the aircraft family.

“The National Transportation Safety Board has dispatched a go-team to Portland to lead the investigation,” said NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy in a press briefing Saturday. “Our priority is securing the wreckage, interviewing the crew, and determining exactly how this door plug came to detach.” The Federal Aviation Administration swiftly issued an emergency airworthiness directive, temporarily grounding all 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with similar door plugs. “We are working closely with the manufacturer and the operator to ensure the traveling public’s safety,” an FAA spokesperson stated. “No aircraft will return to service until we are confident in the structural integrity of the fleet.” An airline representative added, “Our crew’s training and quick response prevented a tragedy. We are providing full support to our passengers and cooperating completely with investigators.”

The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a stretched variant of the popular narrow-body jet. Unlike standard emergency exits, the mid-cabin doors on this configuration are replaced with “door plugs”—solid panels that fill the opening when airlines opt for higher-density seating. The flight was en route from Portland to Ontario, California, carrying 171 passengers and six crew members. The MAX 9 shares its core airframe, flight systems, and certification basis with the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which previously faced a 20-month global grounding following two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the separation likely points to a failure in the plug’s retention hardware or installation process. “Door plugs are held in place by a series of guide tracks, stop fittings, and bolts,” explained Dr. Marcus Chen, a former NTSB investigator and aerospace engineering professor. “If even a few critical fasteners are missing or improperly torqued, the pressure differential at altitude can literally blow the panel out.” The incident will be evaluated against 14 CFR 25.571, the federal regulation governing damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of pressurized fuselage structures. “This rule requires manufacturers to prove that a single structural failure won’t lead to catastrophic decompression,” Chen noted. “Investigators will examine whether the plug’s design, manufacturing, or maintenance fell short of those standards.”

For those on board, the experience was harrowing. “One second we were climbing normally, the next there was a deafening bang and the air just vanished,” said passenger David Lin, who was seated three rows from the breach. “My phone flew out of my hand, and the wind was howling through the cabin. The flight attendants were incredible—they kept us calm while we scrambled for masks.” The Captain, whose identity has not been released, executed a textbook emergency descent, leveling the aircraft at 10,000 feet and declaring a mayday. “The pilot’s handling was flawless,” Lin added. “He got us down safely in under ten minutes.” Family members waiting at the destination airport described scenes of relief and anxiety. “We just want to know why this happened,” said Maria Gonzalez, whose daughter was on the flight. “It’s terrifying to think a piece of the plane just fell off.”

The 737 MAX series has been under intense scrutiny since its return to service in late 2020. While the MAX 9 has not been involved in any fatal accidents, this incident echoes past concerns about Boeing’s production oversight. In 2023, the manufacturer faced whistleblower allegations regarding quality control lapses at its Renton, Washington, facility. The aviation industry has largely maintained that modern commercial flying remains exceptionally safe, but repeated manufacturing anomalies have strained public confidence. “Every incident is a reminder that aviation safety is a continuous process,” said aviation historian Dr. Sarah Jenkins. “The system works when regulators, manufacturers, and operators learn from these events and implement rigorous fixes.”

The NTSB has recovered the missing door plug from a residential yard in Portland, where it landed without causing injuries. Investigators are currently examining the panel, the aircraft’s fuselage, and maintenance records. The FAA has mandated detailed inspections of all affected MAX 9s, requiring airlines to verify the installation of door plug hardware before returning jets to service. Meanwhile, GE Aviation, which supplies the LEAP-1B engines for the MAX family, confirmed it is cooperating with the probe, though preliminary data indicates the powerplants were operating normally at the time of the event. “We are monitoring the situation closely and stand ready to assist with any technical analysis,” a GE Aviation representative said. As the investigation enters its next phase, passengers and industry watchers alike await answers that will shape the future of the 737 MAX program and commercial aviation safety standards.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Engineering and Maintenance Division of the operating carrier, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event. As the organization responsible for the continued airworthiness, operational deployment, and maintenance oversight of the affected aircraft, our technical team has conducted a comprehensive review of flight data, maintenance records, quality assurance documentation, and crew performance metrics. The scope of this document is to articulate our engineering position on the structural and procedural factors that contributed to the left mid-exit door plug separation, evaluate the adequacy of existing maintenance and operational protocols, and provide evidence-based recommendations for systemic safety enhancements. Our analysis is grounded in airframe structural engineering principles, maintenance quality management frameworks, and operational human factors, with direct reference to docket materials, regulatory requirements, and industry best practices. We approach this investigation with a commitment to transparency, recognizing that aviation safety is a shared responsibility across manufacturers, operators, regulators, and labor organizations.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, departed a Pacific Northwest hub on a scheduled domestic flight. During the initial climb phase, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the flight crew experienced an abrupt cabin pressure loss accompanied by a loud acoustic event and visible structural debris. The aircraft executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

Docket materials, including the NTSB Preliminary Report (Section 2.1), Flight Data Recorder (FDR) parameters, and Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) transcripts, confirm a rapid cabin altitude increase from 8,000 to 14,500 feet within 18 seconds, followed by stabilization after descent to 10,000 feet. The FDR indicates normal engine parameters throughout the event, with no indications of compressor stall, surge, or thrust asymmetry. Maintenance logbooks (Docket Item 14-C) document that the aircraft underwent a cabin reconfiguration 14 days prior to the event, which required removal and reinstallation of the left mid-exit door plug per Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1234. The work order reflects standard torque application procedures but lacks independent dual-signature verification for the primary retention fasteners.

The Federal Aviation Administration issued an immediate Airworthiness Directive (AD 2024-02-01) mandating fleet-wide inspections of mid-exit door plug retention hardware. Subsequent findings from the manufacturer’s quality audit, referenced in Docket Item 22-A, identified inconsistencies in fastener installation documentation and missing guide bolts on multiple airframes in the same production block. The operating carrier’s maintenance program, developed in accordance with Advisory Circular 120-16G, was fully compliant with all applicable directives at the time of the event. However, the latent nature of the assembly deviation underscores the need for enhanced verification protocols at the interface between original equipment manufacturing and operator maintenance.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The separation of the left mid-exit door plug represents a failure of the fastener retention system at the fuselage-to-plug interface. Our structural engineering team has conducted a detailed review of the recovered hardware, finite element modeling (FEM) of the plug assembly, and operational load data. The analysis indicates that the primary contributing factor was the absence of two guide bolts and inadequate torque application on four primary retention bolts. Under cyclic pressurization loads, the missing guide bolts shifted the load path to the remaining fasteners, creating localized stress concentrations that exceeded the yield threshold of the aluminum alloy retention brackets. Witness marks on the recovered plug frame exhibit progressive fretting and micro-cracking consistent with a manufacturing/assembly deviation rather than in-service fatigue accumulation.

Regulatory compliance for this interface is governed by 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of principal structural elements. The door plug assembly, while classified as a secondary structure, functions as a critical pressure boundary component when installed. The current certification basis assumes proper fastener installation and retention. The absence of guide bolts compromises the alignment tolerance during installation, increasing the risk of cross-threading, improper seating, and uneven load distribution. Our engineering assessment confirms that the plug architecture, as designed, meets ultimate load requirements when installed per specification. The failure mode is therefore attributable to process control breakdowns during final assembly and post-delivery maintenance verification.

From a maintenance quality perspective, our carrier’s program aligns with AC 120-16G, which emphasizes risk-based maintenance planning, quality assurance oversight, and continuous improvement. However, the event highlights a systemic vulnerability in the handoff between OEM production and operator maintenance. The torque verification step relied on manual documentation without digital traceability or cryptographic validation. Industry best practices increasingly mandate electronic torque wrenches with automated data logging, yet this capability was not universally implemented across the maintenance ecosystem at the time of the event. The absence of independent dual-verification for critical fastener installations represents a gap in our quality management system that we have since addressed.

Operationally, the flight deck response was exemplary. The Captain, supported by the First Officer and cabin crew, executed emergency descent procedures within 45 seconds of the initial pressure warning. CVR analysis confirms clear communication, adherence to Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) protocols, and effective crew resource management. The aircraft’s CFM LEAP-1B engines, manufactured by GE Aviation, maintained stable N1, EGT, and fuel flow parameters throughout the decompression event. General Electric Aviation’s post-event telemetry review confirms that the LEAP-1B powerplants possess adequate surge margin and compressor stability to withstand rapid cabin pressure transients without secondary damage. This operational resilience underscores the robustness of the propulsion system and validates the crew’s decision to prioritize immediate descent over troubleshooting.

Comparative fleet analysis further isolates the failure mode. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 utilizes a standard overwing exit configuration without mid-cabin door plugs. Historical maintenance and operational data for the 737-8 fleet show zero analogous events, confirming that the failure is specific to the plug retention architecture and its installation quality control. The MAX 9’s optional mid-exit door plug introduces a unique structural interface that requires specialized verification protocols. Our engineering team has reviewed OEM service bulletins, airworthiness directives, and industry safety alerts, concluding that the current guidance lacks explicit requirements for digital torque logging, independent quality audits, and real-time structural health monitoring for plug interfaces.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the engineering data, maintenance records, and operational evidence reviewed, our position is that the rapid decompression event was primarily caused by inadequate fastener retention and missing guide bolts at the door plug installation stage, compounded by insufficient independent verification during post-delivery maintenance. The failure was not a fundamental design deficiency in the airframe’s pressure boundary architecture, but rather a quality assurance and process control breakdown that allowed a latent assembly deviation to enter service.

Secondary contributing factors include the absence of digital torque traceability, ambiguous handoff protocols between OEM production and operator maintenance, and the lack of real-time structural health monitoring for modular plug interfaces. While the operating carrier’s maintenance program complied with all applicable regulatory requirements, including Part 25.571 and Advisory Circular 120-16G, the event exposed vulnerabilities in verification methodologies that must be addressed through industry-wide standardization.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Mandate digital torque logging with cryptographic verification for all critical fastener installations on pressure boundary components.
- Implement mandatory independent quality audits for door plug installations, with clear accountability matrices between OEM and operator.
- Enhance OEM-operator data sharing for configuration changes, ensuring that maintenance programs are updated with plug-specific verification protocols.
- Update regulatory guidance to explicitly address modular plug retention in damage tolerance programs, including requirements for guide bolt verification and alignment tolerance checks.
- Integrate real-time cabin pressure decay analytics into airline safety management systems (SMS) to enable predictive maintenance and early anomaly detection.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In immediate response to the event, the operating carrier has implemented comprehensive corrective actions across its fleet and maintenance organization. All aircraft have undergone 100% door plug inspections in compliance with FAA AD 2024-02-01, utilizing calibrated torque wrenches, borescope verification, and independent dual-signature documentation. Maintenance training modules have been revised to emphasize plug retention architecture, alignment tolerance verification, and the criticality of guide bolt installation. We have deployed a digital maintenance tracking system (DMTS) that automatically logs torque values, tool calibration status, and technician credentials for all critical fastener installations, eliminating manual documentation gaps.

Additionally, we have enhanced crew training programs to include advanced rapid decompression scenarios in full-flight simulators, focusing on emergency descent profiles, cabin crew coordination, and systems management under high-stress conditions. The Captain and flight deck crew involved in the event have been recognized for their adherence to standard operating procedures and effective crisis management.

Looking forward, we propose the establishment of a joint OEM-operator quality assurance task force to standardize plug installation protocols, develop ultrasonic and acoustic emission monitoring techniques for early detection of fastener degradation, and advocate for regulatory updates to AC 120-16G and 14 CFR 25.571. We also recommend the integration of predictive analytics into maintenance planning, leveraging FDR and cabin pressure data to identify anomalous decay rates before they escalate into structural events.

The aviation industry’s commitment to continuous improvement is demonstrated by our willingness to confront systemic vulnerabilities, implement rigorous verification standards, and collaborate with regulators, manufacturers, and labor organizations to elevate safety performance. We stand ready to support the NTSB’s ongoing investigation and to implement the recommended safety enhancements across our operations.

TO: All Maintenance Stations, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance, Fleet Engineering
FROM: Director of Structural Integrity & Maintenance Programs, Pacific Northwest Operations
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2024-014: Immediate Inspection & Torque Verification of Mid-Exit Door Plug Retention Hardware (B737 MAX 9)
REF: QA-2023-089, WO-737MAX-PLUG-001, FAA AD 2024-02-01 (Preliminary), NTSB Docket Entry Pending

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate inspection, torque verification, and documentation of all mid-cabin exit door plug retention fasteners on the Boeing 737 MAX 9 fleet. The directive is issued in direct response to the January 5, 2024, in-flight separation event and supersedes all prior routine inspection intervals for this component. Compliance is mandatory prior to any further revenue operations.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. airline experienced a rapid decompression event when the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage during climb through 16,000 feet after departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The aircraft returned safely with no fatalities. Initial telemetry and hardware recovery efforts pointed toward a localized structural fatigue anomaly in the fuselage frame, though subsequent detailed analysis and installation sequence review confirmed that missing or improperly torqued retention bolts on the door plug assembly were the primary cause. While this event specifically involves the MAX 9, our internal engineering review has identified cross-fleet procedural alignment requirements. The FAA has issued an emergency airworthiness directive requiring immediate grounding and inspection of affected aircraft. Concurrently, our Quality Assurance team has initiated a fleet-wide audit of all plug-type door installations, including those on the Boeing 737 MAX 8, to ensure compliance with established damage tolerance requirements and structural integrity standards. This alert formalizes the inspection protocol and establishes traceability requirements for all maintenance actions performed under this directive.

DETAILS:
1. Affected Componen

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:15 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, operated by a major U.S. air carrier, experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during the initial climb phase. The aircraft departed from a Pacific Northwest regional airport and was en route to a destination in the southwestern United States when the left mid-cabin exit door plug separated from the fuselage at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident; there were no reported fatalities or serious injuries among the passengers or crew.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information has been compiled from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads, air traffic control communications, and initial maintenance records. Initial information indicates that the aircraft was operating normally during takeoff and initial climb until the reported decompression event. The FDR data suggests a sudden loss of cabin pressure coinciding with a rapid change in cabin altitude parameters, followed by the activation of the emergency descent profile. CVR transcripts, currently undergoing preliminary review, contain crew communications consistent with an uncommanded structural event and subsequent emergency checklist execution.

Initial witness accounts from passengers and cabin crew, collected via post-flight interviews, describe a loud acoustic event followed by rapid airflow, temperature drop, and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Several individuals reported observing a void in the left fuselage aft of the wing, consistent with the reported door plug separation. These accounts remain uncorroborated by physical evidence at this stage and are subject to further verification.

Meteorological data obtained from the departure airport and surrounding MCAS indicate visual meteorological conditions prevailed at the time of the event. Surface winds were light and variable, with visibility exceeding 10 statute miles and no significant convective activity reported along the departure route. Weather conditions are not currently considered a contributing factor, though this assessment remains preliminary.
