Preliminary damage assessment, based on post-flight photographs and initial ground inspection, reveals a complete separation of the left mid-exit door plug assembly. The surrounding fuselage skin exhibits localized deformation and fastener hole elongation in the immediate vicinity of the plug retention structure. Secondary damage includes minor interior panel displacement and cabin lining abrasion consistent with rapid decompression forces. The aircraft’s primary flight control systems, hydraulic lines, and electrical routing in the affected zone appear intact based on initial visual inspection. It should be noted that while this incident involves a 737 MAX 9 configuration, maintenance and operational procedures referenced during initial review align with guidance applicable to the broader 737 MAX family, including the B737 MAX 8, to ensure comprehensive procedural alignment. Additionally, initial maintenance logs indicate that recent inspections were conducted in accordance with standard operator programs, though specific compliance with Advisory Circular 120-16G regarding maintenance program development and execution is currently under review.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Maintenance Records groups have been formally established and are currently conducting preliminary data collection and analysis. The Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and relevant labor organizations have been designated as parties to the investigation under 49 CFR Part 831. All party representatives have been briefed on their roles, responsibilities, and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding preliminary findings.

Physical evidence has been secured and cataloged in accordance with standard NTSB chain-of-custody protocols. The separated door plug components, including the plug panel, retention hardware, and adjacent fuselage structure, have been recovered and transported to a secure examination facility. Initial non-destructive testing (NDT) and dimensional inspections are scheduled to commence within the next 48 hours. The flight data and cockpit voice recorders have been successfully downloaded, and data validation is underway. Maintenance records, crew training files, and recent work orders have been requested and are being compiled for review.

The Powerplants group has initiated a preliminary review of the aircraft’s propulsion system, which is equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines. While initial telemetry indicates normal engine parameters throughout the flight, a detailed examination of engine health monitoring data and recent maintenance history will be conducted to rule out any secondary effects or contributing factors. Coordination with GE Aviation has been established to facilitate technical support and data sharing regarding engine performance trends and maintenance documentation, though no anomalies have been identified at this preliminary stage. All examinations remain in the early phases, and findings are subject to revision as additional data becomes available.

4. NEXT STEPS
Investigative activities will proceed in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with an emphasis on systematic data collection, component testing, and operational review. The Structures group will conduct detailed metallurgical and fracture surface analyses of the recovered door plug and adjacent fuselage sections to determine the sequence of failure and identify any manufacturing, installation, or maintenance-related anomalies. The Systems group will perform functional testing of the cabin pressurization system, door warning indicators, and associated wiring harnesses to evaluate system response during the decompression event.

The Operations and Human Performance groups will conduct structured interviews with the flight and cabin crew, review standard operating procedures, and evaluate training records to assess crew response and decision-making during the emergency descent. Maintenance records will be cross-referenced with manufacturer service bulletins and operator maintenance programs to verify compliance and identify any recent modifications or deferred items. All findings will be documented in accordance with NTSB reporting standards, and any deviations from established procedures will be noted for further analysis.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated to be released within 30 days of the accident date, pending completion of initial data validation and component examinations. Subsequent updates will be issued as significant milestones are reached, including the completion of structural testing, maintenance record analysis, and operational interviews. The investigation will remain open until all technical, operational, and human factors have been thoroughly evaluated. All preliminary information contained in this document is subject to change as additional evidence is collected, analyzed, and verified. No conclusions regarding probable cause or contributing factors have been reached at this time.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:07 Pacific Standard Time (01:07 UTC, January 6, 2024), a rapid decompression event occurred aboard a Boeing 737 MAX 9 during the initial climb phase of a scheduled passenger flight. The event transpired at an indicated altitude of 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 12.4 nautical miles (NM) northwest of Portland International Airport (KPDX), Oregon. The geographic coordinates of the event location were recorded as 45.58°N latitude, 122.71°W longitude. Following the event, the flight crew executed an emergency descent and returned to KPDX, where the aircraft landed without further incident at 17:42 PST. No ground impact or secondary damage occurred during the return flight.

1.2 Aircraft Identification and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737 MAX 9, bearing United States registration N704AL. The aircraft was operated by a major U.S. certificated air carrier conducting scheduled passenger service under the provisions of 14 CFR Part 121. The flight was designated as AS1282, operating from KPDX to Ontario International Airport (KONT), California. The aircraft was configured for 178 passenger seats and 6 crew members, with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 194,700 pounds. At the time of the event, the aircraft was carrying 171 passengers and 6 crew members.

1.3 Nature of the Flight and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted as an instrument flight rules (IFR) operation in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart U. The operator held an Air Carrier Certificate and Operations Specifications authorizing domestic scheduled passenger service. The flight was dispatched under standard Part 121 dispatch release procedures, with fuel load, alternate airport planning, and weight and balance calculations documented in the operator’s electronic flight bag system. The flight crew filed an IFR flight plan with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) prior to departure. All operational parameters, including crew duty time, aircraft airworthiness status, and maintenance release documentation, were verified as compliant with 14 CFR 121.533, 121.535, and 121.537 at the time of dispatch.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The pilot-in-command held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 2847193, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on October 12, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded as 10,247 hours, with 2,814 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The captain’s most recent line check was completed on November 18, 2023, with satisfactory performance documented across all evaluated maneuvers, including emergency descent procedures, rapid decompression response, and abnormal checklist execution.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The second-in-command held a Commercial Pilot certificate, certificate number 3198472, with airplane single-engine land, multiengine land, and Boeing 737 type ratings. The first officer possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on September 5, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded as 3,612 hours, with 1,189 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer’s most recent proficiency check was completed on December 3, 2023, with satisfactory performance documented in simulator-based emergency scenarios, including cabin depressurization, engine-out procedures, and crew resource management (CRM) protocols.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crew members met the recent flight experience requirements of 14 CFR 121.439, having completed three takeoffs and landings within the preceding 90 days. The operator’s training records indicate that both pilots completed recurrent training in accordance with 14 CFR 121.409 and 121.411 during the fourth quarter of 2023. Training modules included high-altitude emergency descent, rapid decompression recognition, oxygen system deployment, and checklist discipline under simulated stress conditions. The captain’s last simulator session included a scenario involving uncommanded cabin altitude increase at 15,000 feet, with performance evaluated against standard operating procedures (SOPs). The first officer’s training log reflects completion of a line-oriented flight training (LOFT) scenario on December 14, 2023, focusing on abnormal pressurization events and crew coordination. No training deficiencies or remedial actions were documented for either pilot in the 12 months preceding the event.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Airframe and Engine Specifications
The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 9, manufacturer serial number 44442, with a total airframe time of 1,214.6 hours and 892 cycles at the time of the event. The airframe was equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, serial numbers 892144 (left) and 892145 (right). The LEAP-1B powerplants were manufactured under the joint venture between GE Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines, with final assembly and certification conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 33. Engine time since new was 1,214.6 hours for both units, with no unscheduled removals or major overhauls recorded. The operator’s fleet includes multiple variants of the Boeing 737 family, including the BOEING 737-8, which shares commonality in flight deck architecture, systems logic, and maintenance program structure. Cross-fleet maintenance tracking and component interchangeability are managed through the operator’s centralized maintenance control system.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records indicate the aircraft was maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in compliance with 14 CFR 121.367. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check) was completed on August 22, 2023, at 1,089.2 hours. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were documented as complied with, including AD 2023-18-05, which addressed fuselage skin fastener inspection criteria for 737 MAX series aircraft. The left mid-exit door plug (designated as the 12L door plug per Boeing configuration documentation) was last inspected on September 14, 2023, during a scheduled cabin interior check. Maintenance log entries from that date indicate visual inspection of the door plug retention hardware, guide track alignment, and stop fitting engagement, with no discrepancies noted. No deferred maintenance items (DMIs) related to the door plug, pressurization system, or fuselage structure were active at the time of dispatch.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The aircraft was equipped with a dual-channel cabin pressurization system controlled by the cabin pressure controller (CPC), which regulates outflow valve position to maintain a maximum cabin altitude of 8,000 feet during cruise. The left mid-exit door plug is a non-operational exit configuration component installed in lieu of a functional emergency exit door. The plug assembly consists of a reinforced aluminum panel, four primary retention bolts, two guide tracks, and four stop fittings designed to transfer differential pressure loads to the surrounding fuselage frames. The plug is secured via a series of high-strength fasteners torqued to manufacturer specifications, with secondary retention provided by the guide track interface. The cabin altitude warning system is configured to activate at 10,000 feet cabin altitude, triggering an aural alert and automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks per 14 CFR 25.1447. The aircraft’s flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered intact and downloaded for parameter analysis.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Weather Conditions at the Time of the Accident
At the time of departure, surface conditions at KPDX were characterized by light winds, scattered cloud layers, and visibility exceeding 10 statute miles. During the climb phase, the aircraft encountered a transition from visual meteorological conditions (VMC) to instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) as it passed through 8,000 feet MSL. The ambient temperature at the event altitude of 16,000 feet was recorded as -14.2°C, consistent with the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) deviation of +1.8°C. Wind direction and speed at 16,000 feet were 265° at 28 knots, with no significant wind shear or turbulence reported by preceding traffic.

4.2 METAR/TAF Data and Pilot Reports
The KPDX METAR issued at 17:00 PST (01:00 UTC) read: KPDX 051700Z 10008KT 10SM FEW030 BKN050 08/02 A3012 RMK AO2 SLP198 T00830022. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) valid for the period indicated no significant weather changes, with ceilings remaining above 5,000 feet and visibility unrestricted. Pilot reports (PIREPs) filed by aircraft operating in the Portland terminal area between 16:30 and 17:15 PST indicated smooth air, light chop above 12,000 feet, and no convective activity. No SIGMETs or AIRMETs were active for the departure route or event location.

4.3 Atmospheric Conditions at Event Altitude
Atmospheric pressure at 16,000 feet MSL was approximately 16.8 inches of mercury (inHg), with a standard lapse rate of 2°C per 1,000 feet. The cabin differential pressure at the time of the event was calculated at 5.2 psi, based on FDR data and standard pressurization schedules. The rapid decompression event resulted in an immediate cabin altitude increase to approximately 14,800 feet within 3.2 seconds, triggering the cabin altitude warning system and automatic oxygen mask deployment. No meteorological phenomena, including icing, turbulence, or lightning, were identified as contributing factors to the structural event.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage during the climb phase and was recovered approximately 1.4 NM northwest of the event coordinates, in a residential area at 45.59°N, 122.73°W. The component was located on a residential roof with minimal secondary damage. The aircraft sustained localized fuselage damage along the left side, spanning frames 12 through 14, with tearing of the outer skin, deformation of the stringer structure, and exposure of the cabin insulation blanket. No other major structural components were displaced or separated. The aircraft landed with the damaged fuselage section intact, and post-flight inspection confirmed no loss of flight control functionality, hydraulic system integrity, or engine performance degradation.

5.2 Component Examination Findings
The recovered door plug was transported to a secure examination facility for detailed analysis. Visual inspection revealed that all four primary retention bolts were absent from their respective mounting holes. The bolt holes exhibited clean, unthreaded edges with no evidence of fatigue cracking or progressive failure. The guide tracks showed localized deformation consistent with uncommanded lateral displacement under differential pressure loading. The stop fittings remained attached to the fuselage structure, with no signs of overload fracture. Non-destructive inspection (NDI) using eddy current and ultrasonic methods confirmed no subsurface cracking in the surrounding fuselage skin or frame structure. Metallurgical analysis of the recovered fastener holes indicated that the bolt threads were intact, suggesting the fasteners were not installed or were improperly retained prior to flight.

5.3 Structural and Systems Analysis
Examination of the aircraft’s pressurization system revealed normal operation of the outflow valve and cabin pressure controller throughout the flight. The FDR recorded a sudden drop in cabin differential pressure from 5.2 psi to 0.1 psi within 1.8 seconds, followed by stabilization at 0.0 psi as the cabin equalized with ambient pressure. The emergency descent was initiated at 17:08:12 PST, with the aircraft descending to 10,000 feet MSL at a rate of approximately 4,200 feet per minute. The oxygen system deployed automatically, with mask deployment confirmed by cabin crew reports and FDR cabin altitude parameters. Post-flight inspection of the flight control surfaces, landing gear, and engine mounts revealed no anomalies attributable to the decompression event. The aircraft was subsequently grounded for detailed structural evaluation in accordance with manufacturer service bulletins and FAA guidance.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
The operator’s standard operating procedures for rapid decompression events are documented in the Flight Operations Manual (FOM), Section 4.12, and align with 14 CFR 121.310 and 121.311. The emergency descent checklist requires immediate donning of oxygen masks, establishment of crew communication, initiation of descent to 10,000 feet or minimum safe altitude, and declaration of emergency with air traffic control. Maintenance procedures for door plug inspection are governed by the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM), Chapter 52-40, which specifies torque values, fastener retention verification, and guide track alignment checks. The operator’s quality assurance program includes random audits of maintenance documentation, with compliance tracked through an electronic maintenance tracking system. All maintenance personnel involved in the aircraft’s recent inspections held valid FAA Airframe and Powerplant (A&P) certificates and were trained on Boeing 737 MAX series door plug configurations.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
Historical data indicate that door plug and exit door retention issues have been documented in previous Boeing 737 series aircraft, though the specific configuration of the mid-exit door plug is unique to the MAX 9 variant. The FAA issued Service Difficulty Reports (SDRs) in 2019 and 2021 referencing improper fastener installation on non-operational exit door plugs, resulting in corrective action through manufacturer service bulletins. In 2022, a similar event involving a different operator resulted in a cabin depressurization at 14,500 feet, with subsequent investigation identifying missing retention hardware. The manufacturer issued a fleet-wide inspection directive in response, requiring verification of all door plug fasteners and guide track engagement. The operator’s maintenance program incorporated these directives into its scheduled inspection intervals, with compliance documented in the aircraft’s maintenance log.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The design and certification of the aircraft’s fuselage structure and door plug system are governed by 14 CFR Part 25, specifically §25.365 (pressurized cabin loads), §25.783 (fuselage doors), and §25.1447 (equipment standards for supplemental oxygen). Advisory Circular AC 25.783-1 provides guidance on door retention mechanisms, fastener installation procedures, and inspection criteria for non-operational exit configurations. Maintenance and operational requirements are further defined under 14 CFR 121.367 (maintenance programs), 121.373 (airworthiness responsibility), and 121.409 (training requirements). The FAA’s Airworthiness Directive 2023-18-05 mandates enhanced inspection protocols for fuselage skin fasteners and door plug retention hardware on 737 MAX series aircraft. All applicable regulatory requirements were documented as met at the time of dispatch, with maintenance records, training logs, and operational checklists available for review. The investigation continues to examine component manufacturing records, maintenance documentation, and operational data to establish a complete factual record of the event.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the Structures and Materials Group of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in support of the investigation into the rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly, associated retention hardware, adjacent fuselage structure, and correlated flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) parameters. The physical examination and materials testing were conducted between January 10 and January 18, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with supplemental dimensional metrology performed at the Boeing Commercial Airplanes Everett facility under NTSB oversight.

Items examined included:
- Left mid-exit door plug frame assembly (Boeing P/N 65-12345-678, S/N 987654321)
- Twelve (12) retention fastener locations (four (4) fasteners unrecovered, eight (8) recovered)
- Guide track assemblies (upper and lower)
- Stop fitting brackets and fuselage doubler sections
- FDR/CVR data files (UTC timestamps 18:42:00 to 19:15:00)
- Maintenance documentation and work order records for the subject plug

All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) Chapter 4, Section 4.2, and referenced applicable Boeing Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-00-00, D6-13747 Structural Design Manual, and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Advisory Circular 25.571-1D. Measurements were recorded using calibrated digital micrometers (±0.0005 in), coordinate measuring machines (CMM), and optical profilometry. Material characterization followed ASTM E8/E8M-21, ASTM E1086-20, and AMS 2750E standards.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a derivative of the 737 MAX family certified under Type Certificate A16WE. The mid-exit door plug is a structural closure panel installed in lieu of an optional Type III emergency exit. The plug assembly consists of a machined 2024-T3 aluminum alloy frame, forward and aft guide tracks, upper and lower stop fittings, and twelve (12) titanium alloy retention bolts (AMS 5731, Ti-6Al-4V, P/N 65-12345-679) that secure the plug to the fuselage skin and underlying stringer structure. The design incorporates a pressure seal gasket, shear pins, and a mechanical interlock system intended to transfer cabin pressure loads to the primary fuselage structure.

The certification basis for the plug installation complies with 14 CFR Part 25, specifically Section 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure), which mandates that all pressurized fuselage components withstand limit load conditions without permanent deformation and ultimate load conditions without failure. The plug is rated for a maximum cabin differential pressure of 9.1 PSI, with a design safety factor of 1.5 applied to ultimate loads. The structural design is consistent with the baseline architecture utilized on the Boeing 737 MAX 8, with minor dimensional adaptations for the extended fuselage length of the MAX 9 variant.

The subject aircraft, manufacturer serial number 44442, was delivered to the operator in November 2023. At the time of the event, the airframe had accumulated 1,247 flight hours and 462 flight cycles. Maintenance records indicate that the left mid-exit door plug was removed on December 15, 2023, for cabin reconfiguration and reinstalled on December 22, 2023, under work order WO-2023-8841. The reinstallation procedure required torque verification of all twelve retention bolts to a specification of 180–200 in-lbs (15.0–16.7 ft-lbs), followed by a safety wire installation and a post-installation pressure test. The aircraft was returned to service on December 23, 2023, with no deferred maintenance items.

The propulsion system consists of two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines (GE Aviation P/N 123-456-789, S/N 555666777), each rated at 28,000 lbf thrust. The LEAP engine FADEC systems and associated nacelle structures were reviewed for potential contribution to aerodynamic or vibratory loading; no anomalies were identified. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airworthiness directives applicable to the 737 MAX series were current, and no outstanding service bulletins related to the mid-exit plug retention system were pending at the time of the event.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly revealed that the plug frame separated from the fuselage along the forward and aft guide track interfaces. The upper and lower stop fittings remained attached to the fuselage structure, while the plug frame, guide rails, and pressure seal gasket were recovered intact. Four (4) retention bolt locations (positions 3, 5, 8, and 10 per Boeing installation diagram 65-12345-680) were found empty, with no fasteners recovered. The remaining eight (8) bolts were recovered from the aircraft interior and surrounding debris field.

Dimensional metrology of the bolt holes in the plug frame and fuselage doublers indicated nominal diameters of 0.3125 in (5/16 in) with no evidence of elongation, galling, or thread stripping. However, witness mark analysis on the recovered fasteners revealed inconsistent torque application. Using a calibrated torque wrench (±2% accuracy) and thread engagement verification per NASM1312-11, the eight recovered bolts exhibited residual torque values ranging from 42 to 68 in-lbs, significantly below the specified 180–200 in-lbs range. No safety wire was present on any of the recovered fasteners.

Material characterization was performed on the plug frame, fuselage doubler, and recovered fasteners. Optical emission spectroscopy (OES) per ASTM E1086-20 confirmed the plug frame composition as 2024-T3 aluminum alloy (Cu: 4.4%, Mg: 1.5%, Mn: 0.6%, Fe: 0.5%, Si: 0.5%, balance Al). Hardness testing (Rockwell B scale) yielded values of 78–82 HRB, consistent with the T3 temper specification. The fuselage doubler material was identified as 7075-T6 aluminum alloy, with hardness values of 145–150 HRB. No evidence of intergranular corrosion, exfoliation, or stress corrosion cracking was observed.

Fractographic examination of the guide track mounting interfaces revealed clean, ductile overload separation features. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the bolt hole peripheries showed no fatigue striations, beach marks, or crack initiation sites. The separation morphology is consistent with a sudden, high-magnitude tensile and shear load event rather than progressive fatigue failure. The pressure seal gasket exhibited circumferential tearing and localized extrusion, indicative of rapid pressure equalization.

Test procedures included:
- Tensile testing of recovered fasteners per ASTM E8/E8M-21: Ultimate tensile strength averaged 132 ksi, yield strength 120 ksi, consistent with AMS 5731 Ti-6Al-4V specifications.
- Hardness mapping across the plug frame: Uniform distribution, no localized softening or heat-affected zones.
- Chemical analysis of fastener threads: No evidence of hydrogen embrittlement or galvanic corrosion.
- CMM mapping of guide track alignment: Forward track offset by 0.018 in aft of nominal, aft track offset by 0.022 in forward of nominal, exceeding the Boeing allowable tolerance of ±0.010 in.

Photographic documentation (NTSB-STR-2024-001 through 015) captures the recovered components, bolt hole conditions, torque verification setup, and fracture surface topography. All measurements and test results were recorded in the NTSB Laboratory Data Management System (LDMS) under case file 24-001-STR.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters were extracted from the solid-state memory unit and decoded using NTSB-approved software (FDR-Decode v4.2.1). The data stream was sampled at 1 Hz for cabin pressure parameters and 4 Hz for flight control and engine parameters. The following timeline was reconstructed from UTC timestamps:

18:42:15 – Takeoff roll initiated, runway 16L.
18:43:02 – Rotation, 145 KIAS.
18:43:45 – Gear retraction, 10,000 ft MSL.
18:44:10 – Cabin differential pressure (ΔP) begins scheduled increase, 0.0 PSI.
18:45:30 – ΔP reaches 4.2 PSI, cabin altitude 8,200 ft MSL.
18:46:12 – ΔP reaches 6.8 PSI, cabin altitude 11,400 ft MSL. Aircraft at 16,000 ft MSL, indicated airspeed 285 KIAS, vertical speed +1,800 fpm.
18:46:13 – Sudden ΔP drop to 0.2 PSI within 0.8 seconds. Cabin altitude spikes to 15,800 ft MSL.
18:46:14 – Vertical speed transient peaks at +2,400 fpm. Indicated airspeed decays to 240 KIAS. Pitch attitude increases to +12.5°.
18:46:18 – the Captain initiates emergency descent, thrust levers retarded to idle.
18:46:25 – ΔP stabilizes at 0.1 PSI. Cabin altitude 16,200 ft MSL.
18:47:00 – Aircraft levels at 10,000 ft MSL, airspeed 260 KIAS.

CVR audio analysis confirms an abrupt acoustic event at 18:46:13, characterized by a sharp bang followed by high-velocity wind noise and structural vibration. Crew coordination indicates immediate recognition of rapid decompression, with the pilot in command declaring an emergency and initiating the emergency descent checklist. No abnormal engine parameters, fire warnings, or system fault messages were recorded.

Engine performance data from the GE Aviation LEAP-1B FADEC systems (N1, EGT, FF, N2, VSV position) remained within normal operating envelopes throughout the climb and descent phases. At the time of the event, N1 was stable at 82.4%, EGT at 612°C, and fuel flow at 4,850 lbs/hr. No compressor surge, turbine overtemperature, or thrust rollback was detected. The LEAP engine vibration monitoring system (VMS) recorded a transient spike of 0.8 ips (inches per second) at 18:46:14, consistent with aerodynamic buffeting from the open fuselage aperture, not mechanical imbalance.

Comparison with normal operational parameters per the Boeing 737 MAX 8/9 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) indicates that the cabin pressurization schedule was functioning within design limits. The maximum allowable ΔP for the 737 MAX series is 9.1 PSI; the event occurred at 6.8 PSI, well below the structural limit. The rapid pressure equalization rate of 6.6 PSI/sec exceeds the FAA-certified venting rate of 0.5 PSI/sec, confirming an uncontrolled structural breach rather than a controlled outflow valve malfunction.

QAR/ACMS data corroborates the FDR timeline, with no discrepancies in altitude, airspeed, or engine parameters. The data indicates that the separation event was instantaneous and not preceded by abnormal structural vibrations, control surface oscillations, or pressurization system warnings. The absence of fatigue-related acoustic emission signatures in the FDR vibration channels further supports a sudden mechanical retention failure rather than progressive structural degradation.

5. SUMMARY

The examination and analysis of the left mid-exit door plug assembly, associated retention hardware, and flight data parameters yielded the following factual findings:

- The plug frame separated from the fuselage due to inadequate retention fastener installation. Four (4) of twelve (12) specified retention bolts were absent from their designated locations. The eight (8) recovered bolts exhibited residual torque values of 42–68 in-lbs, significantly below the manufacturer-specified range of 180–200 in-lbs.
- No safety wire was installed on any of the recovered fasteners, contrary to Boeing installation procedure 65-12345-680.
- Dimensional metrology revealed guide track misalignment exceeding allowable tolerances (±0.010 in), with forward and aft tracks offset by 0.018 in and 0.022 in, respectively.
- Material characterization confirmed that the plug frame (2024-T3 aluminum), fuselage doublers (7075-T6 aluminum), and retention fasteners (Ti-6Al-4V) met all applicable chemical, mechanical, and hardness specifications. No evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, hydrogen embrittlement, or manufacturing defects was identified.
- Fractographic analysis of the separation interfaces revealed ductile overload features consistent with sudden tensile and shear loading. No fatigue initiation sites or progressive crack propagation were observed.
- FDR data indicates that the cabin differential pressure at the time of separation was 6.8 PSI, well within the certified limit of 9.1 PSI. The pressure equalization rate of 6.6 PSI/sec confirms an uncontrolled structural breach.
- Engine performance parameters from the GE Aviation LEAP-1B turbofans remained within normal operating limits. No thrust anomalies, compressor stalls, or mechanical vibrations contributed to the event.
- The aircraft's pressurization system operated in accordance with the Boeing 737 MAX 8/9 FCOM schedule. The outflow valve, cabin pressure controller, and safety relief valves functioned nominally prior to the structural breach.
- The structural design of the mid-exit door plug complies with Section 25.571 damage-tolerance requirements. The failure mode is attributable to improper fastener retention rather than inherent design deficiency or material degradation.
- The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airworthiness directives and operator maintenance records were current. The reinstallation work order (WO-2023-8841) did not include documented torque verification or post-installation pressure test results.

All findings are based on physical examination, materials testing, dimensional metrology, and flight data analysis. No operational, environmental, or aerodynamic factors were identified that contributed to the separation event. The data supports a factual conclusion that the rapid decompression resulted from the loss of mechanical retention of the left mid-exit door plug assembly.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS VANCE, SENIOR MAINTENANCE QUALITY AUDITOR
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 10:30 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Seattle, Washington
Interviewer: Investigator J. Reynolds, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety

Q: Mr. Vance, thank you for coming in today. For the record, please state your full name, your current position, and your relationship to the flight in question.

A: Yeah, sure. Marcus Vance. I’m a Senior Maintenance Quality Auditor for the airline. I’ve been with the company for, uh, twenty-two years now. Mostly line maintenance, moved into quality assurance and audit about six years ago. As for the flight... I was a revenue passenger on Flight 1282. I was traveling from Portland to Ontario, California. Seat 24A, left side, just forward of the wing.

Q: Understood. Can you walk me through the departure and initial climb? Approximate times, if you recall.

A: Yeah. We pushed back from the gate at... I want to say 16:42, maybe 16:43 local time. Engine start was normal. I could hear the LEAP-1Bs spooling up, that distinct high-pitched whine you get on the MAX series. Taxi was uneventful. We lined up on 28L, took off at approximately 16:48. Climb was smooth. I was actually reviewing some internal audit checklists on my tablet, so I wasn’t really paying close attention to the flight deck or the cabin initially. We were climbing through... I’d guess 14,000, maybe 15,000 feet. The seatbelt sign was still on. Then, at about 16:56, it happened.

Q: Describe the event as you experienced it. What did you see, hear, feel?

A: It was... instantaneous. There was a massive bang. Not like an engine backfire or a tire blowout. It was a structural, almost explosive sound. The whole cabin just... depressurized. I felt the pressure drop in my ears immediately, like when you’re diving into a pool but way more violent. The temperature plummeted. I mean, within seconds it was freezing. I looked out the window, and the left mid-exit door plug was just... gone. Completely gone. The frame was exposed to the slipstream. There was a violent rush of air, like a freight train roaring through the cabin. Oxygen masks dropped everywhere. I saw a phone, a jacket, maybe a seat cushion just get pulled out into the slipstream. It was... it was chaotic, but it only lasted a few seconds before the initial pressure equalized.

Q: How did the flight crew respond?

A: The pilot in command... I didn’t see him, obviously, but the PA came on maybe thirty to forty seconds later. His voice was calm, but you could hear the background wind noise. He announced an emergency descent, told us to secure our oxygen masks, and that we were returning to Portland. The aircraft banked left, I think, to get back on course. The flight attendants were already moving. They were checking passengers, securing the cabin, making sure everyone had their masks on. It was... honestly, it was textbook. Given the circumstances, they handled it exactly how they’re trained to.

Q: From your maintenance background, what are your initial thoughts on how a door plug could separate in flight?

A: Well, I’m not a structures engineer, but I’ve worked on the MAX line for years, and I’ve audited the door installation procedures. The plug doors aren’t like the main entry doors. They don’t have the same locking mechanisms. They’re held in by guide tracks, stop fittings, and a series of retention bolts. The cabin pressure actually seats them tighter once you’re at altitude. For it to blow out like that... it suggests the retention hardware wasn’t properly torqued, or the stop fittings weren’t fully engaged. I know the Federal Aviation Administration has been looking at the assembly process, and rightfully so. There’s a whole section in Advisory Circular 120-16G about cabin pressure integrity and maintenance documentation, but honestly, this feels like a workmanship or quality control issue, not a fundamental design flaw. The damage tolerance requirements for the fuselage are pretty strict, but they assume the door is actually installed correctly. If the bolts aren’t there, the pressure just pushes it out.

Q: Can you elaborate on the damage tolerance requirements you mentioned?

A: Sure. Basically, the airframe has to be designed to sustain a certain level of damage—cracks, fatigue, minor impacts—without catastrophic failure. It’s a fail-safe philosophy. But that’s for material degradation over time. A missing door plug isn’t a fatigue crack. It’s a missing component. The structure around it... I mean, the fuselage skin is designed to handle the loads, but the plug itself is just a panel. If the installation isn’t verified, the structure can’t compensate for it. I’ve seen similar issues on older 737s, but never on a MAX. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 uses the same basic door plug design, right? Or at least similar. I think the MAX 9 has a slightly different configuration for the mid-exit, but the principle is the same. The engineering is sound. The execution... that’s what we need to look at.

Q: Were the engines operating normally during the event?

A: Yeah, the LEAP-1Bs were running fine. I could hear them through the wind noise. No surging, no vibration, no unusual EGT spikes that I could tell. GE Aviation has a solid track record with those engines, and I didn’t notice any engine-related issues. The decompression was purely from the door. The aircraft handled the aerodynamic loads well, which tells me the flight control computers and the airframe itself were doing their job.

Q: How long was the descent and return?

A: Maybe... fifteen, twenty minutes? We leveled off around 10,000 feet, then continued back to PDX. The cabin was freezing, obviously. People were using the oxygen masks. I helped a woman in 24B get hers on. She was hyperventilating, pretty shaken up. The flight attendants were incredible. We landed safely around 17:28. Taxi to the gate, emergency slides deployed on the right side, I think. Everyone got off. No serious injuries, just some minor cuts from debris and a lot of shock.

Q: Is there anything else you observed or would like to add for the record?

A: Just... the sheer force of it. I’ve been in aviation for over two decades. I’ve seen engine failures, hard landings, severe turbulence, but nothing like that. The fact that the PIC handled it so well, and the crew managed the cabin... it’s a testament to training. But the root cause... it’s going to come down to the assembly line. I know the FAA is grounding the fleet, which is the right call. They need to inspect every single plug door. Torque marks, retention bolts, the whole works. I hope the investigation looks at the quality control process. Not just the mechanics, but the sign-off chain. Sometimes things get rushed. I’m not saying that happened here, but... it’s a possibility. The aircraft is safe when maintained properly. The MAX 8, the MAX 9, they’re good airplanes. But you can’t bypass the basics.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Vance. We’ll follow up if we need clarification on any of the maintenance procedures you referenced.

A: Yeah, of course. I’ll be available. Just... let me know if you need the audit logs or the specific work order references. I can pull those up.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND COMPLIANCE REPORT
DOCKET NO. FAA-2024-0112 | NTSB ACCIDENT NO. DCA24MA056
DATE: March 15, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) & Flight Standards Service (AFS)
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO RAPID DECOMPRESSION EVENT INVOLVING BOEING 737 MAX 9 AIRCRAFT

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the formal regulatory response and compliance assessment regarding the in-flight rapid decompression event that occurred on January 5, 2024, involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registered N704AL, operated under 14 CFR Part 121. The event is referenced under NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA056. This correspondence addresses compliance with Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-02-09, issued under Docket No. FAA-2024-0112, and responds to preliminary NTSB Safety Recommendations A-24-01 through A-24-03. The regulatory framework governing this response is anchored in 14 CFR Part 21 (Certification Procedures for Products and Parts), 14 CFR Part 25 (Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes), and 14 CFR Part 121 (Operating Requirements: Domestic, Flag, and Supplemental Operations).

2. BACKGROUND
The subject aircraft, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, was manufactured under Type Certificate No. T00001SE and operates under an approved Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and Operations Specifications. The incident occurred during initial climb at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) following departure from a Pacific Northwest airport. The left mid-exit door plug, a non-egress fuselage panel installed in lieu of an emergency exit, experienced catastrophic structural separation, resulting in rapid cabin decompression. The flight crew, under the command of the Captain, executed emergency descent procedures in strict accordance with 14 CFR § 121.333 and the approved Quick Reference Handbook (QRH), ultimately diverting to a suitable alternate airport without further incident or loss of life.

Historically, the Boeing 737 MAX family, including the BOEING 737-8 and MAX 9 variants, received amended type certification following extensive review of flight control system modifications and structural integrity parameters under 14 CFR § 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure). The door plug configuration was approved via Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) processes and incorporated into the original type design under 14 CFR § 25.783 (Fuselage Doors). Prior to this event, the Federal Aviation Administration had issued multiple airworthiness directives addressing manufacturing quality control and fastener torque verification for fuselage panels, notably AD 2023-18-05. However, the specific failure mode observed on January 5, 2024, revealed latent deficiencies in the production acceptance criteria and post-delivery maintenance verification protocols.

The propulsion system, comprising CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, remained fully operational throughout the event. While GE Aviation, as a principal partner in the LEAP-1B program, maintains strict compliance with 14 CFR Part 33 (Airworthiness Standards: Aircraft Engines), the structural separation event necessitated a comprehensive review of airframe-to-engine interface loads and secondary structural fatigue parameters. The FAA initiated immediate oversight actions under 14 CFR § 121.373 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations) to evaluate operator compliance with manufacturer service bulletins and mandatory inspection intervals.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive regulatory audit of the operator’s maintenance program, manufacturer production records, and certification documentation has been completed. The analysis yields the following determinations:

a. Compliance Status: The operator demonstrated substantial compliance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations). Maintenance records indicate adherence to the approved Aircraft Maintenance Program (AMP) and compliance with all applicable Airworthiness Directives prior to the event. However, the manufacturer’s production quality assurance system exhibited a critical deviation from 14 CFR § 21.137 (Quality System) requirements. Specifically, torque verification logs for the mid-exit door plug retention hardware were incomplete, and final inspection sign-offs lacked traceable conformity to the approved engineering data. This constitutes a violation of 14 CFR § 21.125 (Responsibility of Type Certificate Holder) and 14 CFR § 21.173 (Quality System).

b. Regulatory Oversight Actions: The Federal Aviation Administration immediately issued Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2024-02-09, mandating repetitive inspections of all affected door plug installations across the 737 MAX fleet. Oversight personnel from the Aircraft Evaluation Group (AEG) and Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) conducted unannounced ramp inspections and maintenance facility audits. The Captain’s operational response was evaluated against 14 CFR § 121.547 (Pilot in Command Authority) and found to be exemplary, with no regulatory deficiencies identified in crew resource management or emergency procedure execution.

c. Gaps in Regulatory Framework: The investigation identified systemic vulnerabilities in the delegation of authority under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart J (Organization Designation Authorization). The current framework permits Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) holders to self-certify certain production conformity inspections, which, in this instance, allowed non-conforming hardware installation to proceed without independent Federal Aviation Administration verification. Furthermore, the MMEL provisions for door plug structural integrity do not adequately address in-flight separation scenarios, necessitating a revision to 14 CFR § 25.783 and associated advisory circulars. The structural commonality between the BOEING 737-8 and MAX 9 variants requires harmonized inspection protocols to prevent cross-fleet oversight fragmentation.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings outlined herein, the following corrective actions, compliance timelines, and oversight measures are mandated:

a. Corrective Actions Required:
i. The type certificate holder shall implement a mandatory, non-delegated inspection protocol for all mid-exit door plug retention hardware, in accordance with revised engineering data approved under 14 CFR § 21.99. All torque values shall be verified using calibrated instrumentation, with results documented in the aircraft permanent maintenance records per 14 CFR § 43.9.
ii. Operators shall revise their approved maintenance programs to incorporate enhanced structural integrity monitoring, including eddy current and ultrasonic testing of door plug attachment points, as specified in Service Bulletin 737-53A1234.
iii. The Federal Aviation Administration shall initiate rulemaking to amend 14 CFR § 21.137, restricting ODA self-certification privileges for critical structural fasteners and fuselage pressure boundary components.

b. Timeline for Compliance:
i. Initial fleet-wide inspections shall be completed within 14 calendar days of AD 2024-02-09 issuance.
ii. Permanent engineering modifications and revised maintenance program approvals shall be submitted to the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) within 90 days.
iii. Full compliance with revised ODA delegation limitations shall be implemented no later than 180 days from the effective date of this directive.

c. Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule:
i. The FAA shall conduct quarterly compliance audits of the manufacturer’s production quality system and operator maintenance facilities for a period of 24 months.
ii. A joint NTSB-FAA technical review board shall convene biannually to assess the efficacy of corrective actions and evaluate emerging fatigue data related to the LEAP-1B engine mounting structure and adjacent fuselage panels.
iii. The Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) shall be revised within 120 days to explicitly address door plug structural anomalies, ensuring alignment with 14 CFR Part 121.344 (Minimum Equipment List) and operational safety thresholds.

This regulatory response is issued under the authority of the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, in accordance with 49 U.S.C. § 44701 et seq. All affected parties are directed to acknowledge receipt and submit compliance documentation to the designated Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) and Principal Operations Inspector (POI) within the prescribed timelines. Failure to comply shall result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR Part 13.

HEADLINE: Mid-Air Door Plug Separation Forces Emergency Landing of Boeing 737 MAX 9; All Aboard Survive

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: PORTLAND, Ore. —

A commercial airliner operated by a major U.S. carrier suffered a catastrophic mid-air failure on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, when a fuselage door plug tore away during climb, triggering a rapid decompression event at 16,000 feet. The Boeing 737 MAX 9, which had departed from Portland International Airport bound for Ontario, California, executed an emergency return and landed safely with no fatalities reported among the 171 passengers and six crew members aboard.

The sudden breach in the aircraft’s pressurized cabin caused oxygen masks to deploy instantly and sent loose items, including personal electronics and clothing, flying toward the opening. Pilots initiated an emergency descent to a breathable altitude, navigating the compromised jet back to Portland within minutes. The incident has prompted immediate regulatory scrutiny and a temporary grounding of similarly configured aircraft across the country as investigators race to determine how a critical structural component detached in flight.

“We are treating this as a top-priority investigation,” said National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy in a Saturday press briefing. “Our go-team is on the ground, and we have already recovered the missing door plug from a residential backyard. Preliminary data indicates a failure in the retention hardware, but we will not speculate until the metallurgical and engineering analysis is complete.” While the NTSB’s initial focus centers on the retention hardware, independent aerospace structural engineer Dr. Elena Rostova suggested that inconsistencies in the final assembly torque procedures could have played an equally critical role, emphasizing that both component integrity and installation protocols warrant parallel examination. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) swiftly issued an emergency airworthiness directive, halting operations of 171 similarly configured aircraft. “Safety is our absolute priority,” an FAA spokesperson stated. “We are working closely with the manufacturer and the operator to ensure every affected jet meets stringent airworthiness standards before returning to service.” The airline’s chief communications officer released a brief statement expressing relief that all passengers and crew were unharmed and pledging full cooperation with federal investigators.

1. INTRODUCTION
This submission is presented by the Engineering and Maintenance Division of the operating carrier, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event. Our organization’s role in this investigation encompasses the provision of operational telemetry, maintenance tracking records, crew performance documentation, and post-event fleet inspection results. The scope of this document is to present a technical assessment of the factors contributing to the separation of the left mid-exit door plug, evaluate the adequacy of existing maintenance and quality assurance protocols, and outline evidence-based recommendations for systemic safety improvements. While the investigation remains active, our analysis draws upon flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts, maintenance logs, and structural engineering evaluations to establish a clear, fact-based position. We recognize the inherent complexity of modern aircraft certification, production ecosystems, and maintenance handoffs, and this submission is intended to support the NTSB’s mandate to identify causal factors and advance aviation safety through transparent, data-driven analysis.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, departed a Pacific Northwest airport on a scheduled domestic flight. During climb, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the aircraft experienced a sudden, uncommanded rapid decompression event. The left mid-exit door plug, an optional fuselage component installed in lieu of a standard passenger door, separated from the airframe. The aircraft’s pressurization system responded as designed, and the flight crew executed emergency descent and diversion procedures in accordance with established protocols. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport with no injuries to passengers or crew.

Docket materials, including the NTSB’s preliminary factual report and our internal maintenance tracking system, confirm that the aircraft had been delivered to our fleet approximately two months prior to the event. The mid-exit door plug configuration was installed during final assembly and subsequently verified during post-delivery acceptance checks. Maintenance records indicate that the aircraft underwent a routine scheduled inspection within the preceding 30 days, with no discrepancies logged for the door plug retention system. However, subsequent teardown and forensic examination of the recovered door plug and surrounding fuselage structure revealed that multiple retention fasteners were either improperly torqued or entirely absent from their designated guide tracks. The absence of these fasteners directly compromised the structural integrity of the plug retention mechanism under normal pressurization loads.

Flight data confirms that the aircraft was operating within certified envelope parameters at the time of the event. The Captain, supported by the first officer, immediately recognized the decompression, donned oxygen masks, initiated the emergency descent checklist, and communicated with air traffic control. CVR transcripts reflect disciplined crew resource management and adherence to standard operating procedures. Engine performance data, monitored via the aircraft’s health management system, showed nominal operation of both CFM International LEAP-1B turbofans throughout the flight. General Electric Aviation’s engine health monitoring protocols, which are integrated into our predictive maintenance framework, recorded no anomalies that would suggest a contributing mechanical or aerodynamic disturbance. The event was isolated to the fuselage door plug retention system, with no evidence of secondary structural damage or systems failure.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS
The separation of the mid-exit door plug represents a failure of the retention hardware installation and verification process, rather than a fundamental design deficiency. The door plug system is engineered to withstand maximum differential pressure loads as defined by the aircraft’s type certification basis. Under Section 25.571 of the Federal Aviation Regulations, the airframe must demonstrate damage tolerance and fatigue resistance under repeated pressurization cycles. The plug’s retention mechanism, comprising guide tracks, stop fittings, and high-strength fasteners, is designed to distribute structural loads across the fuselage skin and frame. When properly installed and torqued to specification, the system provides redundant load paths that prevent uncommanded separation.

Forensic analysis of the recovered hardware indicates that the primary failure mode was the absence or improper seating of critical retention bolts. Torque verification logs from the final assembly and post-delivery maintenance phases show inconsistencies in documentation, with several fastener locations lacking digital torque confirmation or secondary inspector sign-off. This gap in quality assurance allowed improperly installed hardware to enter service. The engineering data aligns with established industry standards for structural fastener installation, which require calibrated torque tools, cross-verification by independent technicians, and traceable digital records. Our review of comparable fleet data, including the BOEING 737-8, which utilizes a different door configuration but shares similar maintenance philosophies, demonstrates that rigorous adherence to these standards effectively mitigates retention hardware failures.

The operational environment during the event further supports the conclusion that the failure was installation-related rather than load-induced. FDR data indicates that the aircraft was climbing at a standard rate, with cabin differential pressure increasing predictably. At 16,000 feet, the pressure differential was approximately 4.2 psi, well within the certified operational envelope. The sudden loss of pressurization occurred without preceding structural warnings, vibration anomalies, or aerodynamic disturbances. This profile is consistent with a sudden mechanical release rather than progressive fatigue or overload.

From a human factors and maintenance management perspective, the incident highlights vulnerabilities in the handoff between manufacturing final assembly and operator acceptance. While our maintenance program complies with Advisory Circular 120-16G, which outlines requirements for maintenance program development and reliability tracking, the integration of manufacturer-supplied documentation into our digital maintenance tracking system revealed discrepancies in fastener installation records. The absence of a unified, real-time verification protocol for optional equipment installations created a latent condition that remained undetected until the event.

It is also important to acknowledge the broader production ecosystem. The LEAP engine program, managed by CFM International with significant contributions from General Electric Aviation, exemplifies a mature, highly controlled manufacturing and quality assurance environment. The contrast between the engine program’s rigorous torque verification, digital twin tracking, and supplier quality gates and the door plug installation process underscores the need for standardized quality management across all airframe subsystems. The FAA’s oversight framework, while robust, relies heavily on delegated authority and manufacturer self-certification for certain production phases. This incident demonstrates that optional equipment installations, particularly those involving structural retention hardware, require enhanced independent verification and regulatory alignment.

4. CONCLUSIONS
Based on the available evidence, our technical position is that the rapid decompression event was caused by the improper installation and inadequate verification of retention fasteners on the left mid-exit door plug. The failure was not attributable to aerodynamic loading, material fatigue, or systems malfunction, but rather to a breakdown in the quality assurance and documentation processes during final assembly and post-delivery maintenance. The absence of redundant torque verification, coupled with inconsistent digital record-keeping, allowed improperly secured hardware to enter service.

We recognize that modern aircraft production involves complex supply chains, delegated certification authorities, and rapid delivery schedules. However, the fundamental principles of structural integrity and maintenance traceability must remain uncompromised. The Captain’s professional response and the aircraft’s inherent design redundancy prevented a catastrophic outcome, but the event exposes systemic vulnerabilities in how optional structural components are installed, verified, and tracked.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Implementation of mandatory, digitally logged torque verification for all structural retention fasteners, with independent cross-check requirements.
- Standardization of quality assurance protocols for optional equipment installations across all production and maintenance facilities.
- Enhanced regulatory oversight of manufacturer-to-operator handoff documentation, particularly for structural components subject to pressurization loads.
- Integration of real-time structural health monitoring for door plug retention systems, utilizing strain gauges and acoustic emission sensors to detect early-stage hardware degradation or loosening.
- Development of a unified industry standard for fastener installation verification, aligned with best practices from high-reliability programs such as the LEAP engine manufacturing ecosystem.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS
In immediate response to the event, our organization grounded the affected aircraft type and initiated a comprehensive fleet-wide inspection program. All mid-exit door plugs were subjected to 100% physical inspection, torque verification, and digital documentation review. Any discrepancies were corrected in accordance with manufacturer service bulletins and FAA airworthiness directives. We have also implemented enhanced technician training focused on structural fastener installation, torque tool calibration, and quality assurance documentation.

To address systemic vulnerabilities, we have revised our maintenance program to incorporate mandatory dual-inspector verification for all structural retention hardware. Our digital maintenance tracking system has been upgraded to require photographic evidence and calibrated torque data for each fastener location, with automated alerts for missing or out-of-specification entries. We have established a joint quality review board with the manufacturer and regulatory representatives to audit production and maintenance handoff processes, ensuring alignment with Section 25.571 damage tolerance requirements and AC 120-16G maintenance program standards.

Looking forward, we propose the development of a standardized, industry-wide fastener verification protocol that integrates digital twin technology, blockchain-enabled maintenance records, and real-time telemetry for critical structural components. We will continue to collaborate with the FAA, the manufacturer, and labor organizations to refine training curricula, enhance quality management systems, and promote a culture of proactive safety reporting. Our commitment to operational excellence and passenger safety remains absolute, and we will continue to support the NTSB’s investigation with full transparency and technical rigor.

TO: All Maintenance Stations, Line Operations, Quality Assurance, Engineering Support
FROM: Director of Airworthiness & Maintenance Engineering, Pacific Northwest Division
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2024-007: Mid-Exit Door Plug Retention Hardware Inspection & Torque Verification
REF: FAA AD 2024-02-51, Internal QA Bulletin 2023-114, WO-737-9901 Series, MTS Event Code DOOR-PLUG-01

PURPOSE:
Issue immediate directive for 100% inspection of mid-cabin exit door plug retention hardware across the 737 MAX fleet. Establish standardized torque verification, documentation, and reporting protocols. Ensure compliance with emerging regulatory guidance and internal airworthiness standards.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event when the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage during climb through 16,000 feet. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport. Preliminary data indicates missing or improperly torqued retention bolts on the plug assembly. While this event involved the MAX 9 variant, our active fleet includes the Boeing 737 MAX 8, which utilizes identical door plug architecture, fastener specifications, and pressure boundary design. The Federal Aviation Administration has issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive mandating immediate inspections. Our internal review aligns with 14 CFR 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure) and Advisory Circular 120-16G (Air Carrier Maintenance Programs), which require proactive identification of structural fastener anomalies before they compromise pressure boundary integrity. Initial crew reports, including statements from the Captain regarding abnormal cabin pressure indications and wind noise prior to the event, underscore the need for rigorous hardware verification. Additionally, while the propulsion systems remain unaffected, General Electric Aviation has issued a parallel service bulletin for concurrent inspection of adjacent pylon-to-wing interface fasteners on aircraft equipped with the LEAP engine to ensure no secondary structural stress propagation occurred during the decompression event.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all maintenance personnel shall execute the following procedures for every 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 in the active fleet:

1. Hardware Identification & Access:
   - Locate mid-exit door plug retention bolts per AMM Chapter 53-10-00.
   - Reference Part Number (P/N) 737-900-PLG-BOLT-04A and associated locknuts (P/N 737-900-PLG-NUT-02B).
   - Remove interior trim panels per Work Order WO-737-8842-REV3.

2. Torque Verification & Inspection:
   - Verify torque on all 12 primary retention bolts using calibrated digital torque wrenches (Tool ID: TW-4400 series, calibration valid within 30 days).
   - Target torque: 185 ± 5 in-lbs.
   - Inspect for missing bolts, improper safety wiring, cracked washers, or evidence of fretting/corrosion.
   - Document all findings in the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS) under Event Code: DOOR-PLUG-01.

3. Corrective Action Thresholds:
   - Any bolt reading below 175 in-lbs or above 195 in-lbs requires immediate replacement.
   - Missing hardware triggers a Ground Stop for that aircraft until Engineering issues a disposition.
   - All replaced fasteners must be batch-tracked and logged per QA Form 88-12.

4. Documentation & Traceability:
   - Complete QA Checklist 2024-007A for each aircraft.
   - Upload high-resolution photos of each bolt head and torque wrench readout to the Digital Maintenance Archive (DMA) folder: /QA/2024/DOOR_PLUG_INSPECTION.
   - Cross-reference with the aircraft’s original build records to verify factory torque sign-offs.

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Line Maintenance Supervisors: Initiate inspections on all parked aircraft within 24 hours of receipt. Prioritize aircraft with >500 flight cycles since last heavy maintenance.
- Base Maintenance Planners: Schedule all active aircraft for inspection within 72 hours. Coordinate with Flight Operations to minimize schedule disruption.
- Quality Assurance Auditors: Conduct random spot-checks on 15% of completed inspections. Verify torque tool calibration logs and MTS entries. Report discrepancies to the Airworthiness Office within 4 hours.
- Training Department: Distribute updated Quick Reference Card (QRC-737-PLUG-01) to all A&P technicians by EOD January 14. Conduct mandatory 30-minute virtual briefing on revised torque procedures and documentation standards.
- Engineering Support: Review all non-conforming findings. Issue structural disposition within 12 hours of report submission. Coordinate with Boeing and the FAA for any fleet-wide engineering changes.
- Compliance Deadline: 100% of the 737 MAX fleet must be inspected, documented, and cleared by January 19, 2024, 23:59 PST.
- Reporting: Submit daily completion status to the Maintenance Control Center (MCC) via the Fleet Readiness Dashboard. Any aircraft failing inspection must be grounded immediately and reported to the Director of Airworthiness.

This alert supersedes all prior guidance regarding mid-cabin door plug maintenance. Failure to comply will result in immediate suspension of maintenance privileges and potential regulatory action. Direct all technical questions to the Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or the Quality Assurance Hotline (Ext. 5512).

SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:15 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft operated by a major U.S. commercial carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during initial climb. The incident occurred at an altitude of approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level following departure from a Pacific Northwest regional airport. Preliminary information indicates that the left mid-cabin exit door plug separated from the fuselage structure, resulting in cabin depressurization and minor injuries to several occupants. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident, and there were no fatalities.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information has been compiled from initial data downloads, maintenance records, and preliminary interviews with flight and cabin crew members. Initial information indicates that the aircraft departed normally, with no reported anomalies during preflight inspections or engine start sequences. During the climb phase, at approximately 16,000 feet, the flight crew reported a sudden loud noise followed by a rapid loss of cabin pressure. Oxygen masks deployed automatically, and the crew initiated standard emergency descent procedures.

Initial witness accounts from passengers seated in the vicinity of the left mid-cabin exit row describe a sudden explosive sound, followed by a rush of air and the apparent absence of the door plug structure. Several occupants reported minor injuries consistent with rapid decompression, including ear discomfort and superficial lacerations from loose cabin items. No serious injuries or fatalities have been reported.

Meteorological data obtained from the departure airport and surrounding National Weather Service stations indicate that weather conditions at the time of the event were generally favorable for flight operations. Surface winds were light and variable, visibility exceeded 10 statute miles, and cloud cover was scattered at approximately 4,000 feet above ground level. No significant convective activity, turbulence, or icing conditions were reported along the initial departure route.

Preliminary damage assessment, based on initial photographs and post-flight visual inspection, reveals a complete separation of the left mid-exit door plug from the fuselage. The surrounding fuselage skin, window frames, and adjacent structural members exhibit localized deformation and fastener displacement. Interior cabin components in the immediate vicinity, including overhead bins, seat tracks, and sidewall panels, sustained secondary damage consistent with rapid pressure differential and aerodynamic forces. The aircraft’s primary flight control systems, hydraulic systems, and electrical buses remained operational throughout the event.

It should be noted that the aircraft involved is equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured under the oversight of General Electric Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines. Preliminary examination of engine parameters and maintenance logs indicates normal performance throughout the flight, with no recorded exceedances or fault indications. While the primary focus of this investigation remains the door plug separation, comparative data from the broader Boeing 737 family, including the BOEING 737-8 variant, will be reviewed to assess common design features, manufacturing processes, and maintenance protocols. All preliminary observations are subject to revision as additional data is recovered and analyzed.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has initiated a formal investigation and activated the following investigative groups: Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Maintenance Records. Each group has been tasked with collecting, preserving, and analyzing relevant data within their respective disciplines. The investigation is being conducted in accordance with NTSB protocols and applicable federal regulations.

Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and relevant labor organizations. All parties have been briefed on their roles, responsibilities, and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding investigative materials. The NTSB has established a secure evidence repository at the departure airport and has coordinated with local law enforcement to secure the perimeter and preserve the accident site.

Evidence secured to date includes the aircraft’s flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), which have been successfully downloaded and are undergoing preliminary data validation. Maintenance logs, work orders, and component tracking records for the affected door plug and surrounding structure have been obtained. The separated door plug and associated hardware have been recovered and transported to a secure NTSB facility for detailed forensic examination. Additional evidence includes passenger and crew statements, air traffic control recordings, and meteorological data.

Planned examinations include a comprehensive metallurgical and structural analysis of the recovered door plug, fastener inspection, and non-destructive testing of the fuselage attachment points. The FDR and CVR data will be cross-referenced with maintenance history and operational parameters to establish a timeline of events. The Powerplants group will conduct a detailed review of the LEAP-1B engine performance data, while the Structures group will evaluate the door plug installation procedures and quality control documentation. All examinations will be conducted under controlled conditions, with findings documented and subject to peer review.

NEXT STEPS
The investigative teams will continue to process and analyze the secured evidence, with a focus on reconstructing the sequence of events leading to the door plug separation. Additional interviews with maintenance personnel, quality assurance inspectors, and manufacturing representatives will be scheduled to clarify installation and inspection protocols. The NTSB will coordinate with the aircraft manufacturer to review engineering drawings, service bulletins, and airworthiness directives relevant to the mid-exit door plug configuration.

A preliminary data review meeting is scheduled within the next 30 days to consolidate initial findings and identify any emerging safety concerns. The investigation will proceed through the standard phases of evidence collection, analysis, testing, and reporting. As the investigation progresses, the NTSB will issue periodic updates to the public and relevant stakeholders. A final report, including factual findings, analysis, and safety recommendations, will be issued upon completion of all investigative activities.

It is emphasized that all information contained in this document is preliminary and subject to change. No determination of probable cause or contributing factors has been made at this time. The investigation remains ongoing, and all conclusions will be based on a comprehensive review of all available evidence.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date and Time
On January 5, 2024, at 17:12:34 Pacific Standard Time (PST), the accident flight departed from Portland International Airport (KPDX), Portland, Oregon. At 17:28:15 PST, while climbing through approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL), the flight crew experienced a rapid decompression event. The aircraft subsequently initiated a descent and returned to KPDX, landing at 17:52:08 PST. The total flight duration was 39 minutes and 34 seconds.

1.2 Location
The departure airport is located at latitude 45°35′19″N, longitude 122°35′52″W, with a field elevation of 31 feet MSL. The rapid decompression event occurred at approximately latitude 45°48′12″N, longitude 122°41′05″W, over the Willamette Valley region of Oregon. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a filed route to Ontario, California.

1.3 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufacturer serial number 44450, registered as N704XX. The aircraft was owned and operated by a major U.S. scheduled air carrier holding a valid Air Carrier Certificate issued under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The operator maintained the aircraft under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP).

1.4 Nature of Flight
The flight was a scheduled domestic passenger operation conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121. The flight manifest indicated 171 passengers and 6 crewmembers on board. The flight was dispatched under standard operational control procedures, with all required documentation, weight and balance calculations, and fuel load records completed prior to departure.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain
The Captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The Captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on November 12, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 8,472 hours, with 1,214 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The Captain had completed 42 flight hours in the 30 days preceding the accident and 118 flight hours in the 90 days preceding the accident.

2.2 First Officer
