The First Officer held an ATP certificate with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. A first-class medical certificate was issued on October 3, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 3,188 hours, with 792 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The First Officer had accumulated 38 flight hours in the preceding 30 days and 104 flight hours in the preceding 90 days.

2.3 Training and Qualifications
Both flight crewmembers had successfully completed the operator’s recurrent training program within the preceding 12 calendar months. Training records indicate completion of line-oriented flight training (LOFT), crew resource management (CRM) modules, and emergency procedure simulations, including rapid decompression and emergency descent protocols. The Captain served as the pilot flying (PF) for the accident flight, while the First Officer served as the pilot monitoring (PM). Both crewmembers were current in accordance with 14 CFR 121.439 and 121.441.

2.4 Duty and Rest Compliance
Review of the operator’s crew scheduling records and electronic duty tracking system confirmed that both flight crewmembers were in compliance with 14 CFR Part 117 flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements. The Captain reported for duty at 14:30 PST, and the First Officer reported at 14:45 PST. Both crewmembers had a minimum of 10 consecutive hours of rest prior to the start of the duty period. No fatigue-related factors were identified in the pre-flight or in-flight operational records.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications
The Boeing 737-9 MAX is a twin-engine, narrow-body transport category airplane certified under 14 CFR Part 25. The aircraft was equipped with a maximum takeoff weight of 194,700 pounds and a maximum landing weight of 174,200 pounds. At the time of the accident, the aircraft had accumulated 1,847.3 total flight hours and 1,092 total flight cycles. The airframe was manufactured in 2023 and delivered to the operator in March 2023.

3.2 Maintenance History
Maintenance records indicate the aircraft was maintained in accordance with the operator’s FAA-approved maintenance program. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check equivalent) was completed on December 18, 2023, at 1,798.1 flight hours. During that visit, the left mid-exit door plug was inspected per manufacturer service bulletin 737-53A1289. No discrepancies were documented at that time. The aircraft was released to service on December 20, 2023. Subsequent line maintenance checks were performed on December 28, 2023, and January 2, 2024, with all required inspections signed off by authorized inspection personnel.

3.3 Cabin Pressurization and Door Plug Systems
The aircraft cabin pressurization system was designed to maintain a maximum cabin altitude of 8,000 feet at a cruise altitude of 41,000 feet. The left mid-exit door plug, designated as a Type III emergency exit, was installed in lieu of an operational door to accommodate the aircraft’s seating configuration. The plug assembly consisted of a structural panel, four primary retention bolts, two guide tracks, and a perimeter inflatable seal. The retention bolts were specified to be torqued to 180 ± 10 inch-pounds. The pressurization control system utilized dual outflow valves and a cabin pressure controller to regulate differential pressure. At the time of the event, the cabin differential pressure was approximately 4.2 psi, consistent with the aircraft’s climb profile through 16,000 feet MSL.

3.4 Propulsion Systems
The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured by GE Aviation. The left engine (serial number 88421) had accumulated 1,847.3 hours and 1,092 cycles. The right engine (serial number 88435) had accumulated 1,847.3 hours and 1,092 cycles. Both engines were maintained under an on-condition maintenance program approved by the FAA. Engine health monitoring data indicated normal parameters for exhaust gas temperature (EGT), fuel flow, N1, and N2 throughout the flight. No engine-related anomalies were recorded prior to, during, or after the decompression event.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Conditions
On January 5, 2024, a high-pressure system was centered over the Pacific Northwest, resulting in stable atmospheric conditions. Surface temperatures at KPDX were 8°C (46°F) with a dewpoint of 2°C (36°F). Winds were light and variable, shifting to 180° at 5 knots by 17:00 PST. Visibility was unrestricted at 10 statute miles. No convective activity, turbulence, or icing conditions were forecast or reported in the departure and climb-out corridors.

4.2 Surface and Terminal Forecasts
The METAR for KPDX at 17:00 PST was: KPDX 051700Z 18005KT 10SM FEW040 08/02 A3012 RMK AO2 SLP201 T00830022. The TAF issued at 16:30 PST forecasted VFR conditions through 23:00 PST, with winds remaining below 10 knots and no significant weather phenomena. The forecasted freezing level was at 6,500 feet MSL.

4.3 In-Flight Weather and Pilot Reports
The flight crew received standard pre-flight weather briefings, including AIRMETs and SIGMETs. No AIRMETs for turbulence or icing were active along the route. During the climb phase, the crew reported clear skies and smooth air. No pilot reports (PIREPs) of structural icing, severe turbulence, or wind shear were filed in the vicinity of the accident location. The outside air temperature at 16,000 feet MSL was approximately -12°C (10°F), with a standard lapse rate observed.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The aircraft sustained no ground impact. The primary structural separation involved the left mid-exit door plug, which detached from the fuselage during climb. The door plug was recovered approximately 14.2 nautical miles from the departure airport, located in a residential area at coordinates 45°51′08″N, 122°44′19″W. The plug was found largely intact, with minor surface abrasions consistent with aerodynamic forces and ground contact. No other major airframe components were separated from the aircraft.

5.2 Door Plug and Fuselage Examination
Examination of the recovered door plug revealed that all four primary retention bolts were absent from their respective mounting locations. The bolt holes in the plug exhibited clean, unthreaded edges, indicating the bolts were not present at the time of separation. The guide tracks on the fuselage side showed minor scoring and deformation consistent with sudden lateral displacement. The perimeter inflatable seal was torn and partially extruded from its channel. The fuselage cutout surrounding the door plug location exhibited no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or pre-existing structural damage. The surrounding skin panels remained intact, with fastener holes undisturbed.

5.3 Cabin Interior and Systems Examination
The cabin interior sustained localized damage consistent with rapid decompression. Overhead bin latches in the left mid-cabin section were disengaged, and several service items were displaced. Passenger oxygen masks deployed automatically in the affected zone. The cabin pressure controller recorded a rapid pressure drop from 4.2 psi differential to 0.8 psi differential within 3.2 seconds. The emergency descent was initiated by the flight crew at 17:28:42 PST, with the aircraft descending to 10,000 feet MSL within 4 minutes and 18 seconds. No fire, smoke, or hazardous material release was observed.

5.4 Component Testing and Analysis
The recovered door plug was transported to an NTSB-approved materials laboratory for detailed examination. Non-destructive testing (NDT) of the plug structure revealed no metallurgical defects, manufacturing anomalies, or stress fractures. The bolt retention system was analyzed using coordinate measuring machine (CMM) techniques, confirming that the mounting holes were within manufacturer tolerances. The inflatable seal material was subjected to tensile and compression testing, with results indicating compliance with original equipment specifications. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD) or improper installation tools was identified on the plug or surrounding fuselage structure.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Maintenance and Safety Policies
The operator maintained a Safety Management System (SMS) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.373. The SMS included mandatory reporting protocols for structural anomalies, cabin pressure irregularities, and maintenance discrepancies. Maintenance personnel were required to follow manufacturer installation procedures and utilize calibrated torque wrenches for all critical fastener applications. The operator’s quality assurance program conducted random audits of door plug installations, with the most recent audit completed on November 15, 2023. No non-conformances were documented during that audit.

6.2 Previous Similar Events and Service Bulletins
A review of the operator’s maintenance tracking database and the FAA Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) system identified two prior reports involving door plug seal degradation on the same aircraft type, both resolved through routine replacement. The manufacturer issued Service Bulletin 737-53A1289 in October 2023, providing enhanced inspection procedures for door plug retention hardware and guide track alignment. The operator incorporated the bulletin into its maintenance program on November 1, 2023. No fleet-wide grounding or mandatory airworthiness directive was in effect at the time of the accident.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The aircraft was certified under 14 CFR Part 25, Subpart C, which addresses structural integrity and pressurization requirements. Maintenance and inspection procedures were governed by 14 CFR Part 43 and Part 121, Subpart L. The operator’s maintenance program was developed in accordance with Advisory Circular 120-16G, Air Carrier Maintenance Programs, which outlines requirements for continuous airworthiness, component tracking, and quality control. The AC emphasizes the importance of standardized installation procedures, torque verification, and post-maintenance functional testing for pressurized cabin components. All applicable regulatory requirements were documented in the operator’s Operations Specifications and Maintenance Manual.

6.4 Flight Data and Cockpit Voice Recorder Information
The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered from the aircraft and downloaded at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory. The FDR recorded 256 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz. Data indicated normal engine performance, autopilot engagement, and standard climb profiles until 17:28:15 PST. At that time, cabin differential pressure decreased from 4.2 psi to 0.8 psi within 3.2 seconds. The aircraft pitch attitude increased by 2.1 degrees, and the autopilot disengaged at 17:28:18 PST. The CVR captured standard crew communications, including the Captain’s declaration of “rapid decompression” and initiation of the emergency descent checklist. No abnormal aural warnings or system alerts were recorded prior to the event. The CVR recording duration was 2 hours, with the final 30 minutes preserved for analysis. All data was verified for integrity and synchronized with maintenance logs and ATC communications.

1. INTRODUCTION
This report documents the specialist examination conducted by the NTSB Structures and Materials Group, in coordination with the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) Group, regarding the in-flight separation of the left mid-exit door plug (MEDP) from a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered door plug assembly, associated fuselage interface structure, fastener hardware, guide track components, and the analysis of recorded flight data parameters. The examination was conducted between January 10 and January 18, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the Boeing Commercial Airplanes Engineering Facility in Everett, Washington.

Items examined included the primary door plug panel (Boeing Part Number 65-12345-678, Serial Number 987654321), four (4) recovered stop fitting bolts, two (2) guide track assemblies, the forward and aft fuselage frame interface brackets, and the complete FDR/CVR data set (Honeywell SSFDR, P/N 980-4700-042, S/N 22A1145). All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53A1234, and applicable ASTM/SAE material testing standards. The investigation was coordinated with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Aircraft Certification Service and the operator’s maintenance control center.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737 MAX 9 is a derivative of the 737 MAX family, which shares common structural architecture with the Boeing 737 MAX 8 baseline configuration. The mid-exit door plug is a structural closure panel installed in lieu of a Type III emergency exit for high-density seating configurations. The plug is designed to transfer cabin pressurization loads, aerodynamic shear, and inertial loads to the primary fuselage structure via a series of guide tracks, stop fittings, and perimeter fasteners. The design certification basis for the plug assembly complies with 14 CFR 25.571, Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure, requiring demonstration of fail-safe load paths and residual strength under ultimate load conditions.

The plug assembly is manufactured from 7075-T651 aluminum alloy sheet and extrusions, with titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V, AMS 4911) fasteners utilized at high-stress interface points. The design differential pressure limit is 9.1 PSI, with a proof pressure of 13.65 PSI and ultimate pressure of 18.2 PSI. The plug is retained by twelve (12) primary perimeter fasteners, four (4) stop fitting bolts, and two (2) vertical guide tracks that constrain vertical and lateral translation during pressurization cycles.

The accident aircraft, serial number 44444, was delivered to the operator in November 2023 and had accumulated 1,247 flight hours and 892 flight cycles at the time of the event. Maintenance records indicate the left MEDP was removed and reinstalled on December 12, 2023, during a cabin reconfiguration modification. The reinstallation was performed under the operator’s FAA-approved maintenance program, which references Advisory Circular AC 120-16G for air carrier maintenance and preventive maintenance programs. The powerplant configuration consists of two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured under license by GE Aviation. Engine maintenance records were reviewed and found to be current, with no outstanding airworthiness directives or service bulletins affecting the nacelle or thrust reverser systems.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS
The recovered door plug assembly was received at the NTSB Materials Laboratory on January 10, 2024, secured in a custom transport fixture to preserve fracture surface integrity. Initial visual inspection revealed gross deformation of the forward guide track mounting lugs, with evidence of plastic yielding and localized buckling. The aft guide track exhibited complete separation from the plug panel, with fracture surfaces consistent with tensile overload.

Fastener hole inspection was conducted using calibrated digital micrometers and optical comparators. The twelve (12) perimeter fastener holes on the plug panel were measured for elongation and out-of-roundness. Holes 1 through 8 exhibited nominal diameters within Boeing BAC5000 tolerance limits (0.2500 ± 0.0015 inches). Holes 9 through 12, located along the lower aft quadrant, demonstrated significant elongation ranging from 0.038 to 0.052 inches, exceeding the maximum allowable limit of 0.010 inches per Boeing Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-10-01. The corresponding fuselage frame interface holes showed matching deformation patterns, indicating load transfer prior to separation.

Four (4) stop fitting bolts were recovered from the accident site. Metallurgical examination of the bolt shanks and threads was performed per ASTM E1444 (Magnetic Particle Inspection) and ASTM E1417 (Liquid Penetrant Inspection). No fatigue striations or crack initiation sites were identified. Hardness testing (Rockwell C scale) yielded values of 38.5 HRC, consistent with Ti-6Al-4V specification. However, torque verification of the recovered bolts using a calibrated digital torque wrench (Fluke 754) indicated residual torque values between 12 and 18 in-lbs, significantly below the manufacturer-specified installation torque of 180–200 in-lbs per Boeing Standard Practices Manual (SPM) 20-10-01.

Chemical composition analysis of the plug panel material was conducted via Optical Emission Spectroscopy (OES) and Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (SEM/EDS). Results confirmed 7075-T651 aluminum alloy composition: Zn 5.1–6.1%, Mg 2.1–2.9%, Cu 1.2–2.0%, Cr 0.18–0.28%, with balance Al. Microstructural examination revealed no evidence of intergranular corrosion, exfoliation, or heat treatment anomalies. Grain structure was consistent with T651 temper, with average grain size of 45–60 μm.

Fretting debris was collected from the guide track interface and analyzed via X-ray Diffraction (XRD). The debris composition consisted primarily of aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) and titanium oxide (TiO₂), indicating prolonged metal-to-metal contact under cyclic loading. The presence of oxide layers suggests the guide track was not fully engaged or properly lubricated during the reinstallation event, leading to accelerated wear and reduced load-carrying capacity.

Non-destructive inspection (NDI) of the fuselage frame brackets (P/N 65-12345-680) was performed using phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) per ASTM E2491. No subsurface cracking or delamination was detected. However, the aft bracket exhibited localized yielding at the fastener interface, with permanent set measured at 0.028 inches. The forward bracket remained within elastic deformation limits.

4. DATA ANALYSIS
Flight data recorder parameters were extracted from the Honeywell SSFDR using the NTSB FDR Readout System v4.2. Data was sampled at 1 Hz for cabin pressure parameters and 4 Hz for flight control and engine parameters. The following timeline reconstruction is based on synchronized FDR, CVR, and ATC radar data.

At 14:22:15 UTC, the aircraft departed runway 16L at 142 knots indicated airspeed (KIAS). The pilot in command initiated a standard climb profile, maintaining 250 KIAS below 10,000 ft MSL. At 14:28:42 UTC, the aircraft passed 10,000 ft MSL, and the cabin pressurization system transitioned to automatic climb mode. Cabin differential pressure (ΔP) increased linearly, reaching 3.8 PSI at 12,000 ft MSL, consistent with normal Boeing 737 MAX pressurization schedules.

At 14:31:08 UTC, the aircraft reached 16,000 ft MSL. FDR parameters recorded a sudden, step-change decrease in cabin ΔP from 5.2 PSI to 0.8 PSI within 0.4 seconds. Simultaneously, cabin altitude rate of climb spiked to +18,500 ft/min, and cabin altitude rapidly increased from 6,200 ft to 14,800 ft over a 12-second interval. The rapid decompression event was accompanied by a transient airspeed fluctuation of ±18 KIAS and a pitch attitude deviation of +2.3 degrees, consistent with aerodynamic buffeting and structural separation.

Engine parameters for both LEAP-1B powerplants remained within normal operating envelopes throughout the event. N1 rotation rates were stable at 84.2% and 84.5%, EGT values were 612°C and 615°C, and fuel flow remained at 2,850 lbs/hr per engine. No compressor stalls, surge events, or FADEC fault codes were recorded, confirming the event was isolated to the airframe structure and not related to propulsion system anomalies.

The pilot in command initiated an emergency descent at 14:31:15 UTC, reducing thrust to idle and deploying speed brakes. The aircraft descended at a maximum vertical speed of 4,200 ft/min, stabilizing at 10,000 ft MSL. Cabin ΔP remained at 0.8 PSI, indicating complete loss of pressurization integrity. The aircraft diverted to Portland International Airport (KPDX) and landed at 14:48:22 UTC with a touchdown speed of 138 KIAS.

Comparison with normal operational parameters indicates the decompression event occurred at a cabin ΔP of 5.2 PSI, which corresponds to approximately 57% of the design limit load. The instantaneous pressure drop and guide track disengagement suggest a structural failure mode initiated by inadequate fastener retention. The absence of progressive fatigue indicators in the recovered hardware, combined with the low residual torque values, supports a maintenance-related installation deficiency rather than in-service fatigue degradation.

5. SUMMARY
The specialist examination of the left mid-exit door plug assembly and associated flight data yielded the following technical findings:

1. The recovered door plug panel (P/N 65-12345-678, S/N 987654321) exhibited significant elongation of four (4) lower aft perimeter fastener holes, exceeding Boeing SRM tolerance limits by a factor of 3.8 to 5.2.
2. Four (4) stop fitting bolts were recovered with residual torque values of 12–18 in-lbs, substantially below the manufacturer-specified installation torque of 180–200 in-lbs.
3. Metallurgical and chemical analysis confirmed the plug panel material as 7075-T651 aluminum alloy and the fasteners as Ti-6Al-4V, with no evidence of material defects, heat treatment anomalies, or in-service fatigue cracking.
4. Fretting debris analysis indicated prolonged metal-to-metal contact at the guide track interface, consistent with improper engagement or lubrication during reinstallation.
5. FDR data recorded a rapid cabin decompression event at 16,000 ft MSL, characterized by a ΔP drop from 5.2 PSI to 0.8 PSI within 0.4 seconds, accompanied by transient aerodynamic disturbances.
6. Engine parameters for both GE Aviation-manufactured LEAP-1B turbofans remained within certified operational limits, with no propulsion-related anomalies contributing to the event.
7. The structural failure sequence is consistent with inadequate fastener retention and guide track disengagement under normal pressurization loads, as defined under 14 CFR 25.571 damage-tolerance criteria.
8. Maintenance records indicate the plug was reinstalled 24 days prior to the event under an FAA-approved program referencing AC 120-16G, with no documented torque verification or post-installation pressure test anomalies.

All findings are factual and based on physical examination, material testing, and recorded flight data analysis. No determination of probable cause is made in this report.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER MARK R. HENDERSON
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 10:15 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Seattle, WA
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Aviation Safety Board

Q: Please state your full name and current position for the record.
A: Mark R. Henderson. I’m a First Officer with the airline, based out of Seattle. I’ve been flying the 737 MAX line for about four years now, total time in the right seat is roughly twelve years across the fleet.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Henderson. I’d like you to walk me through the events of January 5th, starting from your pre-flight preparations. Take your time.
A: Yeah, sure. So, we were scheduled for the 14:30 departure to Ontario. I got to the aircraft around 13:15, did the exterior walk-around with the lead mechanic. Everything looked standard. No fluid leaks, tires were good, control surfaces moved freely. We got in the cockpit, powered up the avionics, ran the pre-flight checklist. The engines were LEAP-1B units, spooled up normally during the start sequence. No abnormal EICAS messages, no maintenance write-ups that stood out. We pushed back around 14:45, got our clearance, and taxied out to 16L.

Q: Describe the takeoff and initial climb.
A: Takeoff was uneventful. Normal rotation, positive rate, gear up. I called out the flap retraction schedule, the Captain was hand-flying. We climbed through 10,000 feet, transitioned to standard pressure, and I was just monitoring the flight director and the navigation display. I’d say we were passing through 16,000 feet—maybe 16,200, I don’t have the exact FMC data in front of me, but it was right around there. And then... it just happened. There was this massive bang. Not like a compressor stall or a tire blowout. It was sharper. Louder. Like a cannon going off right outside the left window. The whole airframe shuddered. I felt it through the seat, my headset rattled against my ears, and the cabin pressure warning horn started screaming immediately.

Q: What were your immediate actions following the event?
A: I looked over at the Captain. He was already reacting, hands tight on the yoke, calling out "Decompression!" I grabbed my oxygen mask, pulled it down, put it on, and established mic communication. I could hear this... this deafening, high-pitched howl coming from the left side. Just wind tearing through the cabin. I turned my head, looked back over my shoulder, and... there was just open sky where the left mid-exit door plug should’ve been. It was completely gone. I could see the cabin interior, oxygen masks deployed, some loose items floating around. It was surreal. I immediately started the emergency descent checklist. The Captain said, "Masks on, emergency descent, level off at 10,000." I pulled the thrust levers to idle, deployed the speed brakes, and we banked slightly right to keep the open side out of the relative wind.

Q: How did the aircraft handle during the descent?
A: Honestly, better than I expected. The MAX 9 is a heavy airplane, but the flight controls were still responsive. We were descending at maybe 3,500 to 4,000 feet per minute. I was calling out airspeed, altitude, and running through the QRH items. "Oxygen... check. Cabin altitude... check. Pressurization... off." The Captain was flying manually, keeping us stable. I’d say we leveled off around 10,000 feet, maybe 10,500. Once we got below the higher altitudes, the wind noise dropped off significantly. It went from this roaring vacuum to just... normal flight noise. I keyed the interphone to the cabin crew. The lead flight attendant answered. She was calm, but you could hear the tension. She reported the door plug was missing, some minor debris in the aisle, but passengers were secured and masks were on. No injuries reported at that point.

Q: What was your communication with ATC?
A: I declared an emergency with Seattle Center right after we started the descent. "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, [Callsign], rapid decompression, descending to 10,000, requesting immediate return to Sea-Tac." They cleared us immediately, gave us a direct vector back to the field. I think we were back over the water, maybe 15 minutes after the event. The Captain ran the approach checklist, we configured for landing, flaps 5, 15, 30. We landed on 16R, I believe. Braking was normal, reverse thrust deployed without issue. We taxied to the gate, shut down the engines. Fire and rescue were already staged, but we didn’t need them. Passengers deplaned via the right-side doors.

Q: Have you flown other variants of this aircraft family? How does this compare to your experience?
A: Yeah, I’ve got time on the BOEING 737-8. The MAX 9 is obviously longer, and the door plug configuration is different. The 737-8 doesn’t have that mid-cabin exit plug; it’s a standard, fully hinged door. So structurally, it’s a different setup. But the flight deck is nearly identical. The LEAP-1B engines are the same across the MAX family, and honestly, they performed flawlessly. No surges, no vibrations, just normal thrust response the whole time. GE Aviation really built a solid powerplant. But this event... it’s not something you train for in the simulator. We do rapid decompression drills, sure, but they’re simulated with a switch. You don’t get the actual structural failure, the noise, the vibration. It’s a completely different animal.

Q: In your training or operational experience, are you familiar with the regulatory framework surrounding door plug retention or structural certification?
A: I mean, we cover it in ground school, but... honestly, in the moment, you’re just flying the airplane. You don’t think about the regs. You just react. But afterward, when I was debriefing with the chief pilot, we started talking about the certification standards. I know we’re trained on 14 CFR 25.571—damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of structure. And the maintenance programs are supposed to align with Advisory Circular 120-16G for continuous airworthiness. But I’m not a mechanic. I don’t inspect the retention bolts. I just trust that the system is built to spec. I know the Federal Aviation Administration has been looking into the door plug installation procedures, and I’m sure they’ll find out exactly what happened. But from a pilot’s perspective, the aircraft handled exactly as it was designed to. The systems worked, the crew worked, and we got everyone back on the ground safely.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add, or any details you feel we haven’t covered?
A: Just that the crew coordination was solid. the Captain was incredibly calm, the cabin crew did exactly what they were supposed to. I’ve been thinking a lot about the maintenance side, though. I know there were questions about whether the plug was recently replaced or inspected. I don’t have the logs, but it’s something that’ll come out. I’ve been flying for twelve years, and I’ve never seen anything like it. I’ll be available for any follow-up questions, simulator debriefs, whatever you need.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Henderson. We’ll be in touch.
A: Yeah, no problem. Just let me know.

MEMORANDUM

DATE: March 15, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Aircraft Certification Service
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO NTSB PRELIMINARY FINDINGS AND COMPLIANCE STATUS FOR EMERGENCY AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE 2024-02-51
DOCKET NO.: FAA-2024-0187
NTSB ACCIDENT NO.: DCA24MA056

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the formal regulatory response to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) preliminary findings regarding the in-flight structural failure event of January 5, 2024. The incident, designated NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA056, involved a Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft operated under 14 CFR Part 121, which experienced rapid decompression following the separation of the left mid-cabin exit door plug during initial climb at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) after departure from a Pacific Northwest aerodrome. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport with no fatalities reported. This document addresses compliance with Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-02-51, references applicable provisions of 14 CFR Part 25, and outlines the Federal Aviation Administration’s oversight posture, corrective action framework, and regulatory enforcement timeline. The referenced regulatory framework includes, but is not limited to, Section 25.571, 14 CFR 25.783, and 14 CFR 121.344, as well as the maintenance program guidance contained within Advisory Circular 120-16G.

2. BACKGROUND
The certification basis for the affected airframe is established under Type Certificate No. T00001SE, with subsequent structural modifications governed by Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) protocols and production approval holder (PAH) quality assurance requirements. The mid-cabin exit door plug configuration was originally evaluated under the damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements codified in Section 25.571 of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Historically, the FAA has relied upon manufacturer-submitted structural integrity analyses, coupled with operator compliance with approved maintenance programs, to ensure continued airworthiness. Prior to the January 2024 event, the regulatory framework governing door plug retention hardware and fuselage pressurization cycles was addressed through a series of service bulletins and routine airworthiness directives, none of which mandated immediate, fleet-wide torque verification of the specific fastener array utilized in the plug retention system.

The operational context of the incident falls squarely within the purview of 14 CFR Part 121, specifically 14 CFR 121.344, which mandates that certificate holders maintain aircraft in accordance with approved maintenance programs and ensure that all structural modifications comply with original equipment manufacturer (OEM) specifications. Furthermore, 14 CFR 25.783 establishes the requirements for fuselage doors, including emergency exits, mandating that such components remain securely latched under all anticipated flight loads and pressurization differentials. The maintenance program guidance referenced in Advisory Circular 120-16G provides the foundational framework for developing and revising operator maintenance programs, emphasizing continuous airworthiness monitoring, defect reporting, and reliability tracking.

In the aftermath of the event, the FAA initiated an immediate fleet grounding and inspection campaign under the authority of 14 CFR 21.99 and 14 CFR 39.13. Concurrently, the NTSB launched a comprehensive investigation into the manufacturing, assembly, and quality control processes at the production facility. Historical data from analogous airframes, including the BOEING 737-8 variant, was reviewed to assess whether similar door plug configurations exhibited latent manufacturing variances. The investigation also incorporated engine performance telemetry from the CFM International LEAP-1B powerplants to reconstruct the climb profile and verify that the structural failure was not precipitated by abnormal aerodynamic or thrust-induced loading conditions.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive audit of the manufacturer’s production records, coupled with operator maintenance logs, reveals systemic deficiencies in the quality assurance protocols governing the installation and verification of door plug retention hardware. The Federal Aviation Administration’s oversight mechanisms, while compliant with baseline regulatory requirements, failed to identify critical deviations in the torque application and fastener retention procedures during the final assembly phase. Specifically, the absence of mandatory, documented torque verification at the point of installation contravenes the intent of Section 25.571, which requires that structural components be evaluated for fatigue and damage tolerance under realistic operational stressors.

The operator’s compliance status, as evaluated under 14 CFR 121.367 and 14 CFR 121.344, indicates that while the certificate holder adhered to the published maintenance program, the program itself lacked specific, high-frequency inspection intervals for the door plug retention system. This regulatory gap was exacerbated by the manufacturer’s reliance on production line quality checks that were not independently validated by the FAA’s Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) unit. The Captain’s immediate execution of emergency descent procedures, in strict accordance with 14 CFR 121.557 and approved flight crew operating manuals, mitigated the risk of catastrophic structural failure and ensured the safe return of the aircraft. However, the incident underscores a critical vulnerability in the regulatory framework: the delegation of critical structural verification to manufacturer-controlled processes without sufficient FAA oversight or mandatory post-production validation.

Furthermore, the investigation identified inconsistencies in the documentation of supplemental type certificate modifications and production line deviations. While the BOEING 737-8 fleet operates under a similar certification basis, the door plug configuration on the MAX 9 variant introduced unique load paths that were not adequately captured in the original damage tolerance analysis. The telemetry data from the LEAP-1B engines confirmed that the aircraft was operating within normal climb parameters, thereby isolating the failure to a structural and manufacturing anomaly rather than an operational or aerodynamic exceedance. GE Aviation’s technical support during the data acquisition phase facilitated the accurate reconstruction of the flight profile, but the primary regulatory focus remains on the airframe manufacturer’s compliance with 14 CFR Part 21 and 14 CFR Part 25.

The FAA acknowledges that the current regulatory framework, as applied to door plug installations, lacks explicit requirements for independent, third-party verification of critical fastener torque values during production. This oversight gap permitted the propagation of improperly secured hardware into the operational fleet, directly contravening the airworthiness standards mandated by 14 CFR 25.783 and the damage tolerance principles of Section 25.571.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings outlined herein, the Federal Aviation Administration is implementing the following corrective actions and regulatory mandates to ensure immediate compliance and long-term airworthiness:

a. Mandatory Fleet-Wide Inspection and Torque Verification: All affected aircraft shall undergo a one-time, detailed inspection of the mid-cabin exit door plug retention system in accordance with the procedures specified in Emergency AD 2024-02-51. This inspection shall include torque verification of all primary and secondary fasteners, with results documented and submitted to the FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service within 72 hours of completion.

b. Revision of Maintenance Programs: Certificate holders operating under 14 CFR Part 121 shall revise their approved maintenance programs to incorporate recurring, high-frequency inspections of door plug retention hardware. These revisions must align with the guidance provided in Advisory Circular 120-16G and shall be submitted to the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) for approval within 30 calendar days.

c. Enhanced Production Oversight: The FAA will suspend the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) privileges for the specific production line responsible for door plug installation until a comprehensive quality assurance audit is completed. All future installations shall require independent FAA inspector sign-off, with torque values recorded in the aircraft’s permanent maintenance records per 14 CFR 121.344.

d. Regulatory Rulemaking and AD Updates: The FAA will initiate a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to amend Section 25.571 and 14 CFR 25.783, mandating explicit, independent verification protocols for all fuselage door plug installations. The proposed rule will be published in the Federal Register within 90 days, with a public comment period of 60 days.

e. MMEL and Operational Restrictions: Until compliance with the revised maintenance program is verified, the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) for affected aircraft shall be amended to prohibit dispatch with any door plug retention system discrepancies. Operators shall implement a mandatory pre-flight visual inspection checklist, with findings reported via the Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) system per 14 CFR 121.703.

f. Follow-Up Review Schedule: The FAA will conduct quarterly compliance audits of all affected operators and the manufacturer’s production facility. The first audit is scheduled for June 2024, with subsequent reviews occurring at 90-day intervals until the FAA determines that sustained compliance has been achieved. All audit findings will be documented in the FAA’s Safety Assurance System (SAS) and made available to the NTSB upon request.

The Federal Aviation Administration remains committed to upholding the highest standards of aviation safety and ensuring that all regulatory frameworks evolve to address emerging structural and manufacturing vulnerabilities. This memorandum serves as the official record of compliance actions and regulatory directives issued in response to NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA056. All referenced docket numbers, ADs, and CFR citations shall be maintained in the official regulatory archive.

Mid-Flight Door Plug Separation Forces Emergency Landing of U.S. Airliner; No Fatalities Reported

By Marcus Thorne, Global Aviation Desk
PORTLAND, Ore. — A commercial flight operated by a major U.S. carrier was forced to make an emergency return to its departure airport on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, after a mid-cabin door plug violently separated from the fuselage during climb. The Boeing 737 MAX 9 experienced rapid decompression at approximately 16,000 feet, but the flight crew successfully guided the aircraft back to the ground without any fatalities.

The incident occurred shortly after takeoff from a Pacific Northwest hub as the aircraft ascended toward its planned cruising altitude. Passengers reported a deafening bang followed by a sudden, violent drop in cabin pressure, triggering the automatic deployment of overhead oxygen masks. According to preliminary flight data, the Captain immediately recognized the pressure anomaly and executed a rapid descent protocol, leveling the aircraft at a lower, breathable altitude before diverting back to the departure airport. The jet touched down safely, though several passengers sustained minor injuries from the sudden pressure change, falling debris, and the force of the emergency landing.

“Our top priority is the safety of the traveling public,” said a Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson in a statement released Saturday. “The FAA is working closely with the National Transportation Safety Board to secure the aircraft, preserve all data, and begin a thorough investigation.” The airline’s chief operations officer echoed the sentiment, stating, “We are deeply grateful to the flight crew for their exceptional handling of a highly unusual situation. Our thoughts are with the passengers and crew who experienced this frightening event, and we are providing full support to everyone on board.” NTSB investigators arrived on scene within hours, cordoning off the aircraft and beginning the meticulous process of documenting the structural failure.

The aircraft involved is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a narrow-body jet that shares core design architecture and manufacturing processes with the widely used BOEING 737-8. Unlike standard emergency exit doors, the MAX 9 features a “door plug” — a reinforced, non-opening panel installed in place of an exit to accommodate different seating configurations. The aircraft is powered by twin LEAP engine turbofans, high-bypass powerplants manufactured by CFM International, a joint venture that includes GE Aviation. These engines are standard across the MAX family and are prized for their fuel efficiency and reduced emissions. Federal regulations, including Advisory Circular AC 120-16G, outline strict maintenance, inspection, and operational protocols for commercial airframes, while Section 25.571 of the Federal Aviation Regulations mandates rigorous fatigue and damage tolerance testing for all pressurized fuselage components to ensure they can withstand repeated pressurization cycles over decades of service.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the failure likely stems from a manufacturing or installation defect rather than routine operational wear. “When a door plug separates at altitude, it’s almost always a question of fastener integrity or structural bonding,” said Dr. Marcus Lin, an aerospace engineering professor and former NTSB consultant. “The plug is held in place by guide tracks, stop fittings, and a series of high-strength bolts. If those aren’t torqued to specification or if a critical component is missing, the pressure differential at 16,000 feet can literally blow it outward.” Lin emphasized that while the scenario is alarming, modern aircraft are engineered with redundant safety margins. “The fuselage is designed to withstand localized failures without catastrophic collapse, which is exactly what we saw here. The structure did its job.”

For those on board, the experience was harrowing. “One second we were climbing normally, the next there was this explosive sound and the air just got sucked out,” said passenger David Chen, who was seated three rows forward of the breach. “My phone flew out of my hand, and a child’s backpack was pulled toward the opening. We just held on and prayed.” Chen’s wife, who was traveling separately, described the agonizing wait for news. “I saw the alerts on my phone and couldn’t breathe. When he finally texted me that he was safe, I just broke down.” Several passengers reported minor lacerations, bruising, and ear discomfort, but all were discharged from local hospitals by Saturday evening.

The incident has reignited scrutiny over the 737 MAX program, which faced a global grounding in 2019 following two fatal crashes linked to a flawed flight control system. While the MAX 9 was cleared to return to service after extensive software and training updates, this latest event raises fresh questions about manufacturing oversight and quality control at the assembly line. Historically, rapid decompression events are rare in modern commercial aviation. The last comparable incident involving a door failure occurred in 2018, when a Southwest Airlines 737-700 suffered an engine fan blade failure that shattered a window, resulting in one fatality. That tragedy prompted sweeping changes to inspection protocols for aging fleets and reinforced the industry’s reliance on redundant safety systems.

The NTSB has launched a full-scale investigation, with a preliminary report expected within 30 days. Investigators are focusing on the aircraft’s maintenance records, the door plug’s installation history, and the manufacturing chain at Boeing’s Renton, Washington, facility. The FAA has temporarily grounded all 737 MAX 9 aircraft in the U.S. fleet pending enhanced inspections of door plug fasteners and structural fittings. “We are not speculating on the root cause,” said NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy during a press briefing. “We are following the evidence, examining every bolt, every record, and every procedure. Safety is not negotiable.” As the aviation industry braces for the findings, passengers, regulators, and airline operators await answers that will shape the future of commercial flight safety and manufacturing accountability.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Chief Engineer, Maintenance & Engineering Division, representing the operator of the subject aircraft in the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative hearing. As a party to the investigation, our engineering and maintenance organization has provided comprehensive access to operational records, maintenance documentation, flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, and internal safety management system (SMS) analyses. The scope of this document is to present a technical assessment of the rapid decompression event that occurred on January 5, 2024, with specific focus on the structural retention architecture of the left mid-exit door plug, the maintenance procedures governing its recent removal and reinstallation, and the operational pressurization environment during the climb phase. 

Our position is grounded in engineering analysis, maintenance quality assurance data, and regulatory compliance frameworks. While the investigation continues to evaluate multiple potential failure modes, this submission synthesizes available docket evidence to identify the primary contributing factors, evaluate systemic vulnerabilities, and propose actionable safety improvements. We acknowledge the inherent complexity of modern transport-category aircraft systems, where design tolerances, manufacturing variability, maintenance execution, and operational profiles intersect. Nevertheless, the evidence strongly indicates that procedural and verification gaps in critical fastener installation, compounded by insufficient post-maintenance inspection protocols, were the dominant contributors to the in-flight separation.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, departed a Pacific Northwest airport on a scheduled domestic flight. During climb through approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the flight crew experienced a sudden cabin pressure loss, accompanied by structural noise and rapid decompression. The aircraft executed a safe return to the departure airport with no injuries to passengers or crew. Preliminary NTSB findings, corroborated by our internal maintenance records and FDR data, confirm that the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage structure.

Docket materials, including Maintenance Log Entry 2023-11-08 and Work Order 4472-B, document that the subject door plug was removed approximately 45 days prior to the incident for cabin reconfiguration and subsequently reinstalled. The reinstallation procedure required precise alignment of guide tracks, engagement of stop fittings, and installation of retention fasteners to manufacturer-specified torque values. Post-installation quality control records indicate that a standard visual inspection was completed, but torque verification documentation and independent sign-off were not captured in the digital maintenance tracking system.

FDR telemetry (Docket Exhibit 12-C, Channel 112) shows a rapid cabin pressure differential spike coinciding with the separation event, followed by an immediate descent and stabilization. The aircraft is powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured by GE Aviation. Engine performance data during the climb phase indicates normal thrust scheduling and bleed air extraction rates consistent with standard pressurization profiles. The BOEING 737-8, which shares the same certification basis and structural design philosophy with the MAX 9 variant, utilizes identical door plug retention concepts across the 737 MAX family, making this event relevant to broader fleet maintenance practices.

Regulatory oversight for this aircraft type falls under the jurisdiction of the Federal Aviation Administration (the FAA), which issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) following the incident mandating immediate inspections of all mid-exit door plugs. The certification basis for the airframe structure, including damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements, is governed by 14 CFR 25.571. Our analysis evaluates compliance with these standards while identifying gaps between regulatory intent and practical maintenance execution.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The mid-exit door plug on the 737 MAX series is a non-opening structural panel designed to maintain fuselage pressure integrity while allowing for cabin configuration flexibility. The retention system relies on a combination of upper and lower guide tracks, lateral stop fittings, and a series of high-strength retention fasteners that transfer cabin pressure loads into the surrounding fuselage frames and stringers. Under normal operating conditions, the plug experiences cyclic loading from pressurization and depressurization, with peak differential pressures typically reaching 8.6 psi at maximum cruise altitude. At 16,000 feet, the cabin pressure differential is approximately 3.8 psi, generating significant outward radial forces on the plug interface.

Engineering analysis of the recovered fastener holes and surrounding structure (Docket Exhibit 19-A, Metallurgical Report) reveals that several retention fasteners were either absent or improperly seated at the time of separation. The absence of these fasteners disrupted the intended load path, causing localized stress concentrations that exceeded the yield strength of the remaining hardware. Finite element modeling conducted by our structural engineering team, validated against manufacturer test data, demonstrates that missing even two adjacent fasteners in the lower retention row can reduce the plug's ultimate load capacity by approximately 34%, rendering it vulnerable to separation under normal climb-phase pressure transients.

Maintenance execution is the critical variable in this failure sequence. The reinstallation procedure requires precise torque application, typically in the range of 180–220 inch-pounds depending on fastener diameter and material specification, followed by witness marking and independent verification. Our review of the digital maintenance management system indicates that while the initial installation was logged, the torque verification step was not digitally captured, and no secondary inspector sign-off was recorded. This represents a deviation from the operator's own quality assurance protocols and highlights a systemic vulnerability in human factors and procedural compliance. The complexity of the task, combined with time pressures and reliance on visual confirmation rather than quantitative verification, created conditions where incomplete fastener installation could go undetected.

Operational data further contextualizes the event. The LEAP-1B engines, produced by GE Aviation, utilize a high-efficiency bleed air system that supplies the environmental control system (ECS) for cabin pressurization. During climb, the ECS modulates bleed valve positions to maintain a controlled cabin altitude rate. FDR analysis shows no anomalies in bleed air pressure or ECS valve positioning prior to the event. However, the transient nature of pressurization during climb introduces dynamic loading on the door plug interface. While the BOEING 737-8 and MAX 9 share identical pressurization control logic, the MAX 9's extended fuselage and additional exit configurations introduce slightly different structural load distributions. These differences, though minor, require meticulous adherence to manufacturer installation procedures to ensure proper load transfer.

From a regulatory and certification perspective, 14 CFR 25.571 mandates that transport category aircraft structures be evaluated for damage tolerance, ensuring that fatigue cracks or missing fasteners do not lead to catastrophic failure before detection. The door plug retention system was certified under this framework, with assumed inspection intervals and maintenance practices. However, the incident reveals a gap between the theoretical damage tolerance model and real-world maintenance execution. The FAA's oversight framework relies heavily on operator compliance with approved maintenance programs, but the absence of mandatory independent verification for critical retention fasteners allowed a procedural lapse to propagate into an in-flight structural failure.

Industry best practices for critical fastener installation emphasize redundant verification, digital torque tracking, and mandatory post-installation functional testing. Comparative analysis with other transport-category aircraft programs shows that operators implementing automated torque wrenches with Bluetooth data logging and mandatory dual-inspector sign-offs experience significantly lower rates of fastener-related discrepancies. The subject aircraft's maintenance program, while compliant with minimum regulatory requirements, lacked these enhanced verification layers, increasing the probability of undetected installation errors.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the engineering data, maintenance records, and operational telemetry reviewed, our position is that the primary contributing factor to the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event was the incomplete installation and inadequate verification of retention fasteners on the left mid-exit door plug during recent maintenance. This procedural deficiency was compounded by insufficient post-maintenance inspection protocols, reliance on visual confirmation over quantitative torque verification, and a maintenance tracking system that did not enforce mandatory independent sign-off for critical structural components.

Secondary contributing factors include design tolerance stack-up in the guide track alignment system, which can mask minor fastener misalignment, and the dynamic pressurization environment during climb, which imposes transient loads on the retention interface. While the LEAP-1B engine performance and ECS pressurization scheduling operated within normal parameters, the interaction between climb-phase pressure differentials and compromised fastener retention created the conditions for in-flight separation.

We acknowledge the complexity of modern aircraft maintenance, where human factors, procedural compliance, and engineering design intersect. However, the evidence clearly demonstrates that the failure was preventable through enhanced verification protocols and stricter adherence to quality assurance standards. The incident underscores the necessity of aligning maintenance execution with the damage tolerance assumptions embedded in 14 CFR 25.571, ensuring that critical structural interfaces are not only installed correctly but also independently verified and digitally documented.

Recommended safety improvements include the implementation of mandatory independent torque verification for all critical retention fasteners, integration of digital maintenance tracking with automated compliance alerts, enhanced training programs focused on structural load path awareness, and revised inspection intervals for door plug interfaces based on actual operational cycles rather than calendar-based schedules. Additionally, we advocate for closer collaboration between operators, manufacturers, and the FAA to standardize post-maintenance verification requirements across the 737 MAX family, including the BOEING 737-8 and MAX 9 variants.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the incident, our organization has implemented immediate and comprehensive corrective actions. Within 24 hours of the event, we initiated a fleet-wide inspection of all mid-exit door plugs, utilizing manufacturer-approved borescope and torque verification procedures. All aircraft were temporarily removed from service until inspections were completed and documented. To date, 100% of the affected fleet has been cleared, with three aircraft requiring fastener reinstallation and torque correction.

We have revised our maintenance procedures to mandate dual-inspector sign-off for all critical structural retention systems, with digital torque wrenches now required for all fastener installations. These tools automatically log torque values, timestamps, and technician identifiers to our maintenance management system, eliminating reliance on manual documentation. Additionally, we have implemented a mandatory post-installation functional pressure test for all door plug interfaces, simulating climb-phase differential pressures to verify structural integrity before return to service.

Our quality assurance division has conducted targeted audits of maintenance execution across all line and base facilities, identifying and addressing procedural deviations. We have also enhanced our SMS reporting framework to include near-miss tracking for fastener installation discrepancies, enabling proactive identification of systemic vulnerabilities. Training curricula for maintenance technicians have been updated to include structural load path education, human factors awareness, and standardized verification protocols.

Looking forward, we propose several additional improvements to strengthen industry-wide safety. First, we recommend that the FAA mandate digital torque verification and independent sign-off for all critical retention fasteners across transport-category aircraft, with compliance tracked through centralized maintenance databases. Second, we advocate for the development of predictive maintenance analytics that correlate pressurization cycle data with fastener integrity trends, enabling condition-based inspections rather than fixed-interval checks. Third, we propose enhanced collaboration between operators, GE Aviation, and airframe manufacturers to standardize bleed air and pressurization transient modeling, ensuring that maintenance procedures account for real-world operational loads.

Finally, we support the establishment of an industry-wide working group focused on door plug and structural retention system safety, with representation from operators, manufacturers, regulators, and labor organizations. This group would develop standardized best practices, share maintenance data, and recommend regulatory updates to close identified gaps. The January 5, 2024, event serves as a critical reminder that safety in aviation depends not only on robust engineering design but also on rigorous maintenance execution, transparent data sharing, and continuous improvement. Our organization remains committed to these principles and will continue to support the NTSB's investigation with full transparency and technical expertise.

TO: Fleet Maintenance Supervisors, Line & Base Maintenance Technicians, Quality Assurance Inspectors, Engineering Support Staff
FROM: Director, Fleet Engineering & Quality Assurance / MRO Compliance Division
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2024-014: Immediate Inspection & Verification of Mid-Exit Door Plug Retention Hardware on 737 MAX Fleet
REF: QA-2024-009, WO-737M-8842, FAA AD 2024-02-51 (Preliminary), NTSB Docket Entry #2024-01-05-INC

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert is issued to mandate immediate inspection, torque verification, and documentation review of all mid-cabin exit door plug retention assemblies across our Boeing 737 MAX fleet. The directive establishes interim containment measures, standardizes inspection protocols, and ensures compliance with updated structural integrity monitoring requirements pending final engineering disposition and regulatory guidance.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. carrier experienced a rapid decompression event that caused the left mid-exit door plug to separate from the fuselage during climb through 16,000 feet after departure from a Pacific Northwest hub. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport with no fatalities. Preliminary telemetry and recovered hardware indicate potential retention fastener anomalies and possible deviations from factory installation procedures. The Federal Aviation Administration has issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive requiring immediate grounding and inspection of affected aircraft. While our operational fleet primarily consists of the Boeing 737 MAX 8, the door plug retention architecture shares common design lineage, fastener specifications, and installation protocols with the MAX 9 variant. All maintenance actions must comply with current damage tolerance requirements and align with guidance outlined in AC 120-16G regarding maintenance program development, structural integrity monitoring, and risk-based inspection intervals. Additionally, adjacent fuselage zones and engine pylon interfaces must be evaluated for secondary stress indicators, particularly around the LEAP-1B engine mount attachment points, which share load-path monitoring protocols with the mid-cabin plug structure.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all 737 MAX aircraft in our inventory are subject to the following containment and verification procedures:

1. Hardware Verification & Torque Audit
   • Inspect all four (4) upper and lower stop fittings, guide tracks, and retention bolts on both left and right mid-exit door plugs.
   • Verify part numbers against IPC Chapter 53-40-02, Rev 14. Cross-reference with Work Order WO-737M-8842 for torque specifications (450–480 in-lbs for primary retention bolts, 280–310 in-lbs for secondary guide track fasteners).
   • Mark each verified bolt with approved torque sealant (P/N: TS-994A) and record values in the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS).

2. Documentation & Historical Record Audit
   • Review all historical maintenance records for door plug removal, reinstallation, or adjacent panel work.
   • Flag any aircraft with open or closed work orders referencing QA-2023-112, WO-737M-7719, or any cabin reconfiguration project completed after Q3 2022.
   • Missing, incomplete, or unsigned sign-offs require immediate engineering review and submission of a Nonconformance Report (NCR-2024-008).

3. Structural Interface & Gap Measurement
   • Perform visual and borescope inspection of the plug-to-fuselage interface for fretting, witness marks, paint transfer, or misalignment.
   • Measure interface gap at four quadrants using calibrated feeler gauges. Any deviation exceeding 0.015 inches requires immediate grounding and escalation to Fleet Engineering.
   • Verify that the pilot in command has been briefed on any deferred maintenance items affecting cabin pressurization or structural continuity prior to dispatch.

4. Adjacent Systems & Load Path Verification
   • Inspect overhead bin rails, cabin pressure relief valves, and fuselage stringer attachments within 24 inches of the plug perimeter.
   • Conduct visual and eddy-current inspection of LEAP-1B pylon forward mount brackets for stress cracking or fastener back-out. Document findings per Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 54-10-01.
   • Ensure all inspection tools are calibrated within the last 30 days and logged in Tool Control System TCS-994. Use only digital torque wrenches with audible/visual confirmation.

5. Data Submission & Quality Portal Upload
   • All findings must be documented in MTS under Alert Code 2024-014.
   • High-resolution photographs of each retention bolt, stop fitting, and interface gap must be uploaded to the Quality Portal within 2 hours of inspection completion.
   • Attach completed Work Package WP-737M-INS-04 and calibration certificates for all measurement tools.

ACTION REQUIRED:
• Line Maintenance Supervisors: Ensure all affected aircraft are pulled from service and scheduled for inspection within 24 hours of this alert’s issuance. Prioritize aircraft with >15,000 flight cycles or recent heavy maintenance visits.
• Base Maintenance Technicians: Complete full door plug retention verification per WP-737M-INS-04. Submit completed checklists, torque logs, and photographic evidence to Quality Assurance by COB January 15, 2024.
• Quality Assurance Inspectors: Perform 100% audit of all completed inspections. Validate torque values, documentation completeness, and tool calibration records. Issue immediate grounding authority for any non-compliant aircraft.
• Engineering Support: Review all submitted NCRs and coordinate with OEM technical representatives for disposition. Update the fleet maintenance program to incorporate enhanced inspection intervals pending final FAA guidance.
• Training & Compliance: All personnel performing these inspections must complete the 2-hour refresher module “737 MAX Door Plug Retention & Structural Verification” (Course ID: MRO-737-2024-01) before signing off on any work.

Failure to comply with this Quality Alert will result in immediate suspension of maintenance privileges and escalation to the Director of Safety. All technical discrepancies, tooling issues, or documentation gaps must be routed to the Fleet Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or via the Quality Portal ticketing system.

This document is classified as INTERNAL – OPERATIONAL USE ONLY. All records, inspection logs, and photographic evidence will be retained in accordance with company records retention policy and preserved for regulatory review and investigative proceedings.

1. SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:15 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major U.S. air carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during initial climb. The aircraft departed from a Pacific Northwest regional airport and was en route to a southwestern destination when the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport, where the aircraft landed without further incident; there were no reported fatalities or serious injuries among the passengers and crew on board.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Final factual information has been compiled from initial data downloads, ATC recordings, and early interviews with flight and cabin personnel. Initial information indicates that the flight crew reported a sudden loud noise accompanied by a rapid loss of cabin pressure shortly after passing through 16,000 feet. The Captain immediately initiated emergency descent procedures, donned supplemental oxygen, and coordinated with air traffic control to divert back to the departure facility. Cabin crew accounts, while still being formally documented, suggest that loose objects and personal items were displaced into the cabin aisle, and several passengers sustained minor abrasions consistent with rapid decompression dynamics.

Meteorological data obtained from the departure airport and surrounding weather observation networks indicate that conditions at the time of the event were characterized by scattered clouds at 3,000 feet, visibility exceeding 10 statute miles, and surface winds from the northwest at 8 knots. No significant convective activity, turbulence reports, or icing conditions were documented along the initial climb path. Preliminary examination of the recovered airframe components revealed substantial localized damage to the left fuselage skin surrounding the mid-exit door plug location. The door plug assembly, along with adjacent structural fasteners and sealant material, was recovered from a residential area near the departure airport and has been secured for further metallurgical and dimensional analysis. Initial visual inspection suggests that the separation occurred along the forward and aft retention tracks, though definitive failure modes remain undetermined pending detailed laboratory evaluation.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Air Traffic Control groups have been formally established and are currently conducting preliminary data collection and analysis. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has been designated as a party to the investigation, alongside representatives from the aircraft manufacturer, the operating carrier, and relevant labor organizations. Technical specialists from General Electric Aviation (GEA) have been integrated into the Powerplants group to assist with engine data analysis and to evaluate any potential secondary effects on propulsion systems resulting from the decompression event.

All relevant flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) media have been secured and transported to the NTSB’s Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for readout and validation. Initial data extraction is underway, with preliminary parameters indicating normal engine performance and standard flight control inputs prior to the reported event. The investigation team is also reviewing maintenance records, work orders, and quality assurance documentation associated with the affected aircraft, with particular attention to recent structural modifications and door plug installation procedures. In accordance with established certification frameworks, investigators are evaluating compliance with Section 25.571 (14 CFR 25.571) regarding damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of airframe structure, as well as reviewing maintenance program adherence under the guidance of AC 120-16G (Advisory Circular 120-16G).

Comparative analysis is being initiated to assess structural and procedural commonalities between the affected aircraft and other variants within the same family, including the BOEING 737-8, to determine whether design or manufacturing factors may be relevant to the current event. All recovered debris, including the door plug, fasteners, and adjacent fuselage panels, have been cataloged, photographed, and placed in secure storage pending non-destructive testing and microscopic examination. The investigation scope has been formally documented to encompass airframe design, manufacturing processes, maintenance history, operational procedures, and regulatory oversight, with all findings remaining strictly preliminary and subject to revision as additional evidence is evaluated.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks will focus on comprehensive laboratory analysis of the recovered structural components, including scanning electron microscopy, hardness testing, and dimensional verification of the door plug retention system. The FDR and CVR data will undergo full decoding, synchronization, and validation, with particular emphasis on cabin pressure trends, flight control surface positions, and crew communications during the decompression sequence. Maintenance records will be cross-referenced with manufacturer service bulletins and airworthiness directives to identify any recent interventions or deferred maintenance items that may have contributed to the event.

The investigation team will also conduct structured interviews with maintenance personnel, quality control inspectors, and flight operations staff to establish a comprehensive timeline of pre-flight activities and post-maintenance verification procedures. Coordination with the Agency will continue to assess fleet-wide implications and to evaluate the adequacy of current inspection protocols for similar aircraft configurations. All investigative groups will submit preliminary technical reports to the Board within 30 days, which will be synthesized into a formal factual update.

Given the complexity of the structural and procedural elements involved, the investigation is expected to require an extended period to complete. The NTSB will issue periodic public updates as significant milestones are reached, with a comprehensive factual report anticipated within 12 to 18 months. All preliminary observations documented herein are subject to change as additional data is collected, analyzed, and validated. No conclusions regarding causal factors or operational deficiencies are being drawn at this time, and all findings remain strictly preliminary pending the completion of the full investigative process.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION
1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 1724 Pacific Standard Time (PST), a rapid decompression event occurred aboard a Boeing 737-9 MAX airplane during the initial climb phase of flight. The event transpired at a pressure altitude of approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 12 nautical miles northwest of Portland International Airport (KPDX), Portland, Oregon. The geographic coordinates of the incident location were recorded as 45°38.2′N, 122°48.5′W. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent and returned to KPDX, landing safely at 1742 PST. No fatalities or serious injuries were reported among the 171 passengers and 6 crewmembers on board.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator Identification
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufacturer serial number 44442, registered as N704AL. The airplane was operated by a major U.S. scheduled air carrier under the authority of a Part 121 operating certificate. The operator’s principal base of operations was located in the Pacific Northwest region. The aircraft was configured for 178 passenger seats and featured a standard mid-cabin exit door plug configuration on both the left and right sides of the fuselage.

1.3 Nature of Flight
The flight was conducted as a scheduled passenger service under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The flight departed KPDX at 1711 PST, en route to Ontario International Airport (KONT), Ontario, California. The flight plan was filed under instrument flight rules (IFR) with a planned cruise altitude of flight level 350. The flight was operating in accordance with the operator’s approved operations specifications and standard operating procedures for domestic scheduled service.

2. CREW INFORMATION
2.1 Captain Qualifications and Records
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating. The captain’s medical certificate was first class, issued on November 12, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 11,450 hours, with 3,210 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain successfully completed the operator’s recurrent training and proficiency check on October 18, 2023, in accordance with 14 CFR 121.433 and 121.441. The training syllabus included emergency descent procedures, rapid decompression recognition, and cabin pressurization system management.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Records
The first officer held an ATP certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating. The first officer’s medical certificate was first class, issued on December 5, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 4,890 hours, with 1,120 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer completed the operator’s line-oriented flight training (LOFT) and proficiency evaluation on September 22, 2023, satisfying the requirements of 14 CFR 121.439. Training records indicated satisfactory performance in all evaluated maneuvers, including abnormal and emergency procedures.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Compliance
Both flight crewmembers met the recent flight experience requirements of 14 CFR 121.439 and 121.440. The captain had accumulated 87 flight hours and 42 landings in the preceding 90 days. The first officer had accumulated 76 flight hours and 38 landings in the same period. Both crewmembers were current in instrument approaches, holding procedures, and emergency descent protocols. The operator’s training department confirmed that all required recurrent training modules, including cabin depressurization and door system familiarization, were completed within the mandated 12-month cycle. No discrepancies were noted in the crewmembers’ qualification files or duty time records for the 72 hours preceding the accident flight.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION
3.1 Airframe and Powerplant Specifications
The accident airplane was manufactured by The Boeing Company and delivered to the operator on October 14, 2023. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 145 total flight hours and 110 total flight cycles. The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured under a joint venture between General Electric Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines. The engines were installed per the approved type design and maintained in accordance with the operator’s continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP). The LEAP-1B powerplants were rated at 28,000 pounds of thrust and were equipped with full authority digital engine control (FADEC) systems. Engine performance parameters recorded during the climb phase indicated normal operation, with no exceedances or fault indications prior to the decompression event.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft’s maintenance records were reviewed for the period from delivery through the accident date. The most recent scheduled maintenance event was a 400-hour/400-cycle inspection completed on December 28, 2023. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) were documented as complied with, including AD 2023-24-08, which addressed mid-cabin exit door plug installation procedures.
