The cabin pressurization system was controlled by the outflow valve and monitored by the cabin altitude warning system. At the time of the event, the cabin altitude was approximately 1,200 feet, with a differential pressure of 4.8 psi.

3.4 Engine and Propulsion Systems
The propulsion system consisted of two CFM International LEAP-1B28 engines, manufactured under a joint venture between General Electric Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines. Engine maintenance records indicated compliance with all manufacturer service bulletins and time-on-wing limits. General Electric Aviation technical support documentation was referenced during the operator's engine health monitoring program, with no anomalies reported in the engine vibration monitoring system (EVMS) or exhaust gas temperature (EGT) margins. Both engines operated within normal parameters throughout the flight, with no thrust reverser deployment or engine shutdown initiated.

3.5 Type Certification and Commonality
The aircraft was type certified under 14 CFR Part 25, with certification basis documentation referencing commonality with the BOEING 737-8 for structural load paths, pressurization system architecture, and emergency evacuation requirements. The door plug design was evaluated under Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) provisions and incorporated into the original type design for the 737 MAX series. Structural analysis documentation indicated that the plug retention system was designed to withstand a maximum differential pressure of 9.0 psi, with a safety factor of 1.5 applied to ultimate load conditions.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
A high-pressure system dominated the Pacific Northwest region on January 5, 2024, resulting in stable atmospheric conditions and minimal convective activity. Surface analysis indicated a weak cold front located approximately 200 nautical miles west of the Oregon coast, with no significant frontal passage anticipated during the flight's operational window.

4.2 METAR and TAF Data
The KPDX METAR at 16:53 PST reported: wind 090° at 6 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, clear skies, temperature 4°C, dewpoint 1°C, altimeter 30.12 inHg. The TAF for KPDX, valid from 17:00 PST to 17:00 PST the following day, forecasted VFR conditions with winds shifting to 120° at 8 knots and no significant weather phenomena. No amendments or special weather statements were issued during the flight's departure window.

4.3 Pilot Reports and In-Flight Weather
No pilot reports (PIREPs) of turbulence, icing, or wind shear were filed along the departure route or within the terminal area. The flight crew reported clear skies and smooth air during the initial climb phase. No convective SIGMETs or AIRMETs were active for the region at the time of the event.

4.4 Atmospheric Conditions at Altitude
At 16,000 feet MSL, the standard atmosphere model indicated a temperature of approximately -15°C, with a pressure altitude of 16,150 feet. The cabin differential pressure at the time of the event was 4.8 psi, consistent with normal climb phase pressurization schedules. No rapid temperature fluctuations or atmospheric density anomalies were recorded by the aircraft's air data computer (ADC) or flight data recorder (FDR).

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The left mid-exit door plug was recovered intact from a residential area approximately 12.3 nautical miles northwest of KPDX, at coordinates 45.638° N, 122.891° W. The plug exhibited no evidence of in-flight fragmentation or thermal damage. The primary fuselage wreckage remained intact and was recovered to a secure hangar facility for detailed examination. No other aircraft components were separated from the airframe during the event.

5.2 Fuselage and Door Plug Examination
Examination of the fuselage revealed a clean separation at the left mid-exit door plug opening. The plug retention fasteners were absent from the forward and aft guide track mounting points. The inner and outer plug panels remained mated, with the perimeter seal exhibiting localized compression marks consistent with rapid pressure equalization. The guide tracks showed no evidence of plastic deformation or fatigue cracking. The stop fittings were intact and properly aligned with the fuselage structure.

5.3 Structural and Fastener Analysis
Metallurgical examination of the recovered fastener holes indicated that the retention bolts were not present at the time of the event. The hole edges exhibited clean machining marks with no evidence of thread stripping, galling, or fatigue initiation. The plug retention system design relied on a combination of mechanical stops and cabin differential pressure to maintain structural integrity. No foreign object debris (FOD) was identified within the plug cavity or surrounding fuselage structure. The fastener torque values documented in the manufacturing records were within specified limits, with no evidence of improper installation or subsequent loosening.

5.4 Cabin Interior and Systems Damage
The rapid decompression event resulted in the deployment of passenger oxygen masks in the affected cabin zone. Interior examination revealed minor displacement of overhead bin panels and localized damage to the left-side cabin sidewall trim. The cabin pressure warning system activated at 10,000 feet cabin altitude, consistent with design parameters. The emergency descent was initiated by the flight crew, and the aircraft descended to 10,000 feet MSL within 4 minutes 12 seconds. No injuries were reported among passengers or crew. The aircraft's structural integrity was maintained throughout the event, and the flight control systems remained fully operational.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
The operator maintained a documented maintenance tracking system in compliance with 14 CFR 121.363 and 121.369. Quality assurance audits were conducted quarterly, with the most recent audit completed on December 20, 2023. The operator's maintenance program included specific procedures for door plug inspections, fastener torque verification, and structural integrity assessments. All maintenance personnel involved in the aircraft's servicing held appropriate FAA mechanic certificates with airframe and powerplant (A&P) ratings.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
A review of the operator's safety reporting system and the FAA's Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) database identified two previous reports involving door plug retention anomalies on 737 MAX series aircraft. Both reports were classified as non-critical and resulted in corrective actions including enhanced inspection intervals and revised torque verification procedures. No prior incidents involving complete door plug separation during flight had been documented in the operator's fleet or within the broader 737 MAX operational history prior to this event.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Advisory Circulars
The aircraft's maintenance and operational procedures were governed by 14 CFR Part 25, Subpart C (Structure), and Part 121, Subpart L (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations). The operator's maintenance program was developed in accordance with Advisory Circular AC 120-16G, Air Carrier Maintenance Programs, which provides guidance on continuous airworthiness maintenance program development, quality assurance, and reliability monitoring. The door plug design and installation procedures were evaluated under 14 CFR 25.365 (Pressurized cabin loads) and 25.783 (Fuselage doors). Compliance with manufacturer service bulletins and FAA airworthiness directives was documented in the aircraft's maintenance records.

6.4 Flight Data Recorder and Cockpit Voice Recorder Information
The aircraft was equipped with a solid-state flight data recorder (FDR) and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which were recovered and downloaded without incident. The FDR recorded 2,048 parameters, including cabin altitude, differential pressure, airspeed, altitude, and control surface positions. Data indicated a rapid cabin altitude increase from 1,200 feet to 14,500 feet within 18 seconds, followed by a controlled emergency descent. The CVR captured standard crew communications, including the initial decompression report, emergency checklist execution, and coordination with air traffic control. No abnormal system warnings or crew deviations from standard operating procedures were identified in the recorded data. The recorders were secured and forwarded to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for further analysis.

1. INTRODUCTION

This report documents the factual findings of the specialist examination conducted by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Structures and Materials Group regarding the in-flight separation of the left mid-cabin exit door plug (MCDP) from a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, operated by a major U.S. air carrier. The examination was initiated following the rapid decompression event that occurred on January 5, 2024, during the climb phase of flight at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (ft MSL). The scope of this investigation encompasses the physical, dimensional, and metallurgical evaluation of the recovered door plug assembly, adjacent fuselage structure, retention hardware, and associated flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) parameters. The examination was conducted between January 10 and January 18, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with supplemental dimensional inspections and engineering data correlation performed at the Boeing Commercial Airplanes facility in Everett, Washington.

Items examined included the primary door plug structure (Part Number 65-12345-678, Serial Number DP-2023-0891), four (4) upper and lower guide track assemblies, twelve (12) stop fitting brackets, twenty-four (24) primary retention fastener locations, and the surrounding fuselage skin, frames, and stringer sections. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, referencing engineering standards established by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the original equipment manufacturer. The examination methodology incorporated macroscopic visual inspection, precision coordinate measuring machine (CMM) metrology, non-destructive inspection (NDI), mechanical testing, and metallurgical analysis. Flight data parameters were extracted, time-synchronized, and analyzed to correlate structural loading conditions with the recorded decompression event.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a derivative of the BOEING 737-8 family, configured with a high-density cabin layout that necessitates the installation of mid-cabin exit door plugs in lieu of operational Type III emergency exits. The MCDP is a non-pressurized, structurally integrated panel designed to maintain the aerodynamic contour and pressure boundary of the aft fuselage. The assembly consists of a 2024-T3 aluminum alloy skin panel, reinforced with 7075-T6 extruded stringers and a perimeter frame, secured to the fuselage via a series of guide tracks, roller assemblies, and primary retention fasteners. The design certification basis for the door plug assembly complies with 14 CFR 25.571, Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure, requiring demonstration of fail-safe load paths, residual strength, and crack growth characteristics under cyclic pressurization and flight loads. The maximum certified cabin differential pressure for the 737 MAX series is 8.6 pounds per square inch (PSI), with a limit load factor of 2.5g and ultimate load factor of 3.75g.

The specific unit under examination was manufactured in October 2023 and installed on the subject airframe during final assembly. The aircraft accumulated 145 flight cycles and 420.3 flight hours prior to the event. Maintenance records indicate compliance with the manufacturer’s structural inspection program and adherence to Advisory Circular AC 120-16G, Air Carrier Maintenance Programs, for scheduled and unscheduled maintenance actions. The aircraft is powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B engines, manufactured by GE Aviation, which provide thrust and bleed air for cabin pressurization via the environmental control system (ECS). The ECS utilizes engine bleed air regulated by the pack valves and outflow valves to maintain cabin altitude and pressure differential during climb and cruise. No maintenance discrepancies related to the left MCDP were documented in the aircraft technical log or maintenance tracking system prior to the event. The door plug retention system relies on a combination of shear-loaded fasteners, guide track rollers, and stop fittings to transfer aerodynamic and pressurization loads into the primary fuselage structure.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The physical examination of the recovered door plug assembly and adjacent fuselage structure was conducted using a combination of macroscopic visual inspection, precision dimensional metrology, non-destructive inspection (NDI), and metallurgical analysis. The door plug was received in three primary sections: the main panel, the upper guide track assembly, and the lower stop fitting bracket. Visual examination revealed significant plastic deformation along the forward and aft guide track interfaces, with localized yielding of the 7075-T6 aluminum extrusions. The perimeter fastener holes exhibited elongation ranging from 0.012 to 0.034 inches, exceeding the manufacturer’s allowable tolerance of 0.008 inches for primary retention hardware. Coordinate measuring machine (CMM) inspection confirmed a maximum out-of-plane deflection of 0.185 inches along the aft edge of the door plug, consistent with asymmetric load distribution during separation.

A detailed fastener audit was performed on the recovered components. Of the twenty-four (24) primary retention bolts specified in the assembly drawing, only fourteen (14) were recovered in situ. Ten (10) fastener locations were found empty, with no evidence of thread engagement or shear fracture. The recovered bolts, identified as NAS1097AD6-12, were subjected to torque verification testing per NASM1312-7 using a calibrated digital torque wrench (Model TQ-4500, calibrated to ±1.5% per ISO 6789-1:2017). Measured installation torque values ranged from 18 to 24 inch-pounds, significantly below the specified installation torque of 45 ± 5 inch-pounds. Thread engagement analysis indicated that the empty fastener locations lacked proper nutplate retention, with witness marks consistent with incomplete installation or post-installation removal. Microscopic examination of the empty fastener holes revealed no evidence of fretting, galling, or thread stripping, suggesting the fasteners were never properly torqued or were removed prior to the event.

Non-destructive inspection of the door plug skin and surrounding fuselage frames was conducted using eddy current testing (ECT) per ASTM E309 and ultrasonic phased array (UTPA) per ASTM E2491. No fatigue cracks, corrosion, or material degradation were identified in the 2024-T3 aluminum skin or the adjacent fuselage longerons. Chemical composition analysis of the skin material, performed via optical emission spectroscopy (OES), confirmed compliance with AMS 4037 specifications for 2024-T3 aluminum alloy, with copper content at 4.42%, magnesium at 1.51%, and manganese at 0.68%. Hardness testing (Rockwell B scale) yielded an average value of 82 HRB, consistent with the T3 temper condition. Tensile coupon testing of representative material samples, conducted per ASTM E8, demonstrated a yield strength of 48.5 ksi and ultimate tensile strength of 68.2 ksi, within the material specification limits.

Fracture surface analysis of the deformed guide track brackets was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 15 kV accelerating voltage. The fracture morphology exhibited ductile tearing with microvoid coalescence, characteristic of overload failure under tensile and shear loading. No evidence of fatigue striations, stress corrosion cracking, or hydrogen embrittlement was observed. Static load testing of a representative guide track assembly, conducted per ASTM E8, demonstrated a yield strength of 68.2 ksi and ultimate tensile strength of 78.5 ksi, within the material specification limits. The failure mode was determined to be progressive fastener disengagement leading to loss of structural constraint, followed by aerodynamic and pressure-induced separation.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) parameters were extracted and analyzed to reconstruct the flight profile and correlate structural loading with the decompression event. The aircraft departed from Portland International Airport (KPDX) at 08:04:12 UTC. The pilot in command initiated a standard climb profile, with indicated airspeed (IAS) maintained at 280 knots and vertical speed averaging 2,200 feet per minute. Engine parameters for both LEAP-1B powerplants, monitored via the engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS), remained within normal operating envelopes. N1 rotation averaged 89.2%, exhaust gas temperature (EGT) stabilized at 612°C, and fuel flow was consistent with climb thrust settings. No engine anomalies, bleed air faults, or pack valve irregularities were recorded.

Cabin pressure differential data, sampled at 1 Hz, indicated a steady increase from 0.0 PSI at takeoff to 8.1 PSI at 15,800 ft MSL. At 08:12:34 UTC, coincident with the aircraft passing through 16,000 ft MSL, the cabin differential pressure parameter exhibited an instantaneous drop from 8.1 PSI to 0.2 PSI within 1.2 seconds. This rapid depressurization was accompanied by a transient vertical acceleration spike of +1.8g, followed by a -0.4g negative load factor as the aircraft experienced aerodynamic buffet and control surface deflection. The outflow valve position parameter indicated a commanded closure to 0% open, consistent with the ECS response to a rapid pressure loss.

The flight control computer (FCC) recorded aileron and elevator deflections of up to 12.5 degrees and 8.3 degrees, respectively, as the pilot in command initiated a descent and return to KPDX. The aircraft’s structural load monitoring system did not record any exceedances of limit load factors prior to the event. Comparison of the recorded pressure differential and climb rate with the manufacturer’s normal operational envelope confirms that the aircraft was operating within certified parameters at the time of separation. The LEAP-1B engine bleed air supply, regulated by the high-pressure compressor stage 9, maintained a steady pressure of 38 PSI, with no evidence of surge, stall, or overtemperature conditions. The rapid decompression event was isolated to the left mid-cabin exit door plug, with no secondary structural damage or system failures recorded in the FDR data stream.

Time-synchronized analysis of the FDR and QAR data streams revealed a 0.8-second delay between the initial pressure drop and the activation of the cabin altitude warning system, consistent with the sensor sampling rate and system logic thresholds. The aircraft’s autopilot disengaged automatically at 08:12:36 UTC, and manual control inputs were recorded within 1.5 seconds. The descent profile was executed at a rate of 3,500 feet per minute, with airspeed reduced to 250 knots below 10,000 ft MSL. All recorded parameters remained within the operational limits defined in the aircraft flight manual.

5. SUMMARY

The specialist examination of the left mid-cabin exit door plug assembly and associated flight data yielded the following factual findings:
- The recovered door plug structure (P/N 65-12345-678, S/N DP-2023-0891) exhibited plastic deformation along the forward and aft guide track interfaces, with localized yielding of the 7075-T6 aluminum extrusions.
- Ten (10) of the twenty-four (24) primary retention fastener locations were found empty, with no evidence of thread engagement or shear fracture. The recovered fasteners measured installation torque values of 18 to 24 inch-pounds, below the specified 45 ± 5 inch-pounds.
- Non-destructive inspection and metallurgical analysis of the 2024-T3 aluminum skin and surrounding fuselage frames revealed no fatigue cracks, corrosion, or material degradation. Chemical composition and hardness testing confirmed compliance with AMS 4037 and T3 temper specifications.
- Fracture surface analysis of the guide track brackets indicated ductile overload failure with microvoid coalescence, consistent with progressive fastener disengagement and loss of structural constraint.
- FDR and QAR data recorded a cabin pressure differential of 8.1 PSI at 15,800 ft MSL, followed by an instantaneous drop to 0.2 PSI within 1.2 seconds at 16,000 ft MSL. The aircraft was operating within certified climb parameters, with LEAP-1B engine performance and ECS bleed air supply within normal limits.
- The pilot in command executed a controlled descent and return to the departure airport, with no exceedances of structural load limits or secondary system failures recorded.
- The door plug assembly was designed and certified in accordance with 14 CFR 25.571, with maintenance and inspection procedures aligned with AC 120-16G guidelines. The FAA has issued airworthiness directives and operational bulletins in response to the event.

All findings are presented as factual observations derived from physical examination, material testing, and recorded flight data. No determination of probable cause is included in this report.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER MARCUS T. CHEN
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 10:15 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Seattle, Washington
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Lin, NTSB Aviation Safety Division
Witness: Marcus T. Chen, First Officer, Flight 1282

Q: Good morning, Mr. Chen. Thank you for coming in. This interview is being recorded for the official record of the National Transportation Safety Board investigation into the January 5th incident. Do you understand the purpose of this interview and consent to being recorded?
A: Yes, ma’am. I understand. I’m, uh, I’m fully cooperating. Whatever you need.

Q: Please state your full name, your title, and your role on the flight in question.
A: Marcus Thomas Chen. I’m a First Officer with the airline. I was the right-seat pilot on Flight 1282 on January fifth. So, co-pilot, handling the radios, monitoring systems, that sort of thing.

Q: Can you walk me through the sequence of events from your pre-flight preparations up to the point of departure?
A: Sure. I, uh, reported to the airport around, I think it was 10:30 in the morning. Standard turnaround. We did the walk-around, checked the logbook, everything was clean. No squawks. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 9, obviously. I’ve got more hours on the MAX 8, honestly, but the transition is pretty seamless. Same flight deck, same procedures. We pushed back on time, started the engines—both LEAP-1Bs spooled up normally, no vibration, EGTs were right where they should be. We taxied out, got our clearance, and took off from runway 16L at about 11:45. Climb was smooth. I was flying the leg, so I had the controls. The captain was handling the radios and monitoring.

Q: You mentioned you were flying the leg. At what point did the event occur, and what were your immediate observations?
A: Right. We were passing through, I want to say, sixteen thousand feet. Maybe a hundred or two hundred feet below that, actually. The autopilot was engaged, we were in VNAV, climbing at a normal rate. And then—there was this… this massive bang. Not like an engine failure. It was louder, sharper. Like a cannon shot, but muffled by the airframe. And immediately after, the whole cabin just… it felt like the air got ripped out. My ears popped hard, and I felt this sudden, violent pressure change. The yoke shuddered a little, but the airplane didn’t really pitch or roll. It just… it just kept going, but the noise was insane. Wind roaring. Like a freight train right behind us.

Q: What did the cockpit instruments indicate at that moment?
A: Master caution lit up instantly. Then the cabin altitude warning horn started blaring. I looked at the pressurization panel and the cabin altitude was just… it was climbing rapidly. I think it hit ten thousand feet in maybe three or four seconds. The pilot in command immediately took control, called “my aircraft,” and I said “your aircraft.” He disconnected the autopilot, leveled us off, and we started the emergency descent checklist. I was running through the memory items, but honestly, the wind noise was so loud it was hard to hear the interphone. I remember looking at the left side of the fuselage on the overhead panel, but the indications were just… chaotic. We didn’t know what had actually blown out at that exact second.

Q: Did you have any visual confirmation of the damage from the flight deck?
A: Not directly. The flight deck windows are forward-facing, and the door plug is mid-cabin, left side. But when we turned back toward the airport, I could see through the left window that the… the structure was just gone. There was a gaping hole. I could see daylight where the wall should’ve been. And there was debris, I think, maybe a seat cushion or something, just… floating out. It was surreal. I mean, you train for rapid decompression, you run the sims, but actually seeing it… it’s different.

Q: How did you communicate with the cabin crew, and what was their response?
A: I tried the interphone right after we leveled off. At first, it was just static. Then the lead flight attendant came on. She was calm, but you could hear the wind in the background. She reported that the left mid-exit door plug had separated, that oxygen masks had deployed, and that they were securing the cabin. I was really impressed, honestly. The training they get under AC 120-16G, the air carrier flight attendant program, it really showed. They didn’t panic. They got everyone on oxygen, checked for injuries, and started moving passengers away from the left side. The pilot in command and I were focused on flying, but knowing the cabin was under control let us concentrate on the descent and the return.

Q: You mentioned returning to the departure airport. Can you describe the approach and landing?
A: Yeah. We declared an emergency with Seattle Center, got vectors back. We were heavy, obviously, hadn’t burned much fuel. The captain handled the approach. We configured for landing, but we had to be careful with the speed because of the… the missing panel. We didn’t want to overstress the remaining structure. We came in on runway 16R, touched down around 12:15, maybe 12:18. I don’t remember the exact minute. The landing was firm but controlled. We vacated the runway, taxied to a remote stand, and shut down the engines. The LEAP-1Bs spooled down normally, no issues there.

Q: Were there any injuries reported, and what was the condition of the passengers and crew?
A: No fatalities, thank God. A few minor injuries from the initial decompression—bruises, maybe a couple of people who hit their heads when the masks dropped. One flight attendant had a minor laceration from flying debris, but she was walking and talking. The passengers were shaken, obviously. Some were crying, some were just in shock. But the crew got them off safely. We had stairs brought to the aircraft, and everyone deplaned in an orderly fashion.

Q: After shutdown, what was your interaction with maintenance and regulatory personnel?
A: We stayed on board until the fire department and the airline’s maintenance team arrived. Then, uh, Federal Aviation Administration inspectors showed up pretty quickly. They secured the aircraft, started documenting the damage. I gave them a preliminary statement, handed over the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, and then we were debriefed by the company’s chief pilot. The FAA guys were thorough. They took photos, measured the hole, started looking at the door plug mounting points. I didn’t get into the technical weeds with them, but I could tell they were already zeroing in on the fasteners and the plug retention system.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add about the aircraft’s performance or your crew’s actions that you feel is relevant to the investigation?
A: Just that… the airplane handled exactly as it’s supposed to. Even with a massive hole in the side, the flight controls were responsive. The engines didn’t ingest anything, which was a huge relief. And the crew resource management was solid. We didn’t freeze. We followed the QRH, we communicated, we prioritized flying the airplane. I’ve been flying for twelve years, and I’ve never seen anything like it. But the training, the procedures, the redundancy in the systems… it all worked. I think the investigation will probably look at the manufacturing process, the door plug installation, maybe the torque values on those bolts. But from a flight deck perspective, we did what we were trained to do.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. We may have follow-up questions as the investigation progresses. Do you have any questions for us at this time?
A: No, ma’am. Just… I hope the families of the passengers get some answers soon. And I hope the airline gets the fleet grounded until they figure out exactly what happened. I mean, it’s a MAX 9, but it’s the same family as the Boeing 737 MAX 8, and people are nervous. I just want to make sure it’s safe before I fly again. But I trust the process. Thank you.

Q: The interview is concluded at 11:02 AM PST. Thank you for your time and cooperation.
A: You’re welcome.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AIRCRAFT CERTIFICATION
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20591

DOCKET NO. FAA-2024-0112
REFERENCE: EAD 2024-02-08 / NTSB SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-24-01
DATE: March 15, 2024

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the formal regulatory response and compliance framework addressing Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) 2024-02-08, issued pursuant to 14 CFR § 39.13, and subsequent National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-24-01. The directive mandates immediate structural inspection, fastener torque verification, and retention hardware compliance for Boeing 737 MAX series aircraft equipped with mid-exit door plug configurations.

NTSB Accident Number: DCA24MA055
Date of Occurrence: January 5, 2024
Aircraft Involved: Boeing 737-9 MAX, Registration N704AL
Event Classification: In-flight rapid decompression due to structural separation of left mid-exit door plug during climb phase at approximately 16,000 feet MSL.

2. BACKGROUND
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) maintains regulatory oversight of all transport category aircraft operating under 14 CFR Part 121. The certification basis for the Boeing 737 MAX family, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 variants, is established under Type Certificate (TC) A16WE, with structural integrity governed by 14 CFR Part 25, Subpart C. Specifically, § 25.571 establishes mandatory damage tolerance requirements for fatigue evaluation of primary and secondary structure, while § 25.783 prescribes design and installation standards for fuselage doors, including plug-type configurations.

Historically, the FAA has issued multiple airworthiness directives addressing production quality variances and software certification deficiencies within the MAX fleet. Prior to the January 2024 event, AD 2019-09-09 and AD 2023-15-02 established baseline inspection protocols and manufacturing oversight requirements. However, the rapid decompression incident revealed systemic deficiencies in the application of approved manufacturing processes at the Spirit AeroSystems production facility, specifically concerning the installation and torque verification of retention fasteners for the mid-exit door plug.

The operator’s Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP), developed in accordance with Advisory Circular 120-16G (AC 120-16G), Air Carrier Maintenance Programs, did not incorporate specific inspection criteria for door plug retention hardware. This omission created a regulatory gap wherein production-level non-conformances were not captured during routine line maintenance or heavy checks. Furthermore, while the propulsion systems, including the CFM International LEAP-1B engines manufactured by GE Aviation, operate under separate certification and maintenance frameworks, the integration of airframe structural loads and engine pylon stress distributions necessitates a harmonized approach to structural integrity monitoring. The FAA’s oversight mandate requires that all structural modifications, whether original equipment manufacturer (OEM) or supplemental type certificate (STC) driven, comply with established airworthiness standards and be fully integrated into operator maintenance programs.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the operator’s compliance posture, manufacturer production records, and regulatory oversight mechanisms yields the following determinations:

a. Compliance Status: Initial forensic examination of the recovered door plug and adjacent fuselage structure indicates non-conformance with approved manufacturing documentation. Specifically, four retention bolts were found to be improperly torqued, and two guide track fasteners were absent. These deficiencies constitute a direct violation of the approved Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) and the manufacturer’s structural repair manual (SRM) specifications. The operator’s maintenance program, while compliant with baseline 14 CFR Part 121.369 requirements, failed to implement targeted inspection protocols for door plug retention hardware, as recommended under AC 120-16G for high-stress structural interfaces.

b. Regulatory Oversight Actions: The FAA initiated immediate unannounced production audits at the Spirit AeroSystems facility and issued EAD 2024-02-08 to mandate fleet-wide inspections. Oversight personnel conducted a comprehensive review of the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) to ensure no operational allowances compromised structural integrity. Additionally, the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) coordinated with the Flight Standards Service (AFS) to verify that all affected operators had implemented mandatory inspection bulletins within the prescribed compliance window.

c. Identified Regulatory Gaps: The certification framework for the Boeing 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9 variants did not adequately account for production quality control variances in aftermarket door plug installations. The damage tolerance requirements under 14 CFR § 25.571 were not fully integrated into the operator’s CAMP for this specific structural modification, resulting in a reliance on manufacturer service bulletins rather than enforceable regulatory inspection intervals. Furthermore, while the pilot in command (PIC) executed appropriate emergency descent and diversion procedures in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.333 and § 121.344, post-flight reporting mechanisms under 14 CFR § 121.703 revealed delays in structural anomaly documentation, highlighting a need for enhanced real-time telemetry and maintenance reporting integration.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
To ensure continued airworthiness and regulatory compliance, the following corrective actions and oversight measures are mandated:

a. Corrective Actions Required:
   i. All operators of Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with mid-exit door plugs shall complete a one-time detailed inspection of all door plug retention fasteners, guide tracks, and adjacent fuselage structure in accordance with Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-53A1285, Revision 1.
   ii. Any fastener found outside of approved torque specifications shall be replaced with OEM-approved hardware, and the installation shall be documented per 14 CFR § 43.9 and § 43.11.
   iii. Operators shall revise their CAMP to incorporate recurring inspection intervals for door plug retention hardware, aligned with the updated Maintenance Review Board Report (MRBR) and AC 120-16G guidance.

b. Timeline for Compliance:
   i. Initial fleet inspection and torque verification shall be completed within ten (10) calendar days of EAD issuance.
   ii. Full CAMP revision and integration of enhanced inspection protocols shall be submitted to the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) for approval within sixty (60) calendar days.
   iii. All non-conforming hardware replacements shall be completed prior to return to service, with compliance records maintained per 14 CFR § 121.380.

c. Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule:
   i. The FAA shall conduct quarterly production quality audits at the Spirit AeroSystems facility and Boeing final assembly lines to verify adherence to approved manufacturing processes.
   ii. Operators shall submit semi-annual compliance reports to the Aircraft Certification Service, detailing inspection findings, hardware replacements, and maintenance program updates.
   iii. The FAA will coordinate with the NTSB to establish a joint structural integrity review board, tasked with evaluating long-term fatigue performance and updating damage tolerance requirements for plug-type door configurations.
   iv. Enhanced reporting protocols shall be implemented to ensure that any structural anomalies identified during flight operations are transmitted to maintenance control within two (2) hours of landing, in accordance with revised 14 CFR § 121.703 guidance.

This regulatory framework is issued under the authority of 14 CFR Part 39 and Part 121. Failure to comply with the mandated actions may result in enforcement action, including but not limited to certificate suspension or revocation, pursuant to 14 CFR § 13.19. All correspondence regarding compliance status shall be directed to the Office of Aircraft Certification, Docket Management Facility, under Docket No. FAA-2024-0112.

HEADLINE: Mid-Flight Door Plug Separation Triggers Emergency Landing of Boeing 737 MAX 9; No Fatalities Reported

BYLINE: [Reporter Name], [News Outlet]
DATELINE: PORTLAND, Ore. —

A commercial flight operated by a major U.S. airline made a harrowing emergency landing on Friday, Jan. 5, 2024, after a mid-cabin door plug tore away from the fuselage at 16,000 feet, triggering a rapid decompression event. The Boeing 737 MAX 9, carrying 171 passengers and six crew members, departed from a Pacific Northwest airport and returned safely to its origin point. Federal authorities confirmed there were no fatalities, though several passengers sustained minor injuries during the sudden loss of cabin pressure.

The incident unfolded just minutes after takeoff as the aircraft climbed through 16,000 feet. Witnesses described a deafening pop followed by a violent rush of freezing air, the immediate deployment of overhead oxygen masks, and loose personal items being pulled toward the breach. Pilots quickly initiated an emergency descent, dropping to a lower altitude where atmospheric pressure is higher and breathable air is more readily available, before diverting back to the departure airport. The rapid decompression forced an immediate, nationwide grounding of similar aircraft as regulators scrambled to assess the structural integrity of the fleet.

“Our top priority is the safety of the traveling public and the crew aboard this flight,” said a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) spokesperson during a late-night press briefing. “We are working closely with the National Transportation Safety Board and the manufacturer to determine exactly what caused the door plug to separate.” The airline’s chief operations officer echoed the sentiment, stating, “We are deeply grateful to our flight crew for their exceptional training and composure under extreme pressure. We are cooperating fully with investigators and will not resume operations on this aircraft type until we have absolute clarity on the cause.”

The aircraft involved is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, a narrow-body jet designed for medium-haul domestic and regional routes. Unlike older models, this variant features a “door plug”—a reinforced, non-opening panel that replaces an unused emergency exit to accommodate additional seating. The plug is secured by a series of heavy-duty bolts and metal guide tracks, and its failure is exceptionally rare in modern commercial aviation. The flight was en route to a West Coast destination when the incident occurred, cutting short what was expected to be a routine two-hour journey.

Aviation safety analysts are focusing on manufacturing tolerances, maintenance procedures, and structural fatigue as potential factors. “When a pressurized fuselage experiences a sudden breach at altitude, investigators immediately look at the fastening mechanisms and the surrounding skin,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, a former NTSB investigator and aerospace engineering professor. “Regulatory standards like 14 CFR 25.571 require manufacturers to prove that critical structures can withstand repeated pressurization cycles without catastrophic failure. If those bolts weren’t torqued to specification or if a guide track was misaligned during assembly, it could explain the separation.” Chen also noted that maintenance crews follow strict inspection protocols outlined in advisory circulars such as AC 120-16G, which governs how airlines monitor, document, and repair structural components over an aircraft’s operational lifespan. “Any deviation from those guidelines, whether during initial production or subsequent line maintenance, could compromise the plug’s retention system.”

For those on board, the experience was terrifying. “One second we were climbing normally, and the next, the cabin was filled with wind and screaming,” said passenger David Lin, who was seated three rows from the breach. “Oxygen masks dropped, and the temperature plummeted. I just held my daughter’s hand and prayed the pilots knew what they were doing.” Lin’s wife, Sarah, who was waiting at the arrival gate, described the agonizing hours before confirmation of the safe landing. “When the news broke, my phone wouldn’t stop ringing. I couldn’t breathe until I heard his voice. It’s a miracle they all made it back.”

The 737 MAX family has faced intense scrutiny since two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019, which were linked to a flawed flight control system rather than structural issues. Those incidents led to a global grounding and extensive software and training overhauls. The current model shares its powerplant with the Boeing 737 MAX 8, utilizing the LEAP-1B engine developed by GE Aviation. While the engines have maintained a strong reliability record, the door plug failure has reignited concerns about Boeing’s quality control processes. “The MAX series has a solid operational history since its return to service, but this incident strikes at the heart of airframe manufacturing,” said aviation historian and safety consultant Rebecca Torres. “It’s a reminder that even with advanced engineering, human error in assembly or inspection can have immediate, dramatic consequences.”

The NTSB has dispatched a specialized “go team” to the scene, and investigators are currently examining the recovered door plug, the aircraft’s flight data recorder, and maintenance logs. The FAA has issued an emergency airworthiness directive requiring immediate inspections of all 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with similar door plugs. Airlines are conducting visual and tactile checks of the fasteners, with many flights canceled or delayed as the process unfolds. “We are treating this as a systemic issue until proven otherwise,” the FAA spokesperson added. “Every aircraft of this configuration is grounded until it passes a rigorous inspection.” As the investigation enters its critical early phase, regulators, manufacturers, and carriers are working around the clock to restore public confidence and ensure the skies remain safe.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Aircraft Manufacturer Engineering and Airworthiness Division, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9. Our role in this proceeding is to provide subject-matter expertise in airframe structural design, manufacturing quality assurance, installation procedures, and continuing airworthiness integration. The scope of this document encompasses a technical evaluation of the mid-exit door plug (MEP) retention system, an analysis of manufacturing and verification processes, a review of operational and flight data, and a structured assessment of contributing factors. We submit this analysis in full cooperation with the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration, and all participating parties, with the shared objective of identifying systemic vulnerabilities, validating engineering assumptions, and advancing industry-wide safety outcomes.

Our position is grounded in empirical data, certified design documentation, manufacturing traveler records, and post-event forensic examinations. While the aircraft design meets all applicable certification requirements and has demonstrated a robust safety record across the fleet, this event has exposed critical gaps in process execution, quality verification, and human-system integration during final assembly. This submission does not seek to assign singular blame but rather to illuminate the intersection of design intent, manufacturing reality, and operational oversight. We acknowledge the complexity of modern aerospace production environments and recognize that safety is a continuous, multi-layered discipline requiring rigorous adherence to approved procedures, transparent data sharing, and proactive risk mitigation.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft departed a Pacific Northwest airport on a scheduled revenue flight. During climb through approximately 16,000 feet, the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage, resulting in rapid decompression. The pilot in command immediately initiated emergency descent procedures in accordance with the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH), stabilized the aircraft, and executed a safe return to the departure airport. No fatalities or serious injuries were reported. The aircraft was equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, which operated within normal parameters throughout the event, as confirmed by engine health monitoring data and post-flight inspection.

The NTSB docket contains extensive evidence relevant to this analysis, including:
- Flight Data Recorder (FDR) and Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) transcripts (Docket Items 14, 17, 22)
- Post-event structural inspection reports and recovered debris analysis (Docket Items 31, 35, 42)
- Manufacturing traveler documentation, torque verification logs, and quality control sign-off records (Docket Items 58, 61, 67)
- Pressurization system telemetry and cabin altitude rate-of-change data (Docket Item 29)
- Maintenance history and operator configuration records (Docket Items 73, 78)

The mid-exit door plug is a structural component installed in lieu of a fully operational emergency exit door when an operator’s seating configuration does not require the additional egress capacity. The plug is retained by a combination of primary fasteners, guide tracks, and secondary retention features designed to withstand maximum differential pressure loads, fatigue cycles, and dynamic flight environments. The subject aircraft’s configuration utilized the standard MAX 9 plug variant, which shares fundamental design architecture with the Boeing 737 MAX 8 but incorporates modified load paths and attachment geometry to accommodate the extended fuselage section.

Review of the manufacturing traveler documentation indicates that the left MEP underwent multiple rework cycles during final assembly. Docket Item 61 reveals discrepancies in fastener installation sequencing, incomplete torque verification entries, and a gap in independent quality inspector sign-off prior to aircraft delivery. Post-event examination of the recovered plug and surrounding fuselage structure confirmed that several primary retention fasteners were either missing or improperly seated, with evidence of fretting and localized deformation consistent with in-flight load transfer prior to separation.

The Federal Aviation Administration responded promptly by issuing an emergency airworthiness directive mandating fleet-wide inspections, and the NTSB initiated a comprehensive investigation encompassing design, manufacturing, quality assurance, and operational factors. This submission draws upon the aforementioned docket materials, supplemented by internal engineering analyses, ground test data, and comparative fleet performance metrics.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The technical evaluation of this event centers on three interrelated domains: structural design and certification basis, manufacturing execution and quality verification, and operational load environment. Each domain is assessed against industry standards, certification requirements, and empirical data.

Structural Design and Certification Basis
The mid-exit door plug retention system was designed to meet 14 CFR Part 25 requirements for pressurized fuselage structures, including ultimate load testing at 1.5 times limit load, fatigue testing representative of 3 flight cycles per day over a 20-year service life, and damage tolerance analysis. The plug utilizes a combination of high-strength titanium and steel fasteners, precision-machined guide tracks, and a dual-seal pressure barrier. Finite element analysis (FEA) and ground pressure testing confirm that the design margin exceeds regulatory minimums when all fasteners are installed per approved torque specifications and sequencing protocols.

Comparative analysis with the Boeing 737 MAX 8 plug configuration demonstrates consistent design philosophy, though the MAX 9 variant incorporates additional reinforcement due to the longer fuselage and altered pressure distribution. Both variants underwent identical certification testing methodologies, and no design-level deficiencies have been identified in the retention architecture. The separation event is therefore not attributable to a fundamental structural inadequacy but rather to a deviation from the approved installation process.

Manufacturing Execution and Quality Verification
Forensic review of the manufacturing traveler (Docket Item 58) and quality control logs (Docket Item 67) reveals a breakdown in procedural adherence during final assembly. The plug installation process requires a defined sequence of fastener insertion, torque application, and independent verification. Docket Item 61 indicates that at least four primary retention fasteners were either omitted or installed without documented torque verification. Furthermore, the rework documentation shows that a secondary quality inspection was not completed prior to aircraft release, violating established internal quality gates.

Human factors analysis of the assembly environment indicates that production rate pressures, shift handover ambiguities, and reliance on paper-based traveler documentation contributed to procedural drift. The absence of digital torque verification integration and real-time quality data analytics allowed deviations to propagate undetected. Industry best practices, as reflected in SAE ARP4754A and FAA guidance on manufacturing quality systems, emphasize closed-loop verification, independent inspection, and digital traceability. The subject event demonstrates that when these controls are compromised, even a robust design can be rendered vulnerable.

Operational Load Environment
FDR data (Docket Item 29) confirms that the aircraft was operating within normal climb parameters at the time of separation. Cabin differential pressure at 16,000 feet was approximately 8.3 psi, well within the certified envelope. The LEAP engine thrust settings, vibration spectra, and acoustic profiles were nominal, with no evidence of abnormal aerodynamic or structural excitation contributing to fastener fatigue or loosening. The pilot in command’s immediate recognition of the decompression event and execution of emergency descent procedures align with established training standards and operational protocols.

The pressurization system functioned as designed, and the rate of cabin altitude increase was consistent with a sudden loss of structural integrity rather than a gradual seal failure. This supports the conclusion that the separation was instantaneous and driven by inadequate fastener retention rather than progressive material degradation or operational overload.

Comparison with Industry Standards and Best Practices
The aviation industry has long recognized that plug-type door installations require stringent quality controls due to their critical role in maintaining fuselage pressure integrity. Advisory Circular AC 120-16G, while primarily directed at air carrier maintenance programs, establishes foundational principles for continuing airworthiness, including rigorous documentation, independent verification, and proactive defect reporting. These principles are equally applicable to manufacturing quality systems. The subject event highlights a misalignment between design certification assumptions and manufacturing execution realities. When installation procedures are not strictly adhered to, and when quality verification is not independently validated, the safety margin inherent in the design is effectively reduced.

Ground testing conducted post-event, including pull-out force measurements and torque retention analysis, confirms that properly installed fasteners maintain retention well beyond operational loads. However, missing or under-torqued fasteners create localized stress concentrations that can initiate progressive failure under cyclic pressurization. The absence of digital traveler integration and automated torque verification represents a systemic vulnerability that the industry must address through technological modernization and procedural reinforcement.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the engineering data, manufacturing records, operational telemetry, and forensic examination, the Aircraft Manufacturer concludes that the primary contributing factor to the mid-exit door plug separation was a breakdown in the manufacturing quality assurance and installation verification process. Specifically, the omission of primary retention fasteners, incomplete torque verification, and the absence of an independent quality inspection prior to aircraft delivery created a condition in which the plug was not secured to its certified design standard. This deviation from approved procedures, compounded by procedural ambiguities in rework documentation and insufficient digital traceability, directly enabled the in-flight separation.

Secondary contributing factors include production environment pressures, reliance on manual documentation systems, and inadequate integration of real-time quality analytics. The design itself remains structurally sound and fully compliant with certification requirements. The LEAP engine performance, flight crew response, and pressurization system operation were all within expected parameters and did not contribute to the event. The pilot in command’s actions were consistent with established emergency procedures and training standards, demonstrating the effectiveness of operational preparedness.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Implementation of mandatory digital traveler systems with automated torque verification and real-time quality gate enforcement
- Establishment of independent, cross-functional inspection protocols for all critical structural installations
- Enhanced human factors training for assembly technicians, emphasizing procedural discipline, shift handover clarity, and stop-work authority
- Integration of predictive quality analytics to identify procedural drift before it manifests as a physical defect
- Strengthened alignment between manufacturing quality systems and operator continuing airworthiness programs, guided by the principles outlined in AC 120-16G

These recommendations are intended to close identified gaps, reinforce existing safety margins, and establish a more resilient quality assurance framework across the production lifecycle.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to this event, the Aircraft Manufacturer has implemented immediate and sustained corrective actions to address the identified vulnerabilities and prevent recurrence.

Actions Already Taken:
- Issued fleet-wide inspection directives in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration, mandating 100% verification of mid-exit door plug fastener installation, torque values, and retention integrity
- Revised the MEP installation procedure to include mandatory independent quality inspector sign-off, with no exceptions for rework or final assembly stages
- Implemented digital torque verification tools with automated data logging and real-time discrepancy alerts
- Conducted comprehensive retraining for all assembly technicians, quality inspectors, and production supervisors, focusing on procedural compliance, human factors, and stop-work authority
- Established a dedicated engineering oversight team to monitor plug installation processes across all production lines, with daily quality audits and direct reporting to senior management
- Enhanced supply chain traceability for critical fasteners and retention components, including serialized tracking and batch verification protocols

Proposed Future Improvements:
- Development and deployment of a digital twin integration platform for final assembly, enabling real-time synchronization between engineering specifications, manufacturing execution, and quality verification
- Implementation of machine vision and automated inspection systems for critical structural installations, reducing reliance on manual verification and minimizing human error
- Expansion of predictive quality analytics using historical installation data, environmental variables, and production metrics to identify high-risk configurations before aircraft release
- Strengthened collaboration with regulatory authorities and industry partners to harmonize manufacturing quality standards with continuing airworthiness requirements, ensuring seamless data exchange and proactive risk mitigation
- Establishment of an independent safety review board with external subject-matter experts to conduct periodic audits of critical installation processes and quality assurance systems

The Aircraft Manufacturer remains fully committed to transparency, continuous improvement, and the highest standards of aviation safety. This event has reinforced the necessity of aligning design intent with manufacturing execution, and we are actively investing in technological, procedural, and cultural enhancements to ensure that every aircraft delivered meets or exceeds its certified safety baseline. We appreciate the NTSB’s rigorous investigative process and look forward to continued collaboration with all parties to advance industry-wide safety outcomes.

FROM: Director of Airworthiness & Quality Compliance, Pacific Northwest Maintenance Division
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2024-014: Mid-Exit Door Plug Retention Hardware Verification & Installation Compliance
REF: QA-2023-089, WO-7742-PLUG Rev. 4, QMS-NC-2024-003, FAA AD 2024-02-01 (Preliminary), NTSB Docket Entry #24-00187

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate inspection, verification, and documentation of all mid-cabin exit door plug retention hardware across the 737 MAX 9 fleet. The directive establishes interim compliance procedures, standardizes torque verification protocols, and ensures full traceability pending final regulatory guidance and manufacturer service bulletins.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 experienced a rapid decompression event when the left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage during climb through approximately 16,000 feet following departure from a Pacific Northwest hub. The aircraft returned safely to the departure airport with no injuries. Preliminary telemetry and post-flight inspection data indicate missing or improperly torqued retention bolts at the plug-to-fuselage interface. 

Internal quality audits conducted over the past 72 hours have identified inconsistencies in historical work order documentation for plug installations performed between Q3 2022 and Q4 2023. Several traveler sheets lack final torque sign-offs, and two aircraft show undocumented hardware substitutions. The Federal Aviation Administration has issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive requiring immediate grounding and inspection of all affected aircraft. Our internal maintenance program, developed in accordance with AC 120-16G guidelines, must be updated to reflect enhanced verification protocols and stricter documentation controls. 

The structural design of the plug assembly relies on strict adherence to damage tolerance requirements, which mandate verified fastener integrity, redundant load paths, and continuous pressure boundary sealing. Any deviation from certified installation procedures compromises the certified pressure boundary and introduces unacceptable risk during pressurization cycles.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all maintenance personnel must comply with the following procedures for 737 MAX 9 aircraft (MSN 44000–44500 series):

1. Hardware Verification & Inspection
   • Inspect all four (4) upper and eight (8) lower retention bolts on both left and right mid-exit door plugs.
   • Verify part numbers against IPC Chapter 53-40-01. Acceptable fasteners: NAS1102-08-12 (upper) and NAS1102-08-16 (lower).
   • Confirm presence of all safety wire, cotter pins, and torque stripe markings per WO-7742-PLUG Rev. 4.
   • Photograph each bolt location before and after inspection. Upload images to QMS-IMG-PLUG-2024.

2. Torque Verification & Documentation Audit
   • Re-torque all retention bolts to 185–195 in-lbs using calibrated digital torque wrenches (Cal Due: within 30 days).
   • Cross-reference historical work orders against the Aircraft Maintenance Log (AML). Any missing torque sign-offs, unsigned traveler sheets, or undocumented hardware substitutions must be flagged as a Level 2 Nonconformance.
   • Submit discrepancy reports via the QMS portal within 24 hours of discovery. Do not release aircraft to service until all discrepancies are dispositioned by Engineering.

3. Structural & Systems Interface Check
   • Inspect plug-to-fuselage sealant continuity. Look for cracking, delamination, or improper cure.
   • Verify that the plug guide rails are free of debris and properly lubricated with MIL-PRF-23827C.
   • Confirm that adjacent cabin pressure relief valves and LEAP-1B engine bleed air ducts show no signs of stress, misalignment, or thermal degradation. While the LEAP-1B powerplant is not directly involved in the plug retention system, bleed air routing and thermal expansion profiles must be verified to rule out secondary structural loading on adjacent fuselage frames.

4. Training & Compliance Alignment
   • All technicians performing plug inspections must complete Module 737-PLUG-04 (updated Jan 10, 2024) via the LMS.
   • Reference AC 120-16G, Section 4.3, for approved maintenance program deviations and engineering justification requirements.
   • Coordinate with General Electric Aviation technical representatives for any engine-related bleed air or thermal expansion queries that may impact adjacent fuselage zones. GE Aviation has issued a preliminary technical bulletin (GE-TB-2024-008) regarding bleed line routing clearances; review and apply as applicable.

ACTION REQUIRED:
• Line Maintenance Supervisors: Ground all affected aircraft until inspection is complete. Assign dedicated inspection teams. Complete all verifications by January 18, 2024, 2359Z. Maintain a daily status log and submit to the Airworthiness Office by 1700 local.
• Quality Assurance Auditors: Conduct random spot-checks on 20% of completed inspections. Validate torque tool calibration logs, technician certification records, and photographic evidence. Submit audit summary to the Airworthiness Office by January 20, 2024.
• Engineering Support: Review all flagged nonconformances. Issue engineering dispositions within 48 hours. Update the Master Maintenance Program (MMP) to include permanent plug retention verification checkpoints at every C-check and heavy maintenance visit.
• Records & Documentation: Archive all inspection reports, torque logs, and photographic evidence in the centralized QMS database. Ensure NTSB and FAA evidence preservation protocols are strictly followed. Do not alter, delete, or overwrite historical maintenance records. All digital and paper records are subject to legal hold.

Failure to comply with this alert will result in immediate suspension of maintenance privileges and potential regulatory action. All personnel are reminded that structural integrity and pressure boundary compliance are non-negotiable. Direct technical questions to the Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or the Quality Compliance Hotline.

Signed,
Director of Airworthiness & Quality Compliance
Pacific Northwest Maintenance Division

SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:11 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9, operated by a major U.S. passenger carrier, experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during the initial climb phase. The aircraft, which had departed from a Pacific Northwest regional airport, was en route to a scheduled destination when the left mid-exit door plug separated from the aft fuselage at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and returned to the departure airport without further incident; there were no reported fatalities, and all occupants were accounted for upon landing.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information indicates that the aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules and was in a final descent configuration when the decompression event occurred. Initial data retrieved from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) suggest a sudden pressure differential and associated structural failure in the vicinity of the left mid-cabin exit. The Captain reported an immediate loud bang, followed by rapid cabin depressurization, loss of cabin pressure warnings, and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Crew members and passengers seated in the immediate vicinity of the affected fuselage section have provided initial statements describing a sudden rush of air, loose articles becoming airborne, and visible damage to the left-side cabin interior.

Meteorological data obtained from the departure airport and surrounding National Weather Service stations indicate that weather conditions at the time of the event were generally favorable for flight operations. Surface observations reported light winds, scattered cloud cover, and visibility in excess of 10 statute miles. No significant convective activity, turbulence reports, or icing conditions were documented along the initial departure route.

A preliminary visual assessment of the airframe, conducted after the

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date and Time
On January 5, 2024, at 17:07:14 Pacific Standard Time (PST) (01:07:14 Coordinated Universal Time, January 6, 2024), a rapid decompression event occurred during the initial climb phase of flight. The event was captured by the aircraft's flight data recording system and corroborated by cockpit voice recorder audio. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) at the time of the occurrence.

1.2 Location
The event occurred en route, approximately 12.3 nautical miles northwest of Portland International Airport (KPDX), Oregon, at geographic coordinates 45°38'12"N, 122°45'30"W. The aircraft was tracking a magnetic heading of 185° and was within controlled airspace under the jurisdiction of the Seattle Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZSE).

1.3 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, manufacturer serial number 44442, registered as N704AL. The aircraft was operated by a major U.S. scheduled air carrier holding a valid Part 121 operating certificate. The aircraft was configured for 178 passenger seats and 6 crew positions, with a maximum takeoff weight of 194,700 pounds. The aircraft was equipped with a left mid-exit door plug configuration, consistent with the manufacturer's optional cabin layout for this variant.

1.4 Flight Operations
The flight was conducted as a scheduled passenger service under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The flight departed KPDX at 17:05:32 PST, bound for Ontario International Airport (KONT), California. The filed flight plan indicated a cruise altitude of 35,000 feet mean sea level (MSL). The aircraft was cleared for departure on runway 10L and followed standard departure procedures, including the PDX ONE departure route. The aircraft was operating within normal weight and balance parameters at the time of departure.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot in Command Qualifications
The pilot in command held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating. The pilot in command possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on October 12, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 12,487 hours, with 4,215 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The pilot in command had completed all required recurrent training and proficiency checks in accordance with 14 CFR 121.409 and 121.433.

2.2 Second-in-Command Qualifications
The second-in-command held an ATP certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating. The second-in-command possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on November 3, 2023, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 3,842 hours, with 1,128 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The second-in-command had completed all required recurrent training and line-oriented flight training (LOFT) sessions within the preceding 12 months.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training
Both flight crew members completed a full recurrent training cycle on December 18, 2023, which included simulator-based emergency procedures, rapid decompression drills, and high-altitude emergency descent training. Training records indicate satisfactory performance across all evaluated parameters. The pilot in command had flown 42 flight hours in the 30 days preceding the accident. The second-in-command had flown 38 flight hours in the same period. Both crew members were current and qualified for the assigned route and aircraft type.

2.4 Duty Time and Rest Compliance
The flight crew's duty period commenced at 14:30 PST on January 5, 2024, and was scheduled to conclude at 22:15 PST. The crew had been provided a rest period of 14 hours and 15 minutes prior to reporting for duty, in compliance with 14 CFR 117.25 and 117.27. Fatigue risk management system (FRMS) data indicated no reported fatigue-related concerns. The crew was within all applicable duty time limitations at the time of the event.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The aircraft was a Boeing 737-9 MAX, delivered to the operator on March 14, 2023. At the time of the event, the airframe had accumulated 1,245.6 flight hours and 892 flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a standard avionics suite, including dual flight management computers, integrated standby flight displays, and a digital flight data acquisition unit. The aircraft's weight and balance documentation confirmed compliance with all operational limits.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records indicate the aircraft was maintained in accordance with an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP). The most recent heavy maintenance check (C-check) was completed on November 22, 2023, with no deferred items related to the fuselage or door plug systems. All applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) were complied with, including AD 2023-18-05, which addressed inspection requirements for certain fuselage fastener installations. The aircraft's maintenance tracking system showed no open work orders or repetitive inspection discrepancies at the time of departure.

3.3 Door Plug Configuration and Systems
The left mid-exit door plug was installed at fuselage station 1016, replacing a standard passenger door to accommodate the operator's high-density seating configuration. The door plug assembly consisted of a structural panel, retention bolts, guide tracks, and stop fittings. The installation was performed in accordance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1234, Revision 2. The door plug was designed to be permanently secured and was not intended for routine removal or operational cycling. The plug's retention system utilized twelve high-strength steel bolts, each torqued to manufacturer specifications.

3.4 Engine and Propulsion Systems
The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, serial numbers 884211 (left) and 884215 (right). The LEAP engine design incorporates advanced composite fan blades, a high-pressure ratio core, and a dual-channel full authority digital engine control (FADEC) system. Engine maintenance records indicate compliance with all manufacturer-recommended service bulletins and time-on-wing limits. The engines were manufactured under the joint venture framework involving GE Aviation and Safran Aircraft Engines. Performance data from the flight data recorder indicated normal engine parameters, with no indications of thrust asymmetry, compressor stalls, or abnormal vibration prior to the decompression event. The propulsion system remained fully operational throughout the flight.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Departure and En Route Weather
At the time of departure, surface conditions at KPDX were characterized by clear skies, light winds, and good visibility. The aircraft climbed through a stable atmospheric layer with minimal turbulence. At the altitude of the event (16,000 feet MSL), the ambient temperature was recorded at -12°C, with a dew point of -18°C. The pressure altitude was 15,840 feet, and the density altitude was 15,910 feet.

4.2 METAR/TAF Data

4.3 Pilot Reports and Atmospheric Conditions
No pilot reports (PIREPs) of severe turbulence, wind shear, or structural icing were filed in the vicinity of the event. The aircraft's onboard weather radar and turbulence detection systems indicated no significant meteorological hazards.
