The cabin pressure differential at the time of the event was approximately 5.8 psi, consistent with a normal climb profile at 16,000 feet MSL.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage and was recovered approximately 1.2 nautical miles from the aircraft's flight path, in a residential area near the city of Vancouver, Washington. The component was located intact on a residential lawn, with minimal ground impact deformation. No other aircraft components were recovered from the area. The aircraft sustained no ground impact damage and returned to KPDX under its own power.

5.2 Fuselage and Door Plug Examination
Examination of the aircraft's left fuselage revealed a clean separation at the door plug interface. The surrounding fuselage skin, frames, and stringers exhibited no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or impact damage. The door plug's guide tracks remained attached to the fuselage structure. The stop fittings, designed to prevent outward displacement, were absent from the recovered component. The door plug panel showed no signs of explosive failure, thermal degradation, or foreign object damage.

5.3 Structural and Fastener Analysis
The door plug retention system utilized twelve high-strength steel bolts, each specified to a torque value of 180 inch-pounds. Examination of the bolt holes on the fuselage revealed no evidence of thread stripping, elongation, or fatigue. The recovered door plug was missing all twelve retention bolts. The bolt heads were not located on the aircraft or in the immediate vicinity. The guide track alignment pins were intact and showed no signs of shear or deformation. The separation occurred without evidence of progressive structural failure or overload.

5.4 Cabin Interior and Systems Impact
The rapid decompression event resulted in the immediate deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Cabin pressure dropped from 8,000 feet equivalent to ambient atmospheric pressure within 2.5 seconds. The cabin altitude warning system activated at 10,000 feet equivalent, consistent with design parameters. No injuries were reported among passengers or crew. The cabin interior sustained minor cosmetic damage to overhead bins and seat upholstery due to rapid pressure equalization. The aircraft's environmental control system (ECS) and pressurization controllers remained functional, and the crew initiated an emergency descent in accordance with standard operating procedures.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
The operator's standard operating procedures (SOPs) for rapid decompression events are documented in the company's Flight Operations Manual (FOM) and align with 14 CFR 121.333 and 121.337. The procedures mandate immediate donning of oxygen masks, initiation of an emergency descent to 10,000 feet MSL or minimum safe altitude, and declaration of an emergency with air traffic control. The pilot in command executed these procedures without deviation. The operator's maintenance program, approved under 14 CFR 121.373, includes routine inspections of door plug installations and fastener retention systems.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has documented three prior occurrences involving door plug separation or fastener retention anomalies on Boeing 737 MAX series aircraft. In each instance, the events were attributed to manufacturing documentation discrepancies or improper torque application during assembly. The FAA issued an emergency airworthiness directive requiring immediate inspection of all affected aircraft. The operator's fleet, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8 variant, was subjected to enhanced inspection protocols following the directive. No similar events were reported on the operator's fleet prior to January 5, 2024.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Advisory Circulars
The aircraft's design and certification comply with 14 CFR Part 25, specifically §25.365 (Pressurized cabin loads) and §25.783 (Fuselage doors). The operator's maintenance tracking and inspection procedures are governed by 14 CFR 121.373 and 121.375. Advisory Circular 120-16G, titled "Air Carrier Maintenance Programs," provides guidance on the development and implementation of continuous airworthiness maintenance programs, including documentation control, inspection intervals, and quality assurance processes. The operator's maintenance program was audited against AC 120-16G requirements and found to be in compliance. The FAA's oversight of the manufacturer's production quality system is conducted under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart G.

6.4 Flight Data and Cockpit Voice Recorder Information
The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and downloaded by the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory. The FDR recorded 2,148 parameters, including cabin pressure differential, altitude, airspeed, control surface positions, and engine performance data. The data confirmed a rapid pressure loss at 17:07:14 PST, with cabin altitude increasing from 8,000 feet to 16,000 feet equivalent within 2.5 seconds. The CVR captured the activation of the cabin altitude warning, crew communication regarding the decompression, and the initiation of the emergency descent. All recorder data was within normal operational limits prior to the event. The recorders were secured and preserved for further analysis.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the structural, materials, and flight data recorder (FDR) examination of the left mid-exit door plug (L-MEDP) assembly and associated fuselage structure recovered from the subject accident aircraft. The examination was conducted under the authority of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft manufacturer, and the operator's maintenance organization. The scope of this investigation encompasses the physical inspection of the recovered door plug components, fastener retention hardware, fuselage skin and frame interfaces, metallurgical and chemical analysis of structural materials, and the correlation of recovered FDR parameters with the documented rapid decompression event.

The primary items examined include the L-MEDP assembly (Boeing Part Number 65-12345-678, Serial Number 00482), the associated upper and lower guide track assemblies, four (4) recovered stop fittings, the forward and aft fuselage skin panels (Station 1016 to 1042), and the complete FDR memory module (Honeywell SSFDR, P/N 060-0800-00, S/N 2144-0892). The physical examination and materials testing were conducted between January 10 and January 18, 2024, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with supplemental structural teardown and fastener torque verification performed at the Boeing Everett Facility, Washington. FDR data extraction, decoding, and parameter validation were completed on January 12, 2024, utilizing the manufacturer's proprietary decoding software and cross-referenced against the aircraft's Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data stream. All procedures adhered to NTSB Investigative Manual guidelines, ASTM E8/E8M-22 for tensile testing, SAE AMS 4037 for aluminum alloy verification, and Boeing BAC5000 series structural fastener installation standards.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9, configured with a high-density passenger layout that necessitates the installation of mid-exit door plugs in lieu of standard Type III emergency exits. The L-MEDP is a non-egress structural plug designed to maintain cabin pressurization integrity and aerodynamic continuity. The assembly consists of an inner aluminum alloy panel, an outer composite fairing, a perimeter structural frame, upper and lower guide tracks, and a series of retention fasteners that interface with the fuselage skin and adjacent frames. The plug is certified under the damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements of 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates that all pressurized fuselage components withstand limit load conditions and demonstrate crack growth resistance over the design service goal.

The design basis for the mid-exit door plug aligns with the structural architecture of the Boeing 737 MAX 8, utilizing identical frame spacing, skin thickness, and fastener load paths. The plug retention system employs NAS6606-10 titanium alloy bolts (per NASM1312-7) torqued to a specification of 180–220 in-lbs, with secondary retention provided by guide track engagement and stop fitting interference. The maximum certified cabin differential pressure (ΔP) for the airframe is 9.1 PSI, with a relief valve set to open at 9.35 PSI. The aircraft is powered by two GE Aviation LEAP-1B27 high-bypass turbofan engines, each rated at 28,000 lbf of thrust, with engine control and monitoring integrated into the aircraft's centralized maintenance computer.

Maintenance records indicate the subject aircraft accumulated 1,247 flight hours and 892 flight cycles prior to the event. The L-MEDP assembly was installed during a post-delivery configuration modification on November 14, 2023, at the operator's maintenance base. The installation was documented under work order WO-88421, referencing compliance with the operator's FAA-approved maintenance program, which incorporates guidance from Advisory Circular 120-16G for air carrier maintenance and preventive maintenance programs. The work order notes the replacement of four (4) perimeter fasteners and the re-torquing of the guide track mounting brackets. No subsequent maintenance actions were recorded for the L-MEDP prior to the January 5, 2024, flight.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The recovered L-MEDP assembly was received in a partially fragmented state, with the outer composite fairing separated from the inner aluminum panel along the forward and lower perimeter. The inner panel exhibited significant plastic deformation, with localized buckling along the aft edge and elongation of four (4) fastener holes. The upper guide track remained attached to the fuselage structure, while the lower guide track was recovered detached, showing evidence of shear loading at the aft mounting bracket. All four stop fittings were recovered; two exhibited rotational displacement, and two showed complete separation from the plug frame.

A detailed dimensional survey was conducted using a calibrated coordinate measuring machine (CMM). Fastener hole elongation measurements ranged from 0.012 to 0.038 inches beyond nominal diameter (0.1900 in), with the aft lower quadrant exhibiting the maximum deviation. The recovered NAS6606-10 bolts were subjected to torque verification using a calibrated digital torque wrench (per SAE AS8879). Three of the four recovered bolts registered torque values between 15 and 42 in-lbs, significantly below the manufacturer's specified range of 180–220 in-lbs. The fourth bolt was fractured at the shank, with fracture surface analysis indicating tensile overload rather than fatigue initiation.

Metallurgical examination of the inner panel and stop fittings was performed in accordance with ASTM E3 and ASTM E407. Cross-sectional samples were prepared, polished, and etched using Keller's reagent. Optical microscopy revealed no evidence of intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, or fatigue striations on the primary load-bearing surfaces. Hardness testing (Rockwell B scale) yielded values of 78–82 HRB for the 2024-T3 aluminum panel, consistent with the material specification per AMS 4037. Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed aluminum alloy 2024-T3 with copper content at 4.32 wt%, magnesium at 1.48 wt%, and manganese at 0.61 wt%, all within Boeing BAC5000-12 tolerances.

Non-destructive testing (NDT) of the fuselage skin surrounding the plug interface was conducted using eddy current (per ASTM E309) and ultrasonic phased array (per ASTM E2491). The NDT results indicated no subsurface cracking, delamination, or corrosion in the adjacent skin panels or frame doublers. The forward and aft frame interfaces showed minor fretting wear consistent with normal operational vibration, with no evidence of structural yielding or permanent deformation.

Photographic documentation (NTSB Photo Log 2024-01-10-001 through 0024) captures the fastener hole elongation, guide track shear marks, and fracture surfaces. The recovered components were preserved in a controlled environment to prevent oxidation or contamination prior to further laboratory analysis. All measurements, material properties, and NDT results were recorded in the NTSB Structural Examination Database and cross-referenced with the manufacturer's engineering drawings (Drawing 65-12345-678, Rev. 14).

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The FDR memory module was successfully extracted and decoded using the manufacturer's proprietary software (Boeing FDR Decoder v4.2.1). The data stream was validated against the aircraft's QAR parameters and synchronized with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) timeline. The FDR recorded 88 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with cabin pressure, altitude, airspeed, and door configuration parameters sampled at 4 Hz during the climb phase.

The flight departed at 08:14:22 local time. During initial climb, cabin differential pressure (ΔP) increased linearly with altitude, reaching 2.1 PSI at 8,000 ft MSL and 4.8 PSI at 12,000 ft MSL. At 08:21:04, the aircraft passed through 15,800 ft MSL with an indicated airspeed of 285 knots and a vertical speed of +2,100 ft/min. At this point, ΔP measured 6.7 PSI, consistent with normal pressurization schedules. At 08:21:07, the FDR recorded an instantaneous drop in ΔP from 6.7 PSI to 0.2 PSI within a single sampling interval (0.25 seconds). Concurrently, the cabin altitude parameter spiked from 8,200 ft to 15,900 ft, and the DOOR CONFIG warning illuminated. The rapid pressure loss was accompanied by a transient increase in vertical speed to +3,400 ft/min, followed by a rapid descent initiated by the flight crew.

The Captain's control inputs, as recorded by the control column and rudder pedal position parameters, indicated immediate pitch-down and thrust reduction. The LEAP-1B engine parameters (N1, EGT, fuel flow) remained stable throughout the event, with no thrust asymmetry or compressor stall indications. The left engine N1 maintained 84.2%, while the right engine N1 held at 83.9%. EGT values remained within the green band (680–710 °C), and fuel flow was consistent with climb power settings.

The FDR data was compared against normal operational envelopes for the Boeing 737 MAX 9. Under standard conditions, ΔP at 16,000 ft MSL should stabilize between 5.8 and 6.2 PSI, with a maximum allowable rate of change of 0.5 PSI/sec. The recorded ΔP decay rate exceeded 25 PSI/sec, indicating a catastrophic breach rather than a controlled vent or valve malfunction. The DOOR CONFIG warning activation at 08:21:07 aligns with the loss of structural continuity at the L-MEDP interface, as the door warning system monitors microswitch status on the guide track and stop fittings.

CVR audio analysis corroborates the FDR timeline, with a distinct acoustic transient recorded at 08:21:07, followed by crew communication referencing rapid decompression and emergency descent procedures. The QAR data stream, sampled at 1 Hz, confirmed identical parameter trends, with minor latency differences attributable to data buffering. All FDR parameters were validated against the aircraft's maintenance logs and calibration certificates, confirming sensor accuracy within ±0.5% for pressure transducers and ±10 ft for altitude encoding.

5. SUMMARY

The physical examination of the recovered left mid-exit door plug assembly revealed significant fastener retention deficiencies, with four (4) critical NAS6606-10 bolts exhibiting torque values between 15 and 42 in-lbs, substantially below the manufacturer's specified range of 180–220 in-lbs. Dimensional analysis confirmed fastener hole elongation up to 0.038 inches, indicating localized plastic deformation under pressurization loads. Metallurgical and chemical testing verified that the aluminum alloy 2024-T3 panel and titanium fasteners met all applicable material specifications, with no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or manufacturing defects. Non-destructive testing of the adjacent fuselage structure confirmed structural integrity, with no subsurface damage or permanent deformation.

Flight data recorder analysis documented a rapid cabin pressure loss at 16,000 ft MSL, with ΔP decaying from 6.7 PSI to 0.2 PSI within 0.25 seconds. The event coincided with DOOR CONFIG warning activation and immediate crew-initiated emergency descent. Engine parameters for both GE Aviation LEAP-1B27 turbofans remained within normal operational limits, with no thrust asymmetry or performance degradation. The recorded data aligns with a sudden structural breach at the L-MEDP interface, consistent with the physical evidence of fastener under-torque and guide track displacement.

Maintenance documentation indicates the L-MEDP was installed and reworked in November 2023 under an FAA-approved program referencing Advisory Circular 120-16G. The absence of post-installation torque verification records and the measured fastener values suggest a deviation from Boeing BAC5000 installation procedures. All findings are presented as factual observations derived from physical examination, materials testing, and flight data analysis. No determination of probable cause is included in this report.

INTERVIEW OF SARAH JENKINS, LEAD FLIGHT ATTENDANT
Date: January 12, 2024
Time: 10:15 AM PST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Portland, Oregon
Interviewer: Investigator M. Davis, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety
Witness: Sarah Jenkins, Lead Flight Attendant (Purser), Flight 1282

Q: Ms. Jenkins, thank you for coming in today. For the official record, could you please state your full name, your title, and your specific role on the flight in question?
A: Yeah, absolutely. I’m Sarah Jenkins. I’m a lead flight attendant—sometimes we just say purser. I was assigned to the forward galley on Flight 1282 on January 5th. So my job is basically cabin crew coordination, passenger safety oversight, and making sure all the service and emergency protocols run smoothly. I’ve been with the airline for about twelve years now, so I’ve seen a lot of different aircraft and situations.

Q: Can you walk me through the pre-flight and boarding process that day?
A: Sure. We reported to the gate around… I want to say 1:30 PM? Maybe 1:40. The aircraft was already parked. It was a Boeing 737 MAX 9, obviously, but in our crew scheduling system it sometimes just populates as a 737-8, which is a little confusing, but we knew it was the MAX variant. We did the standard walk-through, checked the emergency equipment, verified the slides were armed, that sort of thing. The cabin was clean, no weird smells, no unusual noises. We started boarding around 2:15. It was a full flight, maybe 170 passengers. Everything felt completely normal. I remember chatting with the other attendants, just going through the usual checklist.

Q: Describe the departure and initial climb.
A: Okay. We pushed back right on schedule, I think around 2:50. Taxi was maybe ten minutes, give or take. The Captain came on the PA, gave the standard welcome, mentioned the weather, said we’d be climbing through the marine layer pretty quick. We took off from Portland, heading south. I was in the forward galley, finishing up the cabin secure check. We were at about… I’d say 10,000 feet when the seatbelt sign went off. I remember that because I was just about to start the beverage service. The climb felt smooth. The engines—those are the GE Aviation LEAP-1Bs, right? I don’t know the exact specs, but maintenance mentioned them once during a pre-flight briefing. They sounded completely normal. Just a steady, consistent hum. No vibrations, no surging.

Q: Take me through the exact moment the incident occurred. What did you see, hear, and feel?
A: Right. So, we were… I want to say about 16,000 feet. Maybe a little under, maybe a little over. The Captain had just made a quick call to the cabin, said we’d be leveling off soon. I was standing near the forward galley, facing aft, just organizing the coffee pots. And then—*boom*. It wasn’t like a normal turbulence bump. It was… it was a sharp, almost metallic crack, followed immediately by this massive rush of air. Like a vacuum cleaner, but a thousand times louder. The temperature dropped instantly. I mean, it went from comfortable to freezing in a second. My ears popped so hard it actually hurt.
I turned around, and… there was just… a hole. Where the left mid-exit door plug should’ve been. It was just gone. I could see the sky, the clouds, everything. The wind was howling through the cabin. Papers, magazines, a passenger’s phone, a jacket—everything just got sucked toward that opening. I grabbed the nearest jumpseat, or tried to, but the wind was pushing me back. I remember shouting, “Heads down! Stay down!” but I couldn’t even hear my own voice over the roar. It lasted… maybe ten seconds? Felt like an hour. Then the wind noise changed, like it equalized a bit, but it was still incredibly loud.

Q: What were your immediate actions following the decompression?
A: Yeah, so… protocol kicks in. I hit the emergency call button to the flight deck. I think I pressed it twice. I yelled into the interphone, “Captain, we have a rapid decompression! Left side, mid-cabin!” I don’t know if he heard me right away, but he came on the PA almost immediately. His voice was calm, which… honestly, that helped. He said, “Cabin crew, secure yourselves. We’re initiating an emergency descent. Oxygen masks are deploying.” And they were. They dropped all at once. I remember seeing passengers grabbing them, some were confused, a few were crying. I started moving down the aisle, checking masks, making sure people had them on. I had to shout over the wind and the engine noise. I told them to pull the straps, cover their nose and mouth, breathe normally. Standard stuff, but… it’s different when it’s real.

Q: You mentioned training. How did your preparation factor into your response?
A: Well, we drill this. I mean, we go through it every year. The airline’s training program follows the FAA guidelines, specifically… I think it’s Advisory Circular 120-16G? Yeah, that’s the one for flight attendant training and qualification. It covers rapid decompression, emergency descents, all of it. So when it happened, my brain just… switched to checklist mode. I didn’t panic. I knew exactly what to do. I checked the cabin pressure indicators, made sure the oxygen was flowing, verified the door area was clear of debris. I also made sure the other flight attendants were okay. One of them, Maria, was near the affected area. She was shaken, but she was fine. We did a quick headcount, made sure no one was injured by flying debris.

Q: Describe the descent and return to the airport.
A: The descent was… steep. You could feel the G-forces. The Captain was flying it manually, I think, or maybe he had the autopilot engaged, but it was aggressive. We dropped from 16,000 down to, I don’t know, 10,000? Maybe lower. The wind noise lessened as we got into thicker air, but it was still loud. I kept walking the cabin, checking on passengers, handing out water, keeping people calm. The Captain came on again, said we were diverting back to Portland. He gave an ETA, maybe 15 minutes. I relayed that to the cabin. We prepared for an emergency landing, but honestly, it felt more like a precautionary return. The aircraft handled fine. No weird vibrations, no engine issues. The LEAP-1Bs kept running smooth. I mean, I’m not a pilot, but I know what an engine failure sounds like, and this wasn’t it.

Q: What happened after landing?
A: We touched down hard, but safely. The Captain taxied to a remote stand, away from the main terminal. Emergency vehicles were already there. We did a full evacuation? No, wait. Actually, we didn’t evacuate. The Captain decided it was safer to keep everyone on board until the fire department and maintenance could inspect the aircraft. We just stayed seated, kept the oxygen masks on until the pressure normalized. Then we deplaned normally, but slowly. Passengers were… understandably shaken. Some were crying, some were just quiet. We got them off, handed them over to ground staff. I filed my initial report with the FAA through the airline’s safety portal that same night. I also gave a verbal debrief to the chief purser.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add that we haven’t covered?
A: Um… I guess just that… it’s weird how fast it happens. One minute you’re pouring coffee, the next you’re looking at the sky through a hole in the fuselage. I’ve been flying for over a decade, and I’ve never seen anything like it. The Boeing 737-8 and the MAX 9 are supposed to be incredibly safe, and they are. But this… this was a structural thing, right? I heard later it was a door plug. I don’t know the engineering details, but I know the FAA’s going to look into it. I just hope they find out why it happened. For us, the training worked. The Captain’s handling was textbook. We got everyone home safe. That’s what matters.

Q: Thank you, Ms. Jenkins. Your statement is very helpful. We’ll be in touch if we need any clarification.
A: Yeah, of course. Whatever you need. I’m just glad everyone’s okay.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND COMPLIANCE DIVISION

MEMORANDUM

DATE: March 15, 2024
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service & Flight Standards Service
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO NTSB SAFETY RECOMMENDATION AND AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE COMPLIANCE STATUS
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA24MA010; Docket No. FAA-2024-0187; AD 2024-02-09

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This memorandum constitutes the formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Preliminary Safety Recommendation A-24-012, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the in-flight rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9, registration N704AL, on January 5, 2024. The referenced incident occurred during initial climb at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) following departure from Portland International Airport (KPDX). The subject matter encompasses compliance verification with Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-02-09, issued under Docket No. FAA-2024-0187, and the associated regulatory framework governing fuselage pressure boundary integrity, production quality assurance, and operator maintenance program adherence.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737 MAX 9 is certified under Type Certificate (TC) No. A16WE, with the mid-cabin exit door plug configuration authorized via Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) No. ST00001SE and subsequent production delegation under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart G. The applicable airworthiness standards for fuselage pressurization and emergency exit integrity are codified in 14 CFR § 25.783 (Fuselage doors) and 14 CFR § 25.365 (Pressurized compartment loads). Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has relied on the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) framework to delegate conformity inspections and airworthiness determinations to the manufacturer’s authorized representatives.

The operator’s maintenance program, developed in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.368 and aligned with Advisory Circular (AC) 120-16G, “Air Carrier Maintenance Programs,” incorporates the Maintenance Review Board Report (MRBR) and the manufacturer’s Maintenance Planning Document (MPD). Prior to the January 5, 2024 event, no Airworthiness Directives specifically mandated torque verification or fastener retention inspections for the mid-exit door plug assembly on the 737 MAX 9 series. However, the FAA had previously issued Safety Alert for Operators (SAFO) 23-004, addressing general fastener installation practices, which was not explicitly incorporated into the operator’s approved maintenance program.

During the decompression event, the flight crew, under the command of the Captain, executed emergency descent procedures in strict accordance with 14 CFR § 121.333 and the operator’s approved Quick Reference Handbook (QRH). The aircraft’s powerplant, a CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engine manufactured by GE Aviation, sustained no structural or operational anomalies attributable to the rapid pressure differential, as confirmed by post-flight engine health monitoring (EHM) data and borescope inspections. The Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for cabin pressurization and door configuration were subsequently evaluated under 14 CFR § 121.344 to determine dispatch eligibility for the return flight.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive regulatory audit of the manufacturer’s production quality system and the operator’s maintenance execution reveals systemic deficiencies in the oversight of delegated airworthiness functions. The investigation indicates that the left mid-exit door plug was installed without the requisite four primary retention bolts, a condition that contravenes the approved type design data and violates 14 CFR § 43.13(a), which mandates that maintenance be performed using methods, techniques, and practices prescribed by the manufacturer. The absence of these fasteners was not detected during the manufacturer’s final conformity inspection, nor during the operator’s pre-delivery acceptance checks, indicating a breakdown in the quality assurance protocols required under 14 CFR § 21.137.

The FAA’s oversight of the ODA unit responsible for the 737 MAX production line has been reassessed under 14 CFR § 183.43. Findings indicate that the delegation of authority for door plug installation verification lacked sufficient independent verification steps, resulting in an unacceptable risk to the pressurized fuselage boundary. Furthermore, the operator’s maintenance program, while compliant with the baseline requirements of AC 120-16G, did not incorporate enhanced inspection intervals for non-standard fuselage modifications, specifically the mid-exit door plug configuration. This gap in the maintenance program structure highlights a regulatory deficiency in the alignment of MRBR tasks with emergent production anomalies.

From an operational standpoint, the Captain’s adherence to emergency procedures and the crew’s management of the rapid decompression event were consistent with 14 CFR Part 121 training requirements. The LEAP-1B engine, produced by General Electric Aviation, demonstrated robust performance under transient aerodynamic and pressure loads, with no exceedances recorded in the engine’s full authority digital engine control (FADEC) parameters. However, the regulatory framework governing supplemental type certificate installations and production delegation requires immediate recalibration to ensure that all structural modifications undergo rigorous, independent airworthiness validation prior to service introduction.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified regulatory gaps and in accordance with NTSB Safety Recommendation A-24-012, the FAA hereby mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Immediate Airworthiness Directive Compliance: All operators of Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft equipped with mid-exit door plugs shall comply with AD 2024-02-09 within 72 hours of issuance. Compliance requires a one-time detailed visual inspection and torque verification of all door plug retention fasteners, in accordance with Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-53A125, Revision 1. Non-compliant aircraft shall be grounded until corrective action is documented and approved by a designated airworthiness representative.

b. Production Quality System Remediation: The manufacturer shall implement a revised quality management system (QMS) protocol for all fuselage pressure boundary installations, subject to FAA audit under 14 CFR § 21.137 and § 21.143. The revised protocol shall mandate dual-signature verification for all critical fastener installations and require independent FAA oversight of final conformity inspections for a period of no less than 180 days.

c. Maintenance Program Revision: Operators shall revise their approved maintenance programs to incorporate enhanced inspection intervals for mid-exit door plug assemblies, consistent with the updated MRBR and Advisory Circular 120-16G guidance. Revisions must be submitted to the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) for approval within 30 days. The revised program shall include mandatory torque checks at 100-flight-hour intervals until a permanent engineering solution is certified.

d. Regulatory Framework Enhancement: The FAA shall initiate rulemaking under 14 CFR Part 21 to strengthen ODA oversight requirements for critical structural modifications. This includes the establishment of a mandatory independent verification process for all supplemental type certificate installations affecting pressurized compartments. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 120 days, with a public comment period of 60 days.

e. Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule: The FAA Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) shall conduct unannounced ramp inspections and maintenance record audits on all affected operators at 30, 90, and 180-day intervals. Compliance data shall be reported to the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and the Office of Aviation Safety (AVS) for centralized tracking. The NTSB shall be provided with quarterly progress reports until all corrective actions are fully implemented and validated.

This memorandum serves as the official regulatory response and compliance directive. All referenced entities, including the operator, manufacturer, and delegated authorities, are hereby notified of their statutory obligations under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Failure to comply with the stipulated timelines and inspection requirements may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR § 13.19 and § 13.301.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Flight Operations and Engineering Division of the operating air carrier, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the January 5, 2024, rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737 MAX 9. Our organization submits this analysis in our capacity as the aircraft operator, maintenance program holder, and employer of the flight crew. The purpose of this document is to provide a comprehensive technical, operational, and human factors assessment of the incident, grounded in recovered flight data, maintenance documentation, crew debriefings, and established regulatory frameworks.

The scope of this submission encompasses three primary domains: (1) an evaluation of the aircraft’s maintenance history and post-delivery acceptance procedures relative to the mid-exit door plug (MEP) installation; (2) an analysis of the flight crew’s response to the sudden cabin depressurization, including adherence to Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) protocols and crew resource management (CRM) execution; and (3) a systemic review of the regulatory and quality assurance environment governing structural modifications, fastener retention, and manufacturer-to-operator handoff processes. While the operator acknowledges the multi-layered nature of this event, our position is grounded in verifiable data, compliance with approved maintenance programs, and a commitment to advancing industry-wide safety standards. This document does not seek to assign unilateral blame, but rather to identify actionable engineering and procedural gaps that, if addressed, will prevent recurrence across the commercial aviation fleet.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On January 5, 2024, the subject aircraft departed a Pacific Northwest airport on a scheduled domestic flight. During the initial climb phase, at approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level, the flight crew experienced an abrupt loss of cabin pressure accompanied by a loud acoustic event and rapid decompression. The left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage structure, resulting in localized structural damage, loss of cabin pressurization, and deployment of passenger oxygen masks. The aircraft was stabilized, and the crew executed an emergency descent to a safe altitude before diverting to the departure airport. The aircraft landed without further incident, and there were no fatalities or serious injuries.

Recovery of the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) and Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) confirms a nominal climb profile with no abnormal engine parameters, flight control anomalies, or structural warning indications prior to the event. Docket Exhibit 7B (FDR Parameter Log) indicates that both LEAP-1B engines maintained stable N1 and EGT values throughout the climb, with no thrust asymmetry or compressor stall signatures. The sudden pressure differential spike at 16,000 feet correlates precisely with the acoustic event captured on the CVR. Post-flight inspection revealed that the MEP had fully separated, with four of the six primary retention bolts missing and the remaining two exhibiting signs of incomplete thread engagement.

Maintenance records reviewed under Docket Exhibit 12A (Aircraft Technical Log and Work Order History) indicate that the subject aircraft underwent a post-delivery inspection and minor cabin reconfiguration prior to entering service. The MEP installation was documented as part of the manufacturer’s final assembly process, with torque verification records signed off at the production facility. The operator’s acceptance inspection, conducted per approved procedures, did not identify any anomalies. Subsequent line maintenance checks, including pressurization cycle monitoring and door seal inspections, were completed without discrepancy.

The flight crew, led by the Captain, immediately recognized the decompression event, donned oxygen masks, initiated the emergency descent checklist, and coordinated with air traffic control for priority handling. The First Officer managed communications and systems monitoring while the Captain maintained aircraft control and executed the rapid descent profile. Cabin crew followed established emergency procedures, secured the cabin, and provided passenger reassurance. All actions were consistent with approved training and regulatory requirements.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The separation of the mid-exit door plug represents a complex failure mode involving structural design, manufacturing quality control, maintenance verification, and operational response. Our engineering team has conducted a detailed review of the available evidence, cross-referenced with industry standards, certification requirements, and operator maintenance protocols.

From a structural engineering perspective, the MEP is a non-structural plug designed to maintain cabin pressurization and aerodynamic continuity. Its retention relies on a series of high-strength fasteners, guide tracks, and stop fittings that must withstand cyclic pressurization loads, aerodynamic shear, and thermal expansion. The certification basis for this configuration is governed by 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of principal structural elements. While the plug itself is not classified as a primary load-bearing structure, its retention system must demonstrate fail-safe characteristics and resistance to progressive failure under repeated pressurization cycles. The absence of redundant load paths in the current fastener arrangement, combined with the lack of positive locking mechanisms on certain retention bolts, introduces a vulnerability that becomes critical if installation tolerances are not strictly controlled.

Review of the manufacturer’s assembly documentation and operator acceptance records reveals a gap in traceability and verification rigor. The torque values applied during final assembly were recorded, but the methodology lacked independent cross-verification, digital torque logging, or post-installation ultrasonic thread engagement verification. Under AC 120-16G, Air Carrier Maintenance Programs, operators are required to establish robust quality assurance systems that ensure continued airworthiness, including verification of critical fastener installations. However, the guidance assumes that manufacturer-installed components meet design specifications and that operator acceptance inspections are limited to visual and functional checks. This assumption proved insufficient in this case, as the underlying assembly deviation was not detectable through standard line maintenance procedures.

The operational response, however, demonstrates the effectiveness of modern crew training and emergency procedures. The Captain’s immediate recognition of the decompression event, coupled with disciplined adherence to the QRH, prevented loss of control and ensured a controlled emergency descent. FDR data confirms that the descent rate, speed management, and configuration changes were executed within approved envelopes. The LEAP-1B engine performance remained stable throughout the maneuver, with no indication of foreign object ingestion or compressor damage despite the sudden pressure transient. This underscores the robustness of the engine control system and the crew’s ability to manage asymmetric aerodynamic loads during rapid altitude changes.

Human factors analysis further supports the conclusion that crew performance was exemplary. The CVR transcript (Docket Exhibit 9C) reveals clear, concise communication, effective task delegation, and adherence to sterile cockpit protocols during the critical phase. The crew’s training in rapid decompression scenarios, including recognition of acoustic cues, oxygen mask deployment, and emergency descent execution, directly contributed to the safe outcome. This aligns with industry best practices and validates the operator’s recurrent training program.

When compared to similar aircraft configurations, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8, the MEP design shares common retention architecture but differs in fuselage length and pressurization cycle distribution. The MAX 8 does not utilize the same mid-exit plug configuration, which highlights a design divergence that warrants standardized inspection criteria across the MAX family. Industry-wide, the aviation sector has historically relied on manufacturer quality control for final assembly components, with operators focusing on in-service maintenance. This incident exposes a systemic vulnerability in the handoff process, where critical fastener installations lack independent verification, digital traceability, and post-delivery structural health monitoring.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the technical, operational, and maintenance data reviewed, the operator concludes that the primary contributing factor to the mid-exit door plug separation was an assembly quality control deficiency at the manufacturing stage, compounded by inadequate post-delivery verification protocols and limited regulatory oversight of critical fastener installations. The absence of redundant retention mechanisms, combined with incomplete thread engagement and missing torque verification cross-checks, created a latent condition that manifested during normal pressurization cycles.

The flight crew’s response was exemplary and fully aligned with approved procedures. The Captain’s decisive actions, supported by effective CRM and adherence to emergency checklists, ensured aircraft control and passenger safety. The LEAP-1B engines, manufactured by GE Aviation, performed within design parameters throughout the event, demonstrating the reliability of modern turbofan systems under abnormal pressure transients.

The operator’s maintenance program, developed in accordance with AC 120-16G and approved by the Federal Aviation Administration, was compliant with all applicable requirements. However, the incident reveals a broader industry gap: the assumption that manufacturer-installed structural components are inherently airworthy without independent operator verification. This assumption is no longer tenable given the complexity of modern aircraft assembly and the criticality of fastener retention in pressurized fuselage sections.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Implementation of mandatory digital torque logging and ultrasonic thread engagement verification for all critical fuselage fasteners, with data accessible to operators and regulators.
- Standardization of post-delivery inspection criteria across all 737 MAX variants, including the Boeing 737 MAX 8 and MAX 9, to ensure consistent verification of plug installations.
- Revision of 14 CFR 25.571 guidance to explicitly address damage tolerance requirements for non-structural but pressurization-critical components, including retention hardware redundancy.
- Enhanced FAA oversight of manufacturer quality assurance systems, with independent audits of final assembly processes and mandatory reporting of fastener installation deviations.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In immediate response to the event, the operator implemented a comprehensive corrective action plan in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration and the aircraft manufacturer. All aircraft in our fleet equipped with mid-exit door plugs were grounded pending a 100% torque verification inspection. Maintenance technicians utilized calibrated digital torque wrenches and cross-referenced installation records against manufacturer specifications. Any fastener exhibiting incomplete thread engagement, improper torque values, or missing hardware was replaced and re-verified. This process was completed within 72 hours, with zero discrepancies identified in the remaining fleet.

Additionally, the operator revised its acceptance inspection checklist to include independent verification of all manufacturer-installed critical fasteners, regardless of prior sign-off. Quality assurance personnel now conduct random audits of torque logs, and all maintenance records are digitized for real-time tracking and regulatory review. The operator has also updated its recurrent training program to include enhanced rapid decompression scenarios, focusing on acoustic recognition, emergency descent execution, and cabin crew coordination.

Looking forward, the operator proposes the following industry-wide improvements:
- Development of a standardized digital twin for fastener tracking, enabling real-time monitoring of torque values, installation dates, and maintenance history across the fleet lifecycle.
- Establishment of a joint industry-regulatory working group to review and update AC 120-16G guidance, specifically addressing manufacturer-to-operator handoff protocols and critical component verification.
- Integration of structural health monitoring sensors on pressurization-critical components, providing early warning of fastener loosening or structural fatigue.
- Mandatory third-party assembly audits for all aircraft manufacturers, with findings reported directly to the FAA and made available to operators during aircraft acceptance.

The operator remains committed to transparency, continuous improvement, and collaborative safety management. We appreciate the NTSB’s thorough investigation and stand ready to provide additional data, technical expertise, and operational insights as the investigation progresses. By addressing the systemic gaps identified in this submission, the aviation industry can strengthen the integrity of aircraft assembly, enhance maintenance verification, and ensure that rapid decompression events remain rare and safely managed.

TO: Fleet Maintenance Managers, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance Auditors, Technical Records, Maintenance Control
FROM: Director of Fleet Quality & Airworthiness, Maintenance Engineering Division
DATE: January 12, 2024
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2024-007: Mandatory Inspection & Torque Verification for 737 MAX 9 Mid-Exit Door Plug Assemblies
REF: QA-2023-114, WO-737M-8842, AMM Rev. 44, NTSB Docket Entry #2024-01-05-001

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate, fleet-wide inspection and torque verification of all mid-cabin exit door plug assemblies on Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft. The directive supersedes routine interval checks and establishes a one-time compliance requirement to ensure structural integrity, prevent recurrence of in-flight separation events, and align our maintenance practices with emerging investigative findings.

BACKGROUND:
On January 5, 2024, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by our partner carrier experienced a rapid decompression event during climb-out from a Pacific Northwest airport. The left mid-exit door plug separated from the fuselage at approximately 16,000 feet MSL. The flight crew, led by the Captain, executed emergency descent and diversion procedures, resulting in a safe return to the departure field with zero injuries or fatalities. Preliminary teardown data and initial NTSB observations indicate that multiple retention fasteners were either missing or improperly torqued at the time of final assembly. While the definitive root cause remains under investigation, internal quality audits have identified documentation gaps in our technical records regarding plug installation verification and post-maintenance sign-off. 

Several aircraft in the affected fleet are currently scheduled for heavy maintenance and powerplant servicing. To minimize operational disruption, this alert is structured to align with existing General Electric Aviation (GEA) service compliance windows. Maintenance teams should coordinate door plug inspections with scheduled LEAP-1B (L1B) engine borescope checks and performance trending to optimize hangar occupancy and reduce redundant aircraft downtime.

DETAILS:
All maintenance personnel must adhere to the following procedures when executing this alert. Deviations require written approval from the Chief Inspector and Quality Assurance Manager.

1. Scope & Applicability:
   - Applies to all 737 MAX 9 aircraft (MSN 44000–44500 series) in active service, storage, or undergoing scheduled maintenance.
   - Covers left and right mid-exit door plug assemblies (P/N 65-73892-1, P/N 65-73892-2).
   - Includes all associated guide tracks, stop fittings, retention hardware, and cabin pressure seals per AMM Chapter 52-40-00.

2. Inspection & Verification Steps:
   - Remove interior trim panels per WO-737M-9901 to fully expose door plug retention structure.
   - Visually inspect all 12 primary retention bolts (P/N BACB30NX06K) and 4 secondary shear pins for presence, corrosion, thread engagement, and proper safety wiring.
   - Verify torque values using calibrated digital torque wrenches (calibration valid within 30 days). Target torque: 185–205 in-lbs. Apply torque stripe (P/N TS-RED-04) immediately upon verification.
   - Confirm that all four guide track rollers are fully seated, free of binding, and properly lubricated per BAC5008.
   - Perform a cabin pressure decay test (WO-737M-9915) to verify plug sealing integrity post-inspection.

3. Documentation & Records Compliance:
   - Complete Form QA-737-PLUG-01 for each aircraft. Attach torque verification sheets, calibration certificates, and photographic evidence of torque stripe application.
   - Cross-reference with prior maintenance entries. Any discrepancy between physical hardware and technical records must be flagged as a Level 2 Nonconformance and routed to Engineering Review.
   - Ensure all work is signed off by an A&P/IA with current 737 MAX type rating. The Capt. or designated PIC must be notified of completion prior to aircraft release.

4. Fleet Coordination & Downtime Optimization:
   - Aircraft currently in C-check or undergoing CFM LEAP-1B engine inspections per GE Aviation SB-72-0145 should have this alert executed concurrently.
   - Coordinate with Powerplant Maintenance to avoid conflicting access requirements. Door plug inspections require cabin depressurization and interior teardown; schedule accordingly to prevent workflow bottlenecks.

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Line Maintenance Supervisors: Initiate inspections within 72 hours of aircraft arrival at base. Prioritize aircraft with >500 flight cycles since last plug-related maintenance.
- Quality Assurance Auditors: Conduct random spot-checks on 15% of completed inspections. Verify torque stripe application, documentation accuracy, and tool calibration logs. Report findings to the QA Dashboard by 1700 local daily.
- Technical Records: Update fleet status dashboard daily. Flag any aircraft with unresolved discrepancies for immediate grounding until QA sign-off. Archive all completed QA-737-PLUG-01 forms in the permanent airworthiness file.
- Maintenance Engineering: Issue revised AMM supplement and update training modules for door plug installation by January 26, 2024. Coordinate with GEA technical representatives for any cross-system hardware compatibility notes.
- All Personnel: Report any anomalies, missing hardware, or torque deviations directly to the 24/7 Quality Hotline (Ext. 4400) within 1 hour of discovery. Do not release aircraft to service until Alert 2024-007 compliance is fully documented and verified.

Compliance deadline: All active fleet aircraft must be inspected and cleared by January 22, 2024, 2359Z. Aircraft in storage or heavy maintenance must be completed prior to return-to-service release.

This alert is effective immediately and will remain in force until rescinded by the Director of Fleet Quality & Airworthiness. Failure to comply constitutes a violation of internal airworthiness protocols and may result in disciplinary action and mandatory regulatory reporting.

Distribution: Maintenance Control, Quality Assurance, Technical Training, Fleet Management, Regulatory Compliance, Flight Operations Liaison
Classification: INTERNAL – QUALITY SENSITIVE
NTSB Reference: Docket #2024-01-05-001 (Filed per 49 CFR § 831.12)

SYNOPSIS
On January 5, 2024, at approximately 17:12 Pacific Standard Time, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 operated by a major United States air carrier experienced an in-flight rapid decompression event during the initial climb phase. The incident occurred at an altitude of approximately 16,000 feet mean sea level following departure from an airport in the Pacific Northwest region. Preliminary information indicates that the left mid-cabin exit door plug separated from the fuselage structure, resulting in a controlled emergency return to the departure facility with no reported fatalities or serious injuries among the passengers and crew.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Final factual information has been compiled from initial data downloads, ATC recordings, and early interviews with flight crew and cabin personnel. Initial information indicates that the aircraft departed normally and was climbing through the assigned altitude when a sudden loud noise was reported by multiple occupants, followed by a rapid loss of cabin pressure. Oxygen masks deployed automatically, and the flight crew initiated an emergency descent and diversion back to the departure facility. Initial witness accounts from passengers seated in the vicinity of the left mid-cabin area describe a sudden rush of air, localized debris, and a visible opening in the fuselage sidewall. Cabin crew members reported securing the cabin and confirming that all passengers were accounted for prior to landing.

Weather conditions at the time of the event were characterized by marginal visual meteorological conditions with scattered cloud layers, light precipitation, and surface winds from the southwest at approximately 10 knots. Initial meteorological data does not suggest that atmospheric conditions contributed to the structural event, though this assessment remains subject to further review and correlation with flight path data.

Preliminary damage assessment, based on post-flight photographs and initial walk-around inspections, indicates significant localized damage to the left fuselage sidewall at the mid-exit door plug location. The door plug assembly was not recovered at the departure airport, and initial search efforts have been coordinated with local authorities to locate the separated component. Secondary damage appears limited to adjacent interior trim, window frames, and cabin seating in the immediate vicinity. The aircraft’s primary flight control systems, hydraulic systems, and pressurization controls remained functional throughout the event, allowing for a safe return and landing. Initial examination of the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) has been initiated, with preliminary data extraction underway. Early review of the FDR parameters suggests normal engine performance and standard flight control inputs prior to the decompression event.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Air Traffic Control groups have been formally established and are currently conducting preliminary data collection and analysis. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has been designated as a party to the investigation, alongside representatives from the aircraft manufacturer, the operating air carrier, and relevant labor organizations. The investigation will proceed in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with all parties operating under the supervision of NTSB group chairs.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, maintenance records, and initial photographic documentation of the aircraft exterior and interior. The aircraft has been secured at a designated maintenance facility, and access is restricted to authorized investigative personnel. Initial examinations of the recovered maintenance logs indicate that the aircraft was in compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives and scheduled maintenance requirements at the time of the event. However, these records are subject to comprehensive verification and cross-referencing with manufacturer service bulletins.

The powerplant group has initiated a preliminary review of the aircraft’s propulsion systems. The aircraft is equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, manufactured by GE Aviation. Initial data from the engine health monitoring system indicates normal operational parameters throughout the flight, with no recorded exceedances or fault codes prior to the decompression event. Representatives from General Electric Aviation have been integrated into the powerplant group to assist with technical analysis and data interpretation. All engine-related findings remain preliminary and will be evaluated in conjunction with broader structural and systems investigations. The Agency has also requested preliminary operational data from the engine manufacturer to support ongoing analysis.

The structures group has begun a detailed examination of the fuselage skin, door plug retention mechanisms, and adjacent structural members. Initial visual inspection suggests that the separation occurred at the interface between the door plug and the surrounding fuselage frame, though the precise failure mode has not been determined. Non-destructive testing, metallurgical analysis, and component teardown procedures are being scheduled to evaluate the condition of fasteners, sealant, and load-bearing structures. All recovered debris, including interior trim and cabin components, has been cataloged and preserved for further examination.

NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities will focus on the systematic analysis of flight recorder data, structural component testing, and comprehensive review of maintenance and manufacturing records. The structures group will conduct detailed measurements and material testing of the door plug retention hardware, while the systems group will evaluate the aircraft’s pressurization and environmental control systems for any anomalies that may have preceded or resulted from the event. The operations group will continue to interview flight and cabin crew members to establish a detailed timeline of events and crew response actions.

Additional data collection efforts will include coordination with air traffic control facilities to reconstruct the flight path and communication logs, as well as consultation with meteorological agencies to refine the environmental conditions at the time of the incident. The investigation team will also review applicable certification documentation, service history, and any recent modifications or repairs related to the mid-exit door plug configuration. The FAA will continue to provide regulatory and operational context as the investigation progresses.

All findings documented in this preliminary report are subject to revision as additional evidence is collected, analyzed, and validated. The investigation remains in its early stages, and no conclusions regarding the cause or contributing factors have been established. The NTSB will issue subsequent updates as significant milestones are reached, with a comprehensive factual report anticipated within the next 12 to 18 months. In the interim, the Board will continue to coordinate with the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, and the operating carrier to ensure the safe and methodical progression of the investigation. All parties are reminded that preliminary information is not indicative of final determinations and should not be used to draw operational or regulatory conclusions at this time.
